### Lambertus Daneus

**Theophilus:** ...If sorcerers can hinder and weaken the power by which life is sustained—as Thomas Aquinas <note>original: "Thomas von Aquino"</note> extensively disputes and demonstrates in the first *Summa*, the third question, the fourth article—then they can also hinder the power by which life is conceived and given.

<margin>Antonius.</margin> Now I do not know what I should say or think, for I hear such strange things from you.

<margin>Theophil.</margin> What would you think if I also told you what Augustine and Apuleius <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) and Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), the latter famous for his story of a man turned into a donkey.</note> explicitly report? Though I deny it myself and consider it a fabricated thing.

<margin>Antonius.</margin> Dear friend, what is that then?

<margin>Theophil.</margin> They write that sorcerers are also able to transform humans into another shape, namely into wolves, bears, donkeys, and similar animals.

<margin>Antonius.</margin> What? Does the holy Augustine write that?

<margin>Theophil.</margin> Certainly, Antonius, nothing less. Read the eighteenth book of *The City of God* <note>original: "von der Stadt Gottes"</note>, in the 17th and 18th chapters. There Augustine recounts many pagans and Christians who said themselves that they had been so transformed. Specifically mentioned are Damiaenetus, Praestantius, and others.

<margin>Antonius.</margin> It cannot be that a spirit or devil can change our nature or "essence" <note>term: "Wesen" (essence/being) - the fundamental nature of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> as they call it. For this is the work of God alone; just as He alone creates natures, He alone can change them. But for the devil himself, or his dear faithful ones, the sorcerers, it is never possible.

<margin>Theophil.</margin> You are right in that, and therefore Augustine himself writes in another place: Although the people who say they were transformed believe it truly happened to them, they are deceiving themselves. For it is only a pure madness and fantasy that they imagine to themselves, which sticks in their minds either through the hardening and blinding of the devil, or through illness. But I do not doubt that Satan can drive and persuade some to that point: namely, he takes away or numbs and blinds

<column-break/>

their external senses. Afterward, he impresses upon their minds—which are already disturbed by "evil humors" <note>term: "feuchtigkeiten" (humors) - referring to the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed in pre-modern medicine to control health and temperament.</note>—various forms and shapes so strongly that they believe they are transformed, or have been transformed. The physicians also teach that there are certain illnesses in which the patients imagine they are wolves, pigs, cows, mules, or even that they are made of glass or wax and the like. I myself have seen one who believed, and even swore to it, that he was a rooster. Therefore, the true cause of such delusions and deceptions—which can indeed happen through sorcery—has its origin in the fact that their humors and "complexion" <note>term: "Complexionen" - the specific balance of humors in an individual's body.</note> are confused. Consequently, the minds are likewise disturbed through "sympathy" <note>The idea that the mind suffers along with the physical body.</note>, so that they lose their senses and can recognize nothing other than what Satan presents to them. Therefore, when they are so plagued, the error easily comes to them that they believe they were transformed, and yet it is nothing but pure devilish blinding.

<margin>Antonius.</margin> Yet was not Nebuchadnezzar, King in Assyria, also transformed into an irrational animal, and did he not eat grass for seven years, as is written in the fourth chapter of the Prophet Daniel?

<margin>Theophil.</margin> It is written there, but one must not understand it as if the human nature of Nebuchadnezzar was substantially changed into an irrational animal. Only the mind within him changed, so that he no longer wanted to be among people, but after he was cast out, he lived in the wilderness like other wild animals and ate grass like an ox. And although he became hairy over his whole body, his human form was not changed. Furthermore, even if I were to admit that he truly was transformed into an irrational animal, it would not have happened through the help of the devil or through sorcery, but through the power and working of God the Almighty Creator. For God the LORD can bring creatures and natures to nothing and change them as He wills, but the devil cannot at all. Therefore...

# Concerning Sorcerers.

For this reason, one should also consider as vain lies that which is written and said about <term>lycanthropes</term> <note>original: "Lycanthropis," meaning wolf-men</note> or werewolves, although some say it occurs in the northern lands, namely by the waters of the Dnieper <note>original: "Borythene"</note> and the Don <note>original: "Tanai"</note>. Regarding what Varro wrote—that there is a lake in Arcadia where those who sail across it become wolves—I believe it should be understood that the people, because of the great fear and terror caused by the cruel danger of that same lake, only imagine themselves to be wolves. Otherwise, there is nothing to these stories but vain, useless lies and fables.

<margin>Antonius.</margin> You have now explained to me extensively enough which things sorcerers can harm. But I would still like to hear one thing: why can malicious people also harm pious Christian folk with their sorcery and poison? Daily and certain experience demonstrates this.

<margin>Theophil.</margin> O Antonius, that is an easy question to answer. Firstly, it happens so that the righteous God may punish the misdeeds of His children in such a manner. For those whom we consider to be pious, true Christians not only have their particular flaws and failings, but often great sins and vices in them, as it is written in the first chapter of the first Epistle of John:
> "If we say we have no sin, we make God a liar." <note>1 John 1:8-10</note> Therefore, they are not unjustly chastened by God. Furthermore, He provokes His own to patience through such a cross. And just as He tested His servant Job through the unjust murder and robbery of the godless Chaldeans, so He also often tries His own through sorcery, yet for their own best use and welfare. For, as Paul says to the Romans in the fifth chapter: "Tribulation brings patience, patience brings experience, experience brings hope, and hope does not let us be put to shame. For the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us." <note>Romans 5:3-5</note> Therefore, the faithful should bear all tribulation with patience, so that they humble themselves before God and surrender themselves entirely to His will.

<column-break/>

<margin>Antonius.</margin> I see well that my question is not as difficult as I thought. But because you have answered so skillfully the three points I desired to know—namely, what the word <term>sorcerer</term> <note>original: "Sortiarius"</note> means and where it comes from, whether there truly are sorcerers, and what things they can harm with their poisoning—dear Theophilus, please also explain the fourth main point to me: in what manner and form do witches cast spells, and how are they accustomed to doing harm with poison?

### The Fourth Chapter.
#### In what form and manner witches are able to cast spells.

<margin>Theophil.</margin> Well now, Antonius, do you think I am so experienced and practiced in their art that I can give you a report on all things? Do you not know, as I gave you to understand at the beginning of our conversation, that I have no fellowship with either Satan or the sorcerers, nor do I desire to have any, and I wish to know nothing of their secret devilish arts? Nevertheless, I will not refuse your honorable request, but will gladly share what is in my power. This is now your question: in what way and manner do sorcerers perform their knavery and murder? Regarding this, you should believe and hold one thing for certain: that it proceeds through the help, incitement, and teaching of the miserable, loathsome Satan. For all sorcerers have their covenant and fellowship with Satan and are sworn to him, none excepted. Because of this, they also have certain signs or <term>stigmata</term> <note>original: "malzeichen," marks of the devil</note> on their bodies—some under the eyebrows, some in secret places, some even in the mouth, up on the gums—so that they may be hidden and recognized by no one. Although some hold that they are not all marked by the devil, but only those of whom he is doubtful, while those he considers faithful, steadfast servants he leaves unmarked. But I would rather say there is not one among them all upon whom he does not hang a sign of his right and power which he has over them. Therefore, the authorities and judges are accustomed...

# Lambertus Daneus

<margin>Lambertus Daneus <note>A prominent 16th-century French Calvinist theologian who wrote extensively on witchcraft.</note></margin>
...after such misdeeds, when they hold these people captive, they inspect their entire bodies and have all hair shaved off with a razor, so that the <term>warzeichen</term> <note>Literally "true-signs" or "witch-marks," believed to be insensitive to pain or hidden under hair.</note> do not remain hidden beneath. For they have established a <term>Gedings</term> <note>A formal contract or pact.</note> with the Devil and pledged themselves to him in return. Satan has stipulated that they shall henceforth recognize and honor him as their God; they, in turn, stipulate that Satan shall stand by them and be helpful whenever they call upon him. This he also does, by virtue of their covenant, and acts according to their will and desire; in exchange, they again obey his command and bidding.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
But since Satan is a lying spirit and a father of lies, does he actually keep what he promises and vows to them?

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
Satan is not a liar at all times, but he is a deceiver at all times. For he often speaks the truth so that he may thereby deceive his listeners, and also so that he is not held to be deceitful but truthful, he often fulfills his promise. As for example in <term>Mark</term> <note>original: "Marci"</note> in the third chapter, where he said of our **LORD** and Savior Christ: "You are the Son of God," he did not lie, but spoke the truth. But why did he do it? So that he could more easily lead astray those who heard it when he told them other things. Furthermore, in the Acts of the Apostles in the sixteenth chapter, through the maiden who had the spirit of divination, he cried out after Saint Paul and Silas: "These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation." In this, he certainly did not lie either, but he was nonetheless a <term>Brillenreisser</term> <note>Literally a "spectacle-maker," a contemporary idiom for a trickster or someone who pulls the wool over people's eyes.</note> and only wanted to make a way for himself to deceive the people. Thus, even when he keeps his promise and grants the sorcerers what he promised them, he only seeks an opportunity to seduce them more securely and easily, and to make them his own through favor.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
But continue, and say how and through what means the sorcerers work.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
That is the very first and most prominent point of their contract: Above all things, he requires of them that they freely and expressly renounce the right, true God, Creator of all creatures, and Lord over Heaven, Earth, and all that is therein, <term>etc.</term>, and that they shall serve him, Satan—to whom he himself gives over without any concealment—look to him alone, obey his will, and rely on his help alone. This most shameful denial and abjuration of the right, true God is the first step and entrance for these cursed, godless people, and the first binding to the Devil and their sorcery. But when Satan has accepted them in this shameful manner as bond-servants, he presses a mark upon them with his teeth or hand, and bids them to demand and desire whatever they wish him to do for them. He also teaches them how they can secretly and surely avenge themselves on their enemies; for this purpose, he gives them powders, roots, or poison, either from his own hand or through other skillful servants whom he employs. On the following day, the new, foolish servants of the Devil give or sacrifice something of their own back to their Lord and Patron as a sign of their obedience and faithful service—one a dog, another a hen, the third a cat, and the like—which is just like a pledge and assurance of the agreement and denial of God that has taken place. In short, that is the whole business that the Devil is concerned with. However, he does not trust them well and fears constantly that they might desert him; therefore, he calls them together at certain times to special places, into the <term>diabolical synagogue</term> <note>original: "Teuffelische Synagog," a common term for the Witches' Sabbath.</note> or school, so that he may hear how faithfully and diligently they have carried out their command and new office, and whom they have bewitched or killed. Therefore, they come together at specially designated places, but not all at once; rather, whichever ones please Satan, and wherever and at whatever hour of the day or night he wishes to have them assembled. Not just once in a week, a month, or a year, but whenever or as often as their Master and Lord sees fit; and he shows this to them sometimes person-

<column-break/>

-ally.

# Concerning the Sorcerers.

### On the Assemblies and Deceptions of the Enemy

The Devil acts either by himself or sometimes through others. When he acts himself, it happens in human or some other form so that they may recognize him. Thus, sometimes in the presence of many people, only the sorcerer sees the Devil, while others see nothing at all; or others may think they see a man, but do not know who he is or where he comes from. When he calls them through his servants and other sorcerers, he also names the place and the hour at which they should appear at the unholy assembly—which they call the Devil’s Fair or <term>Sabbath</term> <note>The "Sabbath" refers to the legendary nocturnal gathering of witches and sorcerers to worship the Devil.</note>—and so it happens. In cases where some complain of the long distance, or the weakness of their body and the toil, or fear danger from other people, he anticipates all of this himself. For he says: he wishes to lead them to such places where it will not be harmful to their body or health. He teaches how they might accomplish it through the help and power of a staff or rod which he gives them, or through an ointment; he also often provides horses upon which they ride. If they are still afraid, he gives them another teaching on how they should make themselves invisible and arrive there safely. Thus, there is no excuse that he does not know how to meet skillfully. However, he only provides such help so that they shall think he is favorable and inclined toward them, and so that he may entangle them all the more tightly in his bonds. When they now come together, he lets himself be seen as the Prelate and leader of their council in many forms and shapes; sometimes like a man, thereafter like a stinking goat, or otherwise as it pleases him. Then all the sorcerers must renew their sworn oath and covenant, that they will hold and honor him as their God. They also hold
<margin>Dances.</margin>
dances, in which he leads the rows as the captain, or they dance around him with rejoicing, according to certain songs that are composed in his honor and praise. When all this has happened, he asks them again what their desire is, and what poison they need to harm people. And after each one reveals his evil will and desire, he shows him the means and

<column-break/>

ways to avenge himself. Then to some he gives poison that is already prepared by him; some he teaches how they should make and prepare it themselves; to some he gives special characters or letters <note>Magical sigils or symbols used in occult rituals.</note>, along with special words or ointments, through the power of which they can know or experience something, or bring something to pass; and he comforts them, saying that everything shall proceed successfully according to their desire. Should they be in need of his help and presence, he promises to be at hand immediately. Therefore, the sorcerers do harm either with poison—which is partly known to learned and experienced physicians and is regarded as rejected and deadly—or partly it is known neither to us nor to them themselves, and they visibly use no poison to do harm, which is more to be wondered at than the former. Therefore, if they have poisoned someone with poison that is recognizable and deadly, as long as they only confess how and with what they prepared it, the physicians can truly find and demonstrate it. But even if one does not know what it is they have used, or how they prepared it, it is nonetheless no less harmful. Likewise, even if one knows of nothing that they have given to someone, it can still have happened in a hidden way: namely, if they only blow or breathe upon someone, or perhaps chew a poisonous root—which Satan held out to them—between their teeth, and thus ruin and kill people during conversation. Therefore, it is no wonder that some people are enchanted by them whom they have never even touched, for the sorcery can well be performed secretly by Satan at their request, so that he places a poisonous dust or powder, made from roots or other poison, before their noses, from which they are harmed; and he does this by virtue of their covenant and condition, that he must thus comply with and serve them in certain things.

God protect me, Theophilus! You, <term>Antonius</term> <note>Antonius and Theophilus are the interlocutors in this dialogue; Antonius acts as the expert teacher, while Theophilus is the student.</note>, have caused me such horror and terror with your speech that my hair stands on end, and my whole body—

after, that you say they are often <margin>2.</margin> led by Satan to such places. And thirdly, that they are said to bewitch and kill one without <margin>3.</margin> poison. For I do not believe that one can make anything better or worse with mere words, figures, or letters.

I will answer one after the other. As far as the first is concerned: do you not believe, Antonius, that the sorcerers themselves are bodily present at the devilish assemblies and gatherings, even though they boast of it? How then do you think it happens?

I hold it to be a pure fantasy <margin>Antonius</margin> and hardening of the heart by the Devil. And so that you do not think I have no ground for my opinion, many of the old, most prominent teachers are with me on this. You highly praise Augustine to me in these questions, who yet in his eighteenth book of *The City of God* <note>original: "De Civitate Dei"</note>—where he deals with the transformations of human form—teaches that when people think such transformations happen, it comes to them because the fantasy (which is not the least among the five properties and effects of the mind and occupies the foremost part of the brain) is injured and troubled, while the external senses are numbed and hindered by it in a wondrous way. Why then should we not also say and hold the same regarding the presence of sorcerers? It happens that drunken people, when the warm vapors rise from the stomach into the brain, think they see things that are not present. Likewise, it happens to those afflicted with sadness or melancholy <term>melancholy: "Melancholey," historically viewed as a physical imbalance of "black bile" causing depression or delusions</term>. # Concerning Sorcerers.

[Those who believe] such things are more powerful in their effects than the aforementioned causes are thus deluded, and will likely never reach the truth. Therefore, I say that Satan is able to weaken and hinder the qualities of the mind and the powers of the body, as Thomas Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a highly influential medieval theologian.</note> and, before him, Augustine wrote in the seventh book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* <note>original: "de Genesi, ad literā"</note>, chapter 11. Furthermore, Augustine, in the seventy-second epistle to Nebridius, his well-known friend, establishes three kinds of our imagination <term>Phantasey: the faculty of the mind that forms mental images</term>. The first is that which comes to us from external things that we have seen. The second type forms something for itself that a person has never seen or heard. The third, however, comes from what a person has heard. Now, I hold that the sorcerer’s imagination is of the second kind, as it deals with vain, unheard-of things. But so that I may better demonstrate this to you from Augustine, he writes in the 101st epistle to Euodius concerning ghosts or miraculous visions: when they appear to us as physical things, so that we think no differently than that they are truly present, the soul does not leave our bodies for the places where we think we are; rather, it remains in its body even at the very moment when such visions occur from which the imagination springs. The external bodily senses, however, are lulled to sleep within us so that they cannot perform their office when the imagination disturbs us with such visions. Hence it happens, when they have awakened again, that it seems to us we have spoken, drunk, eaten, or seen things, the figures and images of which appeared to and occupied the senses and thoughts. We also read several examples of this in Augustine. For in the 100th epistle, he mentions a physician from Carthage named Gennadius, who was experienced in medicine. When he doubted whether another life was to be hoped for after this one, he saw in a dream the host of holy angels so vividly and heard their singing that he believed nothing else but that he was in heaven, even though the

<column-break/>

body meanwhile lay in the chamber on the bed and was asleep, as he himself confessed. Further, in the 18th book of *The City of God*, in the 18th chapter, he reports of one who spoke as a truth: that he had disputed in a dream with a philosopher of the Platonic sect concerning the writings of Plato, and that the philosopher had explained to him a particular sentence or saying from them which he had not understood before. In the *Book of the Lives of the Holy Fathers*, it is written of one who—not at night or in a dream, but in broad daylight—seemed to see a cow when he looked at his daughter, whom other people, and especially Macarius <note>Saint Macarius of Egypt (c. 300–391), a desert hermit known for his discernment of spirits.</note>, saw and recognized as a human being and a young woman, as she truly was. Yes, what is even more, my dear Theophilus, have you not yourself at one time read in the sixth book of *Genial Days* <note>original: "Genialium dierum", a work by Alessandro Alessandri (1461–1523)</note>, written by Alexander of Naples, in the 21st chapter, of an accused man who believed he had been down in Hell, and even gave the judge certain true signs? For he revealed and betrayed one of the judge's secrets, which was known to no man but him. What is also clearly said in the *Canon Episcopi* <note>A medieval legal document (c. 900 AD) that claimed witchcraft was an illusion; it was a cornerstone of skeptical arguments against the reality of the witches' sabbath.</note> 26. q. 5., as recorded from the Council of Aquileia, that all this talk and thought of the sorcerers are nothing but vain ghosts and pure lies or delusions, which Satan, a true master of such things, gives and presents to them while their bodies remain in one place at all times? Finally, to conclude this my opinion, these are the own words of Augustine—or whoever wrote the book *On the Spirit and the Letter* <note>original: "De spiritu & litera"</note>—which he sets down in the 28th chapter: Therefore they prophesy (meaning the sorcerers) of future things and perform strange wonders, so that they may make people dependent on them and deceive them. Hence, some women are so led astray by diabolical delusion and imagination that they believe and confess they have been at nighttime with the goddess Diana, or

But as to why they themselves should not be present—what cause, I ask you, can hinder it, especially since they return physically and visibly to the place from which they had personally departed? For even the accused man whom you mentioned, who believed he had been in Hell, was gone for two days; and although he was diligently sought for in the prison, he could not be found. Therefore, when they boast of things that are contrary to the nature of our bodies, it is a lie and rightly to be considered a devilish delusion <note>original: "Teuffelsverblendung"</note>. Such things are mentioned in the Council of Aquileia <note>A reference to the *Canon Episcopi*, a medieval legal text often associated with councils like Ancyra or Aquileia, which dismissed stories of night-riding as illusions.</note>, such as riding upon the moon, traveling about and consorting with the goddesses Herodias, Diana, and Minerva—or, as the Germans call her, Lady Holle <note>A figure from Germanic folklore associated with the spirit world and winter.</note>—speaking with the dead, personally seeing the "Twelve Heroes" as they are called, such as Hector, Achilles, Roland, etc., and similar things, which are pure devilish phantoms that Satan places and imagines before people's eyes. second [letter] to the Corinthians in the 12th chapter concerning himself thus: "I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago; whether he was in the body, I do not know, or whether he was out of the body, I also do not know," etc. He was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words which no man can utter. For those are only false bodies which are laid there by Satan in place of the sorcerers in the meantime, and fashioned masks <note>original: "Laruen" (larvae/masks)</note> which he lets be seen instead of their bodies. Do you not think of what Michal, David’s wife, devised and did when she wished to hide the flight of her lord and husband from her father, Saul, and his servants who sought to kill him? Have you not read, I say, what is written in the first book of Samuel in the nineteenth chapter, how she—with cunning, yet without any sorcery or devilish art—laid an image in the bed in place of David’s body (which had escaped), and a goat’s skin at its head, and covered the image with clothes so skillfully and neatly that those who had seen the image with their own eyes thought no differently than that it was David himself? So also, in order that Satan may hide the absence of his pupils when they are sought, he often puts a false body in that place. From this it comes that many believe the sorcerers are not personally or physically present at their assemblies because they were seen [at home] at that time; but they are, as has been said, deceived by the Devil’s masks and images.

# On Sorcerers.

Pliny—an experienced man in all manner of things—also publicly and expressly denied it in the twenty-eighth book of his *Natural History*, in the second chapter.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin> Now I consider you, Antonius, to be far more learned than at the beginning of our conversation, when you only thought of the most prominent schools; but now you let yourself be heard like a learned <term>Physicus</term> <note>A natural philosopher or scientist</note>. Therefore, I shall have more to do with you than before. However, I will also help you out of your doubt and answer you. <margin>Theophilus.</margin> Yes, so you must also confess that sorcerers can do harm with mere words or incantations, and are capable of accomplishing something.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin> It is true, as you say, for they use such ways, means, and methods as belong to and are useful for their sorcery. So I say now: sorceries happen through Satan, either with poison or through other means, even though we do not see them but must marvel at them; otherwise, people think they are performed through mere figures, letters, words, or incantations.

<margin>Antonius.</margin> How can that be?

He does this so that he may be held as credible and powerful, and so he can better persuade them that such great power and effect lies behind those means, just as he claimed. Thus he also makes these loose people all the more bound to him, so that

<column-break/>

they must honor him as their God, and he falsely attributes the might and power of God to created things, so that people will more readily abandon God and become infatuated with creatures—that is, become true idolaters. Finally, just as God the Lord has established for His Church, he also wants to have his own special <term>Sacraments</term> <note>Theophilus argues that magic rituals are a mockery or 'apeing' of holy Christian sacraments</note>, so that he may nullify the true Sacraments; as if he could equal God the Lord, he shows himself thereby to be a true ape. In short, he falsely attributes and applies the power of the designated things to mere signs, to which it does not belong.

<margin>Antonius.</margin> So the enchantment does not happen through mere words, letters, or signs, but rather some poison or other medium must come between them, which is used in a hidden way by Satan, even if he has not taught the sorcerers such means.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin> You understand the matter correctly now; for Satan is exceedingly cunning and skillful at concealing his villainous tricks. Therefore, the Covenant he establishes with sorcerers reminds me entirely of two murderers in the forest who ally with one another. For these same men, so that they can hide themselves more securely and also more easily snatch and murder people, arrange their affairs so that one lets himself be seen on the road, while the other has hidden in the forest behind the hedges and trees. But one can give the other a signal, perhaps with a whistle or some other sound, so that he unexpectedly falls upon and strangles the poor betrayed traveler—even though his companion often does not see or know with what weapon or arms he murders him. This can also be explained to you by another example. Noblemen who have enmity with others often tend to take on wanton, daring servants who, when they give them a wink or some other signal, attack the enemies of those same squires or lords, even if the lords themselves are often not present, though they have commanded it. So also is Satan...

For they believe nothing else than that the power resides in the external things or signs, the nature and effects of which are unknown to them. Rather, just as jugglers who boast of great wonders and arts use their sham-fights and chatter to glue up the ears and eyes of the people so they cannot see how it happens—as when they make three or four out of one nut, a pebble, or similar things, which happens only through the speed of the hands to displace or hide them and know how to lay them down as they please, and no one perceives their deceit. In the same way, Satan acts toward those people whom he does not want to diligently investigate such things; he gives them several useless figures or signs, teaches them special words for them, or otherwise performs a juggling act before their eyes so that they gape at it and are struck dumb, and do not investigate further how it happens. Yet those same external signs or words or other juggling acts have absolutely no effect or power regarding the things that are done and performed through Satan.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
Then tell me also, Theophilus: How and through what does Satan work, if one blames the external means or signs, or likewise, the words and incantations?

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
I am reflecting on that now: Firstly, I hold it for certain and true that Satan can do nothing except through natural causes, means, and ways. And everything he does, whether it happens by himself or through his soothsayers and sorcerers, is either pure delusion and fantasy, or an effect of true natural causes. But things higher than these are impossible for him to do.

<column-break/>

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
Does not the Apostle Paul say, in the second [letter] to the Thessalonians, in the second chapter, that he also performs powerful signs and wonders? As is also written in the Revelation of John in the 16th chapter.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
Dear Antonius, what then do you call signs and wonders?

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
I call "wonder-signs" <note>miracles</note> those things which happen contrary to the power and effect that God the LORD has planted in nature. For example, when iron floats on the water by itself, which is reported in the stories of Elisha in the second book of Kings, chapter 6; when a stone floats in the water, and the water is truly transformed into wine; likewise, when the dead are truly raised and become living again.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
You have spoken correctly and properly regarding what wonder-signs are. For as Augustine writes, one should call a "wonder-work" <note>miracle</note> that which is beyond all power and effect of nature, and which cannot happen through the same. Therefore, what is worthy of the name and should be called a true wonder-work is a pure work of the power of God. But Paul and John in the Revelation do not use the word so precisely in its proper meaning, but somewhat more broadly, and understand by it any work that is new and brings astonishment to people, even if it happens in a natural way and springs from nature. Those things you call wonder-works or signs are much too high for Satan and his art. In Latin, a true wonder-work is called *Miraculum* <note>a miracle; a supernatural act of God</note>. What Satan can do, however, should more rightly be called *Mirum* <note>a marvel; something strange but natural</note>.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
Explain this distinction to me a bit more extensively.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
Common wonders have their causes and effects from nature, even if they are often not known to us or to very few people, or happen in other ways and means...

# Concerning Sorcerers.

as we are accustomed and have learned to perform. For example, when the highly learned and famous artist Archytas of Tarentum <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician (428–347 BC) credited with inventing the first self-propelled flying machine.</note> made a wooden dove fly in the air, it was indeed a marvelous thing, but not a true miracle outside of nature. For such movement occurred in the wooden body through special gears and weights, which were so skillfully prepared and ordered that one part pulled and moved the other; therefore, it was a natural work. Likewise, when that same Archytas (as Plutarch writes of him in the *Life of Marcellus*) at the time of the siege of Syracuse in Sicily, arranged for a young youth to pull and lift a large cargo ship with a hook, it was also to be wondered at, but it happened in a natural way and through special screws according to the rules and teachings of artists.

Thus, many wonderful deeds are performed by experienced physicians and craftsmen even today, but all through the means of nature. Satan also does much higher and greater things than we can grasp with our understanding; because his power and intellect far surpass ours, yet they are still not true miracles.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
How does that happen, then?

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
That has many causes, but primarily three. First, because of the excellence of his nature, compared to which ours is far too lowly and unequal; for he has an angelic, spiritual nature. We, however, are earthly and fleshly; for this reason, he can do many things that are impossible for us. Secondly, because of his great speed; for in a "huy" <note>An idiomatic expression for a "whoosh" or a flash.</note> or a moment, he can easily travel as far as we can in six days with great effort, and even much further, since the air does not hinder his movement. Thirdly, because he knows nature and its effects so well, and has had such excellent experience of all things since the beginning of the world—against which our own experience is worth nothing at all. Therefore, it is easy to imagine that he knows more and can

<column-break/>

accomplish more in natural things than is possible for us to do or understand.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
But what is the reason why he cannot perform true signs or miracles, as you say?

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
First, if he were to do such a thing, he would first have to destroy and bring to nothing the properties and effects that God has instilled in every thing; this he cannot do. For just as the creation and preservation of creatures rests in God's power alone, so too does the power to change and transform them. Secondly, he would also have to grant new effects and properties to the creatures; he must certainly leave that undone, since the Lord God alone is the author and creator of the properties of every thing. Thirdly, because a true miracle is such a work that surpasses the power and authority of all creatures, no matter how skillful and excellent they may be. Therefore, the Apostle Peter, in the 3rd chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, when he made a man lame from his mother's womb straight again through a true miracle, spoke thus: "You men of Israel, why do you marvel at this? Or why do you look at us, as if we had made this man walk through our own power or merit? The God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his child Jesus," etc. With which words it is proven, as you see, that the power and authority to do true miracles and signs belongs to God alone, and He alone is mighty and powerful in this regard.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
Yet the holy angels, likewise the Apostles and other holy men, have also performed miracles.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
God worked those through them, for the power is His alone; it can never be attributed to any creature, since He—as it is written in the prophet Isaiah—gives His glory, which is due to Him, to no other. Therefore, the holy angels, Apostles, and other God-fearing men were only *instrumenta* <note>Latin: instruments.</note>, or tools, which the Lord God used as His servants for the miracles. From this, it does not follow that He also uses the Devil in this way—

# Lambertus Daneus

uses [him] and through him performs such miracles; for He will not share His glory with devils and Satan in the same measure as He shares it with the holy angels and the godly. This is clearly seen from the fact that Moses and Aaron, God’s servants, performed true miracles, which Pharaoh’s wise men—though highly practiced in the devilish arts and his well-trained servants—could not do. Indeed, they themselves confessed that such miracles happened only through the "finger of God" <note>Exodus 8:19</note> and far surpassed the power of nature, as is written in the second book of Moses, chapter 8.

This distinction between Satan and the servants of God—and the fact that God does not grant Satan so much—exists because Satan does not seek God’s honor in his wonders. The good angels and godly people, however, direct all their actions and omissions solely to the glory of God. Therefore, they alone are frequently the instruments of God to perform true miracles, but he [Satan] never is. And although it is true that Satan can do nothing except what, when, how much, and in what manner God permits him, he can neither reverse nor overturn the order that God has planted in nature, for God does not allow him that. Thus, he can also work or bring nothing to pass except through natural things and their power, even though these are often hidden and unknown to us. Furthermore, much of what he accomplishes with speed and in haste appears to be a pure miracle. For he can quickly bring about the means and causes through which he works; for example, he can hastily create clouds from which rain comes; he can quickly condense the air and form it into a visible body or shape and place it before our eyes. Likewise, he has poison <note>original: "Gifft"</note> at hand at every moment with which he does harm, and whatever is desired of him, he can bring hither and thither in a flash. When he practices such agility, we think it

<column-break/>

is a miracle, yet he must make use of natural means and causes just as men do, even if he surpasses them with all kinds of advantages. Therefore, as I have said before, the figures, scribbles, words, blessings, incantations, and similar idolatrous and superstitious things do not at all produce that which is carried out by the sorcerers <term>Zauberer: practitioners of harmful magic or witchcraft</term>. Rather, they are only signs and pledges of the promise made by Satan. The deed itself and the work which they undertake—and which they believe they have performed through such means—is done by Satan himself. But he has ordained the signs or false means to disguise himself, and he simply will not have them regarded as slight, useless, or incompetent. Here we should not be moved by the sentence and opinion of Jerome <note>St. Jerome, c. 347–420 AD, translator of the Vulgate</note>, who doubts this, for he himself wavers; and John Chrysostom <note>c. 347–407 AD, Archbishop of Constantinople</note>, in his sermons on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, chapter three, is expressly against him, as are others who are not to be rejected. As far as the biblical scholars of this time are concerned, it is well known what the highly learned Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli, 1499–1562, a significant Reformed theologian</note> writes about this regarding the 28th chapter of the first book of Samuel. Therefore, to speak of it conclusively: Satan does all these things by virtue of his compact or covenant. It happens in exactly the same way when sorcerers banish and conjure the devil so that he comes and speaks with them personally; because he has ordained and promised the false means or blessing, he intends to make himself present or allow himself to be driven away thereby. Thus Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome—and as great a devilish artist and sorcerer as one could be—very often held personal communion and speech with Satan, as Plutarch, the excellent historian, writes of him in his *Life*. Since I have now, Antonius, answered your three questions, what more do you want?

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
I ask you further, whether the poison that the sorcerers deal with is all deadly?

# Lambertus Daneus

Blasphemers, perjured betrayers of God, shameful servants of the Devil, poisoners, and deceivers. Therefore, such a sorcerer is justly punished by the authorities as an apostate, a perjured arch-heretic, and a poisoner, since he has fallen away from God his Creator and has joined and surrendered himself to the loathsome enemy, Satan. For this reason, the Law of God commands that sorcerers be put to death in the fifth book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note> in the 18th chapter. And elsewhere in the Scriptures, it is reckoned among the most gruesome and damnable sins, 1 Samuel 15. Likewise, the holy Christian Councils of the Holy Fathers also condemn and curse them, namely the second at Constantinople, in the 60th and 61st articles, and 26. *quaest.* 1. 2. 3. <note>referring to sections of Canon Law</note> which are laws of Divine Right. But in Imperial Law, they are punished most severely. For in the *Lex Julia* <note>Julian Law</note> they are condemned to death, which Emperor Leo in *Novel Constitution 65* made even more stringent.

In short, there has never been a truly sensible person, neither in years past nor in our own times, who has not always considered them the worst of people and worthy of the most gruesome punishments.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
Thus I wonder that some judges and authorities are so weak and advise the human race so poorly that they either fear or refuse to root out these terrible beasts—namely, the sorcerers—or refuse to punish them when they fall into their hands.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
I also marvel at this. For truly, by their negligence, they prove that they care little for God their Lord and are public despisers of His service and honor, since they help to protect His declared, sworn enemies and let them live unpunished. But what more do you desire to know from me?

The laws are also not all of one kind; however, the Divine Law is everywhere consistent and uniform with itself, in that it condemns and punishes them everywhere: "You shall not permit a sorcerer to live," it says in the second book of Moses <note>Exodus</note> in the 22nd chapter. They are also praised throughout all of Persia as ingenious and highly intelligent people, and among the heathens, it was often considered a great skill and art if one was experienced in sorcery. # Concerning Sorcerers.
## E

...devoted themselves to the art of magic and sought the help and counsel of sorcerers. For instance, Emperor Nero—as Suetonius writes in his histories—was considered one of the best masters of it, although he later abandoned it and condemned it himself once he noticed its vanity, as C. Plinius <note>Pliny the Elder</note> writes of him. After him, Emperor Hadrian (as the historian Dion reports of him) also applied himself to these arts and sought help from them to heal the dropsy <note>An old medical term for swelling or edema</note> with which he was afflicted. The Hunnish people, as cited above from Gregory of Tours, made use of sorcerers to wage war and achieve victory. One also reads of Cyprian—who afterwards became a Christian and Bishop of Carthage—that before he was converted to the Christian faith, he occupied himself much with and was diligent in sorcery, which he afterwards renounced and rejected through the grace and enlightenment of God. These many and varied examples sufficiently prove that sorcerers and sorcery were always held in high esteem among the heathens who did not know the true God, or at least that such vain and loose deception was not rejected or condemned because it was in common use. 

However, after many useless, absurd, and for the most part loathsome and terrible things were observed in sorcery—such as the invocation of evil spirits, wondrous ceremonies, gestures, and superstition—and as the true Christian teaching and faith gradually began to come to light, it was forbidden by the laws of the Roman Emperors. It was decreed that no one should have anything to do with sorcerers, unless perhaps common or private utility or necessity required it. Therefore, in the *Code of Justinian*, Book 9, Title 18, Law 4, this law of Constantine the Great stands written: <note>original Latin: "Eorum est scientia punienda..."</note> "The knowledge of those is to be punished, and deservedly vindicated by the severest laws, who, equipped with magic arts, are discovered to have either conspired against the health of men or to have turned modest minds toward lust. However, no criminal charges are to be applied to remedies sought for human bodies, or to charms innocently employed in rural places to prevent rains from harming the ripe vintages or to stop them from being crushed by winds and hailstorms; by these acts, no one's safety or reputation is harmed, but rather they ensure that divine gifts and the labors of men are not destroyed. Given on the 10th day before the Calends of June at Aquileia, in the consulship of Crispus and Constantine."

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
That law, dear Theophilus, is truly not too precious, but rather harmful, and more heathen than Christian, if indeed it was given by Constantine, the Christian Emperor.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
I hold that at that time, Emperor Constantine was not yet perfectly instructed in Christian teaching. For you see well what he concedes and permits to the sorcerers: namely, he allows one to practice sorcery as long as it serves someone's good. He would never have permitted this if he had been a true Christian; therefore, this law was afterwards not only changed by Leo <note>Emperor Leo VI</note> but entirely abolished. For he forbids that one should in any way—no matter where it might lead—tolerate or practice sorcerers and sorcery, and he calls it nothing other than an imposition and deception; this latter law was afterwards accepted and praised by everyone. Augustine, in Canon 27, Question 7, teaches that the help of sorcerers is nothing other than a pure fraud and cunning of Satan to harm mankind. Finally, this work of the devil is also condemned in Chapter 2 of the *Decretals* concerning fortune-telling, which judgments are all more than fair.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
What judgments do you mean?

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
I mean that we should have no fellowship at all with Satan, whether it happens directly or through a medium, nor should we in any way accept or use his help, counsel, or deed. For we have the right, true God, with whom we should seek our salvation and refuge in all misfortune and suffering. And dear friend, why would we (over which the Prophet Elijah was also justly angered in 2 Kings 1) seek help and counsel from Beelzebub...

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
That is a weak reason or ground by which to prove anything. One should look to God's Commandment, who simply does not want us to visit sorcerers, for whatever reason it might be done, as it is written in the fifth book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note>, in the 18th Chapter. For what else does Satan seek thereby, than to lead us away from the fear of God and draw us to himself? Especially since the help he gives to our bodies results in the harm and damnation of the soul. For in this way people separate themselves from God, which is the certain death of the soul; and therefore all help from Satan and his sorcerers is a deadly poison to our soul, which is more to be feared and fled from than a rabid dog or the venomous basilisk <note>a mythical reptile said to kill with its gaze</note>. One must never judge or act according to the outcome, whether it be evil or good, little or much, but according to God's Commandment alone. For many a thief enjoys his stolen goods very well and lives well from them; should one therefore say that theft is right? Therefore, even if all people had been helped who seek and desire medicine from sorcerers or practitioners of the devilish arts, and it could also benefit us, nevertheless, because it is expressly forbidden by God, we should not accept it

when it is offered to us, let alone seek and desire it ourselves. For if we seek our refuge with anyone other than God, we thereby demonstrate our unbelief, mistrust, apostasy, and shameful contempt of God; through this heavy sin, we bring His wrath and disfavor upon ourselves and fall into eternal death and hellish damnation.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
So I hear plainly: it is not permitted for us at all to call upon sorcerers for help and counsel, even if it concerns health, body, or life?

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
Some make a distinction and say: if the authorities <term>Obrigkeit: the governing civil powers or magistrates</term> permit and command it, one can use their help and medicine with a good conscience; otherwise it is not permitted, nor is it fair or right. They think that because the authorities command it, and we did not run to them of our own accord, we commit no sin. But if we do it of ourselves, we call upon them, flatter and coax them, and affirm them in their sorcery, and that is a great sin. But if, they say, it is required and desired without our asking, then their help happens to us against our will; we keep a good conscience and bear no guilt for their sins, for what the authorities command is as much as if God Himself commanded it, whom one is therefore bound to obey. That is the ground upon which they build their distinction. But mark this, Antonius, how weak, loose, and void this excuse is. Firstly, Paul forbids generally in Romans 3 that we should do evil so that good may result from it, no matter who commands it—be it judge, authority, or someone else. Furthermore, I hold that it is permitted for us to conclude from like to like: if a judge or authority were to command us to worship idols, steal, commit adultery, or otherwise serve the Devil, would it be right, or could we obey this command with a good conscience? No, indeed; no sensible person would admit that. Likewise, if the authorities command that a sorcerer assist us with his devilish art, or—

whoever bids us run to them and desire help, and we do the same, we then consent to their wickedness and commit a great sin. Therefore, even if the highest authority on Earth gave the command, or even if we were robbed of all physical help and had to lie in bed miserable, lame, and sick for our entire lives, it is still not permitted by God for us to desire or use any help or means of sorcery and the devilish art. For it cannot happen without us—as much as lies within us—immediately cutting off the honor and power of God the Lord and assigning them to the Devil, because we make use of his help and allow ourselves to be satisfied by it, whom we nevertheless thoroughly renounced once in Holy Baptism. Furthermore, neither the life nor the death of any human being stands in the power and might of the Devil, but stands alone in the will and omnipotence of God. However, one can well advise and permit that if someone, who is otherwise a sorcerer, could help or make someone healthy without idolatrous, rejected means, and also without the fellowship of Satan, according to the rule and teaching of physicians <note>original: "Artzet"</note> through the means ordained by God, it would not be against God, but fair and right for us to accept that same help and advice for our benefit. For as long as the means applied and given to us are not mixed or defiled with damnable and cursed devilish sorcery, but are used according to the order of God and natural causes, they can and may well be accepted, whether it be man or woman, citizen or peasant, who gives them to us or teaches us to use them. Also, not all are sorcerers who are often accused of sorcery by the people, and much violence and injustice happens to many people through such slander. Therefore, concluding the talk of this, it follows from the mentioned causes and proof that no one, whoever they may be, should or can visit sorcerers, ask for help, or accept the same, lest they also become a partaker of their sins, or as it were enter into their order, and deny the true God, their Redeemer and Savior, as often as they, the sorcerers, have fellowship with the Devil or desire and learn the knowledge of medicine <note>original: "Artzney"</note> from him.

### The Seventh Chapter.
#### How we should guard and preserve ourselves from sorcerers and their sorcery.

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
**A**h, Theophilus, how then can we guard ourselves against them, or if we were bewitched, who would want to heal us and make us healthy again?

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
As far as the cure or healing of bewitched people is concerned, I do not shrink from saying with Augustine <note>referring to St. Augustine of Hippo, a foundational Christian theologian</note> that even the most experienced physicians are for the most part blind in such illnesses and know no help or medicine to give, as they are strange, new, and hidden; for they come out of Satan's workshop and are attached through his cunning, but are generally unknown to men. Nevertheless, in such misfortunes, one should not despise the help of natural means and medicine, but should use them nonetheless and try everything from medicine that is useful and serving, so that we—if it is God's will—may come to health again. For God the Lord can also bless His ordained means so that they serve and help us toward health in a miraculous way, since medicine is an exceedingly noble gift of God for the benefit of man, as it is written in Sirach 38 <note>original: "Sprach 38"; a reference to the Book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus which praises physicians</note>, which has great effect and has often, as even now, healed the bewitched again. But when one has tried everything and no help or improvement follows, one should still not run to the sorcerers and make a bad thing worse, and risk the soul <note>idiom: "die Seel in die schantz schlagen" - to gamble with the soul</note> so that the body may be preserved, which unfortunately happens far too much nowadays by godless and perjured people. What should one do then? One should wait for help from God the Lord with patience and comfort oneself in His Divine Providence. Therefore, we will also commend ourselves to Him, call upon Him, sigh to Him, and approach Him with a true conversion of our hearts.

# Concerning Sorcerers.
## E iij

the Devil, according to their nature, flatter and fawn upon people, whom they nevertheless mercilessly and horribly attempt to execute and kill. Finally, let this also be a remedy and good advice from me to protect oneself against their mischief: namely, that one should diligently warn and exhort the authorities, judges, and magistrates <note>The "Obrigkeit" refers to the established governing bodies of the early modern period.</note> to cease other vain and inquisitive questions regarding this matter, and instead be entirely intent on how they may investigate, seize, and earnestly have these vile people executed with due punishment. For no more gruesome or terrible pestilence can come among the people than the devilish sorcerers, concerning whom the last law, *concerning evildoers* <note>original: "tit. de maleficiis" — a reference to a specific title in Roman Law (the Codex Justinianus) dealing with sorcery and poisoning.</note>, commands that they should be apprehended by anyone who recognizes them and taken into custody; so cruel and evil have these people always been held to be. If we, dear Antonius, who have the power from God to give laws, also directed our laws so that everyone in his territory had the power to judge and sentence such apostate arch-enemies and villains—so that they might not finally escape the hands of the judge through long legal processes or the usual appeals back and forth, which has often occurred. Since every administrator or regent in his province has full power to judge and have killed murderers and those who secretly and craftily plot against our lives—who in Latin are called *assassins* <note>original: "Assassinatores"</note>—why is this power not also given to them over the aforementioned sorcerers? For it is a much worse and more intolerable deed to kill someone with poison than with the sword, and much more evil to attack one secretly than openly to one's face. Finally, dear Antonius, I have not wished to withhold this from you as the final conclusion of our entire disputation <note>A formal academic or theological debate.</note> for your warning: namely, that everyone should diligently note and understand from the matters just discussed how necessary it is for him to commend himself to God at all times, so that he does not fall into the snare of the evil sorcerers,

<column-break/>

or be harmed by them; for they are certain enemies, and moreover quite secret and cunning. Thereafter, that we likewise at all times diligently thank God the Lord, who protects us from the harmful wiles of the hostile adversary, Satan, so that we do not also miserably fall into the accursed order of sorcerers and the denial of His Divine Name. And thirdly, you see, Antonius, how the goodness and providence of God the Almighty heavenly Father over the human race is so exceedingly great, and how gloriously it is to be lauded and praised. The goodness indeed appears from this: that although there have been so many sorcerers at all times who have so insolently, faithlessly, and perjuriously denied God openly and accepted Satan in His place as their god, He has not long ago destroyed the entire world to its foundation, for which He had such good reason and right, and such great cause. The providence, however, is seen in this: that after Satan has applied such great diligence to lead humans away from their salvation and blessedness which they have from God, and accomplishes this so powerfully and craftily, yet God the Lord even today, out of pure grace and mercy, protects the greatest multitude from his assaults and wiles, checks and restrains him, brings his plots to naught, and helps so that the greatest and best part retains the upper hand and the victory. Before whom, our dear God, the godless must tremble, so that they stop and cannot do harm according to their evil wantonness, and so that the elect and children of God do not also fall away from the right faith, but remain steadfast and persevere. To the same sole, eternal, almighty, and gracious God be praise, honor, and glory in eternity, Amen. Do you now, dear Antonius, desire anything further from me?

<margin>Antonius.</margin>
Nothing at all. For you have sufficiently explained and proven the entire matter to me, so that I am satisfied, and I give you great thanks from my heart for this kindness. Now may God protect you, my Theophilus.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
And you also, my dear Antonius.

-> End of the Second Treatise. <-

# The Third Little Treatise
## Concerning Sorcerers, Witches, and Monsters. <note>original: "Inholden" – a term for wood-demons or malevolent spirits, often used interchangeably with witches.</note> Principally, however, what kind of work Sorcery is, and what sickness, harm, and hindrance arise from it. Also, what counter-remedy is to be used against it.

-> By the Worthy Mr. Jacob Vallick, Pastor at Groossen. <-

### Jacob Vallick, Pastor at Groossen, wishes the diligent reader grace and Christian enlightenment.

<margin>Romans 1.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 12.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 13.</margin>
<margin>Revelation 3.</margin>
Friendly and diligent dear reader: Often have I reflected upon the terrifying and lamentable error of the people, which has existed for nearly the longest time in the world—not only among the simple and unlearned, but also among many highly learned and sensible people—concerning Sorcery, into which nearly all have fallen, and that without doubt on account of our sins. For since we are God’s people and yet have not served or honored God with the honors which belong to Him, God has therefore given us over to a perverse mind so that we have fallen into all errors, as the Prophet also says: "Lord, all those who have forsaken thee shall be put to shame." The Psalmist also says: "They have all sinned, altogether they have become useless, and the whole world lies in wickedness." This error of sorcery has spread so far among men that one soon imagines that no one suffers a deficiency unless it comes through sorcery. For instance, if someone becomes sick, or otherwise receives some harm, such as his beasts dying off, fortune being against him, or his temporal nourishment otherwise declining, one immediately imagines that he is bewitched and that the same arises through Sorcery—just as if God sends no punishment to any man. Yet God Himself says: "Whom I love,

<column-break/>

<margin>Hebrews 12.</margin>
I punish." And Paul says, "Whom God loves, He chastens, and scourges every child whom He receives." Such passages of the Holy Scripture we should take to heart, and patiently receive with thanksgiving everything from the hand of God that He sends us, whether it be good fortune or misfortune, as the good and patient Job did. No matter how much or what kind of misfortune came upon him, he nevertheless said: "The Lord has given, the Lord has also taken away again." If we have received the good from the hand of God, why should we not also suffer the evil? As it has pleased the LORD, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord. If we loved God and acknowledged Him as our Father out of His goodness, we should without any doubt receive everything He sends us as obedient children from our Father. We would not be so inconstant as to immediately attribute to Satan the punishments or trials which are sent to us, because we hold for certain and know that neither the Devil nor his companions can inflict anything unless it be permitted to them by God. Do we not have clear testimony of this from Job? Satan was not able to do the slightest little thing to him; he had to have permission from God for it. Does not Christ Himself say that no one can pull even a hair from our head without the will of our Heavenly Father? The Devil could [not even enter] the Gadarenes' <note>original: "Gargases" – likely a reference to the Gadarenes/Gergesenes and the miracle of the swine.</note>

<margin>Job 1.</margin>
<margin>Job 1, 2.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 10. Luke 12, 21.</margin>

# Preface

...the Gadarene swine <note>original: "stafener Schwein"; a reference to the miracle in Matthew 8:28-34</note> could not be harmed; Christ had to permit it first. What, then, could he [the Devil] prevail against a human? Why then should we doubt? Can even a leaf fall from a tree without the will of our heavenly Father? If the Father loves us—as He undoubtedly does—who then can be against us? In truth, it is neither useful nor pleasant for a true Christian never to have a Cross <note>The "Cross" here refers to suffering or trials sent by God to test faith.</note>. Woe to those Christians for whom all things go according to their will and who never have adversity, for such is a certain sign that they are abandoned and despised by God. True Christians, who are loved by God in truth, receive all chastisement <term>chastisement: spiritual discipline or physical suffering intended to improve the soul</term> with gratitude and dignity, as if from their dearest Father, however much their flesh may strive against it. For they know that it stands written:

<margin>Proverbs 3, Hebrews 12</margin>
> My child, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not be impatient with his punishment. For whom the Lord punishes, he loves, and he takes pleasure in him, like a father in a son.

For those whom the Lord has chosen, and who fall into error, He says:

<margin>Jeremiah 64 <note>Likely a citation error in the original for Jeremiah 30:11 or 46:28</note></margin>
> I will punish you justly, and will not spare you as if you were innocent.

Therefore, all pious Christians should say with Tobias:

<margin>Tobit 11</margin>
> O Lord God of Israel, I give you praise and thanks; you have punished me, and you have healed me.

Thus we should diligently note, dear friendly reader, that David says through the Spirit of God to all people:

<margin>Psalm 4</margin>
> You children of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted? How long will you love vanity and seek after lies?

For truly, this error of sorcery <note>original: "Zauberey"</note>, which has been so manifold in the world until now and still persists, has arisen from nowhere else than this: that we love vanity and seek lies, and that people have given themselves little to the love of God and a Christian life through diligent listening and reading of the Divine Word. For when people do not live according to the word of God, Satan disguises himself as an angel of light and also receives power from God to deceive people under the appearance of truth.

<column-break/>

Just as happened among us at Elten <note>A town in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany</note>, in the years written as [15]21, 23, and 24. At St. Anthony’s farmstead <note>original: "Meyerhoff"</note> there was a devil in the form of a little dwarf; he called himself Eckerken. He performed many strange things: at night he threw the sheaves down onto the threshing floor which the servants were supposed to thresh during the day; those servants who were negligent in their work, he beat; he fed the horses and lay down at night with the maidservants. He struck the people who traveled across the heath by the farm. He pulled the women by their secret and hidden hair <note>A euphemism for pubic hair, often mentioned in folklore regarding lecherous spirits</note>; those who traveled by wagon, he overturned their wagon; those on horseback, he pulled them from their steeds. As one man, named Wessel von Berffelt, told me himself—to whom this also happened—this little dwarf let no one pass by that farm; one first had to give him an *Ort* or a half *Stuber* <note>Small denominations of contemporary currency</note>. This lasted for about two or three years, until an old witch <note>original: "Hexe"</note> was burned who lived there and confessed that she had arranged this through her dear bridegroom, Satan, as is known to the whole countryside.

In addition to this, it often happens, as highly experienced physicians indicate, that many people—due to strange illnesses which they call melancholy <note>original: "Melancholiam"</note> and frenzy <note>original: "phrenesin"</note>—imagine that they are something or see something, when in truth they are not and do not see it, as I have often experienced myself, of which further report shall be found in this booklet.

We shall also find in this booklet that some people commit much mischief among the common folk, falsely boasting that they can give counsel against sorcery, recognize hags <note>original: "Unholden"; refers to malevolent spirits or witches</note>, and can lead anyone to whatever places they might desire. They stir up the simple folk to such an extent that one person conceives a very evil suspicion <note>original: "argwohn"</note> against another, which suspicion sometimes remains as long as a single person of that lineage survives. # Preface

false belief or delusion, which one has imagined regarding certain creatures, often corrupts nature and shall utterly ruin it. For (to provide a better understanding) there is perhaps a person who enters a house where a rumor has spread that they can perform sorcery <note>original: "zauberen"</note>, even though such a thing is invented and a lie. This same person enters the house where such unbelieving and suspicious people dwell; by chance, cows or horses die there. The suspected person gives the suspicious man an apple, or some other fruit, which is pure and good in its nature; nevertheless, the suspicious man shall often develop an illness which either plagues him for a long time or from which he even dies. For an evil and strong suspicion is capable of much in these matters, as I have found to be true myself. For once a group of young companions were together, among whom was a young fellow who boasted that he could give something to young maidens and virgins to make them fall in love with him. A good person heard this, who was honorable and pious, as nothing else had ever been heard of her. It happened that they agreed that this same fellow should give her something. For she considered herself so perfect and strong that such a thing could in no way be harmful to her. Now, however, the good fellow knew nothing of these things, nor did he have any prepared poison or love potion <note>original: "philtrū" (philtre)</note> with him; rather, he had only a piece of cake in his pocket. That, he said, was the prepared herb with which he (as said before) could awaken love; this he gave to the person to eat. Immediately she played the fool with him and said, "Oh my friend, how I love you now, what am I doing?" etc. When it became evening, everyone went home, and there was no more thought of this thing. But the virgin went to bed and could not rest or remain still, so deeply did this matter weigh on her mind, and she kept saying to herself: "I wish that I had not taken this devilish work <note>original: "Teuffelisch Werck"</note>; what possessed me to taste this more than others?" At last she stood up, and labored for so long

<column-break/>

until she came to the aforementioned fellow, for she could not sleep or rest until she was defiled by him, etc. This was caused by nothing other than the strong imagination and the firm suspicion. However, it is commonly said: many are easily led astray, and he who likes to dance is easily whistled for, etc. Yet hear another thing which was told to me, and without any <margin>A Story <note>original: "Historia"</note></margin> doubt is true. It happened that four or five men were eating and drinking together in a tavern, among whom was one who was "beaten with a wooden sword" <note>A contemporary idiom for someone who is easily fooled or simple-minded.</note>, so that one could easily persuade him of anything. They first talked him into believing that his face was swollen; they also, during the following night, sewed his trousers and coat to make them tighter. Early in the morning, one of his companions came to his bed and told him again that he was severely swollen. When he tried to dress himself and found that his clothes were too tight, he was terribly frightened. Immediately his other companions came to meet him on the street (for the matter had been planned this way) one after another, and all with one voice told him how severely swollen he was, etc. The good man went home, lay down in bed, and had himself provided with the Holy Sacraments <note>The last rites, indicating he believed he was dying.</note>, and died through such vain persuasion. This happened because he took the false persuasion to heart and thereby was overcome by a deadly terror, as you have now heard. In such a manner, I say, a false opinion causes much evil; as I have lived through and seen much of this, to recount it all here would be far too tedious.

Although this is so, dear reader, one will nevertheless find that the world has not been entirely free from true sorcery, as the Biblical and also pagan writings testify, which has caused much evil among the people in all lands. # A Dialogue or Conversation
### concerning Sorcery: of which the first persons speaking together are
->Mechtilt and Elizabeth.<-

<column-break/>

MECHTILT: Look there, my neighbor Elizabeth comes running here in such a hurry; where can she be thinking of going so fast? ELIZABETH: I do not know, my neighbor, what this means; I might as well just run away entirely. MECHTILT: Good morning, neighbor Elizabeth. ELIZABETH: May God give you a good morning. MECHTILT: Dear neighbor, what does it mean that you are so restless? ELIZABETH: My dear neighbor Mechtilt, I will lament this to you: All my horses are sick, two of my cows have died, and from the others I have left, I can get no butter. Now, the milk is good, yet it has no butter in it. And likewise, my husband is also incapacitated <note>original: "vnuermūgē" - lacking strength or impotent</note>; for though he still walks and stands well enough, he has no appetite to eat or drink. Everything is going backward for me <note>original: "gehē mit mir dē Krebsgang" - literally "walking like a crab," meaning things are deteriorating.</note>. People tell me I must be bewitched; yet I do not know what to say about it; I am almost entirely discouraged and in despair. MECHTILT: Dear me, what are you saying now? Why should you be bewitched? One often suffers lack and infirmity without being bewitched. What person could be so desperate that they would bewitch someone? ELIZABETH: I do not know; an old devil and witch lives near me; I do not doubt that she is the one doing it to me. For she came in days past and borrowed a loaf of bread from me; at that same time I was churning butter and I got some—and fine butter it was, too. Immediately, she could not marvel at the butter enough, nor would she stop, but wanted to taste the butter; therefore she broke a piece off the bread, took some butter on it, and ate it. Besides this, she would not stop until I also had to give her a bowl of buttermilk to drink. And immediately such thoughts came into my mind: "Look, you are giving this to this witch; surely she will bewitch you." And from that time on, two of my cows died, and from one I have been able to get neither milk nor butter; besides that, all my horses are now sick. In the summer, when the plums were ripe, she gave my husband a handful of plums, and from that time on he has also been unfit. In this way, I am firmly of the opinion that she is doing me this evil. MECHTILT: Oh, my dear neighbor, do not talk so foolishly about a matter for which you have no certain proof. In truth, that is a great, yes—

# Concerning Witches and Monsters

and it is in truth so; for I know several women who have given such things <note>likely referring to love potions or charms mentioned on the previous page</note> to young fellows, and it happened according to their desire. Dear friend, show me one word or work of hers that is worthy of blasphemy; have you also, in all the days of your life, seen anything in her that she should not do? **ELYZ.** Of her doings I know nothing in particular, for I have not often paid attention to her; however, one seldom finds her in the church, except during the sermon. Main points must be noted if one wishes to treat this matter correctly.
First, what "to bewitch" <term>zauberen: to practice magic or sorcery</term> means, and what kind of work that is.
Secondly, one must know that sorcery is of two kinds. First, Spiritual, as when the conscience of a person is bewitched. Secondly, Worldly, as when the body and temporal goods are bewitched.
Thirdly, one must diligently observe that the Devil is our sworn enemy, and where he cannot damage us by himself, he uses his children and faithful servants for that purpose, such as sorcerers, traitors, deceivers, murderers, thieves, and the like.
Fourthly, one must know with what cure or remedy one should treat sorcery. Fifthly, how one should be warned and protect oneself so as not to be bewitched.
Now, initially, "to bewitch" is a word that means as much as "to deceive." As if I were to say, "the person is bewitched," it is the same as saying "the person is deceived" and brought to that state; in this manner Saint Augustine describes sorcery. In this way, Saint Paul asked the Galatians who had so bewitched them that they did not believe the Gospel and did not remain steadfast in what Paul had taught them. In this manner, sorcery is a work by which a person is bewitched in a way that is beyond nature, yet through natural means, in a deceptive fashion, whereby he comes into error, into unbelief, into sickness of the body, and into damage of property. DIEDER: Worthy Sir, can one also find people who are able to harm someone through sorcery? PSAR: Yes, indeed, for many excellent writers testify to the same. Firstly, it is known that St. <margin>St. Augustine, Book 10 of *The City of God*, chapter 19</margin> Augustine divides the art of sorcery into three parts.
