The third part he calls *Pharmacia* <note>The use of drugs or potions</note>, and it is when someone is given something to eat or drink which is prepared through sorcery, by which someone becomes sick or dies, or otherwise receives some other misfortune. As the same Augustine also writes, he has heard <margin>St. Augustine, Book 18 of *The City of God*, chapter 10</margin> how in Italy there were said to have been stable-women—that is, such women who let out horses and donkeys for hire to travelers and wayfarers. These same women had prepared a special cheese through sorcery; if they then lacked rental horses, they would immediately give a person this cheese to eat, and they would immediately become donkeys or horses, which had to carry loads and people for money. In such a way it happened to Apuleius, as he writes of himself in the book of the *Golden Ass*, that he retained his human understanding and yet for a time was transformed into a donkey. Just as one named Prestantius told his father that he had eaten of the aforementioned cheeses and was immediately transformed into a horse, which had to carry great and heavy burdens.

Namely, that the impoverished people begin to rob, practice usury, and steal; they become whores, knaves, rogues, thieves, and murderers. # Concerning Witches and Monsters.

Medicine dispels the sickness of the soul, but with what medicine shall one cure bodily enchantment? PASTOR: God the Almighty has left His power to us in words, in herbs, and in stones; and everything that God the Lord created, He created for the benefit of mankind. All such things we may use to God’s honor and our own benefit, according to the occasion and the time. For such things receive their power and effects through the word of God. All such outward

<margin>Tobit 6.</margin>
means were used by Tobias <note>A reference to the Book of Tobit in the Apocrypha, where the Archangel Raphael instructs young Tobias on how to drive away a demon.</note>: When Sarah, a daughter of Raguel, had seven husbands, all of whom Satan strangled on the first evening when they went into her bedchamber, the Angel Raphael gave the younger Tobias such advice: that he should take the liver and gall of the fish which would show itself to him by the water (which is said to have been a pike, as the Doctors <note>Refers to learned theologians or scholars of the church.</note> teach). He was to lay these upon coals, and the smoke would drive away the Devil, as indeed then happened. Thus, such a liver of a pike shall still be powerful today to drive away all kinds of sorcery, when it is used with a firm faith and fiery prayer. The ancient physicians write of certain herbs before which Satan flees; such is *Hypericon*, that is St. John’s Wort, which they therefore also call "Devil’s Flight" <note>original: "Teuffelsfuhe"</note> because Satan flees from it. Such power is also said to be held by the herb *Morsus Diaboli*, called Devil’s Bit. This same herb has a bite in the root after the birthday of St. John, but not before that day; and such a bite, it is said, Satan bites into it because he is an immeasurable enemy to that herb. Where this herb is pulverized on St. John’s Night before midnight and hung in houses, there Satan or any sorcerer can do no harm. The same power is also said to be held by Mugwort, *Ingrim* <note>likely Periwinkle or a similar protective herb</note>, and Palms; drinks made from these and given to the enchanted person will help. These same herbs are also customarily

<column-break/>

hung by the beds of the sick who are seized by hot sickness <note>fever</note>, and also by women in labor. Also by those who, through hot melancholy, feel a certain terror within them that seeks to lead them astray. One also pulverizes these and hangs them around one's neck. Now, however, one should prepare this medicine in such a manner. Take these three kinds of herbs:

<margin>The Cure.</margin>
*Hypericon*, *Morsus Diaboli*, and *Ingrim*; these should be boiled down in water and wine, an equal amount of each. To this one shall add three spoonfuls of honey and a piece of salt as large as an egg. This shall be boiled together until reduced by half, and one should drink of it in the morning, at noon, and in the evening, each time a spoonful, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This should be done for nine whole days, and on each day the drink will expel something from you; after that, come back to me, and I will give you further advice.

In addition to this, I give you here frankincense and juniper berries, among which is also mixed some of a pike’s heart; you shall burn this in your bedchambers during these nine days in the evening. This dispels all sorcery and the evil workings of Satan.

I also give you *Mägdwachs* <note>literally "Maiden's Wax," a type of prepared wax or salve used in folk medicine</note>, in which some of a pike’s liver is embedded; you shall make this into small cushions and hang them around the neck. For as long as you wear such a thing on your neck, no sorcerer, witch, or monster will be able to inflict any evil upon you in any way. DIEDRICH: Well, worthy Sir, we will use these pieces with diligence, and we have a firm confidence that they will help us. PASTOR: May Almighty God give you what is blessed for you. ELIZA: We desire nothing else, and we wish to show ourselves grateful toward Your Reverence. PASTOR: Go in peace, and the Lord Christ be with you, and with us all.

# Concerning Witches and Sorcerers/ A
### Christian, useful, and necessary report for these our dangerous times, drawn from the Word of God, spiritual and secular laws, as well as various other histories.

Originally composed 123 years ago by Ulrich Molitoris of Constance, Doctor of Laws, in the form of a Latin dialogue, and now recently and most faithfully translated into German and divided into specific dialogues by Conrad Lautenbach, Pastor at Hunawihr.

## Report concerning Witches and Sorcerers, in honor of the Illustrious and High-born Prince and Lord, Lord Sigismund, Archduke of Austria, Styria, Carinthia, etc. Composed by Ulrich Molitoris of Constance, Doctor of Laws, also Lecturer in the High School <note>The University</note> at Pavia, and Advocate in legal matters.

<columns>2</columns>

Illustrious, high-born Prince, most gracious Lord, my humble services are at Your Princely Grace’s disposal. As in years past a particular plague of witches and sorcerers, or enchantresses, arose in Your Princely Grace’s lands, and several women who were suspected of this heresy <note>original: "Ketzerey"</note> were taken into custody, who also confessed much under painful interrogation <note>term: "peinliche Frag" — a legal euphemism for interrogation under torture</note>, concerning which Your Princely Grace’s counselors held various and differing opinions, where one concluded this and another that; finally, I also was remembered by Your Princely Grace. And because Your Princely Grace is by nature desirous of the truth, I was commanded by Your Princely Grace’s counselors to set down my opinion

<column-break/>

on this matter in writing.
Although it is both laborious and dangerous: laborious because I am otherwise burdened with other business; dangerous, however, because of the envious and the slanderers, who criticize everything that they cannot improve—indeed, which they cannot even understand due to their sheer coarseness—and defame and blaspheme with poisonous tongues. Furthermore, even excellent people have never been able to sufficiently settle this business. Nevertheless, I acknowledge my duty to serve Your Princely Grace with my body and my modest understanding to the best of my ability, and I will in no way spare myself, provided that Your Princely Grace may be served. I therefore submit this my work to Your Princely Grace and to your high—

# Preface.

<margin>
Conrad Stürtzel / Doctor of Laws.
</margin>
...to the highly intelligent counselors / and especially to the highly learned / distinguished Lord Conrad Stürtzel, Doctor of both Laws <note>original: "beyder Rechten Doctorn"; referring to Civil and Canon Law</note>, Your Princely Grace’s Secretary / and my old schoolmaster. And because dialogues among the ancient orators and speakers / are generally more pleasant and delightful to read / I have also wished to set this report in the form of a conversation / between two or three persons.

<margin>
Conrad Schatz / Mayor of Constance.
</margin>
Since I have many times held good conversation with the wise and distinguished Lord / Conrad Schatz / Mayor and Magistrate of this praiseworthy city of Constance / for many years / as a man of understanding and eloquence / who has also very often heard the renunciations and confessions of such women <note>referring to accused witches</note> / I have deemed it good / to set this report according to the form and shape of a dialogue / between Your Princely Grace, the aforementioned Lord Conrad, and myself. I will therefore, with Your Princely Grace’s favor, proceed to the matter / and comprise the entire subject at the beginning of this report into several points of inquiry.

I have, however / Illustrious / high-born Prince / and most gracious Lord / set this dialogue to the honor of Your Princely Grace / and for the benefit of all good-hearted Christians / and I pray / that Your Princely Grace will graciously recognize and accept this work of mine. If also anything herein has been overlooked / or otherwise set down / than is fitting / and in accordance with the truth / do not ascribe the same to my own presumption / but rather to my ignorance. I herewith humbly commend myself into Your Princely Grace’s protection and shield. May He <note>God</note> preserve Your Princely Grace as an ornament of the Fatherland / and a Prince beloved and esteemed by both Him and all the people, long fresh and healthy. Given at Constance on the 10th day of January / in the Year of Christ / 1489.

->Your Princely Illustriousness's<-
->humble counselor and servant<-
->Ulrich Molitoris, Doctor.<-

### Contents of this present report.

I. Whether sorcerers and witches, with the Devil's assistance / can actually produce hail / storms and frost and thereby ruin the land. Dialogue 1 and 9.
II. Whether witches and sorceresses, through the Devil's cooperation / may inflict harm upon men and young children / and send sickness and paralysis. Dialogue 2, 9.
III. Whether they can make man and wife unfit for matrimonial acts / and take from them their manhood and child-bearing power. Dialogue 3 and 9.
IV. Whether they are able to transform the faces of men / and give them another shape. Dialogue 4 and 10.
V. Whether sorcerers and witches can ride upon greased pitchforks / wolves and other animals / traveling from one place to another / to revelry and dancing / eating and drinking there / knowing one another / and engaging in all kinds of pastime. Dialogue 5 and 11.

<column-break/>

VI. Whether the Devil can practice fornication <note>original: "Bulschafft"</note> with these same monsters and witches in the shape of a man. Dialogue 6 and 12.
VII. Whether children may be begotten from such a mingling. Dialogue 7 and 12.
VIII. Whether sorceresses and soothsayers, through the Devil's instructions, can know secrets / discover the plots of Princes / and reveal future things. Dialogue 8.
IX. Whether one ought to burn such tempted, evil women / according to the content and direction of the Laws / or punish them in other ways. Dialogue 12.

# Concerning Witches and Sorceresses.

->DIALOGUE I.<-

->The beginning of this conversation is made by the Illustrious,<-
->High-born Prince and Lord, Lord Sigismund,<-
->Archduke of Austria, etc.<-

<margin>SIGISMUND</margin>
Dear and faithful Doctor Ulrich, because we hold a particularly favorable will toward you, for you have served us well, we have a special desire to converse with you, above others, regarding the present questions.

<margin>ULRICH</margin>
Illustrious, high-born Prince, although it greatly pleases me that Your Princely Grace recognizes me as capable for this conversation, Conrad Schatz, our City Master <note>A high-ranking municipal official or magistrate</note>, is also present—a sensible, experienced man and my very good friend. If it is not against the wishes of Your Princely Grace, we would also like to hear his opinion first.

<margin>Conrad Schatz</margin>

<margin>SIGISMUND</margin>
Yes, we are satisfied with that, for we are well aware that he possesses high understanding and witty conversation. Since we wish to deliberate concerning witches and sorceresses <note>original: "Hexen vnd Unholden"</note>, the first question arises:

> Whether witches and sorceresses can actually produce hail, thunder, and rain through their deeds.

<margin>CONRAD</margin>
Although I find myself unskilled in such weighty matters, which give even the most learned people much to do—and as Socrates used to say, I only know that I know nothing—nevertheless, at Your Princely Grace's request, I will speak a little on the matter and provide cause to reflect further and better upon the business.

<margin>Objections.</margin>
SIGISMUND. Very well, then begin.

<margin>CONRAD. I. Common report.</margin>
There is a proverb among the philosophers: Not everything is false that is commonly said. Now, the common report goes that witches are said to have made thunder and hail, thereby doing great damage to the fruit in the fields and to mankind. They also confess to this themselves during the penal inquiry <note>interrogation under torture</note>, and it is known from daily experience,

<margin>II. Own Confession.</margin>

<margin>III. Experience.</margin>

<column-break/>

that they have taught each other such arts.

<margin>SIGISMUND. I. Counter-argument.</margin>
However, one must not always rely on common report or believe every rumor. For one person always speaks from the mouth of another. Nor are we satisfied by the confessions they make during the racking and severe martyrdom <note>torture</note>, since often one must confess out of fear and pain during the penal inquiry to things they have never done. We would prefer to investigate and understand these matters, which cannot be seen with the eyes, based on good grounds and certain causes. For a proper disputation rests upon solid testimonies and proofs.

<margin>ULRICH</margin>
Experience is truly not to be rejected in the examination of matters, for experience teaches all things, as it stands in the chapter *where there is danger*, concerning elections, book 6 <note>original: "cap. vbi periculum, de elect. libro 6" — a reference to Canon Law</note>. Hence the common proverb: *Believe Rupert the expert*, that is, believe one who has experienced it.

<margin>SIGISMUND. Proof that witches make no weather. I. The incapacity of women.</margin>
That witches and sorceresses are capable of nothing in this regard, I prove thus: For if women could and knew how to bring about such things, then princes and lords would not need to summon their vassals in times of war, or take on mercenaries to attack the enemy, to ruin land and people, or to burn cities and villages. Rather, it would be enough to demand such a sorceress, protect her with safe conduct, and incite her to attack and damage the enemy in his own land with thunder, hail, and storms. But we see well that they are not capable of such, even if they were appointed and used for it by princes and lords (from which may God preserve us), and even if they themselves would gladly do it. From this, it is to be concluded that they do not have the power.

Here, indeed, the Canon Laws <note>Ecclesiastical or Church laws</note> also agree and testify that a person who is otherwise not "cold" <note>impotent</note> by nature may nevertheless be rendered unfit for marital acts through sorcery. We also have a specific title in the Decretals <note>Papal decrees</note> concerning "cold" and bewitched persons. Therefore, Pope Hilmarus <note>likely referring to Hincmar or a similar citation in the Decretum Gratiani</note> says in the chapter *Si per sortiarias* <note>Latin: "If by sorceresses"</note>, 33rd Question, 1st Causa: "When sexual intercourse does not follow due to God's secret but always righteous judgment and the devil's instigation, the bewitched should, with a repentant heart and humble spirit, fully confess all their sins to God and the priest, etc." There, every text says that marital acts are hindered through the devil's instigation. And although this Canon alone would be sufficient for resolving the present matter (since the Canons should be approved and accepted by everyone, as is also stated in Chapter 1 *de constit.*), the ancient teachers also discuss and acknowledge this very thing. For Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says in the 4th book *Super Sententias*, distinction 34: "Sorcery brings it about that a man may not be able to sleep with one woman, but may well be capable with another." But sometimes their manhood is taken from them in such a way that they can perform with all other women, but are unable to master one alone."

For Simon is said to have told the Emperor Nero: "So that you, dearest Emperor, may know that I am the Son of God, have me beheaded, and I will rise again on the third day." Thereupon the Emperor commanded the executioner to behead him; the executioner certainly thought nothing else than that he was striking off Simon's head, though he had only beheaded a ram. Simon, however, gathered the pieces of the ram together and hid himself with them for three days. On the third day, he stepped before Nero again and said: "Let my blood that was shed be washed away, for here stands the man who was beheaded; I have risen again on the third day according to my promise." When Nero saw this, he was violently terrified and fell into the thought that Simon was indeed the Son of God.

# Ulrich Molitoris

» ...women called *Stabulariæ* <note>Latin: "stable-women" or "innkeepers"</note>, or hostesses, in those regions were said to be experienced in this art. Here Augustine speaks only from hearsay, saying: it was reported to him by certain people. Therefore, Augustine’s words conclude nothing definitive; for with a witness who only relies on hearsay, nothing can be proven.

<margin>ULRICH</margin>
Your Princely Grace speaks wisely of this, yet we wish to step closer to the matter. Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a 13th-century encyclopedist</note> describes in his *Speculum Naturale* <note>The "Mirror of Nature," a massive medieval compendium of knowledge</note>, in the 109th chapter of the 3rd book, a history which William of Malmesbury, a monk of Bury, also relates. Namely, that in the time of Peter Damian, two old women—whom Augustine calls *Stabularias*, hostesses, who lodged people for their money (for *Stabulum* actually means a common and public inn)—lived under one roof by a highway. Both practiced sorcery, and whenever a guest came to the house alone, they transformed him into a horse, a sow, or a donkey, sold him to merchants, and made money from it. One day they took in a young fellow who earned his living with juggling and acrobatics; they turned him into a donkey and made a good profit from him, for whoever passed by had to marvel at the strange behavior of the donkey. For he went wherever the old woman told him to go, since he had lost only his speech, but not his reason. Now when a rich man in the neighborhood heard that the old women had a great profit from the donkey, he bought it from them dearly enough. But the old women warned him that he should not let it go into the water. Therefore, the donkey did not come into any water for a long time. Finally, however, when they were no longer careful with him, he lay down in the nearest puddle,

<margin>VII. Foreign guests transformed into animals by their hostesses.</margin>

<column-break/>

rolled around in it for a long time, shed the donkey's shape, and came back to himself. When the donkey-boy met him and asked if he had not seen his donkey, he answered: "I am that same donkey." The boy reported it to his master; the master brought it before the most holy Pope Leo. The old women were confronted and had to confess it. But as the Pope still placed this matter in doubt, Peter Damian—a very learned man—gave him further report and cited the example of the sorcerer Simon <note>Simon Magus, the biblical magician</note>, who had given Faustinianus his own face <note>A reference to a legendary transformation in the Clementine Recognitions</note>. Thus Peter Damian, a highly learned doctor and reputable man, concluded before the Pope that such a thing might well have happened.

<margin>SIGISMUND</margin>
You bring us to such a point with so many histories and proofs that we do not know which way to turn.

<margin>ULRICH</margin>
At the end (in the following 10th Dialogue) we shall treat further of this question.

Perhaps the spirit enters into a body and takes on a shape that is useful for his intended work, and carries out what he desires in and with that same body. For we read in the Holy Scripture, namely in the last chapter of the Prophet...

# Concerning Witches and Sorceresses.

<margin>
IIII.
Natural
indications.
</margin>
**Sigismund.** Is it not then God alone who—as the Almighty Creator and Searcher of Hearts—knows, foreknows, and proclaims all hidden and future things?

**Ulricus.** Certainly He is. Nevertheless, the Devil can also prophesy future things. For we see also that naturalists <note>original: "Naturkündiger"</note>, astrologers <note>original: "Sternseher"</note>, and other experienced people proclaim future things.

**Sigismund.** Although they also prophesy of future matters, it does not necessarily follow that it must be fulfilled exactly so, or that it must certainly happen by necessity because of their prophecy.

**Ulricus.** Your Princely Serenity speaks rightly of this. For all things stand in God's hand. He also requires no counselor, since He understands all things best by Himself.

**Sigismund.** We would nevertheless like to understand how the Devil could know and proclaim future things beforehand?

<margin>
How and from where the Devil knows and reveals future things.
</margin>
**Ulricus.** Regarding this, let Your Princely Serenity hear the words of Saint Augustine, which are also cited in the Decree, in the chapter *Sciendum* <note>Latin: "It should be known"</note>, question 37, case 4: One should know that the devils are by nature of a spiritual essence, surpassing earthly creatures far in understanding and speed; and because of their natural agility, they are easily superior not only to humans and cattle in swift running, but also to the birds in the air in flying. Since they then have these two advantages by nature—namely, that they are of sharp-witted understanding and quick movement—they can also oftentimes speak of a thing before it happens, at which humans, being of an earthly, coarse understanding, greatly marvel. In addition, the devils have also for a long time now—as long as their lives have lasted—been able to experience much more than any human in his short life. According to these qualities, with which their spiritual being and nature is endowed, they can prophesy and accomplish many things. But because humans

<column-break/>

can neither say nor do the like, they therefore think the devils are well worthy of being served and shown divine honor, especially because curiosity also pricks them, and they would gladly be held in high and good standing before the evil world. And since the question here concerns the Devil's prophecy, one must know that they commonly prophesy such things as they themselves are willing to do. For they oftentimes receive power to sicken people, to poison the air, and to put evil into the minds of the children of this world, especially where they know that people will gladly follow them. From this, they then—in a wonderful and invisible way, according to their subtle nature—creep into the bodies of humans before they are aware of it, take possession of their thoughts, and suggest to them, both in sleep and otherwise when they are awake, a delusion of a presumed command. But sometimes they also do it themselves. They proclaim, however, such things as are not for humans to know, but which they understand in a natural way and from certain signs. For a physician is not to be considered a soothsayer or a god because he knows how to speak of matters that another, who is inexperienced in this art, does not understand. Should it then be a wonder that, just as a physician perceives and indicates future illness or health from the complexion, form, and condition of the human body: so also the Devil, from certain signs and observations of the course of the heavens (which is hidden from us humans), can proclaim future weather? The devils can also know and prophesy future but currently secret things, not only from the words of humans but also from outward gestures with which they reveal the thoughts of their hearts; which afterwards other people, who do not perceive these things, consider to be pure miracles. Thus far Augustine.

**Sigismund.** Should one then also believe them?

**Ulricus.** No, by no means.

<margin>
The soothsaying Devil is not to be believed.
</margin>
**Sigismund.** Why is that?

<summary>Ulricus explains that the Devil's ability to predict the future is not divine, but stems from his superior spiritual nature, speed, long experience, and observation of natural signs. He warns that these "prophecies" are often just the Devil's own intentions or medical-like observations of human behavior and nature.</summary>

**ULRICUS.** One reads in the legends of both Apostles, Simon and Jude <note>referring to the apocryphal Golden Legend accounts of Simon the Zealot and Jude Thaddeus</note>, that Wardach the Babylonian king asked the advice of sorcerers and soothsayers as to how the war he intended to wage against the King in India would turn out. Thereupon the idols and devils answered him that it would result in a great war, and many people on both sides would perish in the battle. When Wardach heard this, he fell into great sadness, but the Apostles Simon and Jude laughed at it. When the King said: "I am in great anguish, and yet you laugh at it," the Apostles answered: "You should not let yourself be anxious; we have brought peace with us into the land. Today you shall travel nowhere; tomorrow at the third hour your legates, whom you have dispatched, will return, and with them the ambassadors of the King in India, who will willingly accept the peace upon the proposed terms and make a covenant with you." Likewise, the soothsayers laughed and said to the King: "Your Royal Majesty should not believe these foreign, unknown, and lying men who claim these things, lest they be considered spies and traitors. The gods, who cannot lie, give you this answer: you should look out for yourself and diligently guard your treasures." But what happened? On the very next day, the ambassadors returned and brought the King exactly the message that the Apostles had indicated to him. Thus the devils were themselves deceived and missed the truth, which they undoubtedly would have preferred to tell if it had been in their power and authority, considering that their lying prophecy turned out to their own disadvantage. But because they did not know future things, they were themselves mistaken and missed the mark. Thus Your Princely Grace sees that the devils are also often deceived themselves. Here, however, it is diligently to be noted how the devils are accustomed to behave when they are to prophesy about doubtful things. How do they do it? Augustine says in the mentioned chapter, *Sciendum* <note>Latin: "It is to be known"; a reference to St. Augustine's writings on the divination of demons</note>: When they are mistaken and speak the untruth, they lay all the blame on their servants, as if they had not correctly noted or executed the matters, so that they might nonetheless not lose their faith and reputation among them.

<margin>
Doubtful answer of the devils.
</margin>
Give me an example of this?

SIGISMUND.

**SIGISMUND.**

**ULRICUS.** One reads of a Prince who wanted to wage war against the Romans and therefore asked his gods—that is, the devils and soothsayers—for advice regarding the victory. Because they did not know what outcome the war would take, and yet had to give an answer so that people would not think they did not know how the war would end, they gave this doubtful answer: *Romanos te vincere certum habe* <note>original Latin: "I hold it certain that the Romans you will conquer." This is a famous grammatical ambiguity: it can mean "You will conquer the Romans" or "The Romans will conquer you."</note>. That is: "You should know for certain: that the Romans your warriors shall overcome." This may be understood in two ways, so that if the Prince had overcome the Romans, his prophecy would stand, and one could also not complain about his answer even if the Prince were beaten by the Romans. Such dark and doubtful answers they are commonly accustomed to give. They also oftentimes deceive people knowingly and intentionally, and report to them lyingly. For they are full of hatred and envy, and have their pleasure and joy in it when they can lead people astray and deceive them with errors and lies. Therefore it is very dangerous to give them belief, since it is not known to man when they are themselves deceived, or when they desire to deceive people according to their custom. Thus Your Princely Grace understands how and when they know secrets and can prophesy future things, and that their words—as no truth is to be found therein—are not to be believed.

From this, it can be seen that not everyone was blinded, but that the holy Macarius still retained his sight.

<margin>SIGISMUND</margin> This story truly serves our purpose well.

<margin>ULRICH. Otto, Bishop of Constance.</margin> At one time, the Right Reverend Lord Otto, Count of Sonnenberg and Bishop of Constance—a man of great experience and a great lover of the liberal arts—held a conversation with me on this matter. He introduced this story and, in this disputation concerning blinding <note>The term "verblendung" refers to optical illusions or demonic deceptions of the senses</note>, moved me greatly with his high authority and particular skill, especially since I was in his Grace’s service, protection, and patronage.

<margin>SIGISMUND</margin> We would very much like to know how it could be possible for one thing to be seen as another?

<margin>ULRICH. Various ways of blinding.</margin> For the improvement of others, I will point out two or three means of such blinding. According to my simple understanding, and according to the opinion of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in his *Commentary on the Second Book of Sentences, Distinction 8*, and other learned men, it seems to me that the Devil can blind our senses when he awakens a fantasy or a "glare" <note>original: "geplerr," referring to a blurred or deceptive image</note> in the thoughts or memory of a person and presents and impresses it upon the outward powers of the senses, just as often happens in a dream. For when a fantasy comes before us in sleep and dreams, and reaches out into the external members—such as the eyes or ears, wherein sight and hearing fulfill their power and effect—it often seems to us as if we see or hear something. And this also happens to people in broad daylight and outside of sleep,

<column-break/>

so that they think they see many things that are not there, as is evident in those burdened with madness or hot fevers. Furthermore, when one dwells too much on a thing and broods upon it too intensely, it happens that one often takes things that are similar and alike for the thing itself. As Augustine says, a man took such pleasure and was so infatuated with the image of a woman that even while awake, it seemed to him as if he were mingling with her in a fleshly manner. Since this method is not unknown to the Devil, I say that he may well displace and befool the senses and understanding of a man in such a way that he takes one thing for another. For he whose bile overflows with excess moisture finds that everything he eats and drinks tastes bitter, even if it is sweet. Also, when the blood and hot vapors settle in the eyes, everything one looks at appears red. Thirdly, I say also that the Devil can bring it about through a medium that one thing gains the appearance of another; and according to the opinion of Saint Bonaventure, many times chaff is seen as snakes when a light, prepared for that purpose with special art, is placed nearby. Jugglers <note>original: "Gäuckler," meaning illusionists or street performers</note> mostly deal in such arts. Since the Devil is a master and paragon above all jugglers, he can without doubt carry out these things more quickly and subtly. Additionally, sometimes one does not see the thing itself, but only a phantom and likeness of it. Thus Saint Augustine maintains that the Apostle Peter saw a vessel let down from Heaven to Earth, in which were all kinds of four-footed beasts, creeping things, and birds, as stands in the 10th chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, which were not actually living animals, but only likenesses of them. In such a vision, Benedict saw the whole world. For one reads in his Legend that the whole world was seen by him at once in a sunbeam.

<summary>Ulrich Molitoris explains how the Devil creates illusions by manipulating human humors, memories, and external light, citing authorities like Aquinas, Augustine, and Bonaventure. He argues that "witchcraft" transformations are often sensory deceptions rather than physical changes.</summary>

For one reads that when the aforementioned Germanus stayed overnight in a house, and after supper the table was prepared anew, Germanus wondered at this and asked the host for whom he was setting the table again. Whereupon the host answered: "For the good men and women who wander by night." Therefore, Saint Germanus resolved to stay awake that same night. He saw a great number of devils, in every way appearing like men and women, sitting at the table, and he commanded them not to depart from there. He also woke everyone in the house and asked them if these people were known to them. When they said they were simply neighbors, both men and women, he sent them from house to house and found them all in their beds. Germanus also adjured the spirits so that they had to confess that they were evil spirits and were thus deceiving the people. There one sees that the evil spirits can transform themselves into and appear in a human's form, so that one thinks the phantom <note>original: "Gespenst"</note> is that very same person. This history also teaches that a person can be at one

<margin>Ulrich</margin> Your Princely Grace understands me correctly, and <term>Vincent</term> <note>Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1184–1264), a Dominican friar and encyclopedist</note> leans toward this opinion as well in the 2nd Book of his *Natural History* <note>original: Naturalis historiæ</note>, in the 128th Chapter.

<margin>Conclusions on Witchcraft.</margin> Firstly, that the Devil—neither by himself nor through the help of other people—can move the <term>elements</term> <note>earth, air, fire, and water</note>, cause harm to humans and livestock, or make men unfit for the <term>marital act</term> <note>impotence caused by "tying the knot" or sorcery</note>, unless it is permitted and allowed by God in His secret counsel and always righteous judgment. Secondly, even when God

<column-break/>

according to His secret counsel and righteous judgment allows the Devil to do harm, the Devil can still harm no one further than what is permitted to him by Almighty God.

Thirdly, although the Devil, by God's permission, can blind the eyes of people due to their unbelief or the other aforementioned reasons, and can displace their other senses so that they believe they are in places and ends where they have not gone, or see something that is not there, or appears different than it is in itself—yet he cannot, in truth, give another form to a human or an animal.

Fourthly, that such wicked women do not travel many miles during the night, come together, and hold costly banquets and high living; rather, the Devil only suggests the form of such a thing to them in a dream or through a strong <term>delusion</term> <note>original: verblendung</note>, as previously mentioned. Such and similar things occur to these people in their sleep; when they then awake, they believe it all truly happened in that way.

Fifthly, that the Devil can father children neither in the form of a man nor a woman, but that the children who are sometimes found are either stolen from elsewhere or are otherwise phantoms.

Sixthly, that God alone knows future things and recognizes the thoughts of men. The Devil, neither by himself nor through his sorcerers and soothsayers, has any certainty of future things, except what he himself—as a sharp-witted and swift spirit—understands from the stars and the movement of the elements, or what is already in progress or at the door, or what he himself intends to do by God's permission, or what he incites other people to do, or what he otherwise presumably gathers from their customs and gestures. In all of which he is nevertheless often deceived himself and deceives other people.

How can you let a Christian woman drive you back so? Tell me, I pray, why does she have such power and strength?" He answered: "I cannot tell you; I saw a terrifying sign and was struck with fear by it. If you wish to learn the power of this sign, swear to me that you will never desert me." When he had rendered the oath, the Devil spoke: "I saw the sign of the Crucified One, and I was terrified by it and became powerless, melting like wax before a fire." Cyprian said: "Then I hear truly that the Crucified One is mightier than you?" The Devil answered: "Yes, he is mightier than us all, since he damns all those who have turned away from God to the fires of Hell." Cyprian said: "If that is the case, I will find my way to the Crucified One without delay, so that I may become his friend and need not expect such punishment." The Devil said: "But you have sworn to me." Cyprian: "I despise you along with all your vain power; I renounce you entirely, mark myself with the Cross, and say: Praised be you, O Christ, and you, Devil, depart from me." Thus the Devil had to retreat with mockery and shame, and Cyprian became a Christian. From this one sees what great power the sign of the Holy Cross had, and still retains to this day. May Christ mark us with it, he who offered himself for us on the wood of the Cross and made us blessed; he who lives and reigns, highly praised in eternity, Amen.

<margin>Cyprian converts to the crucified Christ.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Ephesians Chapter 6.</margin>

We wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, namely, against the lords of this world who rule in the darkness of this world, against the evil spirits under heaven. For this reason, take up the armor of God, so that when the evil hour comes, you may offer resistance, accomplish all things well, and hold the field.

Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and wearing the breastplate of righteousness, and your legs shod, ready to spread the Gospel of peace, so that you may be prepared. Above all things, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the fiery arrows of the wicked one. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God. And pray always in every concern with requests and supplication in the Spirit, and watch thereto with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints, and for me.

<margin>1 Peter Chapter 5.</margin>

Be sober and watch, for your adversary the Devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Resist him, firm in faith, and know that the very same sufferings are experienced by your brothers in the world.

->Prayer.<-

> Almighty, Merciful God, Heavenly Father, you have not ordained us for wrath, but that we might be preserved and saved through your grace. So we pray to you from our hearts: be our assistant throughout our entire life, and command your holy angels, who stand before your face at all times, that they take care for us and protect us in body and soul from all the promptings, deceit, and blinding of the Devil and evil spirits, so that we may persevere in you until the end, through your beloved Son our LORD Jesus Christ, Amen.

# A Christian and Necessary
### Dialogue concerning the evil, apostate angels, or unclean spirits, which are called devils.

### Diligently compiled by the Worthy Mr. Adrian Rheynmann, Minister of the Word of God in the city of Weiden in the Upper Palatinate, etc.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
Dear and faithful friend Eusebius, since you have studied the Holy Scriptures somewhat more diligently than I from your youth, and have undoubtedly learned this from them: that we are indebted to one another, not only in bodily matters, but also (which David in Psalm 51 considers the best work and highest service to God) to instruct one another with God's word: I ask you, would you briefly answer me several questions regarding the evil, apostate spirits, which are called devils.

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
The Lord Christ describes the devil right and well in John 8, where he says to the Jews: "You are of your father the devil, he was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, and the truth is not in him; when he speaks a lie, he speaks of his own, for he is a liar and the father of lies." And Paul says in Ephesians 6: "Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the cunning attacks of the devil, for we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against princes and powers, namely against the lords of the world who rule in the darkness of this world, against the evil spirits under heaven."

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
Tell me what other definition is commonly used.

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
An evil angel is a spiritual being or person, created by God as pious, righteous, holy, and free, but who fell away from Him by his own wantonness, and became the first cause of sin, as well as an enemy of God and the entire human race; he must therefore be eternally subject to the wrath of God and damnation.

<column-break/>

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
What kind of word is "Devil"?

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
In Greek it is <gloss>Diabolos</gloss> <note>original: "Διάβολος"</note>, in Latin *calumniator*, a sycophant or slanderer, who twists the words in one's mouth and interprets everything one says and does—no matter how precious it is—in the worst possible way.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
Surely the devil has other names in the Scriptures?

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
Certainly; for just as he is a master of a thousand arts <note>A "Tausentkünstler" refers to a deceptive magician or jack-of-all-trades</note>, so one might well give him a thousand names. He is otherwise called "Satan" in Hebrew, which is: *adversarius*, an adversary; for he sets himself against all holy Divine order, and where he can offer resistance to a Christian, he spares no diligence, 1 Thessalonians 2: "Satan hindered us." And by this name all those may be called who set themselves against God and His word; therefore even Peter, who had only recently made a beautiful confession of Christ, had to hear in Matthew 16: "Get thee behind me, Satan; thou art an offense, for thou mindest not the things that are of God, but those that are of men." The Pope boasts that he is a successor and follower of Peter; we may believe him in this, for he follows Peter in no part so much as in this: he minds not what is Divine, but what is human—indeed, what is devilish—wherefore he is rightly called Satan, that is an adversary, and Antichrist, that is, against Christ.

Also, in 1 Peter 5, the devil is called a lion because of his tyranny and strength, wherefore we should rightly fear him and not despise his power, as some foolish people—who do not know the devil—are accustomed to say: "the devil is not so black..."

# Adrianus Rheynmannus

as black as he is painted. If one of us were in a wilderness and heard a lion roaring ferociously, how he would be terrified and flee from it! How much more should we fear this, our sworn enemy, who stalks us secretly and does not merely harm the body, but devours the soul. He is also called the "Great Dragon" in the Revelation of John because of his poisonous envy which he bears against us (Wisdom of Solomon 2). In Job chapter 3, he is called "Leviathan," and in Job chapter 40, "Behemoth"; for "Leviathan" is the name for all great, monstrous fish, and "Behemoth" for all great beasts, by which the devil's power is indicated. Likewise, in Tobit 3, he is called "Asmodeus." Likewise in 2 Kings 1 <note>original: 4. Regū 1; in older German Bibles, 1 & 2 Kings were counted as 3 & 4 Kings</note>, Matthew 10, and elsewhere frequently, "Beelzebub."

<margin>Theophilus</margin> In your description, you said the devils were created by God; do you not thereby make God the author of sin?

<margin>Eusebius</margin> They were created good by God, but turned away from God out of their own free will. It is a gruesome error that the Manicheans <note>Followers of Manichaeism, an ancient dualistic religion that taught the universe is a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> invented two gods—one good and one evil. The good one was said to have created angels, heaven, earth, and humans; but the evil one created sickness, devils, harmful animals, etc. But there is only one God, who has revealed Himself in His Son; He is the Creator of heaven, earth, angels, devils, humans, and all things at once, with His Son and the Holy Spirit, as it stands in John 1: "All things were made through the same Word, and without the same nothing was made that was made." The devils, however, were originally a good creature, just as the angels still are; for Moses says: "God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was all very good."

<margin>Theophilus</margin> God created poisonous snakes and other things that are harmful to humans; therefore His creatures cannot all be good. And the prophet Amos, in chapter 3, testifies: "Is there a disaster in the city that the Lord has not done?" Likewise Isaiah 45: "I am the Lord and there is no other, I who make the light and create the darkness, I who give peace and create evil; I am the Lord who does all these things." Likewise Sirach chapter 11: "Evil and good, life and death, all come from God."

<column-break/>

<margin>Eusebius</margin> There are three kinds of things that one calls "evil," and we must distinguish between them. First, <term>malum culpae</term> <note>Latin: "evil of guilt" or "evil of fault"</note>, which is sin; and God did not create this evil, for He is the enemy of sin, as David says in Psalm 5: "You are not a God who is pleased by godless behavior; whoever is evil does not remain before You; You are the enemy of all evildoers." Likewise Psalm 144. The Lord is righteous in all His works; the devil, however, is the first cause of sin, and after that our free will, which obeyed the devil and did not resist him. Secondly, there is <term>malum poenae</term> <note>Latin: "evil of punishment"</note>. When God punishes for the sake of sin, it seems to humans to be evil, yet it is a good thing—not only in the eyes of God, but also to all right-thinking people. For God is just and cannot leave sin unpunished; and when a wicked boy is punished, we all acknowledge it and say: "How good it is, how rightly it happened to him; he well deserved it." And here belong the verses you cited: Amos 3, "Is there a disaster in the city that the Lord has not done?" That is: is there any punishment that the Lord has not undertaken against this city? He sent them various plagues and visited them earnestly. Likewise Isaiah 45; and also Ecclesiasticus 11: <note>original Latin: "Bona & mala, vita & mors à Deo sunt, vel dispēsantur hominib."</note> "Good and evil, life and death are from God, or are dispensed to men." God sends us fortune and misfortune or adversity; therefore Dr. Martin <note>Martin Luther</note> translated it into German as: "Fortune and misfortune, life and death are from God." Thirdly, there is <term>malum materiale</term> <note>Latin: "material evil"</note>. Snakes, harmful animals, poison, and the like we call evil, and God created these—but not so that they should merely harm us. That they have become harmful happens because of our sin; thus "material evil" is nothing other than "punishment evil," and God is the <term>Author mali poenae</term> <note>Latin: "Author of the evil of punishment"</note>; He wills the punishment, yet only insofar as it is a punishment. And although some things harm us, they do not harm us at all times. For example: we call fire an evil thing when it often burns down house and home, and yet fire is a good material which we can in no way do without if we wish to preserve our lives. Likewise, we call a sword an evil thing because people are killed with it; an animal is called evil because it bites, gores, and strikes about; but we should, on the other hand, pay attention...

<summary>Eusebius explains to Theophilus that God is not the author of sin, distinguishing between sin (caused by free will) and the "evils" of punishment and nature, which serve divine justice or have been corrupted by human fallibility.</summary>

The light is indeed a precious creature of God, yet if someone has weak eyes, he must not blame the light, which can do nothing about the fact that his eyes are feeble.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
Prove to me from the Holy Scripture that the devils were created good in the beginning?

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
If it could not be maintained otherwise, you should give credit to the single testimony of Christ, who is the truth itself, and says in John 8: The devil did not stand in the truth. <note>original: "Der Teuffel sey in der warheit nit bestanden"</note> Now, if he did not stand in the truth, he must indeed have once been truthful. And so also says Jude in his Epistle: the angels did not keep their principality, but left their own habitation. And in 2 Peter 2: God did not spare the angels who sinned. And thus says Augustine in the book *On the Nature of the Good against the Manichaeans*: <note>Latin: *de natura boni contra Manichæos*</note> "The angels were made evil, not by God’s creation, but by their own sin." <note>original: "Angeli mali facti sunt, non ex conditione Dei, sed ex proprio peccato."</note> Likewise in the second book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* <note>Latin: *de Genesi ad literā*</note> against the Manichaeans, in the 25th chapter: Everything is from God. But who made the devil? He made himself; for he became a devil not by nature, but out of sin.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
What kind of sins were those through which the evil angels fell?

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
Holy Scripture does not indicate this, but Augustine, in the book of questions to Orosius, holds it to be because the devil is a proud spirit; he was cast out by God for the sake of his pride. Likewise to Count Julian: the devil is an angel separated from God through pride. So also says Isidore: After his creation, the devil considered the highness of his nature and the depth of his knowledge, and became proud against his Creator—so much so that he even undertook to compare himself with God. And again: "By one lapse of pride, while he compared himself to God, both the devil and man fell." <note>original: "Vno superbiæ lapsu dum Deo se confert, & diabolus cecidit & homo."</note> That is: through pride the devil and man fell, because he wants to be equal to God.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
When is this supposed to have happened?

<column-break/>

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
It is held that it happened shortly after his creation; there would have been a little time between the creation and the fall. And so says Isidore: "The apostate angel was deprived of the contemplation of the Creator, for as soon as he was made, he burst into pride, and was cast down from heaven before man was created." <note>original: "Priuatus est apostata Angelus cōtēplatione creatoris, nam mox vt factus est, in superbiā erupit, & de cælo priusquā homo conderetur, præcipitatus est."</note> That is, the rebellious angel was robbed of the sight of his Creator (which the good angels enjoy). For soon after he was created, he fell into pride, and before man was made, he was plunged down from heaven.

But after such a great hole had been made in the Kingdom of God, God created the human race; for thus the Holy Trinity concluded by a wonderful counsel in Genesis chapter 1: Let us make man an image that is like us. Thus God created us humans so that we were wise, understanding, righteous, truthful, and endowed with all virtues, also incorruptible and immortal; for as heard above, we must not understand the image of God as the <term>Anthropomorphites</term> <note>A sect that believed God had a physical human body.</note> do.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
How then did we lose such magnificent goods?

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
When the devil saw that he was rejected by God and deprived of eternal salvation, and that we humans were to take his place, he begrudged us this. He sought day and night how he might lead us away from God so that we would come into the same damnation. He transformed himself into a snake, which at that time was undoubtedly the most beautiful animal. He spoke to Eve the woman, as a weak vessel who was easier to deceive than the man, who might have offered him resistance, and said in Genesis 3: "Indeed, should God have said: you shall not eat of all kinds of trees in the garden?" Then the woman said to the snake: "We eat of the fruits of the trees in the garden, but of the fruits of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said: do not eat of it, nor touch it, lest you die." Then the snake said to the woman: "You shall by no means die the death, but God knows that on whichever day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, and know what is good and evil." Then the villain thinks—as Paul calls him in Ephesians 6—

thought to himself: "I also wanted to be like God and despised Him, therefore I was cast out; you shall also become such gods, just eat; it shall benefit you as grass benefits a dog." And there the venomous serpent laughed at his own misery, saying further: "God knows that on the day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be as God." That is to say: "You are now wise and understanding, but when you eat, you will become even cleverer, yes, as wise as God Himself is, and God does not grant you this, which is why He forbade it to you." Thus he makes an envious God out of Him and craftily deceives the human race, so that we have lost our holiness, righteousness, and eternal life, and are subjected to temporal misfortune and eternal damnation. Had Adam not sinned, all these things that are now contrary to us could have done us no harm; if we had been thrown into the fire, we would not have been burned; we would not have sunk to the bottom in water; we would not have needed to obtain clothing, food, and drink with so much toil and labor. We would have lived there in the beautiful pleasure garden <note>The Garden of Eden</note> without any want, as Augustine says in Book 14 of *The City of God* <note>original: "lib. 14. de ciuitate Dei"</note>. We would have had food so that we did not hunger, drink so that we did not thirst, nor would we have needed to fear any sickness. All fish in the water, all birds in the air were under our power, as God says in Genesis 1: "Rule over the fish in the sea, over the birds under the heavens, and over every beast that creeps upon the earth." If we had beckoned and called to a little bird, it would have sat still and allowed itself to be caught. But paradise, the beautiful pleasure garden, has become a vale of tears; for the sake of sin, all pregnant women must have pain, all craftsmen and laborers great toil; the animals are wild and disobedient, just as we also became disobedient. Thus hunters must set traps and lie in wait for game, and fowlers for birds; thus fishermen must devise many advantages to catch fish; and we must fear wolves, bears, otters, and other animals and defend ourselves against them—this is purely the punishment for sin. One reads of Daniel, that the cruel lions did not tear him apart (Daniel 14); likewise, they would not have been able to harm us. Of Elijah, that the greedy ravens nourished him; likewise, everything would have been willing and inclined to serve us. So we must now endure this temporal punishment and should diligently thank God that He has redeemed us from eternal damnation through the seed of the woman, that is, through Christ, who was born of a woman without male seed.

<margin>THEOPHILUS</margin>
Since God foresaw the fall of Adam, why did He not avert and prevent it?

<margin>EUSEBIUS</margin>
There are some godless people who say flippantly: "Adam and Eve necessarily sinned, it had to be so, and God ordained it thus." But the Devil blows such thoughts into us so that we might begin to blaspheme God along with him—He who has no pleasure or delight in sin. And it does not follow that it had to happen because God knew it beforehand; rather, because it would happen, God saw it beforehand. This rule is well worth noting: *Things do not happen because they are foreseen, but they are foreseen by God because they are going to happen* <note>original: "Res nõ ideo eueniunt quia præuidentur, sed ideo præuidentur à Deo, quia sunt euenturæ."</note>. God had created our first parents with free will, so that they could fall or stand, and they could well have chosen not to obey the Devil, especially since they were so faithfully warned.

<margin>THEOPHILUS</margin>
Why has God cast away the entire human race, when only two people sinned? Must we now also pay for what we did not enjoy?

<margin>EUSEBIUS</margin>
God had created our first parents understanding, righteous, and immortal, so that they should keep such goods not only for themselves, but also for all their descendants. These same goods have now been lost, so that not only they, but all their descendants must be deprived of them.

<margin>THEOPHILUS</margin>
It is a miserable thing that we should be punished eternally for a sin that is committed here in time; could God not be satisfied with a temporal punishment?

<margin>EUSEBIUS</margin>
That God punishes sin, which is performed in time, eternally, happens because He is also eternal. We see that one punishes much more severely a person who strikes a prince or a king than if he strikes a peasant or otherwise common man

<margin>THEOPH.</margin> The devils are cast out into Hell with chains of darkness, says Peter <note>2 Peter 2:4</note>, and the godless go into Hell; where now is Hell?

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin> That I cannot tell you for certain. Some have said it is in the outermost places of the Kingdom of Norway. Some, however, say it is in Britain, where St. Patrick’s Purgatory <note>A famous pilgrimage site on Station Island in Lough Derg, Ireland, believed to be an entrance to the afterlife.</note> is. But it is an uncertain thing; what is certain, however, is that it is beneath the earth. But to say it is in this or that specific place and to point at it with fingers, that is the work of fables, just as some have even presumed to calculate the miles. For Richard <note>Likely Richard of St. Victor or Richard of Middleton, medieval theologians.</note> says: *Hell is in the center of the earth, and according to the measurement of certain astronomers, it is distant from the surface of the earth by three thousand, two hundred and fifty miles, in the middle of the diameter.* **That is: According to the calculation of some astronomers, Hell is said to be in the middle of the earth, three thousand, two hundred and fifty miles from us, etc. Let such things go, and simply let Hell remain beneath the earth.**

<margin>THEOPH.</margin> How can one know, however, that it is beneath the earth?

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin> Firstly, one knows it from God’s word: Numbers 16 says: the earth swallowed Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, and they went down alive into Hell. Paul says in Ephesians 4: Christ descended into the lower parts of the earth. And to the Philippians 2, he says: that at the name of Jesus every knee must bow, of those in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth; that is: not only the angels in heaven and men on earth, but also the devils in

<column-break/>

Hell must humble themselves, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

Secondly, the Fathers and old teachers of the Church have also held that Hell is beneath the earth. For Basil says: *Hell is a common place in the innermost part of the earth, shadowed on all sides and dark, which has a certain opening tending into the deep, through which the descent lies open for damned souls.* <note>original Latin: "Infernus est locus cõmunis in intimo terræ..."</note> That is, it is a common place, inside the earth, dark and shadowed everywhere, and has an entrance through which the damned souls travel across. Likewise, Jerome says on the 4th chapter of Ephesians: The lower parts of the earth are the Hells. Thirdly, experience teaches this: where else would the warm baths and boiling-hot waters that spring out of the earth come from? Likewise, the eternal, unquenchable fires in the mountains? We see that God already has fire and water in reserve for the eternal punishment of the damned. Etna, a mountain in Sicily, which Strabo also mentions, has now burned for a long time and cast out fiery stones; and in the year 1536, in May, the fire broke out so violently that it drove the black ashes so far that a good part of the land of Calabria in Italy was covered by them; sulfurous streams also flowed out, like molten glass, which did great damage and burned everything that was in the way.

<margin>Theophilus</margin> I recently heard someone say: if the priests did not preach about hell, and the shepherds said nothing of wolves, then no one would give them anything. Such Epicurean Sadducees <note>A derogatory term for materialists who deny the immortality of the soul or divine providence.</note>, who so completely mock and cast to the wind what the Holy Scripture says about hell, should indeed be moved by such visions to believe in a hell. Now, what do you hold regarding the fact that the Papists have divided hell into four parts?

<margin>Eusebius</margin> I consider it a loose fiction which one should not believe, since not a single word of it stands in Holy Scripture. First, they said that at the very bottom is the true hell. Above that, the place for unbaptized infants. After that, *purgatorium* <note>original: "purgatoriū"</note>, the Purgatory; and at the top *Limbus patrum* <note>original: "Limbus patrum"</note>, the Limbo of the Fathers. Regarding the true hell, in which the damned angels and humans are, you have just heard that we believe it is such a place, more terrible than we can ever imagine or describe. Of the hell for unbaptized infants, we hold nothing at all, as you previously heard regarding the good angels.

<margin>Theophilus</margin> Nevertheless, children are also damned if they are godless. But I thought it would indeed be fair that their damnation be a little mitigated, since they have not acted as coarsely with their sins as the adults?

<margin>Eusebius</margin> We should not anxiously search into God’s judgment, but rather commend everything to Him and pray for mercy. Nevertheless, it is to be noted that there have been certain heretics even in our times who taught that all sins are equal, and the punishment equal as well. But Christ himself makes a distinction between sins. In Matthew chapter 5, he says: he sins more heavily who says to his brother *Racha* <note>A biblical term of contempt, likely derived from Aramaic.</note>—that is, who shows an angry gesture—than he who is simply angry in his heart. Likewise, he sins even more heavily who says: "You fool"—that is, who shames or reviles his neighbor. And He sets a specific punishment for every transgression, such as the Judgment, the Council, and hellfire. There, one is indeed sharper than the other: he who is brought before the 

<column-break/>

judgment, his case still stands reasonably; he can still be set free if he has a just cause. But if one comes before the Council, he does not escape without consequence; he has earned a punishment without any mediation—they go straight to counsel and agree on how harshly he shall be punished. But if one comes into hellfire, then God have mercy, for there is no more hope of redemption. There we hear clearly that God wants to punish one sin more heavily than the others. Thus Christ also says in Luke 10: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!" etc. Yet it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. Likewise, in John 19 <note>The text says "Joan. 16," but the quote refers to John 19:11.</note>, he says to Pilate: "He who delivered me to you has the greater sin." And that we know such distinctions of sins and punishments is useful to us. For many a man, when he hears that he is a sinner just for being angry with his brother, thinks: "Then I will just kill him outright; since I must go to hell anyway, I might as well earn it in full." Likewise: "If he is an adulterer who looks at his neighbor's wife to lust after her, then I will just commit adultery with her fully, it all amounts to the same thing," etc. But we should know that God wants to be more merciful to those who sin out of weakness than to the others who act too coarsely and lie in public, scandalous sins.

<margin>Theophilus</margin> What do you hold regarding the third hell, Purgatory?

<margin>Eusebius</margin> Exactly as much as the Pope, all monks, and priests—which is to say, nothing. For the fact that they preach so much about it happens solely because it has filled their cellars and chests, purses and pockets; otherwise, they would not have seen to it that they sang so many Vigils and Soul-Masses <note>Requiem masses for the dead.</note>. The fourth hell is said to be *Limbus patrum*, in which the Patriarchs are said to have been until the coming of Christ; and some of the Fathers also held this to be true, which is why it was also taught: Christ descended into hell after his death and led the old fathers out. Jerome says regarding the 4th chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians: "The lower parts of the earth are the hells, into which our Lord and Savior descended, so that he might lead the souls of the Saints who were held locked therein with him into heaven like a conqueror." Likewise, Augustine in Book 20 of *The City of God* <note>original: "de ciuit. Dei"</note>, chapter 15: "The fathers before the incarnation of Christ were in hell, yet far from the pain of the unbelievers, until the blood and descent of Christ..."

# Concerning Evil Spirits.
->I iiij<-

<margin>THEOPH.</margin>
...led Christ out into those same places. Some are unwilling to admit this, although I thought the testimony of Augustine, Jerome, <note>St. Augustine and St. Jerome, influential 4th-5th century Church Fathers.</note> and other Fathers should carry weight?

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin>
There are various opinions of the learned on this matter, which I will not recount. We should allow God's word to carry more weight than the Fathers, and not make Articles of Faith out of every word—something they themselves did not desire. Therefore, St. Augustine writes to St. Jerome thus: "Dear brother, I do not believe that you would want your books to be held as equal to the books of the Apostles and Prophets; for I read all other books outside of Holy Scripture in such a way that I do not believe everything they say simply because of who said it, however learned and holy they may be, unless they prove it to me with Scripture or with clear reason." I also want readers to approach my books just as I approach the books of others. 

However, some believe—and I hold this to be true as well—that we who live after Christ's incarnation come to the same place: when body and soul separate (namely, if we belong to Christ, into Abraham’s bosom into eternal life; or, if we are godless, into the abyss of hell, from which there is no redemption), our fathers <note>The Old Testament patriarchs.</note> have also come there. For there is no difference between the salvation of the fathers and our own; they were made blessed through faith just as we are, except that time makes a distinction. They believed in the Messiah or Christ who was to become man, suffer, die, and rise again; in Him they placed all their trust, hope, and confidence. We believe in that very same Christ who has already accomplished everything pertaining to the redemption of the human race: namely, He suffered, died, was buried, descended into Hell, rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and will soon come again for Judgment.

<margin>THEOPH.</margin>
Can you also prove this opinion?

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin>
So says Peter in Acts 15: "Why do you now tempt God by putting a yoke on the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, in the same manner as they." These, however, were their Gospels: when God said to the serpent, "The seed of the woman shall crush your head"; likewise to Abraham, "In your seed shall all the nations on earth be blessed." That is, through Christ, who is born of your seed

<column-break/>

and descendants, all nations, Jews and Gentiles (who are cursed because of sin), shall be blessed. But this blessing is this: that they shall obtain grace, forgiveness of sins, righteousness, the Holy Spirit, and salvation. Likewise, there are many other clear sermons about Christ which they well understood and to which they held with firm faith.

<margin>THEOPH.</margin>
Yet some say that no soul has ever entered heaven, and none shall enter until the Last Day, but rather our souls are elsewhere in a place of rest until they are judged on the Last Day either to eternal life or damnation.

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin>
That is against Holy Scripture. I know well that some hold this out of simplicity; but those who wish to stubbornly defend it do wrong. Therefore, hear some testimony that our souls, as soon as they depart from the body, are led either into eternal life by the angels or into eternal fire by the devils. The history of the rich man and poor Lazarus in Luke 16 proves this powerfully; for Christ says: the poor man was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom, but the rich man sat in hell in the flames.

<margin>THEOPH.</margin>
Yet some hold it to be a parable or a likeness that is said there, and not a history or actual event.

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin>
I believe entirely that it happened just so. Luke (as he is a diligent Gospel writer) would not otherwise have withheld it from us; and the other Evangelists are also always accustomed, when Christ gives a parable, to put these words before it: "He told them such a parable," which does not happen here. So also says Ambrose in the interpretation of the same Gospel: <note>original: "Narratio magis quam parabola videtur quando etiam nomen exprimitur."</note> "It appears more a narrative than a parable when even a name is expressed." And Chrysostom: <note>original: "Parabola vero illa est, ubi exemplum ponitur & tacetur nomina."</note> "That is truly a parable where an example is set and names are kept silent." That is: because Christ calls the poor man by name, it is not a parable, but a history. Thus thinks Luther in the *House Postils*.

<margin>THEOPH.</margin>
Nevertheless, Christ does not say that the poor man was led into heaven, but into Abraham’s bosom.

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin>
Abraham’s bosom is actually the eternal life in which Abraham is, and into which all those come who believe in the Son of God with Abraham, as Augustine says in *On the Origin of the Soul*. Lest you think Abraham’s bosom is a physical thing...

<margin>Theoph.</margin> Yet does not the 102nd Psalm <note>Psalm 103:9 in modern numbering</note> say: God is not angry and does not threaten forever?

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> The devils may not comfort themselves with this saying; for David thanks God that He acts toward us humans—who are weak and fragile—as a gracious, merciful Father; that He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.

<margin>Theoph.</margin> From where do you prove that the devils must remain in eternal damnation?

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> In Genesis chapter 3, God spoke to the serpent: because you have done this, be cursed above all cattle and all beasts of the field; upon your belly shall you go and eat earth all your life. Likewise in Matthew 25, Christ says He will address the godless on that day: depart from me, you cursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. If it is an eternal fire, prepared for the devils, then they certainly may wait for no redemption. So also says Peter in 2 Peter 2: the angels who sinned were cast down to hell by God and delivered into chains of darkness, to be kept for judgment. Likewise Revelation 20: And the devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet were, and they shall be tormented day and night, from eternity to eternity. It is said that once a devil in a possessed person was asked how things stood regarding salvation? He answered: if a glowing iron full of sharp razors were pointed up into Heaven, and he had flesh like a human, he would want to climb up it if he were permitted.

<margin>Theoph.</margin> Why can the devils not be saved?

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> Because they are not redeemed as we are. God’s Son became man and not an angel; therefore Isaiah chapter 9 says: A child is born to us, a son is given to us. And in the Nicene Creed <note>The profession of Christian faith</note> it stands: who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven. And in the Papacy <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note> a story was told to the people: that the devil once came into a church, and when they sang the words in the Nicene Creed: *and was made man* <note>original: "et homo factus est"</note>, all the people fell upon their knees, as is

<column-break/>

still customary (for the Cantor always used to knock on the book with his little staff to give a signal). But when the devil saw one man who neither touched his hat nor bowed his knee, he struck him on the scalp and complained: you ungrateful human, if God’s son had taken on angelic nature and redeemed us poor devils, we would jump for joy and thank him in eternity; and you stand there like a block and a stone, etc. Whether it be a history or a poem, we learn two things from it: Firstly: that humans who are ungrateful to Christ for his incarnation are worse than the devil himself, who here offers that if such grace had happened to him as has happened to us, he would behave differently. Secondly: that the devils are not redeemed, of which no one should doubt.

<margin>Theoph.</margin> How does it happen then, that God deals more graciously with us than with the devils?

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> We should not search into such secret counsel of God, but rather thank Him that He has saved us. We know, however, that the sins of man were somewhat lighter than those of the devil, who sins willfully and intentionally; no one gave him cause for it. Moreover, he seduced our first parents, who recognized their sin and humbled themselves before God: they fled before Him, therefore Adam said: Lord, I heard your voice and was afraid. Such fear and terror did not, however, earn him forgiveness of sins—it could not help them—unless they had been comforted again through God’s grace by the Gospel of the woman’s seed <note>A reference to the "Protoevangelium" in Genesis 3:15, interpreted as Christ</note>, the crusher of the serpent, the swallower of sin, the slayer of death, the overcomer of the devil and stormer of Hell, etc. Otherwise, they would have had to despair immediately and be damned, like Cain, Judas, and others. But the devil is a proud spirit, hardened, who without ceasing rebels against God and cannot humble himself, as Caesarius <note>Caesarius of Heisterbach, a medieval chronicler</note> sets down such an example in his dialogues: Once when a priest in the church examined those who wished to receive the Holy Sacrament, and shared the absolution <term>absolution: the formal release from guilt or punishment for sin</term> with each one individually by the command of Christ, a youth stood there, strong of limb, and waited until all the others were finished. Then he also stepped forward at the very last, confessed his sins, and recounted such a heap of gruesome deeds, such as blasphemy, countless murders, adultery, theft, and the like, that the priest...
