The priest became annoyed at listening to him any longer and said: "Even if you were a thousand years old, you could not have committed all these deeds." To which he answered: "Indeed, I am much older than a thousand years." The priest was terrified and said: "Who are you then?" He replied: "I am one of those who fell with Lucifer, and I have confessed only the smallest part of my sins to you; if you were willing to listen, I would tell you much more." But because the priest knew that the Devil could not obtain forgiveness for sins, he asked him why he confessed when there was no hope of forgiveness. The Devil answered: "I stood over there and saw many great sinners come to you, to whom you proclaimed forgiveness, and I hoped that the same might happen to me." Then the priest said fearlessly: "Well then, if you will follow my counsel, you shall obtain forgiveness for your sins like the others you have seen depart from here." The Devil answered: "Yes, why not?" "Then go hence," said the priest, "and fall upon the earth three times a day, and say with a humble, repentant heart: 'Lord God, you who created me, I have sinned against you; forgive me.'" And when the Devil said he could not do such a thing, the priest replied: "Why do you complain about something that is so easy to do?" The Devil spoke: "I cannot humble myself before God in such a way; I will gladly do anything else I am required to do." Then the priest became angry and said: "O Devil, since you are so proud in your heart that you will not, nor can you, humble yourself before your Creator, then begone from me, for you shall obtain mercy neither in this world nor the next." And so he vanished. <note>original: "Hæc ille" — Latin for "Thus he [spoke/wrote]."</note>

<margin>Theoph.</margin>That would be a wondrous thing, if it were truly so.

<margin>Evsebivs.</margin>It may well be, for similar things have happened in our own times. In the year 1534, at Stassfurt in Saxony, the Devil came in human form to Mr. Laurentius Döner, the pastor there, on Holy Eve, as if he wished to confess. He blasphemed and assailed the humanity of Christ in various ways, whom the pastor overcame with the testimony of Scripture until he departed.

<margin>Theoph.</margin>The Devil is also experienced in the Scriptures; therefore, one must be no fool if one wishes to dispute with him.

<margin>Evsebivs.</margin>Certainly; and for that reason he is called *Demon*, that is <note>original: "gnarus, sciens"</note> *the one who is expert or knowing*, who knows much. But one must note that he has the habit of falsely alleging the Scriptures; therefore he is a *Calumniator*, a slanderer. As in Matthew 4, he comes citing half a verse and leaves the other half out, where he says to Christ from the 90th Psalm: "He has given his angels charge over you, that they shall bear you up in their hands," whereas he should have added: "in all your ways." But that did not serve his purpose; he has studied the <term>fallacy of composition and division<note>A logical fallacy where one incorrectly combines or separates parts of an argument to change its meaning.</note></term> better than any <term>Dialectician<note>A scholar of logic and formal argument.</note></term>. He is well-experienced in all arts and gives a man sufficient answer and speech. Recently, someone in Italy asked a <term>pythoness<note>A woman possessed by a spirit, a female seer or oracle.</note></term> which was the best verse in Virgil, and she answered him: <note>original: "Discite iustitiam moniti & non temnere Diuos"</note> "Be warned, learn justice, and do not slight the gods." Since the Devil is learned, and we have now learned from him that he is accustomed to falsifying the Scriptures, we should take care that he does not lead us astray through his false teachers whom he sends out into the world.

<margin>Theoph.</margin>Does the Devil also know future things?

<margin>Evsebivs.</margin>He knows what is happening and what happened many years ago; but what is yet to come, neither men, nor angels, nor devils know, but God alone. Likewise, the Devil does not know what we think, as you heard before regarding the good angels. Therefore Augustine says in his book *On the Definition of Hidden Dignities*: <note>original: "Internas cogitationes animæ Diabolū non videre scimus, sed motu eas corporis ab illo & affectionum indiciis colligi, didicimus experimēto."</note> "We know that the Devil does not see the internal thoughts of the soul, but we have learned from experience that he gathers them from the movement of the body and from signs of the emotions." That is: we know that the Devil does not understand the inner thoughts of man, but that he can deduce them from certain outward signs, as we have learned from experience.

<margin>Theoph.</margin>If the Devil does not know future things, how is it that he prophesied among the heathens? For the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi was without doubt conducted through the Devil.

<margin>Evsebivs.</margin>In Delphi (which city lies in the province of Phocis, on Mount Parnassus) there was a magnificent temple built in honor of the idol Apollo...

<meta>This page continues a dialogue regarding the nature of evil spirits, specifically focusing on the limitations of their foresight compared to divine prophecy.</meta>

# Concerning Evil Spirits

...west, and next to it was a dark hole from which vapors emerged. When the virgins and priests appointed for this task were touched by that air, they lost their senses, and in a state of madness, they gave answers whenever they were asked about a matter. For the Devil can prophesy, but not everything one asks him; rather, he only knows what he intends to bring about. For example: when he intends to incite princes and lords against one another, he can announce a war before it begins. Likewise, when by God’s permission he intends to poison the air, he can prophesy of a death or pestilence. And it is nevertheless to be noted that the *vaticinia* <note>original: "vaticinia" — Latin for prophecies or predictions</note> or prophecies of the Devil are so dark and unintelligible that they leave one in doubt and only cause confusion. 

As when Croesus, the powerful King in Asia, wished to wage war against Cyrus, King of the Persians, he first asked the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi whether he should triumph or be defeated; and he was given this answer: *Croesus, crossing the Halys, shall destroy a great power.* <note>original Latin: "Cresus Halim superans, magnā euertet opum vim." This is a famous ambiguous oracle; the "great power" destroyed turned out to be Croesus's own kingdom.</note> At that time, one could not actually know whether Cyrus or Croesus would overcome, until experience taught that the end came for Croesus and his kingdom, goods, and glory. In the same way, when Xerxes set out against the Greeks, the Athenians asked the Oracle of Apollo for counsel, which answered them: *The people of Athens shall overcome within wooden walls.* This might perhaps have been understood to mean they should build a wooden fence, but Themistocles understood it to mean they must take to the ships and resist the enemy by water. There we see how the Devil only mocks and leads men astray, which is why one should not consult him; for no angel knows of future things unless it is revealed to him by God, as Christ says in Matthew 24: *Of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, but the Father alone.*

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
Should the devils not know how to speak of future things, since men are able to do so, as can be seen with the Prophets?

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
Before the incarnation of Christ, there were several holy men who, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, preached of future things, such as the Patriarchs and Prophets. Therefore Peter says <margin>2 Peter 1</margin>: *No prophecy was ever brought forth by human will, but holy men spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit.* So also says Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, in Luke 1: *God spoke in former times through the mouth of his holy prophets.* And such prophecies are not dark, but bright and certain. For the Patriarch Jacob prophesied in Genesis 49: *The scepter shall not depart from the Jews until Christ comes,* and it came to pass, for the Jews had their own kingdom and were not subject to foreign peoples until the coming of Christ.

Likewise, Isaiah prophesied a good seven hundred years beforehand concerning the kingdom of Christ or the Messiah, as if he saw it before his eyes, and preached of future things as if they had already passed; just as Daniel also speaks of the four monarchies.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
Can the Devil also perform miracles?

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
He is a master of a thousand arts <note>original: "Tausentkünstiger" — a common historical epithet for the Devil, implying he has endless tricks and deceptive skills.</note>; therefore he can indeed do many wondrous things, as one sees that some accomplish many strange things with the black arts. But he cannot perform such miracles as Christ did. He cannot raise the dead, nor hinder the sun's course, etc. Therefore Nicodemus says in John 3 to Christ: *No one can do the signs that you do, unless God is with him.* He can, however, by God’s permission, make the sea and wind stormy, stir up a tempest, make a seeing man blind, and the like; and this is well experienced in our times, where some evil people inflict harm on their neighbors, so that here one goes blind, there one becomes crippled, and such nets are the Devil’s tools.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
Some fear such evil people greatly; but I do not believe that they can always do harm.

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
They are indeed to be feared and avoided; but a Christian should know that the Devil cannot and may not do harm whenever it pleases him, but only when God allows it. Therefore we should live in the fear of God, and He will protect us through His angels; but the wicked are punished in various ways, for God uses the Devil and such "Devil-conjurors" <note>original: "Teuffelsbaner" — those who consort with or command spirits.</note> as a punishment or a rod.

<margin>Theophilus</margin>
How can you prove that the evil spirits cannot exercise their power when and on whom they wish, but only when God grants and allows it?

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> We have a magnificent example of this in the Book of Job, Chapter 1. There, the Devil dares to undertake no more against God than what God permits him. And Christ says: "Upon this confession I will build my Church, and the gates of Hell shall not overcome it." That is to say: the Devil shall certainly try something, and set himself against it with all his might, but he shall have no power against it nor accomplish anything. Matthew 10. Likewise in Luke 22, the Lord speaks to Simon: "Behold, Satan has desired you, that he might sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you," etc. Likewise in Mark 5, the devils beseech Jesus that he let them enter into the swine; which is especially comforting, for if the devils have no power even over irrational livestock, how much less power do they have over us humans, and especially over Christians? They are merely God's <term>instruments|Werkzeug</term> through which God works what He wills, and not what they will. Just as a sword cannot cut or stab whenever it wants, so no creature can harm the Devil <note>The text likely implies "so the Devil can harm no creature"</note> without God's will and knowledge.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin> You said before that the Devil cannot raise the dead. Yet do we not read in 1 Kings 28 that a fortune-teller, by order of King Saul, brought forth the deceased Samuel?

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> It was not Samuel, but the Devil who transformed himself so; Augustine also holds this view in his *Letter to Felicianus*. For Paul says in 2 Corinthians 11: "The Devil can transform himself into an angel of light," how much more so into the form of a prophet. And although it says in the text that Samuel was seen, we should nonetheless not believe it; for the Scripture has a way of speaking, just as we are also accustomed to saying: "I have seen Augustus" or "I have seen Cicero," even if it was not Augustus or Cicero, but rather their image and figure. And thus Pharaoh says in Genesis 41 that he saw seven ears of corn and seven oxen,

even though it was only such a form <note>i.e., a dream-vision</note>. And thus Saul saw an image that seemed to him no different than if he were seeing Samuel, so similar was it to him. However, the Devil prophesies there so that we should not allow ourselves to be tempted; for he can certainly do such things if something is revealed to him by God through the angels.

<margin>Theophilus.</margin> So that I may know the Devil all the better and may guard myself against him, show further what his nature and characteristics are.

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> It is not possible for me to rightly paint the Devil with his actual colors, for his tricks are not all to be recounted. For the devils do the exact opposite; they overturn everything. Whatever good the angels do, they corrupt, so that the dear angels have enough to watch over and defend on all sides.

The angels preach God's word themselves and help promote it, so that it may also be preached purely by us. The devils, however, prevent it, so that it is either not preached at all, or is indeed despised by the listeners. They are the birds which eat up the seed of the Divine word on the path, so that it does not sprout in our hearts nor bring fruit (Luke 8). They stir up false teachings and heresy, as the story of the weeds <note>often translated as "tares"</note> indicates in Matthew 13. Who can recount all the various heresies that existed before and after the times of Christ and the Apostles? And all these the Devil devised and arranged. While the highest Teacher, the Son of God himself, preached, there were in the Jewish land the greatest heretics, such as the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes, who erred horribly—not just in one article of faith, but in many pieces—yet they nonetheless esteemed themselves as great saints. For the Devil can pose as a holy angel so that he is not easily recognized. And when he wishes to arrange a <term>delusion|Schwermerey</term>, he does it not through simple people, but through learned, high-ranking people, who would not be expected to err or teach wrongly. <term>THEOPHILUS</term> <note>Theophilus: A name meaning "Lover of God," often used in dialogues to represent the seeking student.</note> Since you mention the three sects, you give me cause to inquire further: what did each one teach and hold to be true? <margin>EUSEBIUS</margin> <note>Eusebius: A name meaning "Pious," representing the learned teacher.</note> First, there were the <term>Pharisees</term> <note>original: *Phariseer*; from Hebrew *parush*, meaning "separated."</note>, that is, "Interpreters," so named because they explained the Scriptures much like we have Doctors of Holy Scripture today. In this regard, they were as "pious" as our Papists, who boast of the Old and New Testaments, yet would—if they dared—throw them away entirely and burn them, just as they deal with other Lutheran books. For a long time, the Holy Bible was tucked "under the bench" <note>An idiom meaning hidden away or neglected.</note> while, in the meantime, palpable lies from stinking legends were preached to the poor people. Now, although the Pharisees kept the Law and the Prophets, they did not understand them correctly; nevertheless, they wanted to teach other people and be Masters of Scripture. Regarding the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> or the Law of God, they taught: it required only outward obedience from us, and therefore one could easily keep it. They believed that whoever did not kill with his hand, did not commit adultery with his body, and conducted himself so that he remained blameless before the world, God must also be satisfied with him—as can be seen with the Pharisee in <term>Luke 18</term>. Yet the Law of God requires inward, perfect obedience of the heart, will, and all affects or desires in man, which no human can perform because of our corrupted nature. 2. Regarding <term>Justification</term> <note>The theological process of being made righteous before God.</note>, they taught that one becomes pious, righteous, and blessed before God through sacrifices and other ceremonies commanded by <term>Moses</term>, just as the Pope also teaches that our works make us blessed. And such—

<column-break/>

—error arises because the Devil blinds people so that they do not recognize what sin is. They think it is such a small thing that we could pay for it ourselves, yet it is such a heavy burden that God's Son alone—and no other man or angel—can bear the wrath of God against sin. This burden pressed Him so hard that He sweated bloody sweat in His anguish, and an angel came from heaven to comfort Him. <term>Luke 22</term>.

In this case, however, the Pharisees were far more "pious" than our Papists, for they performed such works as were actually commanded by God. The Papists, however, want to make satisfaction for their sins with works that God not only did not command, but strictly forbade in His Word—such as pilgrimages, the invocation of saints, founding monasteries, building altars, reading Masses, and the like. God has a horror and loathing for such works; He will not only not reward them, but intends to punish them severely. And even if they occasionally do works that God has commanded—such as praying, fasting, or giving alms—these still do not please God because they are done out of unbelief. As <term>Paul</term> says in <term>Romans 14</term>: "Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin." Indeed, even if a believing Christian does such works, he still does not merit the forgiveness of sins thereby, for the works are too weak and impure; sin is always running alongside them. Indeed, we may well commit a hundred sins before we do one good work. <term>Luke 10</term>. Where does this leave the monks with their <term>works of supererogation</term> <note>original: *operibus supererogationis*; the Catholic doctrine of "extra" good works performed beyond what God requires, which can supposedly be shared with others.</note>, who claim to have such an abundant surplus of good works that they do not need them all for themselves, but can share them with other people to their benefit? Nevertheless, good works do not go unrewarded, for <term>Paul</term> says in <term>1 Timothy 4</term>: "Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come." But let no one boast of it; rather, when we have done everything, we are "unprofitable servants." <term>Luke 17</term>. # Of the Evil Spirits.
## X ij

No one can withstand the wisdom of God. The second reason that God "looks through his fingers" <note>idiom: to turn a blind eye or permit something</note> and does not restrain the Devil is our own ingratitude. For when we have God’s word at our door but despise it, do not improve ourselves, and become weary of His seed, God is moved to take it away from us again and give it to another people. Therefore, Paul says in 2 Thessalonians 2: *God will send them strong delusions, that they should believe a lie, so that all those who would not believe the truth might be judged.* <note>original Latin/German context: 2. Thessal. 2</note> And in such a manner, Muhammad <note>original: "Machomet"</note> preaches today in all of Asia and Africa, where previously St. Paul, the chosen vessel <term>vessel: a biblical metaphor for a person used by God</term>, preached. It is also to be feared that it will go the same way with our lands, for God can suffer nothing less than the contempt of His soul-saving word. Therefore He threatens in Amos, chapter 8: *I will send a hunger into the land, not a hunger for bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing my Word.* And dear Paul well foresaw what the Devil would stir up, which is indeed a lamentable thing that the wretched people in the Papacy <note>original: "Bapstthumb," referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> do not wish to recognize. For he says in 1 Timothy 4: *The Spirit speaks clearly that in the last times some shall depart from the faith and cling to seductive spirits and doctrines of devils, and forbid to marry and command to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful.* Has not the Pope forbidden marriage to his godless ones and filled the whole world with unchastity? Has he not condemned as heretics those who eat meat on Friday and during Lent? I believe indeed it is clear as day; yet St. Paul calls it the devil’s doctrine. And in 2 Timothy 3: *This you should know, that in the last times there will be terrible times, for there will be men who have an appearance of a godly being, but they deny its power.* Therefore we should take good care that the Devil does not seduce us with such an appearance of godliness, for he attacks quite craftily, just as he deceived and cheated Eve in the form of a beautiful serpent. We should also diligently

<column-break/>

hear God’s word throughout our entire life so that we may learn to comfort ourselves with it when the Devil terrifies us with our sins. For he is especially busy when we lie on our deathbed and are about to die; there he is accustomed to paint before us God’s wrath, hell, and damnation. Whoever is not armed there with God’s word must despair and be damned. The Devil is a spiritual enemy. We do not have to fight with flesh and blood; we will not drive him away with swords and spears, nor with holy salt, water, palms, little crosses, and other such tomfoolery <note>original: "narrenwerck," a Protestant critique of Catholic sacramentals</note>. Instead, there must be spiritual weapons and spiritual armor, such as God’s word, faith, diligent prayer, and the Holy Spirit, who is the true Paraclete, Advocate, Assistant, and Comforter. <note>original: "Paracletus, Aduocat, Beystand vnd Tröster"</note>

And I recall now a story told by Nicolaus Manlius in a sermon on the priesthood of Christ, which is well worthy of being noted, and these are his words: There was in Freiberg in Meissen a good, pious, poor man lying sick, who struggled sorely with death, and his sins also troubled him. The Devil undertook not only to light fiery coals in his heart but came in bodily form, in the shape of a tall man with a large ink-horn and a pen-case, along with a large donkey-hide, and spoke to the poor sick man: "Well then, tell me your sins one after another so that I may write them down and bring them before the judgment seat of God." The good poor man was terrified, but immediately reached for the sayings of Holy Scripture and said: "Well then, sit down, I will dictate to you; write this: *The seed of the woman shall crush your head* <note>Genesis 3:15</note>; let this be your introduction." When the loathsome Devil heard such sharp thunderclaps of God’s word, he took his pen-case and ink-horn and vanished, leaving a stench behind him. Thus was the good, pious man delivered through this power of God’s word.

<margin>THEOPHILUS.</margin>
How finely the Devil can diminish <term>extenuirn: to make light of or minimize</term> and make sin easy for as long as we consent to it; and afterwards, when it is committed and we have long lain in security, he can stir it up and make it great.

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin> Therefore we should learn that he is a cunning enemy who never rests, and we must offer him resistance. Therefore, we wish to conclude our conversation and call upon God, that He might protect us from the Devil, which He, as a strong and invincible Lord, is well able to do, and as a kind Father, is willing to do. Secondly, that God's kingdom come to us; which the Devil does not like to see, but rather wishes that not the Holy Spirit, but he himself should rule us according to his pleasure.

Furthermore, the Devil would like us not to do God's will, but to become disobedient to God, and impatient in the cross and suffering; therefore we pray: *Thy will be done.*

The Devil also begrudges us our daily bread; that is, he wishes that we did not have our temporal nourishment, peace, and health; and if he had so much power, he would poison the air, destroy the fruits in the field through hail and storms, burn and tear down houses, let all herbs and trees wither, dry up wells and water; in short, kill man and beast. As we see in Matthew 8, the devils requested that if the Lord would not allow them to possess men, He should at least permit them to enter the swine, so that (as Theophylactus <note>Theophylact of Ohrid, a medieval biblical commentator</note> says) the people would still come to harm and be saddened by the loss of their livestock; such a "mischief-lover" <term>Schadenfro: one who takes joy in the misery of others</term> is he.

Furthermore, the devils are vengeful spirits, and they also incite us to vengefulness; and those who will not forgive their neighbors, nor speak with them or have fellowship, are true children of the devil. They also cannot rightly pray the "Our Father," which pleases the devil very well; for they pray that God would not forgive them their debts, since they also do not forgive. And the saying of Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose of Milan</note> is true: <note>original Latin: "Si non dimittis iniuriã quæ tibi facta eſt, non orationem pro te facis, ſed maledictionem ſuper te inducis."</note> *If you do not forgive the injury that was done to you, you do not offer a prayer for yourself, but you bring a curse upon yourself.*

# On Evil Spirits.
->P iij<-

[May] God not lead us into temptation; not that God Himself would tempt us, but rather it is a way of speaking: that God would not permit us poor humans to be tempted by the Devil, but rather, if it indeed comes to the point that the Devil sets upon us, that we may stand firm, not consent to his temptation, but instead offer him resistance and hold the field.

<margin>THEOPH.</margin>
How can the Devil tempt us, since he is not seen by us?

<margin>EUSEBIUS.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 4.</margin>
He tempted Christ Himself, and we do not know whether he approached Him in an external, visible form, as one man does to another, or whether he assailed Him in some other way. To us, he rarely comes in bodily form; instead, he watches every person’s customs and external gestures, and from these he discerns to which vice each person is inclined. For although, because of our corrupted nature, we are inclined not just to one sin but to all sins, nevertheless one person has a particular inclination and leaning toward this vice, and another toward that one. To this, he provides us with the occasion, placing it before our eyes, and then our <term>consensus</term> <note>Latin: "agreement" or "consent"</note> follows, so that we easily give our consent, as Isidore says: *Sæpè occasio peccãdi voluntatẽ facit* <note>Latin: "Often the opportunity for sinning creates the will [to sin]."</note>. He assails us with pride, greed, unbelief, vengefulness, unchastity, gluttony, and the like; and this not just once, but often and in manifold ways. Therefore, we should not feel secure as if the Devil were a hundred miles away; he is closer to us than we can imagine—behind and before, it is all full of devils. As the Lord says in Luke 11: When Satan has once gone out, he goes and takes seven others with him who are worse than himself. Thus we must now fight knightly, not consenting to his temptation, but resisting him: as it is written in James 4: Resist the Devil, and he will flee from you.

<margin>Genesis 3.</margin>
He tempted our first parents to see if he could turn them away from God, so that they might despise His commandment and become proud, secure, disobedient, and unbelieving. And he succeeded; they ate of the forbidden fruit and had to die the eternal death. Had they, however, struck the Devil away from themselves with

<column-break/>

God’s word, they and we would have remained eternally wise, understanding, pure, holy, righteous, and immortal. Likewise, in 1 Chronicles 21 <note>original: "1. Paralip. 22." — The text cites the older Latin name for Chronicles.</note> it stands thus: And Satan stood against Israel and moved David to have the people numbered. Then the Lord was angered and spoke to Gad: Go, speak with David and say: Thus says the Lord: Choose for yourself either three years of famine, or three months of fleeing before your enemies, or three days of the sword of the Lord and pestilence in the land, etc. Had David resisted the Devil, God would not have been angered; but because he was puffed up and wanted people in all lands to sing and speak of his great power, and held a review of his army, God let seventy thousand men die. And although David remained alive, it was such a heartbreak to him that he would rather have been dead, wherefore he also says: Lord, what have these sheep done? I have done this evil. For his best counselors and most excellent people died, upon whom much depended for him and the government. Likewise, in Acts 5, the Devil tempted Ananias and his wife Sapphira so that they fell into greed and did not bring all the money from the sold field to the feet of the Apostles; for Peter says: Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back part of the price of the land? And Ananias fell down and gave up the ghost, and likewise his wife. Likewise, the Devil tempted Judas that he should betray Christ; for it stands thus in John 13: The Devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray Him. And because Judas did not resist the Devil, his reward was that he despaired, hanged himself, and must be eternally damned. Likewise, in Matthew 4, we see that he even dares to direct himself at the Son of God; how much more violently will he now attack us if we are lazy in the struggle? He gives Him so much to do that in forty days He thinks of no food and forgets eating and drinking. First, He should not believe that He is God’s Son. Likewise, He should despise the means that God has ordained and cast Himself down from the Temple...

# Adrianus Rheynmannus on Evil Spirits.

Finally, he <note>the devil</note> intends that man should fall away from God and become an idolater for the sake of goods and money, etc. In such a way the devil assaults us continually; therefore, we must hold God's word (which is much sharper than any two-edged sword, Hebrews 4) before his nose, just as the Lord Christ teaches us such an art by his own example.

We see, however, in that same struggle which the Son of God maintains against him, that the devil—as was also said before—can also quote the Scripture, though falsely, and that he never lets up; as soon as he does not succeed in one way, he attacks in another. Therefore, when such thoughts occur to you: "You are a sinner, therefore you must be damned," then say: "There are two kinds of sinners, the repentant and the unrepentant; Christ came for the sake of sinners," as Paul says in 1 Timothy 1: *This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.* <note>original Latin: "fidelis sermo"</note> Thus the devil is struck to the ground at once. But he stands up again and puts such thoughts into your mind: "Yes, but who knows if he will accept you? You have made it too coarse; you should have been more pious and converted yourself sooner." Then take sayings and promises that are universal, which exclude no one, where the little word *all* <note>original Latin: "omnis"</note> encompasses all mankind. Likewise, if he views you thus: "You are sick, poor, despised; God must be your enemy, otherwise he would not so oppress and strike you," then say: "God disciplines us out of love and not out of enmity, so that we are not damned along with the secure, godless world," 1 Corinthians 11. "Though I am poor, I shall not die of hunger; I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging for bread," Psalm 37. My heavenly Father

<column-break/>

knows well, and much better than I, what I need, Matthew 6. And immediately consider the examples of how God nourished the children of Israel in the desert where there was nothing but wood and stone, neither wine nor bread; and how he wonderfully sustained Elijah, the widow of Zarephath, and many others. But the devil says: "Yes, God will nourish you well enough, but you must wait a long time until a roasted pigeon flies into your mouth; you must start some business dealings and take advantage of your neighbor." He can dress it up nicely and—according to 2 Corinthians 11—transform himself into an angel of light, so that you think: "It cannot be such a great sin; I must after all support myself, my wife, and my child; there must also be trade and contracts if this life is to persist," etc. Then remember back to what God says: "One shall not steal," and Paul in Ephesians 4: "One should work with their hands at something honest." If we did such things and also held ourselves to prayer, we would remain safe from the devil and leave many more gruesome sins and vices aside. For Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10: *God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.*

Finally, we conclude this most holy prayer: *Deliver us from evil*—from the tyranny of the devil, from all misery and misfortune. And this prayer our dear Father in heaven hears, for the sake of his Son Christ Jesus, Amen.

So you have now, dear Theophilus <note>Theophilus is likely the intended reader or a generic name for a "lover of God"</note>, briefly heard what a Christian should know about the evil angels. God give us his grace that we may often speak such holy prayer in faith and obtain eternal heavenly goods, as well as temporal welfare, peace, health, and protection against the devils.

->**Amen.**<-

# The First Part of this Book,
## that spirits and ghosts appear, and that many other wonderful things truly occur.

->That melancholy and insane people imagine many things to themselves in which there is nothing.<-

->The First Chapter.<-

<margin>Some say there are no ghosts.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap 'M' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or cleric, within a decorative frame.</image-desc>
At all times, people have been found who did not believe that there were spirits or ghosts. The Epicureans <note>followers of the Greek philosopher Epicurus who generally denied divine intervention in human affairs</note> among the Heathens laughed at everything said about them and held them for fictions intended to frighten young and inexperienced people. Cassius, who was also an Epicurean, undertook (as Plutarch writes) when Brutus told him how he had seen a monster, to attribute everything to natural causes. So one reads in the histories of the Holy Apostles in the 23rd chapter that the Sadducees <note>a Jewish sect of the time of Jesus</note> did not believe that there was a resurrection of the dead, or that there were spirits or angels. In the present day, one finds many pious, honest people who also hold that which is said of ghosts for vain fables; partly because nothing special has encountered them in their lives: partly, and principally, because in former times the world was so gripped by false, fabricated appearances, wonders, and signs, that they henceforth hold these for fabricated things or a false delusion. But be that as it may, it can be proven and made known through many kinds of reports and the testimony of histories, as well as daily experience, that spirits and ghosts exist and appear, and that many other wonderful things truly occur. It is otherwise true in itself that many people persuade themselves they see or hear ghosts, which comes solely from melancholy <note>a condition then thought to be caused by an imbalance of black bile</note> and madness, from a weakness of the senses, and from fear; or when they see or hear people, animals, vapors of the earth, or other natural things, as I will explain hereafter point by point with many examples. Indeed, the majority of those things which are commonly held for ghosts are nothing at all: nevertheless, one still sees, hears, and perceives ghosts

# Of Ghosts / The First Part.

Ghosts and other such things often and much as well. First, no one can deny that those who are by nature melancholic <note>In the 16th century, "melancholy" was considered a physical ailment caused by an excess of black bile, leading to depression or delusions.</note>, or otherwise through great misfortunes that have befallen them, are heavy-minded and troubled, imagine many strange and wonderful things to themselves. They testify perhaps high and dearly that they see or hear this or that, which however is not there at all. As we sometimes experience with those who have great headaches or other illnesses, who do not sleep at night, or are otherwise heavy-minded, and are in part deprived of their senses and reason. Whoever is around such people must often and much—however badly he pities them—laugh when they come along with such wonderful and absurd visions, fables, and foolishness.

<margin>Of one who went into the theater.</margin>
Aristotle writes in his book of wonderful things <note>original: "de mirabilibus auscultationibus"</note> of one at Abydos, a city of Asia, who was not well in his senses, who for many days went to the theater where comedies are usually played; and although no play was being held, and no one was present in the place, yet he sat down, clapped his hands together for joy, and rejoiced as if the play pleased him so well. Afterward, when he came back to himself, he indicated that during the whole time when he had never been himself, he had had a good life. For as the proverb goes: He who thinks it is well, for him it is well.

<margin>Book 2, Epistles.</margin>
Horace reports the same of another and noble man at Argos, who also went to the theater and behaved in the same manner as the previous one; and when his friends helped him through medicine, he was poorly satisfied with them, saying it had never been better for him than when his head was thus turned.

<margin>Of one who thought all ships were his.</margin>
Athenaeus writes in the 12th book of one named Thrasyllus, who was so confused in the head that he thought nothing else than that all the ships that landed in Piraeus, the harbor of the sea, were his own; he counted the ships, ordered the sailors to depart, and when they came back, he rejoiced; and the whole time, he writes, when he was not himself, it was very well for him. Afterward, when the physician had helped him again, he said that in his whole life it had never been better for him than when he was robbed of his reason.

I have seen one named Johann Leonhardus Sertorius, to whom pious, honorable people who knew him well gave good testimony, who had persuaded himself

<column-break/>

that he, like Elijah the Prophet, wished to demonstrate with a magnificent miracle from heaven that our faith was the right faith. He also petitioned several authorities that the Papists <note>Catholics</note> and Evangelicals <note>Protestants</note> might be brought together, and then he would perform the miracle; if not, they should deal with him as they wished.

The like may be said of others who go astray and are robbed of their senses, sometimes because they overthink <note>original: "hindersinnen," referring to mental exhaustion from deep study</note>, as sometimes happens to scholars; sometimes through long-lasting illness, through grief, and other accidents. These deal in strange fables. You find one who persuades himself he has horns like an ox; another, that he is an earthen vessel, and therefore avoids people so that he will not be smashed. Of such a person Galen writes in the 3rd book *On the Affected Parts*, chapter 6. Some persuade themselves they are dead; some that they are great princes and lords; some that they are highly learned Doctors; some that they are Prophets or Apostles themselves, and even undertake to prophesy of future things. Some have been found who believed they were the most wicked people on earth. They imagine to themselves how they have seen, heard, spoken, and done this and that, in which there is no truth.

Galen writes of the frenetic <note>original: "de phreneticis"</note> in the book *On the Difference of Symptoms*, chapter 3, of a physician named Theophilus, who in his illness was otherwise of good reason, but wished to persuade everyone by force that there were trumpeters in the chamber where he lay sick, who left him no rest day or night, and he ordered that they should be chased out of the house. Paul of Aegina, the physician, writes in book 3, chapter 16, that those whom Lycanthropy <note>term: Lycanthropy (a delusion where one believes they are a wolf)</note>—that species of madness—befalls, run out of the houses at night, howl like wolves, and like to be among the graves of the dead until it is day again. Otherwise, the evil enemy <note>The Devil</note> also deludes people so that they think they are wild animals. Of this, Saint Augustine writes in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 7, chapter 11. Those who are bitten by rabid dogs shun the water <note>term: Hydrophobia (rabies)</note>, of which this Aegina also writes in book 5, chapter 3. Some bark like dogs, some snap and hiss, and undertake to bite people. Rufus shows the cause why they...

<margin>Hydrophobia.</margin>

# Ludwig Lavater

<note>original: "Wasser förchten"</note> Fear of water—namely because they imagine they see the form of the dog by which they were bitten reflected in the water. <note>This describes hydrophobia, a symptom of rabies.</note>

<margin>Ephialtes.</margin>
So too is *Ephialtes* or *Incubus* <note>Latin terms for sleep paralysis</note> a sickness that is commonly called the "Schrätele" <note>The "Night-mare" or a pressing spirit</note>. In this state, many persuade themselves that something is pressing down on them, holding their mouths and breath so that they cannot cry out. Likewise, they feel and hear it climbing up onto the bed and back down again.

<margin>Insane People.</margin>
Those who are then completely robbed of their senses and reason, or who by God’s permission are possessed by the Evil Foe, behave with very strange antics and speak of many apparitions and wonderful things; they mistake one thing for another, as is experienced in hospitals where such people are kept. It is written of Ajax the Greek that it pained him so greatly when the armor of Achilles was awarded to Ulysses by judgment, that he lost his mind, drew his sword, and ran among a herd of swine, knowing no better than that he was striking at the Greeks. He hung up two large fattened hogs and beat them with whips and scolded them terribly. For he believed that one was Agamemnon, who had been the judge, and the other was Ulysses, to whom the armor had been awarded, with whom he was especially displeased. When he came back to himself, he was so ashamed of his clumsy actions that he killed himself. In field battles, soldiers have sometimes become so wild that their weapons had to be broken out of their hands, because they took friends for enemies and attempted to harm them.

->Fearful people persuade themselves they see or hear monsters, and it is nothing.<-

### The Second Chapter.

What has been said of the melancholy and of those robbed of their senses may also be understood of the fearful. For when one is fearful by nature, or when fear and terror seize him because of great danger or otherwise, he imagines many wonderful

<margin>Women and children are afraid.</margin>
things that do not exist. Women, who generally fear more by nature than men (wherefore St. Peter, when speaking of the duty of spouses in his Epistle, calls them the "weaker vessel"), persuade themselves much more than men that they have seen or heard this or that. Likewise young people, since they are also for the most part easily frightened: when one speaks of ghosts and monsters at the table, women and children sometimes hardly dare to go out the door alone, fearing something might meet them; and if they hear some rattling, they think the monster is right behind them. But it is nothing but a false delusion. A lazy, fearful, and

<column-break/>

<margin>A fearful soldier.</margin>
faint-hearted soldier views the enemy's army as stronger than it actually is: a rustling leaf (as the Lord threatens his people Israel in the Law, should they not be faithful and honest toward Him) hunts him: if he only hears a nutcracker or a woodpecker pecking in a tree, he thinks the enemy is behind him: if a mouse moves in a house, his heart fails him. In contrast, none of these things bother a brave, honest soldier. Yet it sometimes happens in retreats, when soldiers are separated from their own, that even brave people become "forest-mad" <note>original: "waldschellig," a state of panicked disorientation</note> and take friends for enemies, not knowing where they are. Fear brings all this about.

<margin>Of a murderer.</margin>
Plutarch, a famous writer, writes in his book *On the Late Revenge of the Deity* <note>original: "de Sera numinis vindicta"</note> a wonderful story of one named Bessus, who murdered his own father. Now, for a long time, no one knew who had committed the murder; no one suspected the son. But when he once went to a banquet, he took a pole and poked down a swallow's nest. Those who saw this rebuked him for it, asking why he wanted to harass the poor little birds (as people do not like to see one plague poor birds or animals, for it is generally held that such a person is a crude man). Then he said: "They have lied about me long enough; they are always crying out that I murdered my father." Those present wondered at this speech and reported it to the King, who had him captured and questioned, whereupon he confessed to the murder. Here you see what fear does: the swallows could not speak, yet he persuaded himself they said he had killed his father. Thus, out of fear, a man imagines he hears or sees that which is not there.

# Concerning Specters / Part One

<margin>Theodoric imagines Symmachus before his eyes.</margin> In the history of the Italian war against the Goths, it is written of Theodoric their king (whom people commonly call Dietrich von Bern <note>A legendary figure in Germanic folklore based on the historical Ostrogothic King Theodoric the Great.</note>) that after he had killed those honorable men, Boethius and Symmachus his father-in-law, a fish head was served to him at supper one time. He then imagined that he saw the face of Symmachus, who was gnashing his teeth and looking at him squint-eyed. From this great terror, he fell into a sickness and shortly thereafter departed from this life.

Indeed, when fear takes the upper hand in a person, it causes them to be terrified even by something that should bring them great joy. We have an example of this in the disciples of our Lord Jesus himself in Matthew 14. When they were on the sea at night in great distress from the water, they were terribly frightened when they saw the Lord walking toward them on the water. They thought it was a specter <note>original: "Gespenst"</note> and began to cry out "murder!" <note>A traditional cry of extreme distress or alarm.</note> in great fear and need; yet the Lord himself came to them and rescued them from the present danger. After his resurrection, when he appeared to them with his true body, they were terribly frightened, and as it stands in St. Luke, they thought they saw a spirit. The Lord comforted them, saying they should behold his hands and feet, for it was he himself; they should touch him, for a spirit has not flesh and bone as they see he has. Yet for joy and fear, they could not believe it immediately. Thus you see that fear brought it about that the disciples themselves mistook the Lord for a specter. Therefore, it is no wonder if we also, out of fear, mistake one thing for another and persuade ourselves we have seen spirits when there were none.

<margin>Monsters rarely appear to brave people.</margin> Those who are brave and undaunted rarely see or perceive monsters and specters. As one reads of the Scythians, who were a brave mountain and warrior people—from whom the Turks are said to have their origin and descent—they see or hear nothing of these things at all. Of lions, it is written that they do not allow themselves to be frightened by any boasting or "bogeyman" tricks <note>original: "buzwerck," referring to masks or scary disguises.</note>. For the lion is stout-hearted, brave, undaunted, and a king among the four-footed animals.

->Those who have poor sight or hearing also imagine things that are not there.<-
->The Third Chapter.<-
### Furthermore, if someone has a poor or weak sight, he also mistakes one thing for

<column-break/>

another. It often happens that one who is farsighted (as scholars for the most part wear out their eyes through over-studying) would be terribly ashamed if he had to say and admit what he had mistaken this or that for; thus his sight deceives him. When someone drinks too much <margin>Drunken people see strange things.</margin> so that his eyes begin to glaze over or his head begins to throb like a hare <note>A metaphor for the pulsing or "twitching" sensation of a hangover or heavy intoxication.</note> that someone has carried for a mile or two on a saddle-bow, he sees a thing much differently than it truly is. He thinks two lights are standing on the table when there is no more than one; he tries to grab the glass or the cup and reaches beside it. Pentheus says in the *Bacchae* of Euripides that he sees two suns, likewise two cities of Thebes, for he was not right in his head. So it is common, when the wine has taken the upper hand in the head and become master, that the fellows think everything is running around, the mountains move, the trees dance, etc.

The wise Solomon, in his wise proverbs in the 23rd chapter, warns everyone to guard against the vice of drunkenness, recounting what trouble follows when one takes too much wine. Among other words, he says: "Your eyes shall behold strange things" <note>Proverbs 23:33</note>—meaning visions and strange apparitions. For just as the fearful imagine strange things, so also do the "full-casks" <note>A derogatory term for habitual drunkards.</note> who have willfully ruined their sight. And although God the Lord presents many wonders and signs in the air and on earth to warn mankind and to incite them to true repentance, it is nevertheless well to note that the "drunk fools" who part ways late at night sometimes say they have seen this or that wonderful and terrifying sign, in which there is fundamentally nothing. For had they gone home at the right time and drunk less, this or that would not have appeared to them, for their eyes would not have been distorted. Does it not happen in a drunken state that one mistakes one person for another with whom he has a grievance, and strikes out at him blindly? The aforementioned passage from the wise Solomon may also have this meaning: "Your eyes shall behold strange things," namely women, to desire them; as it is often found that one in a "wine-soaking" accosts women and daughters, which he would not dare to take into his mind if he were sober and empty.

It cites historical examples like King Theodoric and biblical warnings from Solomon to illustrate how the mind deceives the senses.</summary>

# Ludwig Lavater
<note>Ludwig Lavater (1527–1586) was a Swiss Reformed theologian whose work "Of Ghosts and Spirits Walking by Night" was a highly influential Renaissance text arguing that most "ghosts" were either natural delusions or demonic deceptions.</note>

<margin>Some see themselves.</margin>
Aristotle writes that some people, due to a weakness of sight, see their own form to some extent in the air or mist floating before their eyes (doubtless as if in a mirror). They persuade themselves that they see their *manes* <note>Latin: "manes" refers to the spirits of the dead or ancestral spirits.</note>, which is, as we say, their ghosts, and thus they fear their own shadows. How many things do people imagine when they are in the dark and cannot see a thing, believing they see many kinds of colors and shapes? Likewise, from the very thing that one sees, one might imagine strange and wonderful things. Thus, it is obvious that a person's sight can be wonderfully dazzled so that he believes nothing else than that a man is swallowing a sword and spitting out money, knives, or other things; or that one is eating bread and spitting out flour; or drinking wine and having it come out again through his forehead; or one striking off another's head and setting it back on again; or one pulling along a winepress or a beam, etc. Furthermore, one can also bring it about through natural things, such as smoke and other means, that one would swear everyone sitting at a table looks as if they were dead, or as if they had no heads, or as if they had donkeys' heads, or that a grapevine stretched through the entire room, when it is nothing but a pure delusion. Entire books have been written about such things.

It is the same with hearing and the other senses as has just been reported regarding sight. If one's hearing is impaired, it sometimes seems to him that he hears a buzzing or a crackling as if it were windy; he hears a fire flickering; he hears the roaring of wild forest waters; or perhaps lovely singing and the playing of strings, or a bell ringing—and yet it is solely a defect of hearing. Others who are with and around him, who have no defect in their hearing, hear none of these things. Sometimes one truly hears things, such as the walls cracking loudly, etc. But that is a natural sign that the weather is about to change.

<margin>Hearing is deceived.</margin>
One thinks he has touched or felt something that is not there; one who has a fever drinks a lovely sweet wine, which seems to him more bitter than gall; he eats a good broth, yet it seems to him to be neither salted nor seasoned, having no pleasant taste at all. In this, the fault is not with the drink or the food, the cellar or the cook, but rather the throat and taste of the sick person are impaired. Thus, it happens in the same way that one thinks he sees a monster, has heard it, or has touched it (or it him), when there is just as little truth to it; yet he will not easily let himself be talked out of it.

<column-break/>

Now, when terror and fear, and the weakness of sight and other human senses all strike together, then things truly become wondrous. For people imagine a thing of which there is neither "dust nor fly" <note>A German idiom meaning there is no trace or substance to it.</note>, as we say, yet it must be a spirit; and they will not be dissuaded from it, but rather insist they are right, God knows what everyone else might say about it. One reads that not only individual persons, but even entire armies have been so deceived that they believed the enemy was present when he was nowhere in the land. From this, terrible flights and retreats have sometimes arisen.

<margin>Weakness and fear.</margin>
The knight Commines <note>Philippe de Commines (1447–1511), a chronicler and advisor to the French kings.</note> writes in the first book of his history concerning the affairs under Louis XI, King of France, how Duke Charles of Burgundy lay before Paris with other princes. A warning came to them that the King intended to attack them the following day with all his power. In the morning before daybreak, as the Duke of Burgundy's cavalry rode out into the field, they thought they saw a great multitude of spears from afar, and that the King's troops had let themselves out of the city. When it became brighter and they came closer, they saw that in the same place where they thought the enemy had drawn up, there were many high thistles, which they had mistaken for spears from a distance, as the night is indeed very deceptive. Should it then be a wonder if travelers, when it begins to grow dim or is dark night, sometimes mistake stones, bushes, stumps, and other things for ghosts and monsters?

<margin>The cavalry mistake high thistles for spears.</margin>
In the second book of Kings in the 3rd chapter, we read that the Moabites, after the death of King Ahab, revolted against his son Joram, for which reason he called upon King Jehoshaphat for help, taking to the field against them with all his power...

<margin>The Moabites mistake water for blood.</margin>

When the Moabites <note>A people frequently mentioned in the Old Testament as rivals to Israel.</note> heard this, they summoned everyone who could carry a spear or pike and armed themselves for defense. <margin>Many people imagine they have seen or heard monsters.</margin>

### The Fourth Chapter.

But it also happens frequently that not only playful and humorous people, but also mischievous and malicious ones, disguise and mask themselves in order to mock and terrify people. It is common among us that a man or woman—so that children will behave, be obedient, and work diligently—disguises themselves and frightens the children. One tells the children <margin>Stupffnaß.</margin> it is the "Snub-nose" or "Mother Klünglerin" <note>Regional bogeyman figures used to scare children into obedience.</note>. (The ancients called them *empusas*, *lamias*, or *mormolycias* <note>original: "empusas, lamias, mormolycias" — Greek and Latin terms for female demons or hags.</note>; in the writings of Nicephorus Callistus <note>A 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note>, the night-woman is called Gilo). The young children know no better than that it is truly so, and they are often terribly afraid. However, it is not always good to frighten children this way, as they may fall into bad and heavy illnesses through fear and terror, or become restless in their sleep at night. The wise Solomon teaches that one should discipline and punish children with the rod when they do wrong, and thus instill a healthy fear in them; he does not teach that one should mock-frighten them and say someone is going to eat them or put them in a sack.

Sometimes mischievous fellows put on devil’s costumes, or otherwise wrap sheets around themselves, to mock and terrify people, so that many simple folk know no better than that the evil spirit or some other monster has appeared to them in bodily form. Yet it is also

<column-break/>

not always safe or good to joke in this way, for at times it turns out badly, as one may know from various examples. It is common, when young, merry people travel together, that they tease one another at the inn at night, tying a rope to a bedstead or the ceiling, or creeping under a bed and playing their games as if a monster were present.

It has also happened that young, merry, mischievous fellows disguised themselves <margin>Dance of Death.</margin> and danced in the churchyard, and one of them made music by drumming with a dead man's bone upon a coffin. This was reported throughout the entire city by those who saw it, so that everywhere it was said and believed for a truth that a "Dance of Death" <note>A late medieval allegory on the universality of death.</note> had been seen, and it was greatly feared that a massive pestilence would follow.

Furthermore, it is well known that sometimes harlots and rogues have carried on their shameless, unchaste lives for a long time under such a pretense, leaving the simple people in the house under the delusion that a ghost was walking in the house, so that no one would pay attention to them, and they could walk to and from one another more conveniently, how and when they wished. Sometimes such "ghosts" have been caught when they tried to be too secretive, and they were publicly shamed and punished. Sometimes thieves have also done their business under this pretense, carrying away the property of honest people under the cover of night and fog. When they were heard walking to and fro in the house, people thought it was a ghost or monster. Now, I will not say that the evil spirit—who knows the wonderful power and effect of many things—cannot arrange wondrous things through natural means and deceive the senses of men.

<margin>Monks and priests have passed themselves off as spirits and ghosts: just as Mundus under this pretense shamed Paulina, and Tyrannus shamed many Christian women.</margin>

### The Fifth Chapter.

But all this is undeniable: that certain priests were found in years past who dealt in wonderful things, and often in forbidden black arts, and deceived the foolish world (which had good faith in them) in many ways and manners, solely so that they might extort much money or otherwise satisfy their temptations...

Josephus, the historian, reports in the 18th Book of *Antiquities of the Jews*, in the 7th chapter, this wonderful story which occurred in Rome during the time of the Emperor Tiberius, under the guise of the religious service of Isis. There was in Rome a noble, pious, honest, and moreover rich, young, and beautiful woman named Paulina. She was married to Saturninus, a prominent and honest citizen. Decius Mundus, a prominent young man of the knighthood <note>the equestrian order</note>, became enamored of her. However, because he did not dare to suggest anything dishonorable to her, as she was of too high a standing, he became more and more infatuated as time went on. He promised her two hundred thousand drachmas <note>original: "Drachma Attica & denarius Rõ. vulgò putantur idem esse, & 8. cruc. Budæus æstimat" — An Attic drachma and a Roman denarius are commonly thought to be the same, and Budé estimates them at 8 kreuzer</note>, which is approximately 26,000 florins according to Budé's calculation, if she would only grant him one night. And when she refused him this, he determined that he would starve himself to death. Ide, a wonderfully cunning procuress who had once been the servant-girl of Mundus's father, knew of this and gave him hope that if he would give her only fifty thousand drachmas, she would bring it about and arrange it so that the lady would have to grant his wish. The young man was exceedingly well pleased with the matter. Now, when the procuress learned that the good, honorable woman could be won with neither goods nor money, but also knew that she was entirely devoted to the goddess Isis, she devised such a trick: she went to several priests of that same goddess and informed them in all stillness and secrecy how this young man was completely inflamed with love for the noble lady, and she kindly requested them to do well and help so that he might enjoy love with her. She promised, moreover, that she would pay them twenty-five thousand now in cash, and as much again once they had brought the matter to pass. Greed overcame the priests, so that they promised her they would apply all possible diligence so that the matter would proceed. The eldest among them betook himself

<column-break/>

immediately to Paulina and informed her in secret that Anubis <note>the jackal-headed Egyptian god</note> had sent him to her, and because of her beauty, he had fallen in love with her and commanded her to come to him. The good, dear woman was not ill-pleased with the matter; she boasted to several women who were her confidants and friends how she was pleasing to her god. She informed her husband that she was invited to the god's supper and that she was to stay overnight at his bed. Her husband allowed it all the more readily because he well knew that she was of a quiet, chaste, and pious conduct. She went into the temple, and after supper, when it was time to go to sleep, she was locked in by the priests. There she knew no differently than that Anubis was with her the whole night, but it was Mundus. He departed early in the morning before daybreak, before the priests arose. When it became day, Paulina returned to her husband and boasted to him and her female relatives how Anubis had been with her. They could not quite believe it, as the matter did not seem likely; yet, because she was a truthful, honorable, and chaste woman, they marveled at her words. Afterward, three days after this had passed, Mundus encountered her on the street and said to her: "Paulina, you did right to save me the two hundred thousand drachmas that would have been your own, and yet you granted my wish nonetheless. For it matters nothing to me that you despise Mundus, since under the appearance of Anubis, that which I desired has happened to me." With that, he left her. But when the woman noticed the cheat and deception, she tore her clothes and told her husband the whole business, begging him not to leave this great shame unavenged. He went immediately before the Emperor and told him one thing after another, how it had happened. Tiberius, however, after he had diligently and properly investigated all things, had the priests—those great deceivers—hanged, as well as Ide, who bore a primary guilt in the deception by which the good woman was shamed. He had the temple demolished and commanded the image of Isis to be thrown into the Tiber. But Mundus he sent into exile, and to him...

<margin>How the heathens were led by the nose by their priests.</margin>
From this history, one clearly sees how the evil enemy <note>The Devil</note> infatuates the heathens, and how their priests have pretended that the gods appeared to them and spoke this or that with them, though there was no truth in it. Under the name of divine service, they practiced great knavery. For how much of this thing do you think happened where they were not caught, and their harm did not come to light? If these priests helped Mundus <note>A Roman knight mentioned in the previous page's story from Josephus</note> so that he might defile a pious woman, they undoubtedly did such things themselves many times over, under the guise of an appearance of the gods; otherwise, the idea would not have occurred to them so quickly. Nor would that good honorable woman have been so easily satisfied with the matter if it had not been practiced before with many honorable women. Her husband would not have let her go either. Why did the gods need beds in the churches? Do you think they actually lay in them?

To this point, that which Ruffinus, a priest at Aquileia, writes in the *History of the Ancient Christian Church* in the 11th book, chapter 25, serves very well. Those in Alexandria in Egypt had a priest of Saturn named Tyrannus. He said to every one of the nobles and other prominent people who came to the temple to pray—whenever their wives pleased him for lewd purposes—that Saturn had commanded him to send his wife into the temple to stay there overnight. Each man who heard this rejoiced that their god (indeed, an idol) was so well-disposed toward them and deemed them worthy to be called to him. They adorned their wives sumptuously and also gave them gifts (so that if they came with empty hands, they would not be sent back or rejected) and thus sent them into the temple. When they were locked inside while everyone watched, Tyrannus locked the doors, took the keys with him, and departed. Afterward, he crept in silence through a secret passage under the earth into the image of Saturn. This image was open at the back and carefully nailed to the wall. While the candles burned in the temple and the women performed their prayers with great earnestness and devotion, he suddenly began to speak through the image, which was brass and hollow, so that the poor woman, out of fear and joy, began

<column-break/>

to tremble because the great god (indeed, an idol) deemed her worthy to speak with her. But after the unclean idol had spoken with her whatever he wished—either to bring her into greater fear or to incite her to lewdness—he brought it about through artifice that all the lights were extinguished at once, for he pulled something over them. Then he went down and carried out his evil wantonness with the woman whom he had previously terrified and infatuated with unclean speech. After he had practiced this for a long time with the honorable wives of these hardworking people, it happened that one woman, who was modest and chaste, had a loathing for such a deed; she took careful note of all things, recognized Tyrannus by his voice, went home, and informed her husband what a shameful deception it was. He became enraged that such a disgrace had happened to his wife, and indeed to himself; he put this Tyrannus in prison and tortured him. When he confessed that he had dealt in knavery and deceit, all the lineages of the heathens were shamed. For the mothers had committed adultery, the fathers incest <note>original: "Blutschanden" - here implying the corruption of bloodlines through deception</note>, and the children were considered bastards. When this came out and became public, the image and the temple were immediately removed, etc.

# Ludwig Lavater

There was a great discord between the Preachers <note>Dominicans</note> and the Barefoot Monks <note>Franciscans</note> regarding the Conception of the holy Virgin Mary. The Preachers maintained she was conceived in original sin like other humans. The Barefooters held she was conceived without original sin. They came so violently against one another that the Preacher monks undertook to confirm their opinion with false miracles. They consulted in a chapter at Wimpfen as to where they might find a convenient place for this; Bern pleased them best. Thereupon, four of the most prominent Preacher monks of the Observance at Bern took the matter in hand. And because the Sub-prior was one of the four skilled in the black arts, they conjured the devil, who consulted with them on how the matter might be aptly attacked, and he promised to be helpful in their undertaking on the condition that they surrender themselves to him, which they did immediately, signing themselves over with their own blood. During this time, Hans Jetzer, a simple man, was received into their order; he seemed to them useful for this undertaking. They first tested him with stone-throwing at night, with rumbling and gestures as if it were a spirit. The business went not badly at the start. On a Friday, the Sub-prior disguised himself in a linen sheet and came, together with other spirits conjured by him, as a spirit seeking help, with great turbulence into the brother's cell, wherein they had previously given him holy water and relics. The brother was terribly frightened; he said he could not help him and commended him to God and His dear mother. The spirit said he and his brothers could indeed help him if he would strike himself with rods until he bled once a day for eight consecutive days, and have eight Masses read for him in St. John’s Chapel, and lie there with outstretched arms. He indicated to him that he would return the following Friday before midnight with great turbulence, but he should not be led astray by it, for the devils could not harm him as a holy man. The foolish man reported the whole business the next morning to the actual ringleaders, with a plea that they should be helpful to him so that the poor soul might be redeemed. Soon

<column-break/>

this matter was spoken of in the entire city. The Lector <note>original: "Läßmeister" - the primary teacher/preacher of the monastery</note> began to preach publicly about it, boasting of what a blessed state existed in their Observance, which could be perceived by the fact that this spirit sought help and comfort from them, and not from the broken, drunken Barefooters. At the promised time, the false spirit came, along with other evil spirits, with a great storm into the brother's cell; the brother began to adjure him and ask about several matters. The spirit recounted who he was and for what reasons he was so plagued. He thanked him and his Fathers that they had faithfully taken up his cause, mentioning that if they read thirty more Masses for him, held four Vigils, and if the brother struck himself once more until the blood flowed, he would be entirely redeemed from the great pain he had suffered now for 160 years. He spoke many other wonderful things with him, which are not necessary to report here at length. Afterward, the false spirit appeared again to the brother, praising the Preacher order above all others, indicating that many of those who opposed this Order sat deep in purgatory. The city of Bern would also perish if they did not drive out the Barefooters and renounce the pensions they received annually from the King of France. He also mentioned several things that had happened to the brother, which they had previously enticed out of him in confession. He herewith thanked the brother for his redemption, pretending he was entering the seventh Choir of Angels, where he would also read Mass for his benefactors.

He said that in his devotion he had been carried there in a trance by the Spirit. Furthermore, he reported how the image [of the Virgin Mary] had spoken, and how he could not leave the spot unless the four heads of the City Council came to speak with him, and only after he had first been given the Holy Sacrament <term>Hostia: the consecrated bread used in the Eucharist</term>. These Councilmen were summoned, and the brother informed them that Our Lady was weeping over the city's downfall because they accepted pensions <note>Foreign mercenary payments, a major political issue in Switzerland at the time</note> and because they had not banished the Franciscans <note>original: "Barfüsser" or "Barefoot friars"</note> from the city, who attributed a fabricated honor to her regarding the Immaculate Conception. The Councilmen did not say much in response. During this time, the monks brought the brother a colored or poisoned Host, which he would not receive; then they brought him another, which he accepted, and he was then led into the choir with a procession. The brother and the four monks were summoned before an Honorable Council, where they confirmed all these things. However, the four monks feared the worst—that the brother, because he did not trust them, would "talk out of school" <note>reveal their secrets</note>. They therefore attempted to do away with him, poisoning his food several times and even forcing a poisoned Host into his throat, which he spat back out. They tormented him in other ways to such an extent that he fled from the monastery and revealed the matter to everyone. Meanwhile, the Order sent two messengers to Rome to obtain confirmation of these events from the Pope, so that no one would dare speak against them. When these messengers returned with high hopes that their cause was secured, an Honorable Council had the four monks arrested and secured, for they had previously interrogated the brother in prison regarding all details. An Honorable Council spared no expense, effort, or labor, and also sent an embassy to Rome so that the matter could be resolved. After a long time, the four monks and the brother were questioned under torture <note>original: "peinlich gefragt"</note> regarding all points, and when they confessed to them, they were degraded <note>stripped of their holy orders</note> by permission of the Pope and subsequently burned at the stake. It is generally considered that if an Honorable, wise Council of the city of Bern had not persisted so bravely

<column-break/>

and earnestly, the clergy would have hushed up these monks in some fashion and covered up their great knavery. For the monks and priests had great cause to fear that after such things—as indeed happened—they would lose much faith and no longer be held in such high regard as before.

It is also certain that after this fraud of the Dominican friars <note>original: "Prediger Münch"</note> broke out and people looked into their "cabinet of curiosities" <note>original: "Kunstkammer," referring here to their secret tricks</note>, the affairs of the clergy everywhere began to limp. They became increasingly suspicious to many pious, God-fearing people, especially their claims that this or that spirit sought help and comfort from them, that candles lit themselves, that this or that image spoke, wept, or moved from one place to another, or that this or that saint honored the houses of God with precious relics, or that crosses or other objects were sprinkled with the blood of Christ. Even if they produced Papal liberties and confirmations for such things, people would no longer firmly believe them. Likewise, when it was claimed that this or that devout father was carried away in the Spirit and saw many wonderful things, or that Francis or Catherine of Siena had the wounds of Christ <note>the stigmata</note> on their bodies. Furthermore, people began—not without reason—to doubt the disputations regarding the transformation of the bread into the body of Christ, since they had so often poisoned the hosts. Similarly, doubts arose regarding what was claimed about indulgences, confession, vigils, religious orders, purgatory, holy water, pilgrimages, and penance, since it is evident from this history that they claimed many things to the common man that had no basis in truth.

Her husband, because the woman was dear to him, did not wish to break her last will; he gave the Barefoot Friars <note>The Franciscans</note>, in whose church she was buried alongside her father and grandfather, 6 guilders as an honorarium, although they had expected a much better booty. When he afterwards cleared a forest and sold the wood, they asked him to be so kind as to grant them some wood from it, which he refused them; this vexed them greatly. And because they had never been favorable toward him before, they sought ways and means to avenge themselves upon him; they therefore claimed that his wife was lost and damned for eternity. The actual ringleaders or chief authors of this play were Colimanus and Stephanus of Arres, both Doctors of Holy Scripture. Among them, Colimanus was a conjurer of devils <term>Teufelsbeschwerer: an exorcist or one who summons spirits</term> and had at hand all the equipment needed for such a task. They began the business thus: they hid a young monk, who had only recently joined the order, upon the vault of the church. This man, at midnight when the others had come for Matins <note>The midnight prayer service</note>, raised a great tumult. So they immediately began to adjure him, but he said nothing. They ordered him to give a sign by which one might perceive whether he were a mute spirit or not. Then he began to rumble again, which served as a sign. Now that this foundation was laid, they went to several prominent citizens who were not unfavorable to them and indicated that something heavy and great had occurred in their house of God, but did not say what it was, asking only that they should come to Matins at night.

When they had come and the prayer had begun, the youth on the vault began to rumble. When he was asked what he desired and who he was, he indicated he was not permitted to speak. Then he was ordered to answer through signs to the questions that would be put to him. They had, however, made a hole through which he—when he paid attention—could hear and understand the voice of the conjurer
