of devils. Accordingly, he had a tablet or small board in his hand, upon which he struck and knocked when he was questioned, so that it could be heard below. Then he gave a sign that he was her spirit. Then they asked further whether he were damned, and what he had trespassed; whether it happened for the sake of greed, luxury, pride, or because he <note>referring to the spirit of the wife</note> did not show Christian love, or for the sake of the new heresy or Lutheranism <note>original: "Lutherthums"</note>, and what he meant by this unrest and rumbling? Whether the body, which had been placed in consecrated ground, should be dug up again and placed in another location? To all of this, as he had been instructed, he answered through signs, with which he indicated "yes" or "no" according to whether he knocked two or three times on the tablet. But when he gave it to be understood that the cause of his damnation was the Lutheran heresy, and that her body should be dug up again, the monks requested of the citizens they had brought with them that they should give testimony to these things which they themselves had seen and heard, and confirm this transaction which had taken place over the past days. After he had indicated to the other councilors what was to be done, he went to the King and recounted the entire affair to him. However, because the monks relied upon their privileges and ancient traditions, and refused to allow the matter to proceed through ordinary law and justice, the King appointed several members from the Parliament of Paris <note>The high court of justice in Paris</note> to pass judgment on the case and granted them full power to act therein. This was also approved by Antoine Duprat <note>original: "Anthonius Pratensis"</note>, the Chancellor, Cardinal, and Papal Legate in France. Now that the monks had no further excuses in the matter, they were led to Paris and there compelled to give an answer. However, nothing could be extracted from them. They were all secured in separate confinement. The youth was kept in the house of a councilor named Fumé <note>original: "Fumeus"</note> and was questioned often, but he refused to confess anything, for he feared he would afterwards be killed by the monks as one who had shamed the Order. But when the judges promised him that no harm should come to him from the monks and that he would never again fall into their power, he recounted the entire affair, how it had transpired, in proper order. 

Afterwards, when he was brought before the others, he confessed everything; the others, however, although they were overcome and as good as caught in the act, nevertheless rejected the judge and appealed to their privileges and liberties. But it was in vain, for it was recognized by unanimous judgment that they should be led back to Orléans, placed in prison there, and afterwards stood publicly in the principal church, as well as in the city square where wrongdoers are customarily punished, so that they might publicly confess their misdeeds themselves. 

Precisely at this time, the Lutherans (as they are called) were being persecuted, which was the reason why this judgment was never carried out. For because the Lutheran name was so hated, they feared that if they undertook something severe against the members of the Order—even if they had deserved it—the entire Order would be disgraced thereby, and whatever punishment was inflicted upon them would bring joy to the Lutherans. Furthermore, the Order of the Barefoot Friars <note>The Franciscans</note> is held by the common man to be a very holy estate. When they had thus been sentenced at Paris and led back to Orléans, several women, out of great compassion, accompanied them to the gate with weeping and lamentation. And when they were brought to Orléans, each was again placed in a separate prison; there they again insisted upon their privileges, and finally, after a long imprisonment, no further harm came to them, but they were set free. During the time they lay imprisoned, they had no lack of food or drink, intercession, or other things, in which the women especially did their best. It was the common report that, had the persecution and burning of the Evangelicals <note>Protestants</note> not prevented it, it had been the King’s final intention to have their monastery razed to the ground. This is an account in history which shows that spirits are not always heard, even when it is claimed to be so.

The highly learned Erasmus of Rotterdam writes in the 22nd book of his epistles on page 854, a letter to a Bishop, wherein he excuses himself regarding several matters he had presented by way of warning; and among other things, as he also mentions wandering spirits or souls, he writes the following history. There was a parson, near whom lived his (the parson's) close female cousin, a wealthy woman. At midnight, he, the parson, wrapped himself in a sheet or some other white cloth, crept into her chamber, and behaved exactly as if he were a ghost or a soul. He made several things known, hoping the woman would send for an exorcist <note>original: "Exorcisten"</note>—that is, a conjurer—or ask him himself and speak with him. She, however, was not without wits; she secretly arranged for one of her kinsmen to stay a night with her in her chamber. This man, instead of using exorcisms <note>original: "Exorcismos"</note>—that is, instead of conjuring—took a good cudgel or club with him. He drank right well to give himself courage and lay silently on a bed. The monster then 

<column-break/>

came as it had before, and as it behaved poorly and sighed, the exorcist, from whose head the wine had not yet departed, awoke at this, leapt up, and went for the monster. The monster, however, attempted to drive him off with words and gestures. But the drunken fellow gave no heed to this, but said: "If you are the Devil, then I am his mother!" He rushed at him and struck him so with the cudgel that he would have finished him off entirely had not the parson, changing his voice, begun to speak normally, begging for mercy and saying: "I am no soul, but I am Master Hans!" As soon as the woman recognized him by his voice, she leapt out of bed and peace was made.

the aforementioned Erasmus also writes that it was this same parson who, on Holy Pentecost, let live crayfish <note>original: "Krebs"</note> crawl about the churchyard with burning wax candles attached to them. As these crawled around the graves, it was terrifying at night, and no one dared go near. A great cry went up about it. When everyone was terribly frightened, the parson stood in the pulpit and said they were the souls of the deceased, who desired to be redeemed from great distress through Masses and alms. This deceit was revealed soon after; a crayfish or two were found among the stones and shards, which the parson had not gathered up again, upon which the wax candles were still attached.

### The Ninth Chapter.

**O**ne could introduce many more such examples, but these are enough, from which we plainly see where ambition, greed, envy, hatred, strife, idleness, and lechery bring mankind. Nothing is too much for them. What wonder should it be then, if some monks and priests, where one [strives to be] higher...

# Ludwig Lavater

Does one not still see today how one man wishes to be higher than the other, using false apparitions and other such things to gain prestige and a following for himself? It is, as everyone knows, a very evil thing, driven by greed; for when a man wishes to become rich, he cares for no one else. Likewise, before a man will suffer hunger, he seeks out wondrous tricks and ways to secure his food and sustenance. Therefore, it would be no wonder if even now among the monks and priests—who have always had the reputation of being greedy—some were found who, through the "appearance" of souls and other means, managed their little affairs to set up pilgrimages and other things that <note>idiom: "give bacon to the turnips," meaning to provide a rich profit or advantage</note> bring wealth. For indeed, with what tricks does the common idle man occupy himself so that he may gather goods and money? Does not Paul say: those who desire to be rich, whether it pleases God or not, fall into the devil’s snare? What zeal, brawling, envy, hatred, and strife result when one insists on being right, as daily experience teaches. When the preaching monks at Bern <note>A reference to the Jetzer scandal of 1507-1509, where Dominicans faked apparitions to win a theological dispute.</note> saw no other way to maintain their cause, they surrendered themselves—which is a terrifying thing—to an evil spirit and acted upon his counsel.

Are the priests not for the most part still brawling and self-righteous today? Idleness is a cause of all evil; what good should one expect from those who do no work, do not study, but are full <note>drunk</note> day and night? Tell me, has a hardworking peasant or a lazy idler had the time and leisure to plot evil things, such as inventing artillery? One could write much about where lechery leads men. Since many monks and priests have their good, quiet, lazy days, along with their good food and drink, yet are not permitted to enter the state of marriage, should it be a wonder if they fabricated apparitions so that they might better carry out their love affairs? I will say nothing now of how it is to be feared that not a few among them and other such people are utterly wicked, dealing in black magic and other forbidden arts; would it then be a wonder if they occasionally "made" spirits and afterwards claimed it was the soul of this or that person? For where the aforementioned traits exist, a man dares to do whatever comes into his mind; and these are nowhere more common than in monasteries, colleges, and foundations. Therefore, do not let it seem strange to you if in former times there were false apparitions of spirits, and if some still exist today. For the world becomes ever more shameless, insolent, greedy, and godless, etc., as we all commonly complain. Furthermore, the aforementioned clergy have the advantage that the common people never suspect them of dealing in falsehood and deceit; it is believed they are too pious to do this or that, and they may therefore carry out wondrous things that do not quickly come to light, unless God disposes it miraculously, as we have heard in the preceding examples.

<margin>The Popes made apparitions.</margin>
But perhaps the monks and priests are to be blamed all the less for occasionally dealing in such falsehood—and perhaps still doing so—since some of the "Most Holy Fathers," namely the Popes themselves, as their own historians report, were skilled in the black arts and thereby attained the Papacy? <margin>The priests are also sometimes deceived by laypeople.</margin>
Before I proceed further, I must also point out that it may well be that sometimes mischievous people have led the priests by a rope <note>idiom: "led them by the nose" or "fooled them"</note>. For when they see how the priests claim to be able to adjure spirits and redeem souls, they might wrap a linen sheet around themselves and carry a glowing coal in a vessel beneath it, appearing to the priests so that they knew no better than that these were souls desiring redemption. And it is certain that the majority of apparitions are arranged by men in the manner described above.

### The Tenth Chapter.

<margin>Animals.</margin>
Furthermore, many other things happen daily in a natural way, where many people—especially the faint-hearted and superstitious—persuade themselves that monsters or specters are walking. When one hears rats, frogs, polecats, martens, or the cries of other animals, or a horse stamping in its stall at midnight, he breaks into a sweat, thinking a monster is in the house. One sometimes hears a night-owl <note>original: "Noß Eu Lorind"; likely a regional name for a screech owl or similar bird</note> or other strange birds, where many people imagine far different things. In a wooden wall, woodworms sometimes gnaw quite loudly, so that it seems to a person as if he hears a subtle little hammer striking an anvil, or someone hammering and smithing. There, some simple, foolish people persuade themselves that they are "Hearth-men" <note>term: Herdmänlein; household spirits or kobolds similar to brownies or goblins</note>; they have their strange and wonderful fables and poems about them, which they heard from their mothers and grandmothers, how they appeared to the household, served them, rocked the children, and how lucky it is where they are felt in a house. If they were truly seen in such a way, then it was the evil spirit; for

<margin>Woodworm <note>original: "Teredinus"</note>.</margin>

<margin>Hearth-men.</margin>

<column-break/>

one reads elsewhere that the heathens had their *Lares* and *Penates* <note>original: "Lares, vnd Penates"; Roman household gods</note> or house-gods, whom they honored as those who took good care and heed of their house and servants; but they were nothing other than evil spirits who sometimes let themselves be seen by them in outward forms. Olaus Magnus, Archbishop of Uppsala, writes in his *History of the Northern Peoples* <note>original: "völckern gegen Mitternacht gelegen"; literally "peoples situated toward midnight," a common term for the North</note> that even at this time in those lands there are spirits who serve men by night in human form, and tend their horses and other cattle. Likewise, the wind knocks something over in the house, or it blows a shutter open and shut, and you will find people who can hardly be talked out of the idea that they have heard a specter.

<margin>Echo.</margin>
It is also natural that when one calls and shouts in a forest, valley, or on a shore, the voice always repeats or echoes the last words, sometimes so distinctly that one thinks it is another person giving him an answer, yet it is not. Many would be terribly frightened by this, especially at night, if they did not know so well that it was a natural thing.

<margin>Some things shine only at night.</margin>
There are many natural things that shine or glow only at night, such as certain gemstones, the eyes of certain animals, glow-worms, and phosphorescent wood <note>term: Scheinholz; "shining wood" or foxfire caused by fungi</note>, with which even wicked people sometimes frighten others, so that they think nothing else than that they have seen a monster. Hector Boethius writes how a King of Scotland showed some of his men who appeared to his nobles at night in fish-skins and with phosphorescent wood, exhorting them to fight bravely against their enemies and promising them they would be victorious. These men believed angels were appearing to them and took up the cause bravely.

<margin>Ignis Fatuus <note>original: "Zünstler"</note>.</margin>
Sometimes one sees little blue lights going to and fro at night, or "Will-o'-the-wisps" <note>term: Irrwisch; atmospheric ghost lights</note>, which sometimes run together and sometimes apart (like the boys in our lands with torches at the Shrove Tuesday fires); sometimes they go alone, which terribly frightens those traveling at night. But these and other similar things are mostly natural things.

vapors come forth from the earth and are ignited. Thus, the sulfur in the hollows or hidden passages of the earth, which becomes air, also ignites at times and forces its way out. Sometimes a fire rises as high as a tree and suddenly extinguishes again, which may also come from burning matter seeking an exit. How does one read of Mount Etna in Sicily, how in former times it burned cruelly day and night, casting out fire, ashes, and fiery stones? Likewise of Mount Vesuvius in Campania, situated about one German mile from Naples, which—as Saint Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> writes—is said to have burned in such a manner during the time of Emperor Titus and cast out fire that it burned the nearest estates and villages, along with many people and cattle; sometimes also covering the surrounding fields with ashes. Even within our own memory, these two mountains have done great damage. One reads of other mountains likewise in our own times. In Iceland, one finds fires that strike out of the earth, as Olaus <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557), a Swedish writer and geographer.</note> writes of it. Now, just as great mountains and level fields can burn, so also can a small little fire ignite from the earth and take its course. But those who ride or walk across the fields, and see such things but do not know the true natural causes, imagine out of fear that they have seen fiery men or other strange things of which they have perhaps heard from other people. Sometimes they fall into heavy illnesses solely out of fright and fear. Some things are also natural, even if one cannot immediately point out the causes. But to want to attribute everything that appears to natural causes is also too much.

<margin>People are persuaded of many things.</margin>
I do not wish to speak now of those who can masterfully persuade simple, innocent people that this or that has appeared to them or others, which then one person tells another as certain and true, and yet there is nothing to it at all. How much have we experienced where a thing was told so polished—such as how the Devil carried someone away body and soul, or how someone was done away with, and other such things had happened—where it was afterwards found in fact that it was a fabricated fable.

<column-break/>

->That spirits and monsters are perceived, and other wonderful things truly happen, is proven from the histories of the Heathens.<-

### The Twelfth Chapter.

**A**lthough people now—out of melancholy, deafness <note>The original "taubsuche" likely refers to a state of sensory confusion or "stupor."</note>, fear, and weakness of the senses—imagine many kinds of things that are not there, or are deceived by men and animals, and also often hold other natural things to be ghosts and monsters (as I have thoroughly recounted until now and explained with several examples), it is nevertheless certain that it is not all a delusion or a natural thing that is said of those matters. Rather, ghosts and monsters do exist and appear, and other strange things happen against the common course of Nature. For one finds much of this in many prominent historians, and many truthful persons indicate that the like has encountered and appeared to them by day and night. We wish to hear one after another only several histories of the monsters or ghosts that appeared and were described by prominent people.

<margin>A Triton appeared to the Emperor Julius.</margin>
Suetonius Tranquillus writes how Julius Caesar moved with power out of Gaul toward Italy and the city of Rome, and came to the river Rubicon (which separates Italy and Cisalpine Gaul <note>original: "Gallia Citeriorem"</note>). There he stood in doubt whether he should cross over it or not. In that moment, one who was exceedingly large and handsome suddenly appeared there and whistled; then not only the shepherds but also many of the soldiers ran toward him to hear him, among whom were also the trumpeters. Then he snatched the trumpet from one of them, leapt to the river, began to blow a loud alarm, and hurried to the other shore. Then Julius said, "Well then, let us go where the omens <note>original: "Ostenta"</note> of the Gods and the injustice of the enemy call us; I will rightly venture it."

<margin>Theseus appeared.</margin>

This was also the reason why the Athenians afterwards honored him as a hero. Pausanias writes in *Attica* that on this battlefield, namely on the field of Marathon, for four hundred years after this battle took place, one heard every night the neighing of horses and the clashing together of soldiers. And to those who went there specifically to hear these things, nothing happened; but those who came there by chance heard them clearly.

In the *Life of Cimon*, Plutarch writes how the citizens of Chaeronea lured Damon—who had been exiled from the city because of many killings—back into the city with good, smooth words, and afterwards murdered him in the bathhouse. From that time on, many monsters and ghosts were seen in that same place, and much groaning and sighing was heard, so much so that the doors had to be boarded up.

<margin>A ghost appeared to Dion.</margin> In the *Life of Dion*, he writes that Dion, a fearless, brave, and honest man, had a great and terrifying vision. For as he sat alone in the evening in the forecourt of his house deep in thought, there was a sudden commotion, so that he looked toward another part of the porch; there he saw a tall, large woman, who was dressed exactly as the Furies are usually introduced in tragedies or plays. She was sweeping the house with a broom. Dion was terribly frightened by this ghost, called his good friends, and told them what he had seen, begging them to stay with him that same night, for he feared that if he were alone, this ghost would appear to him again. A few days later, his son met with a wretched accident, and he himself was lamentably stabbed to death.

<margin>A spirit appears to Brutus.</margin> In the *Life of Decimus Brutus*, he writes how Brutus, intending to travel with his army from Asia into Europe, had a light in his tent at midnight, though not a bright one;

<column-break/>

it was very quiet in the entire army camp, and he was considering something with himself. In that moment, it seemed to him as if he heard someone walking in toward him, and when he looked toward the entrance, he saw a terrifyingly tall figure standing still by him. He asked who it was and why it came to him. It answered: "I am your evil genius <note>original: "genius oder geist"; a personal spirit or tutelary deity, often seen as a harbinger of fate</note>; you shall see me at Philippi." He was not terrified by this, but said: "I will see you." When this ghost vanished, he called his guards and asked them if they had seen it. They answered that they had seen and heard nothing. He, however, slept no more the whole night; in the morning he told it to Cassius, who (since he was an Epicurean <note>Epicureans generally denied the intervention of gods or spirits in human affairs</note>) made nothing of such things and tried to talk him out of it, attributing it to natural causes. Shortly thereafter, he lost the battle at Philippi against Emperor Augustus and Antony, and ordered his servant to stab him so that he would not fall into the hands of the enemy. Valerius Maximus writes in Book 1, Chapter 6, that C. Cassius saw Julius Caesar in the battle at Philippi; he appeared in a form more majestic than a man, looking fearsome, and pressed upon him with his horse, at which he was terribly frightened and took flight. Afterwards, he killed himself.

He also writes another history, not unlike these, of how another man, Cassius of Parma, who took the side of Antony, also saw such a monster or ghost, and that he was afterwards killed by Caesar Augustus.

Dion Cassius, who diligently wrote many books on the Roman wars—a prominent man who was once governor in Africa and Hungary—writes that Drusus, who led difficult wars against the Germans for Emperor Augustus, came to the river Elbe and intended to lead his army across, but the water rose in such a way that it was never possible for him. At that moment, a woman came to him, of greater stature than any other human, who spoke to him: "Drusus, where do you wish to go? When..."

# Ludwig Lavater

He <note>The historian, likely Suetonius or Cassius Dio</note> also reports other prodigies that occurred before his death, all of which he despised—such as two young men seen riding through all the fortresses with slackened reins, a mournful wailing that was heard, and other similar things.

Pliny the Younger, Governor in Asia, writes in the 7th book of his *Epistles* a letter to Sura, in which he asks—since they have the leisure—that he should write his opinion on ghosts: whether they are something real, whether they have their own form or some divine power, or whether men merely imagine vain and various things out of fear. That he believes ghosts exist is moved by what he heard happened to Curtius Rufus. This man had come to Africa with the Governor when he was still of no reputation, but rather insignificant and unknown. One evening, as he was walking under a portico, the figure of a woman—larger and more beautiful than a human—met him, by which he was terribly frightened. She told him she wished to prophesy to him: that he would come to Rome, be promoted to high offices there, and eventually become Governor in Africa and die in that office—all of which came to pass. When he arrived at Carthage and stepped off the ship (doubtless when he was moving into the Governorship), it is said she met him again on the shore in the same form.

<margin>Pliny writes of ghosts.</margin>

<margin>A monster in Athens.</margin>

Thereupon he relates another story that is just as wonderful. In Athens, there was a beautiful large house that was ill-reputed and unhealthy. At night, one first heard something from afar, as if someone were dragging a chain behind them; soon it came even closer. Thereupon, one saw an old, gaunt man with a long beard and bristly hair; he wore shackles on his legs and a chain on his hand, which he shook. Because of this, it happened that those who lived in this house became melancholy

<column-break/>

and sad; at night they could never sleep, became sick, and died. For even by day, when the image or the monster was no longer present, it seemed to them they still saw and heard it, and they feared it greatly. Thus, no one wanted to move into the house anymore, and it stood empty for a long time. However, it was advertised as being for sale, or otherwise available to rent for a fee. In the meantime, Athenodorus, a philosopher or wise man, came to Athens and read that the house was for sale. When he heard that it was offered for a small amount of money, it seemed to him that something was not right; he asked what the cause was, and nothing was withheld from him. He took it nonetheless—indeed, all the more willingly. When it began to be night, he ordered a bed to be placed for him in the front part of the house and said they should give him his writing tablet and stylus, along with a good bright light. He ordered his servants to go into the inner part of the house. He began to write and to focus his mind on it, so that his spirit, if it were not occupied, would be less likely to imagine things it had heard about. But when it was well into the night, the monster began to rattle the chains and shackles. He did not look around but continued writing. Then the noise became louder and louder. The monster approached him, coming right to the door; then he looked beside him and found that everything was exactly as had been said. It stood still and beckoned to him with its finger, as if it were calling him. He, however, signaled to it with his hand that it should wait a little longer and continued his work. Then it rattled the chains over his head, and when he looked around again, it beckoned to him as before. Then he took the light and followed it immediately. It went slowly, as if it could hardly carry the bonds; it went into the courtyard of the house and vanished. He plucked grass and leaves and marked the spot. The following day, he appeared before the Council and indicated that they should dig there. There they found human bones with chains on them; the corpse had decayed. They gathered the bones and buried them. From that time on, the monster was no longer perceived. Regarding this, Pliny writes that he believes those who report that it is so.

### The Twelfth Chapter.

If we take before us the history of the ancient Christian church, we find not a little of this matter. Sozomen writes in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, Chapter 28, of a blacksmith named Apelles who was famous in Egypt; how one night as he was smithing, a ghost came to him in the form of a beautiful woman who enticed him to unchastity. He snatched a glowing iron from the ash and struck the ghost in the face with it; then it howled and vanished away.

Afterward, in Book 7, Chapter 23, he writes of a riot that occurred in Antioch because of a tax which the Emperor Theodosius had imposed on the city during wartime. In this riot, the people were enraged and struck down the statues of the Emperor and his wife, dragging them about with a rope and speaking unseemly words. But on the night before this riot broke out, he writes, there was a common report that a monster—namely a woman—was seen, who was very large and hideous to look upon; she ran to and fro in the streets of the city, cracking a whip loudly, just as the servants in the theater are accustomed to do when they wish to enrage the beasts. By this, one might well understand that an evil spirit had caused this riot.

<margin>Nicephorus.</margin>
In Gregorius Nicephorus, who also described the affairs of the church at great length, one finds very much concerning wonders, dreams, and visions of the saints; likewise of the ghosts that appeared to them, for he held almost more regard for such things than for others which would have better served the business at hand.

<margin>Monastery.</margin>
Whoever reads the histories written in the following times, especially the chronicles of the monks, finds such things without number. Yet I must mention here that they describe many of these things in such a way that they are not unjustly held to be suspicious—

<margin>Testimony of the ancient Fathers.</margin>
In the writings of the holy Fathers, you will also find several places here and there concerning appearances or ghosts. Saint Ambrose writes of the noble virgin Saint Agnes in Sermon 90 <note>original: "Sermone 90"</note>, who was martyred for the sake of the true faith, that her father and mother, as they kept watch at her grave, saw at midnight a choir or assembly of virgins in cloth of gold, and among them also their daughter Agnes clothed in like manner. She commanded the other virgins to stand still, and turning toward her parents, she spoke to them, saying they should not weep for her as for one dead, but rejoice with her, because she had attained eternal life from God; and when she had spoken thus, she vanished.

<margin>St. Felix appeared at Nola.</margin>
Saint Augustine writes in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead* <note>original: "de Cura pro mortuis gerenda"</note> concerning Saint Felix the martyr, that he appeared to the citizens of Nola when the city was besieged and stormed by the barbarians, those cruel peoples. Concerning Saint Gregory, who has very many such things in his *Dialogues*, more will follow hereafter.

In almost all the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>term: "vitis patrum" - a famous collection of biographies of early Christian hermits and monks</note>, that is, in the accounts of the lives of the holy ancient Fathers, there stands not a little concerning these things, which is not all to be rejected, for some are described by credible persons. For brevity's sake, I will mention only one history. In the life of Saint Chrysostom, one reads that Basilicus, Bishop of the city of Comana (who, together with Lucian the priest at Antioch, was martyred under the Emperor Maximian), appeared to Saint Chrysostom when he was sent into exile, and said, "Brother John, be of good comfort, for tomorrow we shall be together." Before this, he had also appeared to the priest of that same church and had

->In the books of the monks one finds many foolish apparitions.<-

### The Thirteenth Chapter.

Otherwise, one cannot place much reliance upon the legends and books of examples, likewise upon the *Book of the Old Fathers* <note>original: "Altvätter buch"</note> wherein much is also read concerning the appearances of spirits. For much that stands therein has a very poor appearance; perhaps they wished to strike a fear and devotion into the world with good intentions. Yet I will let that rest upon its own merit.

The like may also be said of many subsequent Popish writers, whether they be monks or others who were quite superstitious and reported many things solely from hearsay. But lest anyone should think I write out of malice, I will—so that one may have a sample of it—report just one history, or perhaps more truly a fable.

<margin>St. Severin appeared.</margin>
Petrus Damianus, at first a Benedictine monk and afterward Bishop of Ostia <note>original: "Hostia"</note>, who is held for a holy and learned man in the Papacy, writes that a cleric or man of the church from Cologne, at a time when he rode through a river, saw Saint Severin, the Bishop of Cologne (who had died not long before, and at whose grave many miracles occurred). He fell upon the horse's bridle and held him back, whereat the cleric was astonished and asked how it came to pass that such a magnificent man was detained in such a place. The Bishop said he should give him his hand and feel for himself how it stood with him; he then thrust the cleric's hand into the water, and in an instant it was so scorched that the flesh peeled from the bone and fell away, so that nothing remained of the hand but the bare bone. Then the cleric asked, "How does this happen, since you have such a great name in the church, that you suffer such distress?" St. Severin answered, "Only because I did not diligently speak my Seven Hours <note>term: "sibẽ zeit" - the Canonical Hours or daily cycle of prayers required of clergy</note> at the correctly appointed times. For I was at the Emperor's court, attended almost all the councils, and took upon myself many kinds of business."

By this, the world was reminded: if the pious, holy Bishop—who served the common good in the Emperor’s business—was so miserably tormented for the reason that he prayed the seven canonical hours <note>The "seven times" or canonical hours are the set times of daily prayer in the Christian tradition.</note> all at once rather than at the appointed hours, what will happen to those who, without necessity, speak the seven hours without devotion and all at once, so that they may better indulge in their lusts and vain things? In such cases, the neglect of the things that God requires of us is not considered. But if the Papal Bishops place any value on this history, as they present it, they should consider how they will answer to God for allowing themselves to be made Bishops of this or that Church while having no regard for the same, instead concerning themselves only with worldly matters; or, if they do concern themselves with spiritual matters, it results in them pushing the Gospel and the Word of God into the background and suppressing those who would gladly see God’s honor and teaching make progress.

### The Fourteenth Chapter.

As far as many other distinguished writers are concerned, Alexander of Alexandria <note>original: "Alexander ab Alexandria," a 15th-century Italian jurist and scholar.</note>, a prominent jurist and Neapolitan, writes in Book 2, Chapter 9 of *Genial Days* <note>original: "genialium dierum"</note> about a trustworthy man with whom he was well acquainted. This man had helped bury one of his good friends. And as he afterwards traveled back toward Rome, when night fell, he turned into the nearest inn on the road and lay down to rest. While he was thus alone and had not yet fallen asleep, the form of the aforementioned friend—as pale and thin as he had been when he lay on his deathbed—came to him. As soon as he saw him, he was terribly frightened and asked him who he was. He gave him no answer, but undressed himself and also lay in his bed, moving close to him as if he wanted to touch him. The man lay far out on the edge of the bed-frame, and when the ghost tried to move closer, he gave him a shove with his foot and felt that he was colder than any ice-stool <note>A metaphor for extreme coldness, likely referring to a block of ice or a cold seat.</note>. The ghost looked at him sourly, put his clothes back on, and departed. He also reports other similar histories which are truly said to have happened in his time.

Baptista Fulgosius <note>Also known as Battista Fregoso, a Doge of Genoa.</note>, the exiled Duke of Genoa, writes in his first book of *Memorable Sayings and Deeds of Many Distinguished People*, etc., in the 4th chapter *On Prodigies* <note>original: "de Prodigiis"</note>, that in the courtyard of the house of Matteo Visconti, who was called "the Great" (the *Vicecomites* or Viscounts were prominent, renowned citizens of Milan who later became Dukes), in the evening after the sun had set, an armed man on a horse was seen, of a more magnificent form than any other human. After he had been seen by many of them for about an hour—not without great terror—he vanished. Three days later, at night, two of them on horseback were seen in the same form at the same place, fighting with one another, who afterwards also vanished like the previous one. Shortly thereafter, Emperor Henry VII passed away, who had been very well-disposed toward the Visconti family.

Immediately after the history just mentioned, he relates another more wonderful one: namely, when Ludovico Alodisius, Lord of Imola, dispatched his secretary or one of his trusted servants to Ferrara for certain matters, the father of Ludovico, who had died shortly before, appeared to him on the road. The highly learned Philip Melanchthon <note>A key leader of the Protestant Reformation and collaborator with Martin Luther.</note> writes in his book *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note> that he himself has seen several monsters or ghosts, and knows many credible people who have testified highly and dearly that they have not only seen ghosts but also spoken with them for a long time. The other was tall and looked like a Discalced Monk <note>term: Barfüsser münch (literally "barefoot monk"), referring to a Franciscan friar.</note>. And as the one who had taken her husband's form went toward the hearth, he greeted the good woman and said to her she should not fear him, for he came to command her with something. Meanwhile, he told the tall monk to go into the room. Afterward, he spoke with her and begged her to appoint Mass-priests to hold Mass. When he wished to depart, he desired that she should offer him her hand. But because she was terribly frightened and not immediately willing, he promised her that no harm should come to her. So she offered him her hand, and although her hand did not become lame, he nevertheless burned it in such a way that it remained black forever after. Thereupon he called the tall Discalced Monk back, and as they went away, they soon vanished.

<margin>Melanchthon's aunt sees a monster.</margin>

Ludovicus Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives, a Spanish humanist and scholar.</note> writes in Book 1 of *On the Truth of the Faith* <note>original: "de Veritate fidei"</note> that in the newly discovered world <note>Referring to the Americas.</note>, nothing is more common than that spirits encounter people in the cities and in the country even at midday, speak with them, command them to do something, forbid them from something, plague, frighten, or strike them. Others who describe voyages or sea travels report the same.

Dr. Girolamo Cardano of Milan <note>original: "Hieronymus Cardanus"</note> also writes of several such appearances in his books which he wrote *On Subtlety* and *On the Variety of Things* <note>original: "de Subtilitate vn̄ de Varietate rerū"</note>; whoever has the desire may read it for themselves there, for I strive for brevity.

Olaus Magnus Gothus, Archbishop of Uppsala, writes in his *History of the Northern Peoples* <note>original: "Histori von völckern gegen mitternacht"</note> in the 2nd book, chapter 3, that in Iceland <note>original: "Yßland"</note> ghosts appear in the form of known people, to whom the inhabitants offer their hands before they know of the death of those whose form they take; and the deception is not noticed until they vanish. I have wished to show this much from old and new historians and other writings, from which one may see that ghosts exist.

# Concerning Spirits / Part One

They never want to leave him, for they also fear him. Someone goes to sleep, lies down in a bed, and then something comes, tugs at his blanket, or pulls the blanket off him entirely, or lies down on top of the blanket or underneath it; sometimes it walks up and down in a chamber. At times, people have been seen riding or walking—sometimes in a fiery form—whom one knows well but who have been dead for a long time, or have recently died. Sometimes one who perished in a battle, or otherwise died, has called out to his kin so that they recognized him by his voice.

<margin>Spirits seeking help.</margin>
Many have heard spirits slipping by at night, clearing their throats, groaning, and sighing deeply; when they were asked who they were and what was troubling them, they answered that they were this or 그 soul. When asked further how they might be helped, they indicated that if one would hold so many Masses, pilgrimages, and other such works <note>Refers to "good works" in a Catholic context intended to shorten a soul's time in Purgatory</note> for them, they would be released. Afterward, they appeared in clarity <note>original: "Klarheit," implying a bright or holy light</note>, claiming they had been helped, thanked their benefactors, and indicated how they would also pray to God and Our Lady <note>The Virgin Mary</note> for them. However, that it was not always priests or other daring people posing as spirits to do such things (as I mentioned some above) is known by the fact that they appeared in many chambers that were locked, where many had previously searched with a light under all beds and chests to see if anyone was in the room, as many people are still in the habit of doing when they go to sleep.

Thus it has often happened that in a house, one thought nothing else than that someone was in the building throwing the kettles, pots, plates, dishes, tables, chairs, and benches upside down, or down the stairs; yet in the morning, everything was found standing orderly in its place. Conversely, stories are told of some monstrous spirits who lifted a door off its hinges, threw it out, overturned things in the house, and left them lying that way, causing much plague <note>trouble or distress</note> to the world.

One also sometimes hears knocking at night in monasteries, or other solitary places, exactly as if coopers were binding a cask, or other crafts-

<column-break/>

men were completing their work, even though everyone is at rest.

<margin>Where one builds, one hears spirits.</margin>
It often happens where new houses are being built that the neighbors hear carpentry in the night, the snapping of the chalk line, masonry work, and the stirring of lime, exactly as if the carpenters, stonecutters, masons, mortar-laborers, and other workmen were at their labor. Some believe there are natural causes for this—that it seems to a person they hear these things at night because they heard them by day. I will let others dispute over that.

<margin>There are spirits in mines.</margin>
The miners testify that in some discovery pits <note>term: "fundgruben" - productive mine shafts where ore has been found</note> one sees spirits or ghosts who are dressed no differently than the mine-knaves <note>term: "bergknappen" - apprentice or journeyman miners</note>; they run back and forth, and one would think nothing else than that they are working like the miners. They hew ore, scrape it together, haul it out like the "dog-trolley" pushers <note>term: "hundstöffer" - workers who pushed small mining carts called 'dogs'</note>, draw water, turn the windlass, and perform other labors, yet they actually accomplish no work. They also do not quickly do harm to anyone, unless one mocks them or laughs at them; then they might well throw things at the person or injure them in other ways. They are especially sensed in those pits where there is much ore. On the other hand, one also finds harmful and cruel mountain-spirits who at times block the shafts and tunnels from the miners, and show many other evil malices and tricks. Georgius Agricola <note>A famous 16th-century scholar known as the "Father of Mineralogy"</note>, a renowned and noble mine-master who wrote magnificent books on mining, writes that in a pit at Assenberg called the "Rosary," such a spirit killed twelve miners, and although it was rich in metal, it had to be abandoned. Likewise, one was seen in Schneeberg in the St. George pit in a black cowl; he took a mining-lad and hoisted him up high, not without injury to his body. Regarding the "mountain-mannikins" <note>gnomes or earth spirits</note> or spirits, you will also find information in Olaus Magnus <note>A Swedish historian and geographer</note> in the 6th book, chapter 10. Those who travel the sea indicate that in some places where the cannibals dwell, many monsters walk and inflict much suffering on those peoples.

# Concerning Spirits / Part One

...follow a funeral procession, or stand by the grieving.

It is said that if one sees a person's spirit (as they call it) and that person does not die shortly thereafter, it is an indication that they will live to a very old age. However, one should not place any stock in such things; rather, let everyone prepare themselves as if they must depart tomorrow, so that they do not shortchange themselves.

Other wonderful things also occur: when someone is imprisoned for a capital crime <note>literally "for their life"</note>, a wild din is sometimes heard at night in the castles, as if someone were trying to help them escape by force and wanted to smash down door and gate; yet when people arrive, there is nothing there, and the prisoner has heard nothing. Regarding executioners, it is said they mostly know when they must execute or dispatch someone because their execution swords give a sign. Among those labor-weary people who kill themselves <note>a reference to the historical belief that the bodies of suicides possessed supernatural weight or properties</note>, wonderful things also happen. Sometimes they have been led a long way until they could be cast into a great body of water. There, the horses could scarcely pull the wagon down a hill, yet the wagon ran up the hill so fast it nearly overran the horses. When someone has been murdered and the murderer comes near the dead corpse, it has begun to foam, bleed <note>original: "schweissen" - a reference to the 'cruentation' or the bleeding of a corpse in the presence of its killer</note>, or give some other sign. A murderer once sat at a table, and when a cup was overturned, the wine ran through the entire table, not off the edge. One could show many testimonies and histories of these and other wonderful things. But everyone who reads this will well remember some of these and other similar things that have happened to themselves, their friends, acquaintances, and relatives, or that they have otherwise heard from other credible people.

When great changes in governments, deadly and long-lasting wars, uprisings, and other heavy, dangerous courses and times are at hand, many wonderful things mostly happen beforehand against the common course of nature in the air, on earth, and among animals. The Latins call them <term>ostenta</term> <note>displays</note>, <term>portenta</term> <note>portents</note>, <term>monstra</term> <note>monsters/omens</note>, and <term>prodigia</term> <note>prodigies</note>. It is said that sometimes even the horses are mournful, refusing to move forward and never letting their masters mount them when defeats are imminent.

Therefore, one calls it <term>Panic terror</term> <note>original: "Panicos terrores"</note> when a gruesome fear suddenly overcomes someone and they do not know why. Before the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> were defeated at Leuctra, the weapons clattered in the Temple of Hercules. At Thebes at that same time, the gates of the Temple of Hercules, which had been secured with good bolts or bars, suddenly opened by themselves. Appian, who diligently described the civil wars that the Romans waged against one another, also reports the wonders and signs that preceded them. For instance, that people heard the terrifying, gruesome cries of men, a clashing of weapons, and the riding of horses, yet nothing was seen.

Valerius Maximus writes in the 1st book, chapter 6, *On Prodigies* <note>original: "de Prodigiis"</note>, that Gaius Pompey was sufficiently warned not to offer battle to Julius [Caesar]; that when he sailed from the land at Dyrrachium, his servants suddenly became very sad and dejected. This is also said to have happened at Ptolemais. At Pergamon, in secret and hidden places where no one was allowed to go except the priests, drums were heard beating.

<margin>Castor and Pollux.</margin>
The heathens write of Castor and Pollux <note>Twin deities in Greek and Roman mythology, often associated with horsemanship and protection.</note> that they were seen several times in field battles on white horses, fighting bravely against the enemies of the Romans. Plutarch writes in the *Life of Coriolanus* that they were seen in the battle against Tarquinius, and that they immediately announced the victory in Rome; Livy also writes this in book 8, decade 1. In the history of the siege of the city of Magdeburg, one reads that the enemies lying before the city believed—whenever the citizens made a sortie from the city and skirmished with them—that someone rode before their ranks on a white horse, yet the citizens saw no one.

Josephus describes in his books on the *Jewish War* what great signs occurred before the terrifying destruction of the city of Jerusalem: namely, that the bronze gate of the Temple, which was well-bolted, opened by itself at night. Before sunset, chariots were seen driving through the air, and armed armies hovering around the city. On the feast of Pentecost, as the priests went into the Temple at night to perform their divine service, they heard a noise, followed by a voice: "Let us depart from hence." He reports other such things as well, which are not necessary to introduce here at length.

Felix Hemmerlin, Doctor of both Laws <note>Civil and Canon law</note>, Provost at Solothurn and Canon at Zurich—a well-read man, as his writings still extant testify—writes in his book *On Nobility* <note>original: "de Nobilitate"</note> in the 30th chapter: In the history of King Rudolph of Habsburg, one finds that when King Rudolph had defeated Ottokar, the Bohemian king, in battle, he remained on the battlefield overnight; and that many monsters <note>or "unearthly beings"</note> made a wild commotion and outcry around midnight; then, as it vanished, it was seen that they were <term>Lemures</term> <note>In Roman mythology, these were the wandering and vengeful spirits of the dead.</note> or the spirits of the dead. In the 26th chapter, he writes that in the Year of our Lord 1280, as the priest at Zurich preached in the Great Minster, a stone split apart by itself near the burial place of the holy martyrs St. Felix and Regula, our patrons (as they were called in former times). It let out such a crack, as if a clap of thunder had come, so that all the people in the church were no less terrified than if a vault had collapsed. In the same year, on the 3rd day of October, the greater part of the city was disastrously burned; and subsequently, great unrest arose among the people because of the [Papal] Ban and the Imperial Outlawry. When one counted 1440 years from Christ's birth, a similar crack or bang was heard at midnight at the Great Minster in Zurich, on the 12th day of September, on the Church Anniversary. Following this, the old seven-year Zurich War ensued. Further, in the 33rd chapter, he writes that in the Year of our Lord 1444, before the brave battle that the few Confederates <note>The Swiss "Eidgenossen".</note> fought against the entire military power of Louis the Dauphin of France at St. Jakob by the Leper House outside Basel, one heard in that same region for several nights in succession how people fought with one another and cried out. Many other such things I intentionally omit.

->Of Ghosts / The First Part.<-

<margin>Evidence from Holy Scripture that monsters appear and other strange, wonderful things happen.</margin>

### The Seventeenth Chapter.

Yet you may say: I hear of no testimony from Holy Divine Scripture regarding these things, and especially whether there be monsters <note>original: "Ungeheur" - here meaning supernatural apparitions or portents</note> or ghosts? **Answer:** It is not without evidence; one does not find much, but certainly something of it. In the Holy Gospel of Matthew, chapter 14, it is written of the disciples of our Lord Christ that when they were on the sea at night and stood in great danger because they had a headwind, and the Lord came walking upon the water toward daybreak, they were sorely terrified, cried out, and believed they saw a monster. By this one clearly sees that they knew of ghosts which appeared to men on water and land. Likewise, when the Lord appeared to them after his resurrection and wished to assure them of his true resurrection, they thought they saw a spirit or ghost. There the Lord does not deny that there are spirits or monsters and that they let themselves be seen at times; rather, he confirms it by making a distinction between himself and the ghosts. But further regarding these two testimonies will follow later in its proper place.

You find an even greater instance in the second book of Samuel <note>modern Bibles list this as 1 Samuel 28</note> concerning Saul, who, when he was invaded by the Philistines and stood in great anxiety, went to a witch and commanded her to awaken Samuel for him, so that he might ask him for advice regarding the present war. Then she awakened one, and Saul believed no differently than that it was Samuel, who spoke with him about how the war would turn out. Whether it was the true Samuel, however, will also be explained later in its proper place.

Regarding other wonderful things, one also finds in Holy Scripture, 1 Samuel chapter 5 and 1 Chronicles 14, how David was attacked a second time by the Philistines; the Lord God said he should go behind them, and when he heard the rustling in the tops of the trees, then he should launch the attack, etc. In 2 Kings chapters 6 and 7, it is written how God delivered the city of Samaria, which was

<column-break/>

strictly besieged by Ben-hadad, the King of the Syrians, and saved them from great famine; for in the night they had heard a rattling of wagons, the neighing of horses, and the noise of a great army in their camp. They feared the King of Israel had hired a foreign host of horse and foot to relieve the city. Therefore they fled, leaving behind the provisions, wagons, and other things, etc.

In Daniel chapter 5, you find how King Balshazzar sat at his feast and saw a hand distinctly over against the candlestick, which wrote upon the wall how it would go with him.

In the second book of Maccabees, chapter 1, you read that to Heliodorus—the servant of Seleucus, the King in Asia, who wished to rob the temple in Jerusalem—there appeared a horse upon which sat a terrifying rider who rode toward him. At his side stood two handsome youths who scourged Heliodorus. In 2 Maccabees chapter 10, it says how Judas Maccabeus fought with the enemy, and when the battle was at its fiercest, the enemy saw five magnificent men from heaven on horses with golden bridles, who rode alongside the Jews, and two stayed beside Maccabeus, etc. Furthermore, an armed man appeared to Maccabeus in a shining garment with golden armor, shaking his spear to indicate that he would achieve a magnificent victory, 2 Maccabees chapter 11.

I do not cite this because these books of the Maccabees should be held in equal value with the true primary books of the Old and New Testaments, but because they are placed with the Bible and have always been read. For even if one never proved dogmas <note>original: "Dogmata" - core church doctrines</note> or the main points of teaching from them, they have nonetheless been held in great esteem.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of who witnesses apparitions and the historical/spiritual conditions under which they appear, following the previous section on the nature of spirits.</meta>

# Ludwig Lavater

...not only (as some have thought, of whom Plutarch writes in the *Life of Dion*) by children, women, or those whom physical illness has greatly weakened, or otherwise by the simple-minded, but also by brave, honest people who are not melancholy or easily frightened, but fresh, healthy, and of sound mind. Yet it has always happened that some encounter these things far more than others—such as travelers, watchmen, hunters, wagoners, and sailors, who are on the roads, waters, and in the forests, mountains, and valleys not only by day but also at night. You will find one person who never encounters anything of the sort in his entire life; on the other hand, you find another who encounters much of it. Just as one finds people who see strange worms <note>likely referring to visions of vermin or perhaps "earth-spirits" in folklore</note>, while others constantly encounter many things on the road. The common saying that "Ember-day children" <note>original: "fronfasten Kind"; children born during the Ember weeks, traditionally thought in German folklore to possess the "second sight" to see spirits</note> see and hear more ghosts than other people is a superstitious fantasy. Those who are stiff and firm in true faith encounter less, for the most part, than the superstitious, as is the case in other matters. A superstitious person uses a blessing to heal this or that ailment of a horse, and it works; he conjures a snake and it lies still; he has a blessing to staunch blood and it stops; he has a divining rod and where metal is buried, it inclines. A true believer, who despises these things (as they are forbidden in Divine Law and even in Papal Law and Right), even if he were to use them, they would achieve nothing. Thus, ghosts appear to him much less than to the superstitious, because he knows what to make of them. You find people who imagine themselves to be somewhat greater if many of these things appear to them. Among us, when we were still stuck in much superstition, there were many more of these appearances than there have been since the Gospel has again been preached cheerfully and clearly; the reason for this I will show hereafter.

<margin>Ember-day children.</margin>

<margin>One sees and hears a thing, the other does not.</margin>

It also often happens that one person sees and hears a thing distinctly, while another who stands or walks with him sees and hears nothing at all.

<column-break/>

As is read in the history of the Prophet Elisha <note>original: "Helisei"</note>, who saw the fiery chariots and horses on the mountain, but his servant saw nothing until the holy Prophet prayed to God that He might open his eyes for strength and comfort, so that he might also see this magnificent wonder. Likewise, it is written in Acts chapter 9 how our Lord Christ struck down Paul before Damascus and spoke with him; there his companions heard the voice. Afterward, in chapter 22 <note>The OCR says "12. cap.", but the text refers to Paul's speech in Jerusalem, which is Acts 22</note>, when Paul himself tells the people in the camp before the commander Lysias how it happened, he says they did not hear the voice of the one who spoke with him—which is not a contradiction. For this is the meaning: they certainly heard the voice or the sound, but did not understand what the Lord said to Paul. Plato writes in *Theages* that Socrates had a secret spirit <note>original: "geheimen geist"; referring to the *daimonion* of Socrates</note> that warned him where he should be on his guard. He did not see it, but others heard it. Sometimes young children see something that no one else can see.

<margin>The question is resolved.</margin>

<margin>The demon of Socrates.</margin>

<margin>At what time ghosts appear.</margin>

As far as the time is concerned when these monsters are most seen, one finds in histories that after the thousand years following Christ's birth—of which St. John prophesied in his Revelation that the Devil would be loosed from his chains, that is, to cause and bring about much error, superstition, shame, and vice—indeed, after the passing of these years, everything was full of these appearances. For people relied almost more upon them than upon the Holy Scripture itself. A spirit appeared and said: if one establishes this or that, a pilgrimage, a chapel, etc., it would be dear and acceptable to God the Lord. Then the bishops and parish priests did not inquire further whether it could be supported by Holy Scripture or not. Ghosts appeared in former times and still appear by day and night, but especially at night, and more before midnight when people wake from their first sleep than after midnight. Likewise on Fridays, Saturdays, etc., on fast days, to strengthen superstition. But it is no wonder that these things are felt more by night than by day, for he, from whom the majority of these things...

<margin>Where or in what places the spirits appear.</margin> These things are heard and seen in all places and ends, but especially on battlefields where skirmishes and great battles took place in former times, or in those places where homicides have otherwise occurred; at places of execution, and in the woods, where perhaps black magicians <note>practitioners of necromancy or dark arts</note> have conjured the unclean spirits. God the Lord threatens the Babylonians in <term>Isaiah chapter 13</term>—where they previously had their precious palaces and their dances—that there the <term>Fauns</term> and <term>Satyrs</term> <note>original: "Fauni vnnd Satyri"; forest and field spirits from classical mythology</note> or field spirits shall leap.

For by God’s permission, the Devil carries out his wondrous game in those places where much pride and tyranny was practiced against poor people.

<margin>How or in what form the spirits appear.</margin> The manner and measure of the appearance of spirits is unequal, as one may understand to some extent from those examples I cited above. For they show themselves in many kinds of forms. Sometimes in the form of a person known to us, who is still living or has long been dead. Sometimes in the form of an unknown person. To the Forest Brothers <note>hermits</note> and monks, many spirits appeared in the form of women to incite them to lewd matters. They also appear in the form of animals, be they four-footed animals—such as in the form of a dog, a sow, a horse, a goat, a cat, a hare—or flying or crawling animals, such as in the form of a raven, an owl, or a snake, of which the heathens had many in their houses and honored them. Sometimes the spirits appeared in a pleasant form, other times in a gruesome, terrifying one. Now one came riding by

<column-break/>

on a horse, then he went on foot, or crawled on all fours. Now a fiery man was seen, then a bloody man, or one whose guts hung out from his belly; sometimes only a shadow was seen, then only a hand, then something that the ghost carried in its hand, such as a stick and other such things. Sometimes it allowed itself to be seen like a burning wisp of straw. Sometimes only a dark voice was heard, as if someone were speaking out of a pot. Sometimes ghosts have been heard walking up and down in a chamber, leafing through a book, counting money, placing stones in a board game, or knocking. Sometimes one otherwise hears a wild rumbling and pounding, likewise a wondrous noise, din, and clattering as if several pieces of artillery were being fired from afar. The monster has also sometimes grabbed one under the arm or by the hair and walked alongside him.

<margin>The Raging Hunter.</margin>

<margin>What the ghosts accomplish.</margin>
These ghosts, monsters, spirits, or whatever one wishes to call them, sometimes block the paths of travelers, lead them away from the right road, terrify and plague them so that they sometimes turn ice-gray in a single night, cause people to be unable to sleep peacefully at night, and sometimes pull them out of their houses, so that they must leave the same standing empty, not without their particular loss. Sometimes they turn things over for people, give them shoves and jerks, throw things at them, and thus inflict damage upon their temporal goods, their bodies, and sometimes even their lives, if God permits it to them. It often happens that those who have seen or heard something, or as we say, "those whom an evil wind has blown upon," break out in sores around the mouth, their face swells up, and sometimes they even fall into the "deaf-sickness" <term>Taubsucht: likely referring to epilepsy or a state of catatonic stupor</term>, as all this has often and much been seen and experienced. They also often drive the cattle wild in the meadows and commons.

So much for the first part of this book, in which, as I hope, it is sufficiently proven that although there are many who persuade themselves they have seen or felt monsters when there is nothing there, or mistake one thing for another, there are nonetheless monsters, and likewise other wonderful things often and frequently occur. Furthermore, it has been indicated to whom primarily, where, when, how, or in what form these things appear, and what signs they sometimes leave behind.

Whoever would now wish to deny and mock this manifold and unanimous testimony of those who lived in ancient times, and also in our times and are still living, I would not know what one should believe or trust in such a person, or what one should take him for. For just as it is a great frivolity when one believes every "full and drunken tap" <note>A derogatory term for a drunkard or a babbler</note>—whether he be (as they call it) Spiritual or Worldly, especially a partisan one—in everything he claims regarding such appearances and other wonders and signs: so on the contrary, it would be a great impudence if one were to wantonly and shamelessly deny and reject all that which is told as truth by many impartial historians, by Holy Fathers, and other prominent, honorable persons.

# The second part of this VI. Treatise/ that specters and other wondrous things are not the souls of men/ but either good or evil angels/ or otherwise warnings from God.

->The Belief of the Heathens/ Jews and Turks regarding the souls that have departed from the body.<-

### The first Chapter.

AS far as the second part of this report is concerned/ one must indicate what those things might be/ which in the manner described above/ by night or day/ are heard/ seen and felt. Whether they be the spirits or souls of the deceased/ and what the Ancients held concerning them/ likewise what the Holy Divine Scripture teaches us about them.

The wise Heathen <note>original: "Heyd"</note> Plato, believes the noble and aristocratic souls travel upward/ as they are purer: but the others who are sluggish/ and stained by fleshly lusts/ wander here below near the graves/ and he considers those to be the monsters <note>or "apparitions"</note> that are often seen. Other Heathen writers <note>original: "Scribēten"</note> also write that this moves them/ that they believe that the souls of men remain after their death/ for it is certain/ that many monsters wander here and there/ as one hears and sees: they also often speak with men/ wherefore the majority of them have held these to be souls. The holy ancient Teacher Tertullian also writes in his book *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note>, the wise among the Heathens/ who held that the soul is immortal (for some/ like the Epicureans have believed/ body and soul perish together) have taught/ that the souls of the wise when they depart from the body/ have their dwelling in the heights/ the others travel down to hell.

In addition, the Heathens hold it to be true/ that if the bodies of the deceased are not properly committed to the earth/ then their souls must wander for a long time/ before they may come to rest. Therefore it was quite terrifying among them (the Heathens)/ if one was not buried/

<column-break/>

but rather cast away/ as one reads especially among the Poets. Hector begs Achilles in Homer most earnestly/ that he should not cast his body to the dogs and birds/ but let it be given to his dear old father King Priam/ and his mother Hecuba/ so that they may bury him honorably. Patroclus appears to Achilles in sleep/ desiring of him/ that he hold a burial for him/ otherwise he may not enter the gate of hell/ for the souls of those who are buried/ thrust him away. Which example the holy Tertullian cites/ and contradicts this false and erroneous opinion. Palinurus begs Aeneas in Virgil/ that he throw earth upon him/ that is/ that he make him a grave. <margin>Empty tombs.</margin> *Cenotaphia* <note>original: "Cenotaphia"</note> empty tombs/ they called the graves into which one did not go/ but were made in his honor.

Furthermore, the Heathens have alleged/ that the souls of those who died before their time/ and especially those who were executed/ such as those hanged/ drowned/ beheaded/ etc. wander as long as they would have lived/ had they not previously perished by misfortune/ which opinion the Holy Tertullian also refutes. Plato writes in *The Laws* <note>original: "de Legib."</note> book 9. that the souls of those who were killed/ often pursue the murderers to harm them.

<margin>The faith of the Jews.</margin> Among the Jewish people the general belief has been/ that the souls of the deceased are either in rest/ namely if they depart in the faith of the promised Messiah/ or else are in damnation/ if they died without repentance for their sins. For Job speaks in the 7th Chapter. As a cloud passes away/ so those who go down into hell/ do not return/ etc. If you say/ Job was a Heathen/ so it stands that David/ when he in

In the Book of Wisdom (which, as the ancients indicate, was written by Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher; the Book of Wisdom is now considered part of the Apocrypha</note>), it says in the 3rd chapter: "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment shall touch them." On the other hand, it is written that the souls of the unbelieving go into hell. In the 49th Psalm, it speaks of the rich who turn away from God and His commandments because of their wealth: "They shall lie in hell like sheep; death shall feed on them; hell shall be the dwelling of them all," etc. If the Jewish people had held the opinion that souls went into Purgatory, they would undoubtedly have had, among so many forms of sacrifice which they held for the sins of the living, some sacrifice for the redemption or at least the comfort of souls in Purgatory. But that souls return, allow themselves to be seen, and request help—you do not find that in the Old Testament, but rather the opposite. In 2 Samuel 12, David says of his young son that he cannot call him back; he will go to him, but the son will not return. However, that long after the time of Christ there were some among the Jews who held that souls wander after they have departed from the body may be understood from what some of their Rabbis write: that the soul of Naboth (who was killed because he would not give his vineyard to Ahab) was the spirit who offered himself to deceive Ahab, as he wished to see his destruction.

<margin>Turks.</margin>
The Turks <note>A common early modern term for Muslims</note> also believe the souls are immortal and go either into rest or into pain and distress. But whether they hold that souls also return and wander upon the earth and appear to men, I can find nothing specific in their Alcoran <note>The Quran</note>.

->The Papist <note>A Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics</note> Doctrine of Souls and the Appearance of Spirits.<-

---

->The Second Chapter.<-

In the Papacy, it was formerly publicly taught and written that the ghosts seen and heard by men are either evil or good angels, or the souls of those who are in Bliss, in Purgatory, or in Damnation. The majority, however, are said to be souls who desire help and redemption from men. But so that their teaching on this matter may be better understood, I must set it forth somewhat more extensively from their own books.

<margin>Four places where souls go.</margin>
The Papist teachers, in their commentaries on the 4th Book of the *Master of Sentences* <note>Peter Lombard, whose "Sentences" was the standard medieval theology textbook</note>, designate four places to which souls go after they have departed from the body. Three are eternal, but one is only for a specific, certain time. The first place they call *Cœlum empyreum* <note>original: "Cœlum empyreum" - the highest heaven</note>, the Heaven, which is a lodging for the blessed and is otherwise called Paradise in the Scriptures. The second place is Hell beneath the earth, a dwelling for devils and for unbelievers who have grown to adulthood, as well as for false Christians who depart from here in a mortal sin without repentance. The third is said to be *Limbus puerorum* <note>original: "Limbus puerorum" - the Limbo of Infants</note>, the place for young children born of either believing or unbelieving parents who depart from here without Holy Baptism. These live there eternally without a sensible punishment, but they shall not see the face of God. And for this reason, they should not be buried in consecrated ground. The fourth place, they say, is *Purgatorium* <note>original: "Purgatorium" - Purgatory</note>, which is prepared for those who depart from here without mortal sin; or if they have committed mortal sin, they have had repentance for it, yet they have not done sufficient penance, or they have departed from here with only venial or daily sins.

<margin>Cœlum empyreum.</margin>
<margin>Hell.</margin>
<margin>Limbus puerorum.</margin>
<margin>Purgatory.</margin>

Regarding this place, namely Purgatory, the Papist Doctors teach wonderful things. Some say Purgatory is also beneath the earth like Hell. Some say Hell and Purgatory are one place, though the pain or punishment is unequal, according to whether the soul has deserved a great or small punishment. Additionally, there are many places of punishment on Earth in which the souls of the deceased are purified.

# Concerning Spirits / The Second Part.
