For it is said that in this or that mountain, water, or valley, this or that soul has been seen, especially in the place where they had sinned. And these are said to be *particularia purgatoria* <note>original: "particularia purgatoria" — specific or private purgatories</note>, special places of cleansing appointed by God for certain individuals for specific reasons before the Day of Judgment; after which judgment, the general Purgatory, along with these special ones, shall cease. Some teach that the pain in Purgatory is just as great as the pain in Hell, with the only difference being that Purgatory has an end, while Hell does not. They claim a person would more easily endure all the suffering that all humans from Adam until the Last Day have suffered, rather than the slightest punishment in Purgatory for just one day. Likewise, they say our earthly fire, when compared to the fire of Purgatory, is like a mere painted fire. See the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to established academic theologians of the Church.</note> on the fourth book of the *Sentences*, distinction twenty <note>original: "Sententiarum, distinctione vigesima" — referring to Peter Lombard's *Sentences*, the standard medieval theology textbook.</note>. They also have the question of by whom the souls in Purgatory are punished. On this, one does not say the same as the other. Richard of Middleton <note>original: "Richardus de Media villa" — a 13th-century Franciscan theologian.</note>, a barefoot friar, writes in his commentary on the *Sentences* that he believes the souls are carried to the place of pain by good angels, but are not punished by them, because they will shortly become their fellow citizens in heaven. Likewise, they are not punished by unclean spirits (for after a person has died, those spirits no longer tempt the souls), but rather by the justice of God. Yet it may well be that the unclean spirits are present and rejoice in their punishment. I have cited this regarding Purgatory at some length so that you may see that the Doctors themselves are not in agreement on this important article of faith, with which people have been deprived of both their goods and their courage.

<margin>Who punishes the soul in Purgatory.</margin>

Furthermore, they teach that the spirits of the good and the evil sometimes come or are sent from hell to living humans. According to the common law of justice, all souls shall only come forth from hell on the Day of Judgment to be judged; before then, none come out of hell. Yet, by special permission of God, some may return from hell for a short time even before the Last Day, and this for the instruction and terror of those who are still living. They tell of many kinds of visions, how various damned persons—clergy and laity, women and men—appeared to their confessors or others and indicated the cause of their damnation, which I intentionally skip over. But the souls who are in eternal bliss or in Purgatory appear often and much, as can be seen in the *Homilies* of Gregory and in his *Dialogues* <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), whose writings on miracles and the afterlife were highly influential.</note>, who writes that the holy Apostles, Peter and Paul, and other saints appeared to the faithful and led their souls to Heaven. God allows souls to come from both places: partly so that they may comfort and warn the living, and partly so that they may desire help and comfort from them. Yet God does not let them come as often or as much as they might desire.

<margin>The souls return.</margin>

<column-break/>

Furthermore, the Doctors have a question as to whether it is a sin if someone desires of God that souls appear to him? To this they give this answer: If it does not happen out of lightheartedness or vanity, but with good intention—so that one might know how it stands with his friends, neighbors, benefactors, father, mother, and others, in order to come to their aid so they may be released all the sooner—then it is not wrong. For since the souls show themselves and desire help, why should one not also desire such a thing from God? And this is the opinion of Thomas Aquinas <note>The most influential medieval philosopher and theologian.</note>.

<margin>Whether one should desire that spirits appear to him.</margin>

Regarding the place and time when spirits show themselves, no certain rule can be prescribed, for it depends on God; if He wishes to redeem one soon, He lets him appear soon, and in places where he may be heard. Furthermore, they do not always appear in visible form, but invisibly, clearing their throats, or sometimes clapping their hands together, etc. Of this I have already reported in part when I wrote of monsters and portents in general. Yet wherever they are, they say they suffer distress. Moreover, the souls do not appear to everyone, nor do they give an answer to everyone, but perhaps to one among many. Therefore, if one wishes to question them, one must prepare oneself, such as with fasting and prayer, as Daniel did in the 10th and 11th chapters <note>Refers to the biblical Book of Daniel, where the prophet fasts and prays before receiving angelic visions.</note>. Likewise with confession, and—

If he desires alms, what kind of alms should be given, how much, to which persons, and whether they should be given to hospitals, leper houses, or other poor people. Furthermore, by what sign one shall know that he is perfectly redeemed, and why he came into Purgatory. Yet one should put no unnecessary or superfluous, inquisitive questions to him, unless he wishes to reveal it of his own accord. It is also better that one does this on a holiday and fasting before the midday meal, or at night, as is the custom. And if the spirit gives no sign at that hour, one should delay until another time when the spirit reveals itself again. One should, however, leave the holy water and crucifix standing there. For by the secret judgment of God, they reveal themselves at certain hours, and also to certain persons, not to all. One should also not fear that the spirit will injure such a person in body, for if it be a good spirit, it will not readily do anything to them, otherwise it would make itself suspicious.

The Papist <note>Catholic</note> teachers also indicate four principal marks by which one may recognize good spirits from evil ones. Firstly, they say, if it be a good spirit, it may indeed bring some terror with it, but it immediately raises the person up again, as the angel Gabriel did for the holy Virgin Mary when she was terrified by his greeting. They also cite other examples. Secondly, one may recognize the spirits by their visible form. If it appears in the form of a lion, bear, dog, a toad, snake, raven, or like a black shadow, then it is well to be presumed that it is an evil spirit. A good spirit reveals itself in the form of a dove, a human, a lamb, or with a radiance. One must also take heed whether the <margin>Marks by which one shall recognize good spirits.</margin>

# Of Ghosts / The Second Part.

Whether the voice heard be lovely, pleasant, humble, harmonious, sorrowful, or instead terrifying, cruel, and harsh. Thirdly, one must observe whether the spirit says anything that is contrary to the teaching of the holy Apostles and the teachers who are approved and accepted by the Church, or against the faith, good morals, the Papal Law <note>original: "Bäpstlich Recht," referring to Canon Law</note>, the Decrees or findings of the Councils, and the authority of the holy Roman Church. Fourthly, one must diligently observe whether one perceives in its words, works, morals, and gestures any humility, recognition and confession of sins and punishment, sighing, weeping, and lamentation—or instead boasting, threatening, slandering, and blaspheming God. For just as a poor beggar recounts his deficiencies, so also do the spirits who desire help. They have other signs as well, by which one may distinguish the good spirits from the evil, but those previously recounted are the most prominent.

<margin>With what things one comes to the aid of the souls.</margin>
As far as concerns the *suffragia* <note>Latin: "suffrages," or intercessory prayers and acts of devotion</note>, or the help by which the souls are released from Purgatory, their Doctors <note>Scholastic theologians</note> also report four kinds: namely, the reading of Mass, the distribution of alms, praying, and fasting. Under these they include all others, such as going on pilgrimages, going to church, sheltering the poor, decorating churches, etc. In particular, however, they boast of how the sacrifice of the Mass has great power for the redemption of the poor souls. They recount many examples of this, and of the other parts they also have various questions regarding these matters, which whoever has the desire may read for themselves in their books.

<margin>Redeeming the souls is a good work.</margin>
They have not only taught this in their writings but have preached from all pulpits what a great, glorious, and comforting work it is when someone takes pity on the appearing souls who desire help, and faithfully takes up their cause and does that which they desire of him, so that the great pain and distress in which they find themselves may be lessened or even taken away. They claim that the souls thereafter pray most earnestly for their redeemers and benefactors. Conversely, they teach how it is such a heavy and terrifying sin when someone is sought for help—especially by father and mother, brothers and sisters—and yet does not undertake to help them. For if they could not be helped, they would not desire help so earnestly. No one should be so unmerciful that he regrets a small expense for those who placed him in honor and wealth. If these were not the souls of the deceased, but rather the Devil's phantom <note>original: "Gespenst"</note>, they would not command so much praying, fasting, and giving of alms, for the Devil is a "spider-enemy" <note>an old German idiom meaning a bitter or mortal enemy</note> to those things and to all other good works.

->What has grown out of the Papists' teaching on the appearance of souls.<-

### The Third Chapter.

Through this, they have brought the matter to the point that it is commonly held—and almost no one has doubted it—that those things which were seen and heard were the souls of the deceased, and whatever they claimed should be believed without any contradiction. Thus, the truly simple teaching of calling upon God alone through Christ, of trust in His merit and redemption, and of the truly good works of Christian love, has been increasingly darkened and suppressed. People have gradually abandoned the Holy Scripture and elevated human statutes and commands, building more upon them than upon the word of God; for almost no sin was considered as great as when someone acted against human statutes. Upon the speech and answers of these spirits, they have primarily founded Purgatory, and taught that a person may be redeemed from it through his own and other people's works and merits. This has made people careless; for if one believes he can hire or commission people to do this or that for him after death, and that it will benefit him, he has postponed or even neglected the amendment of his life. Therefore, it has happened to him as it did to the five foolish virgins in the Gospel. By this means, many Masses, images, pilgrimages, relics, monastic vows, feast days, confession, and all kinds of ceremonies—in short, everything that is outside of the Scripture—have been introduced.

# Ludwig Lavater

<note>original: "Ludouicus Lauaterus"</note>

...otherwise could not be maintained, [they] came into great and excellent standing. But all this, as is well known, many pious, simple people have spared from their own throats <note>meaning they went hungry to save money</note> so that they might support monks and priests and make offerings to images. They have founded chapels, altars, monasteries, eternal lights, anniversaries, brotherhoods, and other things, so that they might redeem their loved ones from the pain and distress of **Purgatory**. <note>original: "Fegfewr"</note> Through this, the parishes, foundations, and monasteries have increased wonderfully in wealth and income, and have drawn to themselves and acquired the best farms and estates, fisheries, serfs, jurisdictions—yes, even entire lordships, and their own stocks and gallows <note>referring to the right of high justice/capital punishment</note>. For since it was firmly believed that souls return, the majority did whatever was demanded of them.

But so that it may be understood even more clearly how much was staked upon visions and other such wonderful things, and how foundations were established, I will mention only one or two stories. **Johannes Trithemius**, Abbot of Sponheim, writes in his *Chronicle* that the feast of **All Souls' Day** <note>November 2nd</note> began to be celebrated following All Saints' Day for this reason: A monk, on his return journey from Jerusalem, stayed with a forest brother or hermit in Sicily, not far from the burning mountain **Etna**. From him, he understood that many souls were tormented in the flames of that same mountain, but were redeemed through the prayers of the faithful, which he had learned from the testimony of spirits, etc. You can also find this in **Polydore Vergil**, *On the Inventors of Things*, Book 6, Chapter 9. There you see how a feast was established based on the indications and claims of appearing spirits.

<margin>
The Feast of All Souls.
</margin>

<margin>
Origin of the Carthusian Order.
</margin>

The **Carthusian Order**, which is commonly held to be the holiest and strictest of all, also arose from almost the same cause (concerning which the monks of that same order have themselves published a printed book). At the high school in Paris (around the year of our Lord 1080, as Polydore Vergil testifies), a famous Doctor, renowned for his art and pious conduct, passed away. When they wished to bury him in a church, he cried out with a terrifying voice: "I am accused by the righteous judgment of God." Thus, they left the coffin standing, for a great crowd had gathered. On the second day thereafter, he cried: "I am judged by the righteous judgment of God." On the third day: "I am damned by the righteous judgment of God." Some, like **Vincent of Beauvais**, improve the story and say that he sat up in his coffin for the third time. Since, however, no one had believed that this famous, excellent man should be lost, everyone was terrified. **Bruno**, a native of Cologne and a Master of Theology, immediately left everything and moved with six God-fearing men, his companions, into a wasteland or wilderness called **Carthusia**, located in the Diocese of Grenoble. He began to build the first monastery of this Order there, and this Order was thereafter named the Carthusian Order after that place. Many other monasteries were also initially founded for such reasons or otherwise richly endowed.

### The Fourth Chapter.

<margin>
Souls go to heaven or to hell.

<margin>
Souls go immediately to heaven or to hell.

**B**ut that neither the souls of the faithful nor the unfaithful wander here and there after a person has died may be understood from the following arguments or grounds. It is certain that people depart from this time either in true Christian faith or in unbelief. Those who depart from here in true faith, their souls immediately attain eternal life; those who die in unbelief immediately enter eternal damnation. Souls do not turn to dust, nor are they everywhere, and much less do body and soul perish together. Concerning these points, we wish to hear the manifold and sufficient testimony of Holy Scripture.

In the third chapter of John, our Lord Jesus himself speaks, who may know best of it: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son..."

### Testimony of the ancient holy Fathers that the souls of the deceased do not wander upon the earth.

### The Fifth Chapter.

The pious ancient Fathers also understood this matter in this way. For St. Augustine speaks in his book on the words of the Apostle in the 18th Sermon: There are two dwellings, one in eternal fire, the other in the eternal kingdom. <margin>Augustine.</margin>

In his magnificent work *The City of God*, chapter 8 in the 13th book, he says: The souls of the believers who are separated from the body are at rest; but those of the ungodly are punished, until the souls of the believers are made alive again for eternal life, and those of the unbelievers for eternal death (which is called the second death).

Justin, an ancient teacher, writes in *Response to the Orthodox*, question 75: After the souls depart from the body, there will be an immediate distinction between the righteous and the unrighteous. <margin>Justin.</margin>

As far as the souls of the ancients before the birth of Christ are concerned, the Holy Fathers—such as Augustine, Jerome, Nazianzen, etc.—teach that the Lord God kept all those who departed from this world in true faith and relied upon the promised Savior in places and ends where it pleased Him, without pain; yet they were deprived of the Divine countenance. ->The objections of those who believe the souls of the deceased appear are refuted. And first, an answer is given to those who say that God is almighty and can therefore act against the common order.<-

### The Sixth Chapter.

First they say: it is indeed true that according to the common order, the souls of the believers remain in heaven and the damned in hell until the Last Day, and wander nowhere. But is it not possible for God the Lord to grant a dispensation <note>a special exemption from the rule</note> so that souls might occasionally appear to teach or warn people? After all, Samuel appeared to King Saul after his death; Moses, who had died long ago; and Elijah, who had departed in the fiery chariot, appeared to the Lord Christ and the three disciples on Mount Tabor. Lazarus of Bethany also came back from his rest. Likewise others whom our Lord Christ, his Apostles, and before them some of the holy prophets, raised from the dead. Furthermore, the graves were opened when our Lord Christ hung on the Cross, and afterward, on the day of his resurrection, those who lay therein appeared to some believing people. They also point out that the disciples of our Lord Christ believed a spirit or soul appeared to them, whether they understood it to be Christ's or another's. Beyond this, they bring forward the opinions of the ancient Fathers, the Councils, and the common saying of how some have returned. To these grounds I will, with God's help, answer one after another.

<margin>The basis for those who think souls return.</margin>

The first thing put forward is that all things are possible for God. We are not at all against that. It is not impossible that God could summon souls from heaven or from hell to wherever he wished, and use them to teach, comfort, warn, or punish men; but since we have no place or example in the Scripture where any have come from the dead who taught or warned other people in that manner, or that the believers learned or inquired anything from the soul of a deceased person, we cannot build upon it.

# Concerning Ghosts / The Second Part.

<columns>
one should not conclude everything from the omnipotence of God. He does not act against His word, nor against Himself. Prove that He wills for souls to appear in such a form. Saint Tertullian says in *Against Praxeas* <note>original: "contra Praxeam"</note>, God cannot do that which He does not do—not that He could not do it if He willed, but that He does not will it; and He does not will it because it is not fitting. Saint Ambrose writes to Chromatius in *Epistle book 6, Epistle 37*: "What is impossible for Him? That which conflicts with His nature. It is impossible for Him to lie." This impossibility is not a weakness, but a power and majesty, etc. Saint Jerome writes to Eustochium in *On the Guarding of Virginity* <note>original: "de Custodia virginitatis"</note>, "I speak plainly: although all things are possible for God, He cannot bring it to pass that a woman who has fallen should be a pure maiden." Saint Augustine says in *The City of God* <note>original: "de Civitate Dei"</note> book 5, chapter 10: "God's power is not diminished when one says He cannot die, or cannot be deceived. Therefore, He cannot do certain things precisely because He is omnipotent," etc. Theodoret also says that one should speak of God's omnipotence with distinction; otherwise, one would have to say He could commit sin and injustice, etc. Therefore, it is not a valid argument to say, "God can send souls to warn and teach men, therefore these are souls seeking help."

<margin>One should not learn from the dead.</margin>
Hear what our God and Lord says in Deuteronomy, chapter 18: "When you come into the land which the Lord your God will give you, you shall not learn to do the abominations of these nations, so that there be not found among you anyone who makes his son or daughter pass through the fire, or a soothsayer, or an observer of times, or one who heeds the cries of birds, or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or a medium, or a fortune-teller, or one who consults the dead. For whoever does such things is an abomination before the Lord, and because of such abominations the Lord your God has driven them out before you. But you shall be steadfast and upright before the Lord your God." Thereupon He promises them a Prophet whom they shall hear.

<margin>Deut. 18.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 8.</margin>
The holy Prophet Isaiah speaks in the 8th chapter: "If they say to you, O my disciples, children of God: 'Consult the fortune-tellers and the sorcerers, the

bird-diviners, and the charmers,' then answer them: 'Is there then any people that does not consult its God? Should one run to the dead on behalf of the living?' But whoever lacks light, let him look to the Law and the testimony; if they do not speak according to this word," etc.

From this we understand well that God the Lord has explicitly, earnestly, and under great penalty forbidden us from investigating or learning anything from the dead: He Himself wishes to be our more-than-sufficient teacher. In the Holy Gospel it is written: "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them believe them." Thus, God does not send souls to teach us. The common and orderly way through which God wishes to deal with us is His word and Revelation; let it remain at that. Therefore, we should let ourselves be satisfied and hold to the Divine word alone, accepting nothing that does not have its good foundation therein. More will follow on this in the final part.

### The Seventh Chapter.

<margin>II. Some say Samuel returned.</margin>
As far as this example is concerned, which is cited by those who believe that the souls of the departed return to the living on Earth, I will first take up the appearance of Samuel (about which there is much dispute) and demonstrate and prove with good, strong reasons that it was not the true Samuel in body and soul, nor his body which had long since decayed, nor his soul alone, but rather the Devil’s ghost.

Firstly, it stands in the text that Saul consulted the Lord, but He did not answer him, neither through dreams, nor through the Urim <note>sacred lots used by ancient Hebrew priests</note>, nor through the prophets. Since He did not wish to answer him (whom He had rejected) through the living prophets or through other orderly ways, it is well to be presumed that He would much less allow a prophet who had died to return to give an answer. Especially since He earnestly forbade in Deuteronomy 18 (as cited before) that one should learn from the dead or investigate the truth from them. He also does not wish that one should deal with necro-

# Ludwig Lavater

Dealing with necromancy <note>original: "Necromanty"</note> and other such forbidden devilish arts.

Secondly, if the true Samuel had come, it must have happened either through the will of God or through the power and effect of the black art <term>black art: magic or sorcery involving communication with the dead</term>. Now, God did not will it, for He has earnestly forbidden the searching and questioning of the dead, as well as the black art, in His word; the Holy Spirit would have done nothing against this, nor allowed His saints to do so, nor helped those who acted against it. Thus, we cannot say that it was brought about through the evil art. For the evil enemy has no power over the souls of the faithful, who are in the hand of God and in the bosom of Abraham <note>A biblical reference to the place of rest for the righteous dead</note>, that he might pull them down or up how and when he wishes. He does not even have power—if I may mention it with your favor—over a stinking sow. For when he wished to enter into the swine, as it stands in the Gospel, he first had to take permission from Christ; why then should he have power over the soul of a pious man? It is not denied that God the Lord at times permits the Devil and his servants, the sorcerers and hags <note>original: "Vnholden"</note>, much for certain reasons, such as making people and cattle go lame and performing wonderful, unbelievable things. But that God should permit and allow the Devil to awaken corpses, or to force or bring souls—especially from Heaven—back to Earth, I find no example of this anywhere in the entire Holy Scripture. Nor can any sufficient reason be shown for why God the Lord should or would have allowed the Devil such a thing against His general order and earnest prohibition. For what some say—that He did it to terrify Saul—seems to me to be too trivial. Could He not have terrified him through any other means?

Thirdly, such a thing must have happened either with Samuel's will or against his will. That he willingly obeyed the hags, no one can say, since it is against God's command to give counsel or deed to the black art. And if he had been called by the hags during his life, he would not have gone to them; who then would believe that he followed them after his death? Thus, she could not have forced him. For the Devil has no claim upon holy souls, and the black art has no power in itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>Words have no power in themselves.</margin>
That words, when spoken in a particular way, or characters <note>written symbols or sigils</note>, have a wonderful secret power, is a superstitious and heathen thing. For the heathens believed they could lure Jupiter <note>original: "Iouem"</note> out of heaven with certain words, or (as we call it) compel him. Therefore they called him *Elicius* <note>Latin: "The Elicited," an epithet for Jupiter when summoned by magic</note>. Many superstitious people today undertake to heal diseases with conjurations and blessings, or by hanging a slip of paper around the neck in which wonderful words are written. Whether words have an effect in themselves, read Pliny, book 28, chapter 2, and Ludovicus Caelius, *Ancient Readings*, book 16, chapter 16.

Fourthly, if the true Samuel had appeared, he would not have allowed himself to be worshipped by Saul. For in the Revelation of John, in chapters 19 and 22, it stands that he—the holy Apostle and Evangelist—wished to worship the angel who revealed such great mysteries to him, but the angel would not permit it. Here some say that Saul did not wish to show the prophet divine honor, but only outward honor, as is customary toward honorable and well-deserving people. For the Hebrew word *Schachach* <note>original: "שָׁחָה" (shachah)</note> means to bow or fall at someone's feet; and we read that Abigail and Nathan the prophet showed such honor to David (2 Kings 1), and Paul teaches in Romans 12 that one should show honor to another. Thomas Aquinas himself writes on the cited passage from the Revelation of John that he wished to worship the angel with *Dulia* not *Latria* <term>Dulia vs Latria: Dulia is the veneration given to saints/angels; Latria is the worship reserved for God alone</term>; that is, he did not wish to show him divine but only outward honor as a noble messenger of God, yet the angel still did not allow it. In the New Testament, you read in Acts 10 that Cornelius went to meet Peter and fell at his feet, and was...

Fifthly, if it had been the true Samuel, he would have undoubtedly exhorted him to repentance and improvement; he would have told him to wait for God’s help and to trust Him well, or would have otherwise spoken a friendly word and given good counsel, so that he might have been more comforted against the enemies of God’s people and fought more manfully. <margin>Tertullian.</margin>
Sixthly, the holy ancient Fathers also indicate that it was not the true Samuel. The holy Tertullian writes in his book *On the Soul* <note>Latin: *De Anima*</note> on page 687: The Devil passed himself off as Samuel’s soul. He would say he was God himself and would perform even greater signs to destroy the elect, if it were possible, etc.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>

He cites the example of Samuel, who told Saul what would happen to him; yet he adds thereafter that one may understand that passage in another way as well, and that other believers have understood the passage differently. In other places, he insists (as will partly follow) that it is a way of speaking, as when one gives the name of the person to the image that represents them, and that it was not the true Samuel, but a ghost <note>original: "Gespenst," implying a demonic phantom</note> of the devil.

<margin>Rabbis.</margin>
The Jewish Rabbis write on one hand that it was the true Samuel, and on the other that it was merely a ghost; but their testimony, even if they all said it was the true Samuel, should trouble us little. For they are poor, blind people to whom God has given a perverted mind, and who wander in the Holy Scripture like one who has lost his way in a great forest, and they have great and absurd fables in their books.

### The Eighth Chapter.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 46.</margin>
**N**ow we also wish to dismiss the objections and counter-arguments of those who hold that it was the real Samuel. For whoever accounts well for the grounds of his opponent also confirms his own case thereby.

The foremost argument put forward against the aforementioned opinion is taken from the 46th chapter of Ecclesiasticus, or Jesus Sirach <note>A book of the Apocrypha</note>, where it is written: Samuel testified before his end, before he died, before the Lord and his anointed, that he had taken money from no man, nor even a shoe, and no man could accuse him of anything. And when he had fallen asleep <note>A common biblical metaphor for death</note>, he prophesied and announced to the King his end, and let himself be heard out of the earth, and prophesied that the godless people should perish. This testimony somewhat troubled St. Augustine and other pious, holy Fathers. For if the Devil alone appeared, how can it say he had "fallen asleep," that is, died? The Devil does not sleep or die. Here I might point out that the book is not one of the true primary books <note>The Biblical Canon</note> from which disputed articles of doctrine should be confirmed, as St. Augustine also admits in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead* <note>original: "lib. de Cura pro mortuis agenda"</note>. But be that as it may, Sirach only intended to cite the history according to the letter, and did not involve himself in disputing whether it was truly Samuel or not. He speaks as Saul intended it, and as the witch herself believed.

Furthermore, they say that the one who appeared to Saul

<column-break/>

is several times clearly and expressly named Samuel. Now, this would be an injustice and would serve as a disgrace to the holy Prophet if his name were given to the Devil. If it were not Samuel, but the Devil, then the Scripture would have mentioned it somewhere with a word.

To this, I first give this answer: <term>Metonymy</term> <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it, or a representation is called by the name of the original</note>. It is common even in our daily speech that we use a metonymy to name an image after that which it portrays. Thus, we also name a coat of arms after its lord. You say, "That is Julius Caesar, Nero, or St. Peter, St. Paul"; or, "That is Zurich, Strasbourg, the Duke of Zähringen," and they are only their images or shield and helmet. In a play, you call one Saul, the other Samuel, the third David, who only represent their persons. Thus it also stands in Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 1: they wondered at the gifts of Aeneas and at his son Iulus.

> They marvel at the gifts of Aeneas, they marvel at Iulus. <note>original: "Mirantur dona Aeneae, mirantur Iulum."</note>

And yet it was not Iulus, but Cupid who passed himself off as Iulus, or had taken on his form. St. Augustine also writes in the 2nd book of *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture* <note>original: "de Mirab. sacrae scripturae"</note>, in the 9th chapter, that Holy Scripture gives the names of the true and essential things themselves to the likenesses of those things. He cites exactly this example: that the unclean spirit is called Samuel because he passed himself off as him. This brings no disadvantage to Samuel at all; for should it be a reproach to a pious man if a rogue names himself after him or passes himself off as him? The Devil himself sometimes passes himself off as God. The false prophets often presented themselves as servants and prophets of God, indeed, sometimes as the Son of God, the Messiah himself. But the fact that Holy Scripture leaves the people in their delusion, as if it were Samuel himself, and does not mention in passing that it was a ghost <note>original: "gespenst"</note>, happens because everyone should have known beforehand from the Law that the black arts <note>original: "Schwarzkunst"</note> and the questioning of the dead were forbidden. King Saul himself, doubtless at the instigation of the pious Samuel, had previously driven out and rooted out such people.

# Concerning Spirits / The Second Part.

So God has a custom of interpreting figurative speech in such a way. For they are commonly well understood.

Accordingly, the Scripture has the custom of sometimes speaking of things according to the understanding, opinion, and judgment of men, and not as they are in themselves. For example, Jesus is called a son of Joseph, and Joseph is called a father of Jesus, yet our Lord Jesus was born of a pure virgin without the involvement of a man; nevertheless, many Jews held Jesus to be Joseph’s son. In 1 Corinthians chapter 1, the Gospel is called a "foolishness," because the world reckoned or held the greatest wisdom to be foolishness. The Scripture calls those "gods" who were actually nothing of the sort (1 Corinthians 10), because the heathens held them to be gods and saviors. <note>The author refers to the biblical practice of "phenomenological language"—describing things as they appear to human observers rather than their divine essence.</note> Thus the Scripture here uses the words as Saul had them in his heart, who knew no differently than that it was Samuel.

<margin>Jeremiah 10. Psalm 96.</margin>

But they say: he predicted future things to him—that his army would be defeated by the Philistines and that he would perish along with his sons. All of this truly came to pass. Since future things stay in God’s hand alone, the evil enemy <note>The Devil</note> cannot know or predict them. He is, as it says in John 8, a liar and the father of lies. To this, it is not difficult to answer. The Devil knew how all things stood with the Jews and the Philistines. He knew the secret plots and war preparations of both parties. He saw that the Israelites were poorly positioned and were altogether terrified. Additionally, just as Samuel during his lifetime had threatened Saul with God’s disfavor and punishment, and had anointed David as king in his place, the Devil could easily deduce how it would go and that Saul must give way to David. And even if it had turned out another way, he knew that with such a prophecy he would take away Saul’s joy and courage and bring him completely into despair, which is what the Devil pursues day and night.

<margin>Whether the Devil knows future things.</margin>

The Devil does not know future things fundamentally; therefore, when the oracles were questioned, he gave such answers that could be interpreted and understood in two ways. Yet he can deduce one thing from another and guess something. Augustine writes of this in *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note> chapters 26, 27, and 28. The evil enemy has great experience and practice, which brings much to light in all things. Just as one sees with old, experienced people, who see immediately where a thing is heading, which the young and inexperienced cannot contemplate as well. Furthermore, the devils are very quick and agile. A sailor knows when a wind is about to pick up; a farmer also has his marks and signs of the weather; an experienced astronomer can indicate a year and a day in advance when and how the sun and moon will be eclipsed; a physician has his <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "dies criticos" — specific days in the course of a disease when a change for better or worse is expected</note>, the pulse, urine, and other signs by which he sees whether he should estimate a person's life or not. A carpenter or mason sees when a house is about to fall; an experienced soldier sees immediately which side will capture the victory. Should it then be a wonder if the thousand-fold cunning Satan also occasionally guesses or prophesies something? He also sometimes tells a truth solely so that he may give his lies all the more prestige.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, this "Samuel" acts as if he is reluctant for Saul to disturb him and that he must speak with him, and he masterfully uses the words of Samuel. From this, many conclude it was the true Samuel. But what can the Devil not do to seduce men and bring them to despair? One could show examples where some knew no differently than that they had seen or heard this or that person and recognized them by their voice, where it was afterwards found that the same person was not in the country at all, but many miles from that very place. The Devil can do much of that sort of thing.

That certain passages from the writings of some ancient Fathers are cited, which are intended to provide evidence that the true Samuel appeared to King Saul, has partly been heard before. Although St. Augustine in some places expresses a doubt as to whether it was the true Samuel, in other places he sides with those who do not hold it to be so.

<margin>Justin.</margin>
Justin <note>Justin Martyr, c. 100–165 AD</note>, who was one of the oldest and a Greek, writes in his dialogue that he held with Trypho the Jew, that Samuel's soul was called forth at Saul's command by the female soothsayer. But do not let that lead you astray; for immediately after that he says, in his opinion, all souls of the prophets and the righteous were subject to such powers, as one sees in the deed this soothsayer performed. None of the other Fathers would concede that to him. There have also been other Greeks who, from their youth, were occupied with Philosophy rather than Holy Scripture, but later became Christian teachers, who held some opinions that are not in accordance with God's word. Therefore, it is no wonder that this man also stumbles in some things. Furthermore, this same Justin writes in *Responsio ad orthodoxos* <note>original: "Response to the Orthodox," a work formerly attributed to Justin</note> question 52, the opposite: that what was handled by this soothsayer happened through the devil's help, who so blinded the eyes of the onlookers that it seemed to them they saw Samuel, though it was not him. Shortly thereafter: The truth of the words came from God, who permitted the devil to appear to the soothsayer in Samuel's form and to indicate what should happen; for He did not deem him <note>Saul</note> worthy to be shown what was to come through His own people.

<margin>The *Responses to the Orthodox* are not by Justin.</margin>
But if the learned wish to say that this book attributed to Justin is not his—because he cites Origen in it and mentions the Manicheans, who lived after his time—I say: even if it is not by Justin, it is nonetheless by another magnificent learned man, as this work of his testifies, and his writing should count for more in this case than Justin's, as it stays closer to the Scripture. Thus, we set against Justin other holy Fathers who taught from the Scripture that it was not Samuel, such as St. Tertullian and Chrysostom, of whom mention was made above. Regarding St. Gregory, it will follow hereafter that he was indeed pious and learned, but too simple for the guileful, evil world.

<column-break/>

When the holy Fathers speak without the foundation of Scripture, they say themselves that one should not believe them. The Pope has placed into Canon Law, from the sayings of St. Augustine (9. c. *Noli*), that one should believe no Fathers unless they prove their case from the Scripture. Now, many suck only errors out of their books, and that which they say with good scriptural grounds, they let go; they act just like children who only mimic their pious parents in their bad habits. For even pious people have their failures and defects.

->Whether the devil may appear to someone in the form of a pious deceased person.<-

### The Ninth Chapter.

If you ask: can the evil spirit take the form of a deceased, pious, holy person and appear to someone in it? You should not doubt it. For St. Paul says in 2 Corinthians chapter 11 <note>The text says 12, but the reference is 2 Cor 11:14</note>: Satan can transform himself into an angel of light. Satan is a spirit by his nature. He is also called an "angel" because God also sends him out to accomplish something. For the word "Angel" is Greek and means as much as a "messenger." Thus, an evil angel was sent out to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all the prophets of Ahab to destroy him. He was an angel of darkness and error, yet he could present himself as if he were a spirit of truth and light, and he governed the council of those same priests, who without doubt claimed they were assembled in the holy spirit (1 Kings, last chapter). If the devil can do that, should he then not be able to appear in the form of a pious man, speak like him, and do other such things? Among the heathens, he played wonderful games; he brought them to the point that they believed one could, through black arts and sorcery, force souls to appear and learn of future things from them: for this reason, they ran after black-magicians and hags, not only in common matters but also in particularly difficult affairs.

# Concerning Ghosts / The Second Part.

To call forth souls from Hell or from the other world through the black arts <note>original: "schwartze Kunst"; referring to necromancy</note>, he calls the second form of idolatry. For just as in idolatry the devils act as if they were gods, so here they also give themselves out to be the deceased. The devil takes on a body or a form and plays his game. He says further: it is not difficult for the devil to deceive the outward eyes, since he is also able to blind the inner sight. For Pharaoh and the Egyptians believed the rods of the black artists were the bodies of dragons, but the truth of Moses swallowed up the lies. Simon and Elymas the sorcerers also undertook much against the holy Apostles. He writes that even in his day the followers of Simon <note>The Simonians, a Gnostic sect</note> were so bold that they dared to promise they would bring back the souls of the Prophets from the underworld <note>original: "ab Inferis"</note> through their art, etc.

Lactantius writes in *The Origin of Error*, book 2, chapter 17: the evil spirits hide themselves under the names of the dead and spread nets for the living; that is, they give themselves out to be this person or that—for Jove, for Juno, whom the heathens honored as gods—or now for St. Sebastian, St. Barbara, or St. Alexius. In Book 7, chapter 13, he writes that the black artists call forth souls from Hell through sorcery so that they may be seen. Not that it was the opinion of Lactantius that they truly have the power to do so, but rather they say: "this is this or that soul," etc. He indicates that the soul is immortal, which is exactly what their black artists say as well.

Justin, in his *Second Apology for the Christians*, says the evil spirits have deceived women and children by appearing to them, and have terrified men through great wonders so that they held them to be gods. Shortly thereafter he says to the heathens: they should never think that souls are immortal, yet they should believe their black artists who claim they call forth souls, and those who say they are plagued by souls, etc. You will also find such things in Augustine’s *The City of God*.

What wonderful, terrifying ceremonies and superstitious ways they use when they wish to bring forth souls through

<column-break/>

their forbidden arts, you will find in Lucan’s 6th book, where he describes how Erichtho raises one from the dead to please Sextus Pompey, so that he might learn from him what the outcome of the present war—the Pharsalian War <note>original: "bellum Pharsalicum"</note>—would be. This sorcery is called Necromancy <term>Necromantia: divination by conjuring the dead</term> or Psychomancy <term>Psychomantia: the calling up of spirits or souls</term>, which consisted of more than one kind: sometimes the corpses of the deceased appeared entirely, sometimes only as a shadow, and sometimes one heard only a dark voice.

Plutarch writes in the *Life of Cimon* that when Pausanias conquered Byzantium (later called Constantinople), he sent for the noble daughter of an honorable citizen to fulfill his wanton lust with her; her parents, out of fear, dared not oppose him. The daughter prevailed upon his chamberlains to extinguish the light, and as she went silently in the dark to Pausanias's bed, she accidentally stumbled over the lampstand; he woke up, thinking nothing else than that an enemy was coming for him, drew his sword or dagger, and killed the good daughter. Afterward, she appeared to him in a dream, left him no peace, and threatened him that he must receive his earned reward. Therefore, he later traveled to Heraclea to the Oracle where souls are called forth, and when he brought forth her soul, he attempted to appease her. Then she appeared to him and said: when he came to Sparta, nothing more of these things would happen to him, nor would they make him restless. This Pausanias had previously conducted himself quite honorably and well, but afterward he became arrogant over his victories and acted tyrannically; for this reason, he was walled up and died shortly thereafter in prison. One might cite such histories to understand the nature of the raising of Samuel <note>A reference to the Witch of Endor summoning the prophet Samuel in the Bible</note>. In other things, the evil enemy also has great power, if God permits him such; he lacks nothing in skill.

# Ludwig Lavater

Even if it were granted (which the Scriptures do not allow) that God the Lord had permitted Samuel himself to return and prophesy of future things, should it therefore follow that even today such apparitions occur? Or that one should believe and do exactly what they claim? In former times, God the Lord often and frequently sent his angels to the world in visible form; now you do not hear of many being sent to men in this way, nor is it necessary. In the times of the holy Apostles, great wonders and signs occurred, but afterwards, for certain reasons, they ceased. For as much as is necessary for us to know, we have God's word. So much shall be said regarding Samuel.

<margin>Moses and Elijah appeared to the Lord on the mountain: many have come from the dead with body and soul, therefore souls may also return.</margin>

### The Tenth Chapter.

<margin>III. Moses and Elijah appeared to Christ.</margin>

Furthermore, it is cited that Moses and Elijah appeared—as in Matthew chapter 17—on Mount Tabor <note>The traditional site of the Transfiguration</note> with the Lord, to the holy Apostles whom he had called there, and were seen by them; they also spoke with the Lord Christ. Saint Luke reports what they conversed about with him, namely his departure, or his suffering and death. Therefore, the souls of the deceased may return to earth and appear. We have previously admitted that God could send souls back to earth; but whether it is his will, and whether necessity demands it now, would require much more discussion. Moses and Elijah appeared only to the three, not to all the Apostles, nor to anyone else; they did not speak with the Apostles themselves, nor did they command them to build churches in their honor or do anything else of the kind. It was of great importance that those who were to be Christ's witnesses thoroughly understood that the Law and the Prophets gave testimony to Christ our Lord—that he would die for us, and at the end of the world return, awaken the bodies from the dead, glorify <term>clarificieren</term> <note>from the Latin 'clarificare', meaning to make bright or glorious in a theological sense</note> them, and lead them into eternal glory and joy. Therefore, Christ allowed these two magnificent prophets to appear.

<column-break/>

<margin>IV. Lazarus returned.</margin>

Lazarus, as it stands in John chapter 11, returned with body and soul; it was not his soul alone that appeared. This is a testimony of our true resurrection from the dead, which will happen on the Last Day. Just as others were raised by the Lord Christ, by his holy Apostles, and in ancient times by holy prophets. But it is nowhere written that Lazarus or others said where they had been, or how it had been for them in the meantime, or what kind of existence is there. For we should learn and know that from the holy Divine word, not from the dead.

<margin>V. On Easter Day several arose and appeared.</margin>

The same may be said of what is written in the history of Christ's passion, Matthew 27: namely, how when Christ expired on the cross, the graves opened, and subsequently on the day of resurrection the dead arose with the Lord and appeared to many in the city of Jerusalem. It was not the souls of the deceased alone that appeared, warning those still living or telling them to do this or that for the benefit of the dead—such as praying for them, going on pilgrimages, etc.—but rather they returned with body and soul. For by this our Lord Christ wished to testify that through his death he had overcome death for his believers and made it powerless, and that on the Last Day their body and soul would come together again and be with God eternally.

<margin>Whether the holy Apostles thought they saw a soul when Christ appeared to them unexpectedly after his resurrection.</margin>

In the Gospel of Luke chapter 24, it is written how the two disciples came from Emmaus and told the holy Apostles how they had seen the Lord Jesus; in that moment the Lord stood in the midst of them and said: "Peace be with you." They were terribly frightened by him and thought they saw a spirit, etc. By this, some attempt to maintain that the Apostles believed that spirits or souls wander and appear to men. When the ancients spoke of someone who was away from the land or dead, saying if they saw or heard something, "it is his spirit," it may well be that they did not mean his soul, but rather his angels. However, if they meant the soul—as has become the common belief in the meantime, whenever a spirit is seen here or there—then they were in error, as they were in many other things. For souls go immediately to either blessedness or damnation. Had the priests taught them correctly, or had they let them read the Holy Scriptures themselves, they would have held the correct belief regarding these and other matters.

<margin>Concerning the Holy Fathers, Councils, Popes, and the common man to whom souls appeared.</margin>

### Chapter Twelve.

<margin>VII. The Fathers say that souls appear.</margin>

Furthermore, certain passages from the Holy Fathers are brought up against us, such as what Saint Ambrose writes of Saint Agnes, or Saint Augustine of Saint Felix, which were mentioned above. Saint Gregory, in his *Dialogues*, cites many wonderful things, and especially many examples of the dead who are said to have appeared, and how they or their souls recounted strange things and desired help. He also describes how some of the holy Apostles themselves, and others, came to those lying on their deathbeds, and other such things which anyone may read for themselves. Some write that Saint Jerome appeared to Saint Augustine.

Now, I would never deny the holy and pious Fathers and other honorable people. Yet, they do not say that those who appeared were definitely the souls themselves, but rather they speak according to common usage. As far as Gregory’s *Dialogues* are concerned, I must mention—as others have done before me—that he writes much in them that does not seem at all consistent with the truth. Yet the good, pious Father did not do this out of malice, but rather because he believed others too easily and described many things more from hearsay than from having a thorough knowledge of them. Just as one still finds many

<margin>The *Dialogues* of Gregory the Great.</margin>

<column-break/>

pious, honorable people who believe too quickly and allow themselves to be led by others. They feel they would be greatly ashamed if they suggested to someone that there was nothing to a story; they expect to be treated with the same trust, but their simplicity is abused, and they are sometimes badly burned <note>i.e., deceived or discredited</note> for it. Accordingly, in the time of Gregory, people began to give great credence to such appearances. At that same time, the true, simple teaching also began to fade significantly; it matters a great deal in what era a person lived. He himself confessed that his times were the "latter days," for which reason he should have clung more diligently to the Holy Scriptures and believed nothing without them. Some excuse him by saying he filled his *Dialogues* with miracles so that perhaps the hardened hearts of the Lombards <note>original: "Lamparten"</note> might be softened by such examples and become more inclined toward the true religion, which they were so fiercely persecuting at that hour. But that it is neither good nor fruitful to describe such things without any foundation, or to attempt to support the faith in such a manner, is also noted by Ludovicus Vives in *On the Handing Down of Disciplines* <note>original: "de Tradendis diſcip."</note>, Book 5.

Some also cite the Councils, which have approved and confirmed some appearances of souls, as well as the books written about them; some they permitted to be read by the simple-minded for edification alone, while others they rejected entirely.

<margin>VIII. Councils have confirmed that souls have appeared.</margin>

Regarding the Council of Constance <note>original: "Coſtenz"</note>, it is said that it confirmed this appearance: That a Dean gave up his dignity and went into the wilderness to lead a life of penance. After his death, he appeared to his Bishop and informed him that in the hour he passed away, thirty thousand other people had died, among whom only his soul and that of Saint Bernard were saved; three went into Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfewr"</note>, and all the rest into eternal damnation, etc. Now, they argue that the Councils and the Church cannot err, for they are governed by the Holy Spirit. The Lord also says in Matthew 24: In the last times, wonders and signs shall occur, so that if it were possible, [even the elect would be deceived].

# Of Specters / The Second Part
<note>original: "von Gespensten/der ander Theil."</note>

likely, even the elect would be led astray. And yet, it is not the meaning that God's elect cannot be led into error (for one can show the opposite with many noble examples), but rather that they do not persist or remain therein, although they shall escape only with difficulty. Who attended the ancient Councils? Did not the holy Fathers attend them? Now, the pious ancient Fathers have written against one another in many points, and sometimes even against themselves; therefore, they were not always in the right. They themselves constantly point us toward the infallible Word of God. The ancient Councils failed in several articles, as one could prove with many examples. The Council of Rimini <note>A 4th-century council that briefly favored Arianism</note> gave right to the Arians <note>original: "Arrianern"; followers of Arius who denied the full divinity of Christ</note>; the second Council of Ephesus to Eutyches <note>original: "Euticheti"; a monk who taught that Christ had only one nature</note>. Likewise, in the Council held by Cyprian at Carthage, errors were also made, etc. What then must have happened since then, as one well knows from history, regarding those who have overseen the Councils for several hundred years, who governed them, and what was primarily dealt with? Likewise, what for the most part followed immediately upon them? If the ancient Councils could err, should it then be a wonder if those held until now erred? But as far as the appearances are concerned—letting other things fall away and writing of them alone—dear friend, who would tell the Council whether this or that appearance truly happened? For no Council can make a truth out of a lie.

<margin>
IX.
The Popes confirm the appearances of souls.
</margin>
It is just as foolish when people say the Pope (who wishes to be above the Councils) has confirmed this or that miracle that is said to have happened in a monastery. For how should he know it better in Rome, so many miles away, than others who are resident in those very places? I hear it well: if the Pope says this or that soul has appeared—of which he can know nothing, except that certain partisan people write to him for the sake of their own profit, perhaps to arrange a pilgrimage or something else—then one must believe it. And when others who have a grounding in the matter testify to the contrary, must that count for nothing? Dear friend, consider the matter: previously everyone doubted a thing, but once it is confirmed, or if it is otherwise revealed to a spiritual person in a dream, then one is supposed to doubt it no longer.

As far as other persons are concerned, who have seen this or that individual distinctly after their death, standing and walking, heard them speak, and recognized them: I readily concede they have seen and heard something, so that they knew no differently than that they were human souls, and they themselves spoke with them. But that it follows they were therefore souls, I do not concede; much less what some think, that some have appeared to them with both body and soul. For only on the Last Day shall souls return to their bodies. Souls are spirits; spirits are invisible unless they take on some outward form. Therefore, one cannot see souls in this way: for that they take on forms as the good and evil angels do, one does not find that in the Scriptures. Moreover, it is certain that one often sees the forms of those from whom the soul has not yet departed through death (such as when one lies on his deathbed) standing and walking just as well as those who have died and passed away; therefore, these must not necessarily be the souls of the deceased.

Many say that certain acquaintances appeared to them.

one of which is the most common and prominent: that no one may enter Heaven unless they are purified of all their sins. Now, sin clings to us even unto the grave. If one points out to them <note>the proponents of Purgatory</note> that purity does not come from our life or suffering, but that God makes us pious and righteous solely through faith in His Son (who is our only redemption, righteousness, satisfaction, and payment for our sins), they then say that faith is imperfect within us. Indeed, even the most pious complain when they are to depart from here that their faith is not as firm and fervent as it ought to be. Therefore, they argue, God cannot place such a person directly into Heaven; yet, because he still possesses faith, He cannot cast him into Hell. Thus, there is now a middle place called Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfewr"</note>, where souls are purified and improved by fire from the imperfection remaining at death, and are redeemed through the merits of the living and through indulgences. But does this not attribute to our suffering and to temporal fire that which should be attributed solely to the suffering of Christ? Does the Lord Christ not teach us, when we feel the weakness of our faith, to say with the Apostles: *Lord, increase our faith*? <note>Luke 17:5</note> Will God then not hear the prayer of His believers, especially when they lie in the throes of death? God the Lord wishes to save us not because of the worthiness of our faith, but out of pure grace, which is communicated to us through faith. Just as if a rich man distributed food and drink out of grace, and one received it in a wooden vessel, another in an earthen one, and a third in a silver or golden vessel; or if a lord threw out money where one with a withered hand receives it just as well as another with a healthy hand. Saint Paul admonishes the Thessalonians in the 1st Epistle, Chapter 4, that they should not mourn like the heathens for their dead; if there were a Purgatory, he could not have been against such mourning, even if they had behaved poorly, etc. Other arguments introduced for the maintenance of Purgatory were long ago by many

<column-break/>

learned men so thoroughly refuted that one might wonder how anyone would dare to bring them forth again. But if there is no Purgatory, then souls cannot come from there and manifest themselves.

<margin>Whether unbaptized children appear.</margin>
Regarding the fourth place, namely that of the innocent little children, the Papists <note>a term used by Reformers for Roman Catholics</note> cannot well say that they return and appear to people to beg for help; for they teach that because they depart without Baptism <note>original: "Tauff"</note>, they must be eternally deprived of the face of God, and should not even be buried among other Christian people. Oh, how many miserable and sorrowful hearts have been made for many pious mothers by this! And yet they have nothing from Holy Scripture to support this, which does not attribute so much to the outward Baptism performed with water. Should the children in the Old Testament have fared better than those in the New? Now, it stands nowhere that the ancients held that a child who might not live to the eighth day so that it could be circumcised would therefore never see God's face in eternity. The holy King and Prophet David himself says he would go to his child, whom God called out of this time before it was circumcised. Now, it was not David's meaning that he wanted to go to a place where he would never see God's face in eternity; but to dispute much on this point does not serve my purpose. And so I have answered the most prominent indications and objections of those who believe the souls of the good and the evil sometimes manifest themselves to people after they have been separated from the body by death.

<margin>The Angels appear.</margin>
The Lord testifies in the Holy Gospel that young children have their good angels. For in Matthew chapter 18, it is written that the Lord said: "See that you do not despise one of these little ones. Therefore, those who stand continually before the Lord are intimate, dear, and acceptable to Him. From this passage in Holy Matthew, Saint Jerome concludes in his <term>Commentaries</term> <note>original: "Comment."</note> and others, that God assigns to every soul, as soon as He creates it, its own special and

That all Christians have not just one, but many angels whom God uses for their service, may be understood from many places in Scripture. For in Hebrews chapter 1, it says that angels are ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. In Psalm 34 it says, "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them," even though we do not see them.

One reads that they appeared in various forms, warned people, strengthened and comforted them, protected them, delivered them from dangers, and moreover punished the unbelieving. Many examples of this exist, which need not be recounted here. Sometimes they appeared through dreams or visions; sometimes they carried out their command through internal inspiration. And even in our times, warnings have sometimes occurred through visible angels, and many occur through internal inspiration—as when a thing is clearly before a person, or their own heart tells them "it will happen thus and so," and it happens so—that, I believe, happens from God through the service of His angels. The angels mostly take on the form of a human being in which they appear; thus, the appearances of Saint Felix, Saint Agnes, and other pious faithful people may have been appearances of the holy angels.

Where Saint Augustine writes in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead* <note>original: "de Cura pro mortuis agenda"</note> in the 10th chapter, that the deceased appeared to the living in dreams or in other ways and showed them where their bodies lay as yet unburied, and begged them to bury them, he believes these are the workings of angels, through the order and permission of Divine Providence, who uses the good and the evil rightly according to the unfathomable depth of His judgments and decrees. He writes further that if the souls of the departed were burdened with the affairs of those who are still living, and if we could speak with them in dreams whenever we wished, then his dear mother would not leave him for a single night; for she followed him across the sea and over land so that she might be with him and near him, so dearly did she love him.

<margin>Sometimes and for the most part one sees evil angels.</margin>

### The Fifteenth Chapter.

On the other hand, the evil angels are hostile and averse to mankind, attaching themselves everywhere so that they may draw people away from the right and true worship of God, and from trust in the only Son of God, toward various other things. They appear in many kinds of forms. For if the Devil, as Paul says, can transform himself into the form of an angel of light, then he can also pass himself off as a prophet, apostle, evangelist, bishop, and martyr, and appear in their form, or blind us to such an extent that we believe we see and hear them. He also undertakes to prophesy of future things, whether he hits the mark or not. He says he is this or that soul, and that he must be helped in such and such a way, thereby bringing things that have no foundation in the Scripture into great prestige. Through false wonders and signs, he establishes new feasts, pilgrimages, and chapels; through conjurations, blessings, black arts, and sorcery, he undertakes to help the sick, so that his business may have all the more prestige. For how has the Devil blinded the poor heathens and led them around on a fool's rope for a long time? You find wonders in Arnobius, Lactantius, and other old holy fathers. He attached himself to their idols, sometimes spoke through them, moved the images from one place to another, and performed great signs, so that the lame left their crutches lying in the idol-temples and went home without them. This happened especially often in the Temple of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>. Therefore, today one has little reason to boast of such miraculous signs.

<margin>Concerning prodigies, omens, and other such things.</margin>

### The Sixteenth Chapter.

As for other wonderful things—what they might be when a person dies, such as something being seen beforehand, or a fall occurring, and especially when great lords are to perish, that for the most part many wonders precede it. As one reads that before the death of Julius Caesar there was a wild noise everywhere far and wide at night, and many other wonders occurred. Likewise, one reads that before the deaths of other emperors, kings, and prominent persons, something was for the most part heard or seen. Furthermore, what it might be that precedes great changes in governments <note>original: "Regimenten"</note>, deadly wars, uprisings, and other such things.

To this I give this simple answer: as was said before regarding ghosts <note>original: "Gespensten"</note>, if it is not a false persuasion and a vain delusion or natural things, then they are warnings from God, which He performs through His good angels and in other ways, so that one may see that these things do not happen by chance, without God's ordinance, knowledge, and will, but that our

# Concerning Spirits / The Second Part.
<note>original: "von Gespensten/ der ander Thail."</note>

Our death and life, peace and war, the changes of religion, of governments, and the course of events, all stand in His hand and in His power, so that we may learn to fear Him and call upon Him. Alongside this, the Evil Foe <note>The Devil</note> also plays his game to bring mankind into fear, terror, and superstition. However, that these things are not all orchestrated by the Evil Foe may be understood by this: if someone is to be stabbed by one who has been his dear friend until now, or is to drown, fall to his death, or otherwise perish miserably and unexpectedly in another way, the Evil Foe cannot know such things beforehand, for there are no preceding natural or other signs; yet, if some wonderful signs and warnings occur beforehand, they must surely come from God. He warns not only those whom it primarily concerns, but also others who hear of it, are present, and all those to whom it happens. 

But that the Devil also plays his game, I gather from this: a man lies in a heavy sickness, so that not only the physicians but he himself despairs of his life; then one sometimes hears someone making a coffin <note>original: "todtenbaum," literally 'death-tree' or coffin</note> for him at night, or burying him. That will be the Devil’s phantom, for he thinks the man will surely die, yet God raises him up again. Furthermore, by God’s permission, when war and riot are at hand, he may cause a rumbling in armories among the cannons and weapons, a cry of an army in the air, the beating of drums, and other things that have happened many times, as all histories testify.

->It is not impossible for the Devil to appear in many<-
->kinds of forms, and to do wonderful<-

### The Seventeenth Chapter.

That it is not difficult for the Evil Foe to appear in many forms—not only of living or dead men (of which I mentioned something above when I spoke of the appearance of Samuel <note>A reference to the Witch of Endor summoning the spirit of the prophet Samuel in the Bible</note>), but also, what is less, to appear as four-footed beasts, birds, etc., such as a black dog, a horse, or a horned owl, and to orchestrate great, wonderful, and unbelievable things—is manifest. For through long-standing experience and manifold practice, he may well know the effect and power of natural things such as herbs, stones, etc., and thereby arrange strange wonders. Moreover, he is a subtle, nimble, and ready spirit who can skillfully take a thing in hand, which is of no small importance. Through his speed and through the experience of natural things, he can deceive the sight of men and other senses. He can hide a thing that stands there and place another in its stead. Of this, the Holy Scripture, histories, and also daily experience give manifold testimony.

<margin>The conjurers of devils and sorcerers carry out wonderful things.</margin>
How did the Evil Foe deal with the patient Job? What did he bring to pass in a short time? What wonders did Balaam perform through the Devil’s help? Was he not famous in all lands because of his art? What great signs did the sorcerers of Pharaoh bring about through the black art? Did not Simon Magus so delude the Samaritans with his forbidden arts that they held him for a great power of God? The ancients write much of this sorcerer, such as Irenaeus in Book 1, Chapter 16; Eusebius in Book 1, Chapter 13. Hegesippus testifies in the 3rd Book, 2nd Chapter, concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, that he came to Rome and there opposed Saint Peter; he claimed that he wished to fly to heaven. On a certain day, he went up to the Capitoline Hill <note>original: "montem Capitolinum"</note>, a mountain in the city, jumped down from the rock, and began to fly, at which the common people wondered greatly and began to believe his false claim; in the midst of this, he fell down to the ground and broke a leg. Afterward, he had himself carried to Aricia, and died there.

<margin>Simon Magus.</margin>
Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, writes in his Chronicle of the Monastery of Hirsau, of the Benedictine Order, that in the year of our Lord 876, a Jew named Zedechias, who was the personal physician to Emperor Ludwig, performed and brought about quite wonderful things publicly before the Prince and all the people through the black art or sorcery, so that one thought no differently than...

# Ludwig Lavater

->thought and known<- that he swallowed horses and men with armor and weapons, a loaded wagon with hay along with the horses and the driver; that he had cut off people's heads, hands, and feet, placed them in a basin along with the blood that flowed from them, and let everyone see it, only to have them reattached shortly thereafter. People were said to have heard and seen him running, hunting, and engaging in other activities in the air and clouds, just as one does on earth, not without the great wonder of all who were present.

Accordingly, in the year of our Lord 970, Peter and Baianus, sons of Simeon the Monk <note>Simeon I of Bulgaria</note>, reigned in Bulgaria. Baianus was said to have been excellent in the black arts <term>black arts: necromancy or dark magic</term> and performed many wonders thereafter. Whenever he wished, he changed himself into the form of a wolf or another irrational animal. Sometimes he made himself entirely invisible, so that many people wondered greatly at him.

He further relates that in the year of our Lord 1323, when Duke Frederick of Austria—who had been elected Emperor against Emperor Ludwig—was defeated in a great battle between Oettingen and Mühldorf and handed over to Emperor Ludwig, the Emperor had him imprisoned in a fortress. There, a practitioner of the black arts came to his brother, Duke Leopold of Austria, and offered to release the imprisoned Duke through his art and the mediation of a spirit, and to bring him to him within an hour, if he were promised a good reward. When the Duke gave his consent, the magician made a ring and conjured a spirit who appeared to him in human form, commanding that he immediately lead the Duke out of the prison to Austria. This same spirit soon arrived at the prison in Bavaria in the guise of a stranger and told the imprisoned Duke to sit upon a black horse that stood ready, saying he would lead him to his brother Duke Leopold in a short time, and no harm should come to him. A shudder came over the Duke, and he crossed himself <note>The sign of the cross was believed to ward off demonic spirits</note>, whereupon

<column-break/>

the spirit vanished along with the saddled horse. When the spirit returned to the magician without the Duke, he scolded the spirit; but the spirit related how the Duke would not mount, otherwise he would have brought him away. Later, when the Duke was released from prison by other means, he likewise said that such a thing had happened to him. This history is also found in the Swiss and other chronicles.

Even today there are magicians who claim they can saddle a horse upon which they may complete great journeys in a short time. To these same people, when all is said and done, the Devil will give the ride and the horse-pay, the shoeing and the saddle-money all together <note>A proverbial way of saying the Devil eventually collects his due</note>. What wonders is the famous sorcerer Faustus <note>The historical Johann Georg Faust, whose legends inspired the famous literary character</note> said to have performed in our times? Now I will write nothing of the ancient sorcerers, such as Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note> and others, of whom historians tell wonderful things that they accomplished with their forbidden arts. The hags <term>hags: "Vnholden," often referring to witches or malevolent spirits</term> sometimes lame people and cattle if they only touch them, stroking them or gripping them; they do strange things about which entire books have been written. The jugglers <term>jugglers: "Gauckler," meaning street performers or illusionists</term> also bring much about through their agility, dealing in strange pranks, telling one to take a vinegar-dish in the mouth and then spit it out, so that something else falls out, etc. But the magicians, sorcerers, hex-masters, and conjurers of devils are solely the Devil's servants; should their Lord and Master not reserve some masterpieces for himself?

Yet I must also report this: that the evil spirit boasts of many things that he can never perform, such as that he can bring the dead forth from their graves, etc. He may well present their forms to men by God's permission, but over the dead bodies he has no such power.
