# Concerning Spirits / The Second Part.
->P iij<-

If these spirits are not souls, but the devil’s phantoms, why do they direct people toward good? For they say: maintain good judgment and justice, leave other people’s property alone, return ill-gotten goods, guard yourselves against cursing and swearing, gluttony and drunkenness, envy and hatred, lying and cheating; pray earnestly, go diligently to church, etc. Now, the devil has no pleasure at all in these things; nothing would be more contrary to him than if one acted rightly. Therefore, it cannot be the devil who commands one to avoid or do these things. Furthermore, they speak the truth, whereas the devil is called and is the father of lies by Christ himself <note>John 8:44</note>.

To this I give this answer: He does it for his own advantage. If he allowed himself to be seen as he is, he would achieve little. What he does, he does so that people will have faith in him, and so that he may all the better impress other things upon humans, leading and strengthening them in all kinds of error and superstition—so that they comply with those spirits and let the Word of God go. Dear friend, did not his servants, the false prophets, also come in sheep’s clothing in former times and act as if the salvation and welfare of the common man were of great concern to them, when it only happened so that they might come to honor and fill their purses? Do not all sectarians today say they are appointed or sent by God, and that one should guard against sin and vice? Have you never heard that murderers on the road have walked with a man and spoken with him of a pious, honorable life, and additionally of future punishment and reward? And when he expected no evil from them, but thought his body and life were secure, they unexpectedly murdered him? Because the devil can so masterfully disguise himself, he has brought all kinds of superstition, error, and false divine service into the church. The bishops, meanwhile, paid little heed to the Holy Scripture; they did not want to recognize the devil when he came not in a black, cruel form, but in an agreeable and lovely shape; they accepted him as an angel of light <note>2 Corinthians 11:14</note>. He says good things so that he may also, with full authority, drive in the evil—

<column-break/>

—underneath it. He tells the truth so that one believes the lies. Just as in Virgil, Sinon <note>The Greek spy who convinced the Trojans to bring the Wooden Horse into their city</note> also larded his lies with truthful things, so that he could all the better deceive the Trojans.

The evil enemy acts like a false, cheating gambler, who lets a simple, uninformed fellow win many a turn so that he makes him addicted to the game, and afterwards wins everything he has from him. He acts like one who intends to defraud another: he treats him bravely and honestly several times, pays him on the target date as he promised, so that he may afterwards receive a large sum of money from him and then deprive him of it. Thus the evil enemy also acts; he tells the truth several times so that he may afterwards gain belief, and may all the better deceive people with lies, etc. One who has something for sale prepares it for the market; the evil enemy can do that too.

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
Saint Ambrose writes on the first Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians in the 5th chapter, as he interprets the words: *You shall not quench the spirit, prove all things, and hold fast that which is good,* etc. <note>1 Thessalonians 5:19-21</note>. The spirits of this world have the custom of saying good things in a deceptive way, so that they may introduce evil underneath them, so that one accepts the evil along with the good. And because one thinks it is spoken by a [holy] spirit, one does not distinguish the two from each other, etc.

<margin>Chrysostom shows why the devil speaks the truth.</margin>
To this also serves what Saint Chrysostom writes in his second sermon on Lazarus. He reports that many simple people are stuck in the heavy error that the souls of those who did not die a natural death, but were killed <term>violenta morte</term> <note>by a violent death</note>, have become devils. And he shows thereby that the devil brought many of his servants who were in this error to the point that they killed many youths in the hope that they would become devils and serve them.

Thereupon Saint Chrysostom says further: But that is not true, it is not true. What is it then that the devils say: "I am the soul of such-and-such a monk"? Indeed, for that very reason I do not believe it, because—

# The third part of this 6th Treatise: Why God allows ghosts to appear and other wonderful things to happen; also how people should conduct themselves when something of this kind appears and happens to them.

->God exercises his believers with ghosts and punishes the unbelievers.<-
->The first Chapter.<-

<margin>GOD does it for the good of the believers.</margin>

Now follows the third and last part of this simple report: namely, why God the Lord allows spirits, ghosts, and monsters to appear, and other wonderful things to happen; also how people should conduct themselves to whom something of the like appears and happens.

God the Lord lets spirits appear to his elect for their good, and to the damned for punishment; and as all things serve for the good of the believers and God-fearing, so do these things also. If they are good spirits who warn and protect them, they see God's gracious providence and Fatherly love toward them. If they are then evil spirits, as they mostly are, the believers are thereby stirred to true repentance and the improvement of their lives. They also guard themselves all the more diligently every day they live, so that the evil enemy who stands and walks against them does not fell them into sin and vice, and thus gain further occasion to plague them. God also exercises and proves their faith and patience, so that they persist in His word alone and permit nothing that is against it—no matter what appearance it may have—nor act against it even if the ghosts do not wish to leave them immediately. God also allows his own to be tempted by ghosts for this reason

# Concerning Ghosts / The Third Part.

so that they may be all the more humble. In the 2nd to the Corinthians, in the 12th chapter, Paul says: *Lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, namely the messenger of Satan <note>original: "Engel des Teuffels" (Angel of the Devil)</note> to buffet me with fists, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. We would also not so easily believe others who are perhaps plagued by monsters <note>original: "vngeheur"</note>, but would think they were merely imagining it. Furthermore, when other people hear that even pious folk are tested in this manner, they become more patient in their own physical sickness and other concerns, thinking: "Your suffering is a small suffering; it is nothing compared to when the Devil plagues people," etc.

<margin>God punishes the unbelievers.</margin>
As far as the unbelievers are concerned, they too must confess that there are devils. For many would not believe that there were angels or devils if they did not occasionally see such signs that forced them to believe. God permits such things to them as a punishment. For since they do not accept the truth, but willfully wish to be deceived and led astray, it is only fair that they should hear from the Devil's ghost <note>original: "deß Teuffels gespenst"</note> what they should do or leave undone, and be fooled in other ways by the Evil Enemy.

For thus it stands in Deuteronomy, in the 13th chapter: *If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder come to pass, whereof he spake unto thee, saying, Let us go after other gods, which thou hast not known, and let us serve them; thou shalt not hearken unto the words of that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams. For the Lord your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul. Ye shall walk after the Lord your God, and*

<column-break/>

*fear him, and keep his commandments, and obey his voice, and ye shall serve him, and cleave unto him. And that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death,* etc. From this we see not only that God allows wonders and signs to be performed by these rogues, but also why he permits such things: namely, to test his believers, to see how brave and honest they will remain toward him. Even if spirits come and speak of things that shall happen hereafter, we should not allow ourselves to be led away from the one God because of it.

In the Holy Gospel of John, in the 3rd chapter, our Lord Christ says: *This is the judgment <note>original: "gericht oder die verdamnuß" (judgment or condemnation)</note>, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved,* etc. In these words, our Lord and Savior indicates why the world is condemned: namely, because it does not accept the light of the holy, divine Word—indeed, Christ himself, who is the light of the world and is presented to us in the Word—but rather closes its eyes against the bright light and prefers darkness, that is, all kinds of error, superstition, shame, and vice, over the Divine Word. Now, if God condemns the ungrateful world entirely because of its thankfulness, should he not also let them be plagued by ghosts and various seductive apparitions? In John, the 5th chapter: *I am come in my Father's name, and ye receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive.* Our Lord Christ sought their salvation and well-being, but they did not want it; thus it was God's fair and just judgment that they should accept others who sought their own honor and profit, such as Theudas, Judas of Galilee, and other false teachers and rebellious deceivers. Thus, when one will not hear Christ and his servants, it happens by the righteous judgment of God that one must hear ghosts and other such things.

<margin>Pharaoh.</margin>Let us hear several examples of this. Pharaoh despised God and His servants, Moses and Aaron; therefore he was so blinded by God that he allowed himself to be deceived by his black-magicians <term>Schwarzkünstler: practitioners of the dark arts or sorcery</term>, and after a long time, he drowned miserably in the Red Sea.

<margin>Saul.</margin>Saul wanted no mercy from the holy prophet Samuel, who meant well for him, nor would he believe him; instead, he hated him and all those who wished him well and advised him. He ran after a witch so that she might awaken the prophet Samuel from the dead for him, so that he could ask advice from the one he would not listen to during his life. She awakened one who is called Samuel in no other way than how false gods or idols are called gods—which, to speak properly, are not gods but wood and stone; indeed, as St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10, they are devils. This false Samuel did not comfort him; he advised him nothing, but rather made him even more weary and desperate than he was before. It went for Saul just like those children who despise their pious father and mother and will not follow their faithful advice, but rather wish they were well buried: afterwards, it comes to pass that they would travel many miles just so they might enjoy their faithful counsel once more.

The King heard in his voice that he was not in earnest, and therefore adjured him that he should tell him the true ground of the matter. Then he said: he had seen all Israel scattered upon the mountains like a herd of sheep that has no shepherd. And the Lord had spoken: "Do these have no master? Let every man return home again in peace." Ahab spoke to Jehoshaphat: "Did I not tell you before, this man never says anything good to me?" Thereupon the Prophet said further: "Hear the word of the Lord; I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and the whole heavenly host standing beside him on his right and on his left, and the Lord spoke: 'Who will persuade or deceive Ahab so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead?' And one said this, the other that. Then a Spirit came forth, stepped before the Lord, and spoke: 'I will persuade him, or deceive him.' The Lord spoke to him: 'With what?' He answered: 'I will go out and will be a false spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' The Lord spoke: 'You shall persuade him and shall be able to do it; go forth and do so.' Now behold, the Lord has put a false spirit in the mouth of all your prophets, and the Lord has decreed evil against you." When he had spoken such things, Zedekiah ran up, struck him in his face, and spoke: "Has the Spirit of God then left me, that he speaks with you?" Then Micaiah prophesied to him also how it would go for him. The King commanded him to be thrown into prison immediately and given nothing but water and bread until he returned from the war. Then Micaiah said: "Yes, if you return, then the Lord has not spoken through me," and he told all the people to hear and take note of it. But the campaign had to proceed; the Kings equipped themselves with their best military power and took to the field. Thus was Ahab shot in the battle, and Jehoshaphat also came into great danger, etc.

<column-break/>

I cite this history somewhat extensively for this reason: so that one may see how God, by a righteous judgment, sometimes allows spirits to come to those who despise his Prophets and his word, which spirits seduce and deceive them.

The same has also happened to all of Christendom for several hundred years after the times of the holy Apostles; when the Divine word was no longer held in such value as was proper, but rather fleshly temptations were dearer to men: when they no longer wished to suffer anything or come into danger for the sake of faith and truth, but rather one faith was almost the same to them as another. Then God punished them, so that they began to listen to the deceivers who stood by them and justified them in their temptations. They taught from images, which they called "books for the laity" <note>A reference to the medieval concept of *Libri Laicorum*, where religious art was intended to teach the illiterate</note>; they kissed their bones and set them in gold—whose teachings they previously would not accept (if indeed they were even their bones at all). They believed in false apparitions and the Devil’s ghosts, and thus received the deserved punishment for their great ingratitude. And just as youths who will not follow their faithful masters must afterwards obey others with great shame who will lead them to ruin: so it has also gone for many hardworking people, and the longer it went, the further they stepped away from the simple word of God, so that afterwards they no longer knew where they stood; one ran up, the other down, to earn grace and the indulgence of his sins. One believed this spirit, another believed another, etc., as is publicly evident today.

Previously, the same happened to the poor Heathen <note>The non-Christian ancient world</note>, as can be seen from the first chapter of Paul to the Romans and from their own writings. They had many gods; many wonders and signs occurred among them, and many appearances of the gods. They had many oracles <term>Oracula: divine pronouncements or the shrines where they were given</term>, but as soon as they accepted the Holy Gospel preached by the holy Apostles with faith, one no longer perceived or heard anything of those same things. Athanasius writes

Now, after Christ has been preached everywhere in the world, this deafness <note>Likely referring to the silencing of the pagan idols.</note> has ceased, etc. Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) who argued that pagan oracles were silenced by the power of Christ.</note> and others write the same. Since the time that human teachings and decrees have been cast aside and the holy Gospel teaching <note>original: "Euangelisch Lehr"</note> has been accepted with great desire and joy, the appearances of souls or spirits and the visions have gradually vanished. ->What the cause may be that in our times so few spirits are perceived anymore.<-

### The Second Chapter.

The bright radiance of the Divine Word drives away these spirits, who like to establish their affairs in the darkness. The Prince of Darkness shuns the light, and where God is called upon through Christ alone, trusted and believed in, and where one holds to Him alone, there he can accomplish little. Where God's Word is held in high esteem among men, God does not allow the world to be so deceived as it is when His Word is not allowed to stand alone. Here I cannot omit mentioning a witty remark <note>original: "Schimpffred," meaning a jest or mocking retort.</note>. When people were once talking about ghosts, monsters, and apparitions, an Evangelical <note>A Protestant.</note> said to a Papist <note>A Catholic.</note>: "By this you should see and understand that our faith is right and yours is wrong: that from the time the Gospel was preached among us, few ghosts are perceived among us anymore." To this the other gave answer: "Yes, by that you should realize that you are wrong and we are right, for the Devil only pursues those who wish to escape him."

<column-break/>

<margin>St. Benedict sees one evil spirit in the market, but many in the monastery.</margin>
This is not unlike what Aeneas Sylvius (who was afterwards named Pope Pius II) relates in his history of the Council of Basel <note>Held between 1431 and 1449.</note> from the Legend of St. Benedict: When he once visited a monastery in which there were many holy, pious monks, he saw a whole crowd of impure spirits who fought with the holy fathers and endeavored to hinder them in their good works. As soon as he came to the annual fair <note>The market.</note> in that same place, he saw only one evil spirit, who stood idly on a high place. Benedict wondered at this and conjured the Devil to show him the cause. He answered him: "The holy place requires many to storm it, but those who otherwise lie, deceive, swear, and serve me, do not need the impure spirits to urge them on."

Then I ask you, could the heathens not have said the same to the Christians in ancient times when they asked: "Why have the Oracles ceased? That is, why do your gods no longer give answers regarding future things?" Likewise: "Why are there so few apparitions?" But it is the Devil who pursues you; why then do you hold that it is this or that soul that must be helped? Because the Devil well knows that we understand his cunning, he pursues others. Just as when you want to do a mischief to someone at night, and he notices it, you immediately leave him be and go to another who is full of sleep, or who otherwise does not understand such roguery <note>original: "lotterwercks."</note>.

Accordingly, there are other reasons also why one hears little more of these things. A person does not let himself be deceived by you more than three or four times; afterwards, you open your eyes and look closely at his hands. Thus, because fraud and falsehood have been found so often and so much, one does not easily believe false pretenses. "A burnt child," they say, "dreads the fire." Furthermore, one no longer fears or shuns monsters as badly as in former times; you will soon find someone who would seek them out, see them, or even grab them—this is known—therefore no one will easily hide themselves <note>original: "verböggẽ," likely meaning to disguise oneself as a "Bogeyman."</note> or otherwise pass themselves off as a soul or spirit, as often happened before. Children are easily persuaded that a "Black Man" or a "Tall White Lady" is coming to put them in a sack if they do not stop crying, etc. But when they come to their years of maturity, they no longer let themselves be...

Now that we have increased in knowledge therein, and by God's grace can read and understand the Scripture ourselves, we no longer allow ourselves to be aped or led by a fool's rope in these and other matters; we do not believe every apparition. How much, then, did that fraud used by the Monks of Bern <note>A reference to the Jetzer affair of 1509, a famous case of monastic fraud involving faked apparitions.</note> do to drive away spirits? One sets up straw-men <note>original: "hanffbutzē"</note> to drive the birds out of the hemp fields or plots, but after a long while they care nothing for them, seeing that it is nothing that can harm them.

### Why GOD the LORD allows strange events to occur before great changes and at other times.

->The Third Chapter.<-

The precursors <note>omens or warnings</note> of when people are to die, or when otherwise difficult times and great changes are at hand, also serve for the good of the believers and for the punishment of the unbelievers. For by this, God gives it to be understood that nothing happens by chance, but rather our life, success, and misfortune stand in His hand. It is not at all as the Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, here used to mean those who believe God is indifferent to human affairs.</note> think: that whether one lives or dies, whether things go well or ill for one, or whether governments rise or fall, GOD the LORD concerns Himself with none of these or other things. Christ Himself teaches us that the lowly sparrow does not perish without His knowledge and will. Solomon and Daniel say that God holds the hearts of kings in His hand, and that He appoints and removes rulers. It should comfort us more than frighten us when we hear of these things. Accordingly, God warns us through such things so that we are never careless or complacent. For from of old, He has warned His people not only with words but with wondrous events. The heathens also took such things as warnings from their gods, as is found everywhere in their historians. Even if the majority of these things happen through evil spirits, we nevertheless see how GOD cares for us and graciously protects and shields us against the assault of the Evil Foe. For though the Evil One is never idle and sneaks after us to destroy us, he cannot do so, for GOD watches over us. However, the unbelievers—who otherwise care nothing for the preaching of the Divine Word—are terrified by this, so that they do not know which way to turn and must confess that God takes account of all things, and that there are both good and evil spirits. Otherwise, no one could restrain them; they would cause even greater suffering and distress to the believers if GOD the LORD did not instill in them a fear and terror through such things.

<column-break/>

### How those should conduct themselves to whom good or evil spirits appear, or to whom other wondrous things happen: and first, how the heathens and Jews conducted themselves in such cases.

->The Fourth Chapter.<-

For a better understanding of how one should behave when something of this kind appears, be it good or evil, we wish first to hear how the heathens and Jews of old conducted themselves in such cases and what they did.

<margin>How the heathens conducted themselves.</margin>
Among the heathens, the wandering spirits did not only present themselves as human souls, but also indicated what should be done for them: namely, to observe the *Feralia* and *Parentalia sacra* <note>Latin: Roman festivals and sacred rites for honoring deceased ancestors and the dead.</note>—that is, to perform service for the dead—to bury their bodies properly in the earth, to build temples, to observe holidays, and other such things.

Suetonius writes of the Emperor Caligula that his dead body was secretly carried into the gardens (*Hortos Lamianos* <note>Latin: The Lamian Gardens on the Esquiline Hill in Rome.</note>) and buried in haste; afterwards, his sisters dug him up again, burned him according to common custom, and buried him properly in the earth. But before this happened, the gardeners had no rest from the spirits or souls. Likewise, in the house where he perished, there was no rest at night until it was burned down. You will also find in other historians that when people were not properly buried, or if during the course of wars the customary...

Those who neglected ceremonies appeared to their own kin and others, complaining bitterly and desiring that burials and other ceremonies be performed for them. From this arose the *cenotaphia* <note>empty tombs built as memorials for those whose bodies were lost</note>; likewise the seventh day, the thirtieth day, and the anniversaries of death, of which one finds much among the Heathen writers. Something of this is also cited by Gyraldus in his book on burials among the ancient Heathens, and by Polydore Vergil in *On the Inventors of Things*, Book 6, Chapter 10. We heard above in the second part, Chapter 1, how some desired to be buried after their death. Cicero writes in Book 1 of *On the Laws* that Romulus, founder of the city of Rome, appeared after his death to Proculus Julius and said he had been accepted into the number of the gods and would be called Quirinus; he also commanded him to build a temple at the same place where he had appeared to him.

Ovid writes in the 5th book of *Fasti* that Remus appeared to Faustulus and <margin>Lemuria.</margin> Acca in the night, and begged them to see to it that the day on which he was slain by his brother Romulus should be kept as a holiday. Therefore the Romans held the festival *Remuria*, later called *Lemuria* <note>A Roman festival to exorcise the restless ghosts of the dead</note>. In Lucan, one reads of the spirits of Sulla and Marius. So we have heard above how Athenagoras commanded that the bones in the courtyard of the house in Athens, where a monster <note>original: "vngeheur" - often used for a ghost or haunting presence</note> had been, should be properly committed to the earth, etc.

<margin>What the Jews did.</margin> The ancient Jewish people had God's express command that they should not turn to any false prophets or signs of wonder, and specifically should not consult the dead. King Saul himself, at the beginning of his reign, destroyed sorcerers and hags. How the Jews of our own times behave when a monster appears to them is not known to me.

->How Christians who encounter monsters should behave; and first, they should be undaunted and firm in faith.<-

### The Fifth Chapter.

But how we Christians should behave in such a case is (like everything else necessary for our salvation) sufficiently presented to us in Holy

<column-break/>

Scripture. Namely, that first of all, we should be brave, undaunted, and stiff in true faith. For if they are good angels who show themselves, they are sent to us for our good by God; if they are evil angels, they can do us no harm without God's permission. If it is then nothing but a delusion, it would be foolish if one were sorely afraid of it. It is <margin>Fear is natural.</margin> indeed natural that one shudders at such appearances and all hair stands on end. For even pious, believing people in the Old and New Testament were terrified by good angels; yet one should pull oneself together again and "take one's heart in both hands," as the saying goes. When the disciples of our Lord Christ saw the Lord walking on the water and approaching the ship, they took him for a ghost <note>original: "Gespenst"</note>, were sorely frightened, and cried out from great fear; but the Lord Jesus said to them: "Be manly, it is I; be not afraid." You find the like in Luke, Chapter 24, after his resurrection. In the Holy Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 10, he says: "Fear not those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy body and soul in hellfire." It would be a great pleasure to the Devil if we were always sorely afraid of him.

If a spirit acts perversely and throws chairs and benches about, remain undaunted. If he rumbles <margin>Rumbling Spirit.</margin> <note>original: "Rumpel Geist" - the origin of the term 'poltergeist'</note> to frighten you, pay no mind to his thumping and rumbling, but let him go on in his way until he is tired, then he will trot off. If you wish, you may well say to him: "Be gone, Devil! You have nothing to say to me, who trusts and believes in Christ; I am the possessor of this house, you belong in another place," etc. When he perceives that one does not fear him and cares nothing for his rumbling, he will not stay long. Take a familiar comparison: one finds troublemakers who, if they think people fear them, act as if they want to draw their swords <note>original: "von leder zucken" - to pull from the leather/scabbard</note>, then they twitch and strike the stones and live a wild, boastful life; but when they see that one does not fear—

But if the Lord God wishes to test you for a time through the Evil Foe, as he did the patient Job, then endure his wantonness patiently for the sake of the Lord's highest commandment. Where He gives great suffering, He also imparts great grace. It should not seem so very strange to us if at times something of these things is seen or heard.

<margin>The Devil is around mankind.</margin> For the Evil Foe, as Saint Peter testifies, runs about everywhere—understand this to mean in houses, in woods and fields, in water and fire—but he does not always let himself be seen, nor can he, unless God permits it. That we do not always see the evil spirit (for he can take on many forms) or hear him, for that we have God to thank; we would

otherwise not have a single quiet hour. But if God at times allows the evil spirit to appear to us, or to rumble about in the house, it is not to be thought that he was not already there before.

### The Sixth Chapter.

Since the good angels very rarely appear to men—for it is a much different situation with us than with the ancient Fathers, to whom God many times sent His angels—we should, when we rise and go to sleep, bless ourselves all the more diligently; that is, faithfully commend ourselves into God’s gracious protection and shield. Our Lord Jesus Himself taught us, among other things, to pray: "Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." But He says this in Matthew, chapter 17: "The Devil is not driven out except through fasting and prayer." Regarding those who curse and swear and yet undertake to drive out the Devil, I will speak at the end. In Matthew 26: "Watch and pray, that ye fall not into temptation." In Luke 22, He says to Peter: "The Devil has set upon them, but He has prayed for him." He still prays at this hour for us all at the right hand of His Father in Heaven. The pious ancient Fathers also always cried out earnestly to God in all their afflictions, as we know from many examples.

It is also good if one who is plagued by ghosts requests the common intercession of the Church. For we know that the same is powerful in this and other cases, and that the faithful have always desired it in their needs. God also commands us here in this life to pray for one another. But that the saints, after they depart from this life, pray for us, or that we should desire their intercession—of that we have no commandment from GOD, nor any example in the Holy Scripture.

In like manner, the holy Apostles also teach us to offer resistance to the Devil. Saint Paul in Ephesians, chapter 6.

Chapter 6. Saint Peter says in his first Epistle in the 5th chapter: Cast all your care upon the Lord, for he cares for you. Be sober and vigilant: for your adversary goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; whom resist, steadfast in the faith, etc. Where one is frivolous, careless, and lazy, and moreover entirely given over to bodily lusts, to gluttony and drunkenness, to greed, adultery, and other vices, there the Devil finds a good place. Therefore, one should earnestly persevere with watching, praying, fasting, and a pious life, hearing and speaking much and gladly of the word of God, diligently hearing and reading the same; then the Devil and his **specter** <note>original: "Gespenst"</note> will have little room or place. If you have something to manage, carry it out faithfully. If you have ill-gotten goods, return them, etc. Because the world is deranged and asks little after God and his word, it is no wonder if He allows something to appear to humble the people.

<margin>One should resist the Devil with a pious life.</margin>

It is terrifying when men give themselves over entirely to evil so that they have peace from him: for they do not consider that they will be tormented and plagued by the evil enemy in eternity if they do not turn back to God.

->We should hold appearing spirits as suspicious, and not be quick to speak with them, nor wish to learn anything from them.<-

### The Seventh Chapter.

All spirits or apparitions should not be without cause suspicious and suspect to us. For although God always uses the good angels for the service of his believers, they nevertheless appear seldom in our times. For now, since Christ has come into this world, it is a much different thing than in times past. Even if it seems to you that you see a good angel, do not rely too much upon it. If it is discovered afterward by the deed that a good angel appeared to you, who gave you a faithful warning or delivered you from danger, then give thanks to the Lord that He cares for you so faithfully and Fatherly, and submit yourself to His will. If it is an angel who is capable of much flattery and fawning, such as those who desire help, then you have previously

<column-break/>

heard what you should place upon their words. Even men who are capable of much fuss and flattery are suspicious to us; why then should we not hold such spirits as suspect? You should not involve yourself with any spirit by wishing to ask him much about what you should believe or do, or what will happen in future times. Do not ask who he may be, or with what intent he lets himself be seen or heard. For if it is a good spirit, it pleases him well if you wish to hear nothing other than GOD'S Word: if it is an evil spirit, he is a liar.

When God himself asked Adam in Paradise regarding his transgression, and he gave the blame to Eve, and Eve to the serpent who had persuaded her to eat of the forbidden fruit, God did not wish to ask the serpent, or the Devil who spoke through it, as He well knew that he was a liar. If Eve, the mother of us all, had not involved herself in a conversation with the serpent, she would not have fallen into sin and transgression. Indeed, even if the spirits approach us and wish to tell us much, we should simply not listen to them, let alone that one should first wish to adjure <note>original: "beschweren," referring to ritual conjuration or binding</note> them to learn the truth from them. God has forbidden in His law, as heard above, that we should not learn from the dead.

<margin>GOD has given us teaching beforehand.</margin>

God the Lord himself has sent his faithful servants, the holy Prophets, Apostles, and Evangelists, and above all his dear Son our Lord Jesus, into this world, and through them has sufficiently and faithfully informed his believers how and what they should believe, do, and avoid, and how and with what they should serve Him. He has also prophesied through them what great things will occur and happen in governments and in the church until the Day when our Lord Jesus shall sit in judgment and hold the truly universal, impartial Council <note>original: "Concilium"</note>, giving the verdict on who was right or wrong, and making the separation of the true and false believers. Our Lord Jesus himself has also come back from the dead, has shown himself...

# Concerning Ghosts / The Third Part.

## Q ii

...lingered on earth for a time, appeared to his dear disciples and many others, so that we would have no cause to say: "Who has ever returned from there to tell us how things are in that place?"

<margin>God has preserved the Holy Scripture.</margin>
Furthermore, the Lord God has also miraculously preserved the books of the Holy Scripture for our benefit up to this very hour, through difficult and long-lasting persecutions in which so many good books perished, and He will continue to preserve them hereafter.

<margin>God has established the ministry of the church.</margin>
In addition, He has also established the ministry of His holy Word, so that there would always be people until the end of the world to interpret the Holy Scripture and present His saving Word both orally and in writing, informing us of His holy, Divine will. The Divine Word is our light that shall shine for us in this dark world, which is so full of error, as it stands in the 119th Psalm. In the 8th chapter of John, our Lord Jesus says that He is the light of the world; whoever follows Him shall not walk in darkness, etc.

He intends to let the matter rest there. Therefore, we should wait for no other revelation, neither by miraculous means from heaven nor from wandering spirits or "souls," as they are called—though they are not actually souls. But even if these spirits that wander about were actually souls, they would be either the souls of the faithful or the souls of the unfaithful. If the souls of the faithful were to return, they would—like Christ our Lord—point us toward the Holy Scripture and would say, as God the Father said of His Son: "Hear Him." If, then, the souls of unfaithful and wicked people returned, dear God, who would want to listen to them or pay any mind to what they say? Furthermore, that which these supposed souls recount and claim either agrees with the Divine Scripture or it is against it. If it agrees with it, then one should accept it—not because the souls say it, but because it has its foundation in the Divine Word. If it is against it, then it can in no way be accepted. You would not believe a man well known to you, whom you otherwise knew to be truthful,

<column-break/>

if he stood physically before you and said something you recognized to be against the Scripture; should you then believe an unknown ghost? In common law, it would carry very little weight if someone wanted to testify to his case using the dead.

God our Lord could certainly send His angels (whom He uses constantly for our service anyway) to us, and through them teach us the faith, but He has not ordained or intended it so. We read in the Acts of the Holy Apostles in the 10th chapter that He commanded Cornelius through an angel to send for St. Peter, so that Peter might inform him of the faith. He could have easily spared him the journey and let the angel preach himself, but He remains with His common order. Therefore, there is nothing more correct than that we also remain simply with the Holy Scripture; thus we need not fear being deceived and led astray. Had the ancients done so, people would never have stepped so far away from Apostolic simplicity. What is necessary for us to know is sufficiently contained within the Holy Scripture; what is not mentioned therein, we should not desire to know—let alone that we should want to inquire about it from the dead or from the Devil's ghost against God's prohibition. Whatever else there is, we shall understand in the eternal life. Might God not also say to us, if we are not satisfied with His Word, as He said through the holy prophet Elijah to the messengers of King Ahaziah: "Is there no God in Israel, that you go to Ekron to consult Beelzebub?" <note>original: "Ist kein Gott in Israel/ daß jhr gehn Accaron ziehet/ den Beelzebub raths zu fragẽ?" Refers to 2 Kings 1:3.</note> Thomas Aquinas <note>A hugely influential 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note> also says that one should not listen to the devils who deceive simple people and act as if they were the souls of men, terrifying people under that pretense; he testifies that such things occasionally happened even to the heathens. If we could know for certain that the Devil could not appear and play his games, or perform great wonders, then there might perhaps be some sense in giving credence to such appearances:

# Ludwig Lavater

For the evil enemy, as Saint Jerome says <note>original: "Sanct Hieronymus"</note>, does not let himself be seen with his deceit as he truly is. Therefore, we should look about ourselves carefully.

<margin>What one should place upon miraculous signs.</margin>
Furthermore, the right and true miraculous signs <term>wunderzeichen: miracles or supernatural omens</term> are solely a testimony and a seal of the Word, and one should not attempt through them to maintain that which is against the Holy Scripture. Therefore, all miraculous signs that lead us away from the Creator toward the creatures, and attribute to our own merit that which should be attributed to Christ alone—and in short, lead us into error—are to be rejected. If one were to give credit to those "souls" <note>referring to reported sightings of souls from Purgatory</note>, no one would know where he stood. For people would constantly be establishing some new innovation (as has happened before). Therefore, let a ghost be a ghost, and be a pious, upright, and honest Christian.

->Testimony of the Holy Scripture, and an example that one should not believe such appearances, but rather be cautious.<-

### The Eighth Chapter.

That one should not immediately believe everything one hears, but rather be cautious, is taught to us not only by experience and many proverbs, but by the Holy Divine Scripture itself, and especially in matters concerning the salvation of our souls, regarding which we wish to hear only a few testimonies and also examples.

When our Lord Christ sent out his disciples for the first time to teach, he spoke, as it stands in Matthew chapter 10: Be wise as serpents and simple as doves. Guard yourselves against men; how much more should we guard ourselves against the Devil. In Matthew chapter 24, our Lord Christ prophesies how in the last times many false teachers will arise and perform great wonders and signs, and thereby attempt to confirm their errors; therefore, one should be careful. He does not add in vain: "Behold, I have told you beforehand,"

<column-break/>

beforehand, etc. Saint Paul speaks to the Galatians in the 1st chapter with great earnestness: even if an angel were to come from heaven and attempt to preach another Gospel to them than that which had been preached by him, let him be accursed <note>original: "verflucht"; referring to the concept of Anathema</note>. So, if spirits should still come and say things that are not in accordance with the holy Apostolic teaching, we should let them go. In 1 Timothy chapter 4, he prophesies of false teachers who will arise in the last times, and says: "But the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will fall away from the faith and cling to seductive spirits and the teachings of devils: through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared with branding irons: who forbid marrying and command to abstain from foods that God created to be enjoyed with thanksgiving by the faithful." By "spirits," one understands the false teachers who boast of the Spirit; but who would be against it if we also understood this to refer to those wandering spirits <note>ghosts or apparitions</note> who have persuaded the world of many things? In 2 Thessalonians chapter 2, when there were some who claimed the Last Day was at hand, the holy Apostle prophesies: "The falling away and the Antichrist <term>widerchrist: the Antichrist</term> shall come first," and he exhorts them highly, saying: "But we beseech you, dear brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by our gathering unto him (for the elect shall come to him), that you be not quickly shaken in your understanding (from the teaching he preached to them), nor be terrified, neither by a spirit, nor by a word, nor by a letter, as if sent by us, as though the day of Christ were at hand. Let no one deceive you in any way." Which words, in my opinion, may also be aptly understood as referring to appearing spirits. St. John says in his 1st Epistle, chapter 4: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are of God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you shall know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses..."

confesses, etc. <note>original: "bekennt/ etc." referring to 1 John 4:2-3</note> Here St. John does not speak of those spirits that appear in visible form, but of those teachers who boast of the Spirit; but one should not immediately believe the living, much less the dead. But even if our Lord Christ and his Apostles had never so diligently warned us against those miracles and spirits, daily experience nevertheless teaches us to open our eyes and look out for ourselves. For as soon as a thing cannot be maintained by the Scriptures, people want to prove it through miracles and stories. To what end greed, ambition, zeal, and envy have brought the clergy, we know from many examples, and it has also been partly indicated above. Has not one Order wished to be above the others, as far as prestige and temporal goods are concerned? Have they not fabricated new miracles, saints, pilgrimages, and spirits?

<margin>An example that one should not believe too quickly.</margin>
We also have a magnificent example in the highly favored, eternally pure Virgin Mary, that we should not immediately believe every spirit. For when the holy Angel Gabriel appeared to her in visible form, greeted her, and announced to her the Incarnation of our dear Lord Christ, she pondered what kind of greeting that might be, and how that would come to pass, since she knew nothing of any man. Only when she was thoroughly informed of the whole matter did she say: Behold, I am a servant of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word. Why then should we believe every spirit, especially one that comes with things that not only have no basis in the word of God, but are directly against it?

->How the believers in the ancient Church conducted themselves when monsters and ghosts appeared to them.<-

### The Ninth Chapter.

Just as I have related so far from God's word how one should conduct oneself against spirits, so also did the ancient Christians conduct themselves. For they were comforted and brave, applied themselves to a pious, honorable life and all kinds of good works, and above all guarded against that which they knew to be displeasing to God; they also took good care not to give too much belief to those things.

<column-break/>

They commonly (as many people still have the custom) when something of these things encountered them, made a cross before themselves. The holy Tertullian writes in his book *On the Soldier's Crown* <note>original: "de Corona militis"</note>, on page 449: The ancient Christians often marked their foreheads with the cross. Saint Jerome admonishes Demetrias that she should make a cross on her forehead, so that the destroying angel in Egypt might find no place or room with her. Origen, Epiphanius, Chrysostom, and Augustine also write much about the power of the cross. The holy Bishop Athanasius writes in his book *On the Incarnation of the Word* <note>original: "de Human. verbi, eiusq; corpor. adventu"</note>, on page 67: In former times, the devils confused men with vain forms; they fooled people with their play at wells, rivers, in wood and stone. But now, after the Word of God has appeared, the visions and deceptions of the idols have ceased. For when a man only uses the sign of the cross, he drives away their lies and deceit. Thereafter on page 72, before that on page 56, and elsewhere here and there he mentions the like. Lactantius writes in *Divine Institutes* <note>original: "Diuinarum Instit."</note> book 4, chapter 26, and mentions throughout the entire 27th chapter, that whoever marks the forehead with the cross, to him the devil may not come, and may not harm him. He also mentions that the Christians used these ceremonies in the driving out of devils and in the healing of sickness.

<margin>The ancients made a cross for themselves.</margin>
<margin>Whether the cross has a power in itself.</margin>
Not that they attribute such power to the external crosses (otherwise it would be superstition <term>Aberglauben: belief in supernatural forces outside of God's ordained means</term>), but to the Cross, that is, the merit of Christ, which they remembered by this means. Of the holy Apostles and the Apostolic Church, one does not otherwise read that they used the ceremonies of the cross in driving out unclean spirits or sicknesses, or otherwise. The Jews who in Egypt had marked the lintel with blood were not slain; not that the sheep's blood had such power that it could preserve men, but it was a prefiguration of the blood and cross of Christ. But what the Jews did happened not out of their own opinion, but because they had a certain command from God for it.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of spiritual warfare and the history of the early Church's practices regarding exorcism and apparitions, following the previous section on the nature of spirits.</meta>

# Ludwig Lavater

The holy ancient Fathers, by making the sign of the cross, intended to show their trust in the Cross—that is, in the suffering and death of Christ—which takes away and drives out all evil. The Devil does not fear the cross that a person makes, nor the

<margin>The wooden Cross.</margin>

small pieces that are said to be cut from the wooden Cross of Christ and are kept and displayed as relics <note>original: "heiligthumb"</note>; he fears them not at all. Rather, he fears the effect and power of Christ's suffering, through which he was overcome. If someone today gives too much credit to external ceremonies, it is an abuse and superstition, which is rightly scolded. Furthermore, we read in the ancient Fathers that in the early church, they adjured <note>exorcised or commanded</note> the devils.

<margin>On adjuring the Monster.</margin>

You also find in Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD</note>, in his book *On the Soul* <note>Latin: "de Anima"</note>, that the unclean spirits often deceived people by pretending to be others, acting as if they were the souls of the deceased. They did this so that people would not believe that all souls went to the lower world <note>Latin: "ad inferos"</note>, thereby casting doubt on the faith in the Last Judgment and the resurrection of the dead. He reports that they were subsequently adjured and brought to the point where, against their will, they had to confess the truth: namely, that they were unclean spirits and not souls.

The ancients also drove out or adjured the unclean spirits from people, and also from those places where they bothered people with rumbling, knocking, and in other ways, as a story of St. John is read in Abdias of Babylon. For the holy Apostles, and after them many holy people, had the grace from God to be able to drive out devils. This gift and grace lasted in the Church for a good time for the benefit of believers, but later ceased, just as other miracles did. Tertullian writes in his *Apology* <note>Latin: "Apologetico"</note> on pages 858 and 859: one should present someone who claims that the gods speak through him; then the devil, at the command of any Christian, must confess that he is playing a game. Furthermore, he says: if Christians only

<column-break/>

touch or breathe upon a possessed person, the devils must depart against their will. He also mentions adjuration in his other books and writings.

However, they did not use many strange ceremonies and characters <note>magical symbols or sigils</note> in their adjuration, but commanded the evil spirits in a simple manner, in the name of our Lord Jesus the Crucified, to depart from a person or from a place where they had made themselves known. Later, when the gift had ceased, some merely continued the practice out of habit. The holy Origen <note>An early Greek scholar and theologian, c. 185–253 AD</note> writes that one should not adjure the unclean spirits, nor question them, nor speak as if the evil spirit hears; rather, one should persist in prayer and fasting, so that those plagued by the evil enemy may be helped. From this, one notes that in his time, adjuration was still in use, but it displeased him not a little.

That the ancient Christians placed no value on such apparitions is seen in what the holy Cyril writes in his 10th book against the Emperor Julian. Julian accused the Christians, saying the Apostles had taught them to keep watch at graves and to desire visions or dreams. Cyril replied that Julian did the Christians violence and injustice; he was mistaken, for he was attributing to Christians what the Heathens do (for in Isaiah chapter 65, such things are said of the Heathens). The Jews, and the Christians after them who follow the Divine law, do not have the custom of desiring visions to appear to them in dreams, nor do they in a childish way take pleasure in various apparitions; rather, they hate those who teach such things. For it is written in Deuteronomy chapter 13 <note>The text says chapter 11, but the reference to a rising prophet is chapter 13</note>: "If a prophet arises among you," etc.

<margin>Christians do not rely on visions.</margin>

To this also serves what Tertullian reports in his book *On the Soul* on page 688: it is written that the Nasamones <note>original: "Namanæ," a North African tribe</note> watch by the graves of their ancestors and ask how this or that should be undertaken or how it will end. The Celts watch by the graves of their heroes for the same reasons.

<margin>They seek oracles.</margin>

# Of Ghosts / The Third Part.
<sig>Q iiij</sig>

<margin>
The evil spirit appeared to St. Martin.
</margin>
Sulpitius Severus, who composed the life of St. Martin in three books (both of these lived at the same time, approximately 500 years after the birth of Christ), reports in the first book that at one time the Devil appeared to St. Martin in his cell in great radiance. He wore a <term>diadem</term> <note>original: "diadema"</note>, which is a headband adorned with precious stones (such as kings used in former times), upon his head, and had shoes adorned with gold upon his feet, and appeared cheerful and lovely. And as St. Martin was startled by him at first sight, they both remained silent for a good while. Then the Devil said he was Christ and wished to reveal himself to him. But as St. Martin answered nothing to this, he said further: "Martin, do you doubt whether you should believe what you see? I am Christ." And when the Spirit of God revealed to him that it was the Devil, Martin spoke: "Christ did not say that he would return in purple and a crown. I will not believe that Christ has come unless he comes in the form in which he suffered, bearing the marks of the nails with which he was fastened to the Cross." At this, the Devil vanished like smoke and left the cell (with your permission to mention it) so foul-smelling that one could well understand it had been the Devil. Severus writes that he did not have this from hearsay, but heard it from Martin’s own mouth; therefore, one should not consider it a fable.

Thus we have understood how the holy, pious Fathers and the ancient Christians conducted themselves when ghosts and monsters appeared to them.

-> How many kinds of superstition crept in, by which men undertook to drive away ghosts. <-

### The Tenth Chapter.

<margin>
2 Thess. 2.
</margin>
In the meantime, however, much superstition gradually crept in. The holy Paul complains that even in his time the Antichrist had begun to stir and various sects arose; St. John also says that many antichrists were already on the path in his time. Therefore, it is all the less to be wondered at that afterwards and in time, various errors sprang up in the Church.

<column-break/>

St. Augustine relates in *The City of God* <note>original: "de Civitate Dei"</note> in the 22nd book, 8th chapter, as he described several miracles which occurred so that the world might believe in Christ, among others such a history or story: There was a prominent man among them named Hesperius, who had an estate or a farm in which evil spirits greatly plagued his livestock and his servants. Therefore, he asked the priests in the absence of St. Augustine that one of them might go there so that they might depart at his prayer. One went and offered the Sacrifice of Christ there (the ancients called the Lord’s Supper a "sacrifice" <note>original: "Opffer"</note>, but in a different sense than is customary today) and prayed as fervently as he could that the plague might cease. He had, however, received earth from one of his good friends which had come from Jerusalem out of the Promised Land, and had hung the same in his chamber so that no harm might befall him. And that same house was delivered from this plague. From which it is easy to perceive how superstition began to spread, and as often happens, became greater the longer it lasted—just as when one rolls a snowball further, or an avalanche <note>original: "Löuwin" / Lawine</note> starts in the high mountains and covers everything far and wide with snow. Men also early began to pray and offer for souls, as may be noted from several passages of the holy Fathers.

Subsequently, as the bishops and pastors not only failed to correct the old abuses but added more out of "good intentions," the matter became worse and worse. For when monsters appeared, men did not call upon God alone through Christ, but upon the dear saints, regardless of what Paul says in Romans chapter 10 (for I will let other arguments rest for now): "How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?" Now, one should believe in God alone, and for that reason call upon Him through His Son alone.

<meta>This page continues the theological discourse of Ludwig Lavater regarding the nature of spiritual apparitions and the correct Christian response to them, specifically addressing the misuse of the "Hail Mary" as a magical incantation.</meta>

# Ludwig Lavater

<margin>
The Angelic Salutation.
</margin>
There is said to be no better medicine to drive away monsters and ghosts than to pray the *Ave Maria* <note>original: "Aue Maria"; the Hail Mary</note>. However, the *Ave Maria* is not a prayer (which I must mention at the outset) but rather a greeting and a historical narrative of how the Angel Gabriel announced the incarnation of Christ to the Holy Virgin Mary. If you look at the words themselves, you will not find that one asks or petitions for anything with them. When the Angel came to her, he greeted her and spoke, <term>chaire</term> <note>original Greek: χαῖρε; a greeting meaning "rejoice" or "hail"</note>, "God greet you" or "rejoice" (for that is what the Greek word signifies, 
<margin>
To hail is to rejoice.
<note>original Latin: "Auere est gaudere"</note>
</margin>
as does the Latin *Avere*, according to Festus). "You favored one," *Gratia plena* <note>Latin: "Full of grace"</note>, should be understood in a passive sense, as they say in the Schools <note>referring to Scholastic academic theology</note>: that she is filled with grace by God, as the Angel himself interprets it when he later says she has "found favor," that is, God is gracious to her and wishes her well. And you should not understand it to mean that she is a fountain of grace (as some have taught), as if she possessed grace from and out of herself and shared it with those who call upon her as a Mediatrix or greet her with the *Ave Maria*. For neither the Greek word in the text nor other places in the Holy Divine Scripture can support such a view. In the first chapter of Ephesians, it says that God has graced us believers through His grace in the Beloved, that is, in Christ. The same word is used there as the Angel spoke here to the Holy Virgin Mary. Likewise, in the first chapter of John, it is expressly stated that St. John the Baptist testified of Christ with a loud voice and said: "We have all received from his fullness grace for grace." For the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Christ. Other similar passages I shall omit for the sake of brevity. The Holy Virgin herself says, "The Lord has done great things for me," praising the grace that God the Lord showed her without her merit. For no greater grace has ever happened to any woman. But there is a great difference between the one who gives grace and those who receive grace.
With the one who gives grace, one should alone

<column-break/>

seek grace, and not with those who have received grace. In former times, everyone ran to the Holy Virgin and sought and hoped for more grace and help from her than from our Lord Christ Himself. Further, the Angel says, "The Lord is with thee; blessed" or highly praised "art thou among women," which means the Lord has shown you more grace than any other woman. That which follows—"and blessed" or highly praised "is the fruit of thy womb"—are not the words of the Angel, but the words of her cousin Elizabeth, who also greeted her. To this, others out of devotion added "Jesus Christ, Amen." Thus, the Angel did not speak all these words together, as is clearly understood from the text of Luke in the first chapter; not that they are therefore not holy and good. For it is written of Elizabeth that she was filled with the Holy Spirit, but what the Angel did not say should not be attributed to him. One also does not find that in the time of the Holy Apostles and the ages immediately following, this greeting was used as a prayer, or that the Holy Virgin was otherwise called upon. This is mentioned by us not because we begrudge the Holy Virgin Mary her due honor, but so that one does not, against her will, show her the honor that belongs to God and her Son, our Lord Christ, alone. For He is the sole Mediator and Redeemer (1 Timothy 2). Otherwise, one should read and contemplate the Angelic Salutation and other magnificent, comforting passages of Scripture regarding the Incarnation, the suffering, death, and merit of our Lord Christ frequently and diligently, and not take the Holy Scripture out of the hands of the common man, in which he may read these things himself.
<margin>
Holy Water.
</margin>
It did not stop there, however; water was also exorcised or consecrated with special ceremonies and kept in churches, houses, and elsewhere in cauldrons. Among other effects, the power was attributed to it to drive away ghosts. Salt was consecrated in the same manner, with the claim that wherever it was scattered, it would drive away all ghosts and the deception of the Devil—indeed, the Devil himself.

themselves. Furthermore, people have conjured candles, palms, herbs, and other creatures with special gestures and words, so that they might drive away the *phantasmata* <note>original: "phantasmata" — apparitions or illusions</note> or ghosts. Wherever these ghosts appeared, people carried these objects, as well as relics and other things, to those places. Many have also claimed <margin>The sound of bells.</margin> that bells, through their tone or sound, drive the Devil out of the air. All of this can be found more extensively in the books of the Papists <note>A Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics</note> which are written concerning the consecration of such things. When the bells are rung on St. John’s or St. Agatha’s day, they are said to especially drive away ghosts. On St. John’s day, some also lit a bundle of consecrated herbs to chase away the Devil through their smoke. Many also have their own special and wondrous blessings against ghosts. Furthermore, all kinds of services for the dead were practiced; and upon the appearance of wandering souls, eternal Masses, Vigils, and prayers were established and sung every year, as if the souls had not been redeemed immediately.

That the heathens also had their sacrifices for the dead, such as the *Novendialia sacra* <note>original: "Nouendialia sacra" — Roman Catholic or pagan rites performed nine days after a burial</note> on the ninth day, anniversaries, and others, is found here and there among the poets, etc. But the supposed souls desired nothing more earnestly than that many Masses be held for them continually, because these were thought to have a special effect and power to release them from Purgatory.

<margin>The Cistercian Order.</margin> Johannes Trithemius writes in his *Chronicle of the Hirsau Monastery* that around the year of Christ 1098, in the time of Emperor Henry IV, when the Cistercian Order first arose, not far from Worms, a great number of armed men on horse and foot appeared for many days and nights. It was as if they intended to go against an enemy; they ran in troops now here, then there, and around the ninth hour of the night they returned to the nearby mountains from which they had come. After a long time, a monk from the Limpurg Monastery, which lies not far from this mountain, went there with several others. He made a sign of the cross before him and conjured them by the power of the Holy and Un-

<column-break/>

One from the troop answered him: "We are not living warriors, but a ghost-specter; rather, the souls of those who fought in this region and perished in this place some years ago. The weapons, clothes, and horses, which were instruments of sin for us while we were still alive, are now signs of pain for us after death. Everything that you now see around us is entirely fiery to us, although you cannot see our fire." And when the monk asked whether they could be helped by humans, the spirit answered: "With fasting, prayer, and especially through the sacrifice of the Body and Blood of Christ <note>The Eucharist or Mass</note> they might be helped," for which he also begged them. When he had said this, the entire multitude of spirits cried out for the third time, as if with one voice: "Pray for us!" Soon it was as if they all became fire, and as if the mountain burned; it cracked loudly and spewed fire, etc.

<margin>Exorcists, Conjurers of Devils.</margin> Beyond all this, there was a special rank in the Church of those who were supposed to conjure the Devil; these are called *Exorcistae* <note>Exorcists</note>. However, they did not have the grace to drive out devils like the ancient Christians did; instead, they merely engaged in "shadow-fighting" <note>original: "spiegesfechten" — a sham or mock battle</note>. Accordingly, some monks and priests who were instructed in the Black Arts <note>original: "schwarzen Kunst" — magic or necromancy</note> (as such people are seldom found without them) undertook to drive the evil spirits out of houses into the forests or wildernesses and to conjure them. These people practiced strange adventures and claimed that the evil spirit must depart in the name of the Saints, and by the power of their conjuring or strange characters <note>Magical symbols or sigils</note>. In such cases, the Devil may well depart, but like an enemy seeking his advantage; what he does, he does willingly and gladly, so that he may lead people away from true trust in the one God and stick and strengthen them in idolatry. But when Christ and his Apostles drove out the devils, they did so in such a way that the devils, against their will, had...

In addition, people have hung the Gospel of John around their necks, or carried wax in their pockets which has been consecrated by the Pope and is called the *Lamb of God* <note>original: "Agnus Dei"; a small wax disc bearing the image of a lamb, used as a sacramental</note>. There are several books available, especially that of Doctor Jacobus de Chusa the Carthusian, concerning the appearances of souls departed from the body; it was printed in the town of Burgdorf (belonging to the Lords of Bern) in the year of Christ's birth 1475. In this book, among other things, it is shown how one should prepare oneself when a spirit makes itself known: how one should behave when approaching it and at the place where it lets itself be heard, and what questions one should put to it. This was partly dealt with above on page 141. I have heard from some that they were so superstitious that when the priest elevated the Host during the Mass, they quickly passed their hand over their face, believing that they would then see no monsters or phantoms.

But tell me, dear friend, where do the aforementioned practices have any basis in Holy Scripture? Where do Christ and his dear Apostles teach us to drive away the Devil—who is a spirit and therefore has no physical body—with physical things? Where do we have a single example of them resisting the evil spirit in such a manner? Or did the Lord institute his Supper so that one should hunt away ghosts with it in this fashion? Even if the evil spirit acts as if he retreats because of these things, he actually sits all the deeper in the hearts of men through such superstition.

<margin>One should not attempt to drive away the phantom with cursing, swearing, or with the physical sword.</margin>

### The Ninth Chapter.

Here I cannot neglect to mention that some people are also found who believe that if one encounters a phantom, there is no better remedy than for one to curse and swear profanely, so that it will leave him immediately. For they claim that if one prays, the spirit comes closer and closer and plagues him all the more violently. But our Lord Jesus, who knows best of all how one should defend oneself against the Devil's specters, teaches us in more than one place to persevere earnestly in prayer. That

<column-break/>

is the Devil's delight when a person curses and swears; he may act as if he leaves him, but he actually draws closer in an invisible way. A person may otherwise give the Devil or the ghosts their dismissal and say they should go to the abyss of Hell where they belong; they have no claim at all on him, as one who sets his hope and trust in Christ Jesus. For in Romans, Chapter 8, it is written: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh," etc. One can tell the Devil to go his way without needing to swear, bluster, or behave perversely. It is also dishonorable that coarse, godless fellows, when a phantom appears, sometimes speak to it in a crude and shameful manner.

<margin>The phantoms cannot be driven away with the sword. Concerning a coarse Spartan.</margin>

Some, when they see phantoms, draw their swords and want to strike at them, or attempt to drive them out of a window. In Plutarch's *Laconian Apophthegms* <note>original: "in Laconicis"</note>, one reads that a Laconian <note>a Spartan</note>, as he walked past a grave at night and saw a phantom or ghost, ran toward it and wanted to stab it with his spear, saying, "Where are you fleeing, soul, you who must die twice?" It is indeed praiseworthy when one is not terrified by such things, but one should not be too presumptuous either.

Sometimes a man has thought he struck the phantom, but it felt to him as if he had struck a soft pillow. Another thought he had chased the phantom out through a window, but it seemed to him to fall no differently than if dry shingles were flying down into the bushes. Many a man who has attempted to attack phantoms with a weapon in hand is said to have had an arm paralyzed or been otherwise injured in his body. Nothing is to be gained here with the external sword, but rather with the Sword of the Spirit. Those who attempt to strike shadows <note>original: "umbras"</note> or ghosts are true "shadow-fighters." In the Book of Job, it is illustrated through the Leviathan—who cares nothing for a spear—that the evil enemy, who lets himself be seen in all kinds of forms, cares nothing for—

# Concerning Spirits / The Third Part.

nothing for a spear. For the Devil is a spirit; he has neither flesh nor bone, but only takes on an external form. But where there are physical spirits (that is, when sorcerers, priests, whores, and knaves pass themselves off as monsters), there is no stronger or better exorcism than if one were to rush at them with a good cudgel <note>original: "tremmel" - a heavy club or staff</note> and thrash them soundly; for they care nothing for kind or powerful words, but they do care for hard blows.

Hitherto I have spoken of how those should conduct themselves who encounter something; now as for those who encounter nothing, as one finds many who in their whole life have never seen a monster, these have all the more reason to thank God. They should also not be presumptuous and desire to see something, but rather pray to God for others who are plagued by these things. They should not act like the majority of those who, having had no particular illness in their lives, do not believe the sickness of others and think they are telling fables, until the Lord God also casts them into a heavy sickbed. Thus God may also send something to a man’s house and home, so that he may afterwards have compassion for other people.

->How one should conduct oneself when crashes and other such things are heard.<-

### The Twelfth Chapter.

As far as other things are concerned now, such as when one hears crashes, or when other strange, wonderful things occur and happen before great changes (of which mention was made above), one should never place too much weight upon them. For these things often—indeed, for the most part—happen through the Devil's deception; he would love for Man to brood over these things and imagine many gruesome things, so that he might become melancholy, fall into sickness, and have no peaceful day in all his life. Rather, when such things truly happen, they should move us to let fall everything that we have hitherto practiced against God, and to apply ourselves all the more faithfully to His will, and also to prepare ourselves, as the Lord otherwise teaches us, so that when

<column-break/>

He comes and wishes to summon us from here, we may be prepared. Furthermore, we should take up the various other cases that strike us all the more lightly and patiently.

<margin>Plutarch’s Christian opinion.</margin>
Plutarch, a pagan historian, has—in my opinion—not a bad view of these prodigies <note>original: "Prodigiis" - omens or supernatural events</note> and portents. Where he writes of Alexander the Great, that several omens or signs of fate preceded his death, he indicated that Alexander at times inquired nothing at all of these things but despised them all; on the other hand, he held simple things to be signs that they signified some future misfortune. He mentions alongside this how it is a harmful thing when one despises the signs presented to Men by God; likewise, it is harmful when one fears everything. For as in other matters, so also in this one should do neither too much nor too little. He holds the same opinion regarding other wonders. For in the life of Camillus it is written how Camillus, the Roman captain, having conquered and razed the city of Veii, undertook to bring the image of Juno to Rome, as he had made a vow. He appointed people to take the image, sacrificed to the goddess, and prayed that she would be gracious to him and the Romans, as were the other gods who dwelt in Rome. Then the image answered that it was well satisfied with the matter. Those who wrote of this also report many other such wonderful things, prodigies, such as that sweat often issued from the images, that they were heard to sigh, that they turned their faces aside, or that they looked downward. He says that those who lived before his time recorded much of this, and that he heard many wonderful things from those who lived in his own time, which are not easily to be despised by anyone; but human frailty causes one to either give too much belief to these things or to believe them not at all, not without harm. For Men cannot easily hit the middle ground, but are either too superstitious and place too much weight on such things, or they despise them
