Thus the Devil can sometimes secretly steal a child and substitute another for it, with whom he has had dealings for a time, so that she believes the child is hers. Another history useful for this purpose is cited by Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1184–1264), a Dominican friar and encyclopedist</note> in his *Mirror of Nature* <note>original: "naturali Speculo"</note>, from the 4th book of Helimandus <note>Hélinand of Froidmont, a medieval chronicler</note>, chapters 26 and 27: how in Cologne on the Rhine, many distinguished people looked out from a palace upon the Rhine and there became aware of a small ship, which sailed down the Rhine. In front of it swam a white swan, which pulled the ship along by a silver chain. In it stood a new and unknown knight, who leaped from the ship onto the land. There in Cologne he took a wife and fathered many children with her; but after several years the swan returned with the little ship, and the knight leaped back into it and was never seen again. His children and his lineage, says Helimandus, remained alive for a long time thereafter.

That was the Devil, who disguised himself in the form of a knight. But the children he had with his wife were true, natural human children, whom he had stolen elsewhere and exchanged, and at the time of the deceptive birth, he placed and substituted them under his wife, thus blinding other people into thinking they came from the woman.

It can also happen that the Devil does not always steal children from elsewhere, but that he presents himself in the form of a child, and the longer it lasts, the more he lets himself be seen as if he were growing and becoming larger with age.

As for example: Geoffrey of Auxerre <note>original: "Ganfridus Antissiodorus," a 12th-century Cistercian abbot</note> says (as Vincent then reports in the *Mirror of Nature*, book 3) that it truly happened in Sicily that a young fellow, who could swim well, was bathing in the sea by moonlight at night.

He caught a mermaid <note>original: "Meerfrawen"</note> and held her with great strength, and brought her with him to land. He covered her with his cloak and led her home to his house, and took her publicly as his wife. She showed herself friendly toward him and treated him well, but would never speak a single word. But when it began to seem to his companions and neighbors that it was not a right matter, and that she was not a natural human woman but only a deception and a phantom, they advised him to force her to say where she was from and why she did not speak. Now she had conceived and borne a son by him; he took the child one time and threatened the woman that if she would not tell him who and from where she was, he would kill the son. Thereupon the woman began to speak and said: "O you miserable man, you shall know that you lose a good housewife because you force me to speak; for I would have stayed with you always, and it would have gone well for you with me if you had let me remain mute; but now you shall see me nevermore," and with that she vanished. But the son also bathed often in the sea thereafter, and it finally happened that the mermaid, his mother, swam up to him, seized the son, and led him away, so that he too was never seen again afterward.

The mermaid and also her son were two living devils, one of whom disguised himself in a woman's form, and the other in the form of a child. For if this son were not a true human child—whom the Devil might have stolen elsewhere—he would have drowned in the sea after he was led under the water by the mermaid; and if he had been drowned and dead, the sea, according to its custom, would have pushed and cast him out onto the land or shore. For the sea suffers no dead thing. But none of that happened. Therefore, etc. <note>The author uses "Ergo" to conclude his logical proof that the beings were demonic.</note>

Some also report—as one might think—that the Devil, acting as a swift <term>Physicus</term><note>A natural philosopher or physician</note>, could create such an object and a strong impression or imagination in a person who is otherwise naturally lustful, so that their <term>Semen</term><note>Seed/Sperm</note> escapes them. He then catches this and might pour it into another witch or "vessel of the Devil." As those loose hags say: it feels like a cold, wet sack or rag when he has to do with them. I leave this thought to each individual's judgment, and certainly hold that he, as a meddling spirit, often carries out wonderful and strange things with his witches. But that children should come from such seed is nothing <note>i.e., impossible/false</note>, as we shall hear.

Another person might also have this <term>speculationem</term><note>theory or speculation</note>: that the versatile and swift Devil might change his custom, being sometimes a <term>dæmon Incubus</term><note>original: "dæmon Incubus"; a male-form demon believed to lie upon sleepers</note> in a man's shape, and sometimes a <term>dæmon Succubus</term><note>original: "dæmon Succubus"; a female-form demon</note> in a woman's shape, and can thus have to do with both woman and man. When he is a Succubus, he receives the human seed from a man, and then goes to godless, lewd women who are devoted to him; with them he acts as an Incubus and pours that same seed into them, and from this, children are later born—conceived and born not from a spirit, but from human seed which the Devil has poured in.

I cannot reject this theory of the <term>Succubo & Incubo Diabolo</term><note>The Succubus and Incubus Devil</note>, as it is certain that he can disguise himself in a thousand forms. But that children may come from this stolen seed is nothing, because it becomes cold, powerless, and through being carried back and forth, it is altered and becomes useless for birth. And <term>Conciliator</term><note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316), a famous physician and philosopher known as "The Conciliator"</note> in the *Book of Medicine*, <term>differentia 25</term><note>Section or distinction 25</note>, explains this matter correctly and says: "You should know that the genitals of the man are a prince and lord of the procreative power." This is also testified by <term>Galenus</term><note>Galen of Pergamon, the influential Roman physician</note> with more words and better understanding, where he says: "Although the genitals of humans have a special power for procreation, 

<column-break/>

the first origin does not come from them, nor can they accomplish such a thing by themselves alone. For the first beginning comes from the heart through the internal and living power, which can then well temper and prepare its measure and kind, through which the genitals have heart and power for procreation, but not perfectly," etc.

From this saying, I conclude that the Devil cannot nor may not receive or effectively gather human seed, which has its origin and power primarily from the heart and its heat and warmth. And even if the Devil, through the help of evil and desperate people and by God's permission, obtains and keeps the seed, yet from that pouring-in alone, without other powers and virtues (as just stated), nothing living, good, nor powerful can be born.

Otherwise, however, the Devil as a Succubus or Incubus can have to do with a person to inflict harm upon them, as happened in Zurich in Switzerland: a butcher's apprentice was traveling at night following his trade and was also thinking of lewdness. A beautiful woman appeared to him, as he thought; he slept with her and committed unchastity with her. But he immediately became so ill that his genitals and all belonging to them became inflamed and rotted away. That was the Devil as a Succubus.

There was also a common slut in the same place who was slept with at night by the Devil in human form; she also became ill immediately, and her body was so ignited with <term>kalter Brand</term><note>Gangrene</note> that no cutting <note>surgery</note> helped, and she died before the ninth day; for she became so wretched that all her entrails fell out. These are punishments and warnings from God, so that everyone may learn to avoid the great and heavy sin of lewdness.

I could not keep silent about these examples and histories, in order to better settle the preceding questions, the basis of some of which...

For even the strong angels of God are appointed—not only over us adults, but as we read in Matthew, chapter 18—over the young, innocent children and infants, to serve them and to protect them.

This I have thus briefly, in great haste, gathered together for the good instruction of everyone, and out of Christian good intention, I neither should nor would withhold it. ### The 10th Little Treatise.
### Report
# On the investigation, trial, and recognition of female witches by cold water, in which the opinion of Wilhelm Adolph Scribonius is refuted, and the origin, nature, and truth of this and other purgings <term>purgation: a legal ordeal or trial used to determine guilt or innocence</term> are discussed. Useful and necessary for all authorities and rulers to know. Composed and published by Hermann Neuwalt, Doctor of Medicine and Professor at the Julius University. But now translated from the Latin into the German language by

### Master Henricus Meibom, Professor of
### Poetry and History at the Julius University.

# To the Noble Lords, Lord
### Adolph and Lord Ernst, Counts of Holstein,
### Schauenburg, and Sternberg, Lords of Gemen,
->My gracious Lords.<-

Noble, gracious Lords, it is not only difficult and laborious to eradicate a habit that has crept in among the common rabble and become established over many years—sitting deep in their hearts and bearing the appearance of truth—but it is almost equally difficult to lead learned people, who have embraced a certain delusion and opinion, away from their undertaking and bring them back to the right path. The former appeal to old custom, and whatever has the appearance of being ancient, they do not depart from it; acting as if truth depended upon a statute of limitations <note>original: "verjahrung," a legal term for prescriptive right or expiration</note>, just as the Papists have taught. The latter, however, wishing to be wiser, claim they can provide good evidence which ought to be believed. Thus, the matter is contested with great ambition, but if one considers the situation, such things happen with great danger.

For although many things are forced upon us, gain belief, and gradually take root, we ought to consider the matter diligently and not hold everything that has crept in under a false appearance and received approval from superstition as equal to God's word. To this category belong those practices that have fallen into common use and please and delight the people. Others, who are far too clever, wish it to be considered wrong to look at custom; they seek colored, false grounds and reasons, thinking they have hit the mark perfectly and have climbed so high that the matter they speak of is hidden from reason and in no way subject to it.

I have recently seen such an example in a writing composed by Wilhelm Adolph Scribonius <note>A philosopher and physician (c. 1550–1600) who defended the legality of the water ordeal</note>, in which he undertakes to prove with testimonies and good reasons that it is right to throw sorceresses <note>original: "Zauberinnen," specifically female witches</note> into the water, contrary to all

<column-break/>

other judgments and opinions. The opinion in which he is stuck is not only scandalous but amounts to a contempt of God; it is in itself dishonorable and also harmful, since we must wish that we may keep our reason undisturbed alongside a healthy body—that is, so that we do not go about pregnant with false delusions, dragging them with us, and thus be corrupted at the core. For, to say nothing here of the superstition and abomination that springs from the transgression of the First Commandment, this matter is entirely inhuman—not only that one human should harm and injure another, but that this invention, so contrary to reason, is the Devil's find and suggestion. He gave it to some godless gallows-birds <note>original: "Diebhenckern," a derogatory term for criminals or low-lifes</note>, who further showed it to the inquisitive rabble and have practiced it until now without punishment. No one knows the beginning of it; the first inventor is also uncertain. But that it is an old custom is to be learned from the Devil's cunning and mockery <note>original: "afferey," literally 'apery' or mimicking</note>, who from the beginning of the world has wanted to imitate God in everything—insofar as, in the opinion of the learned, this investigation was devised and introduced to the people following the example of the suspected wives in the Old Testament <note>A reference to the "Ordeal of the Bitter Water" for suspected adultery in Numbers 5</note>, as will be reported in detail hereafter. For histories testify and experience shows that this trial <note>term: "Probstück" (test-piece/ordeal) - a judicial test used to determine guilt or innocence through physical endurance or divine intervention</note> has also been used to investigate many other things.

But since this practice of identifying sorceresses has crept in among some, and is especially taking root in Westphalia so that it is becoming almost like a custom <note>original: "Süzüg," likely a regional variant for a prevailing habit or 'sweet' obsession</note>, necessity demands that one inquire after its initial origin, so that many people may be saved and superstition may be weeded out. Thus, we may not offend against Divine Majesty by tolerating such a thing, which cannot be done without blaspheming God's name.

# To the Honorable and Very Wise
### Messrs. Heinrich Floreken and Dietrich Kothman,
### Mayors, School Overseers, and Councilors of the laudable
### City of Lemgo, his highly favored
### Lords and Friends.

Very Wise and Highly Learned Messrs. Mayors: When I arrived at your city of Lemgo on the twenty-fifth day of the harvest month <note>September</note>, two days later—exactly on the eve of Michaelmas <note>September 28th</note>—three sorceresses <note>original: "Zäuberinnen"</note> were brought from life to death by fire, by decree of the Council, on account of their manifold and gruesome misdeeds. That same evening, another three, who had been named by the aforementioned as their accomplices and associates, were seized by the city servants and placed in prison. On the following day, however, at nearly two o'clock in the afternoon, they were thrown into the water outside the city gate for the further investigation of the truth, so that it might be seen whether they would sink or not. Indeed, their hands and feet were tightly bound and their clothes removed; the binding was applied in the following manner: the right hand was fastened to the left big toe, and likewise the left hand to the right big toe, so that they could not move their entire bodies at all. Thereupon, in the presence of several thousand people, they were thrown into the water, each of them three times; but just like a piece of wood or a log, they floated on top, and none sank.

And what was also greatly to be wondered at: as they were being led from the dungeon through the city to the aforementioned place on prepared carts, the rainy weather that had just begun ceased at that very moment—almost in the instant the sorceresses first touched the water—to such an extent that while they floated upon the water, the sun unexpectedly shone forth and the sky became quite beautiful and clear. But as soon as they were pulled out again, it began to rain heavily.

<column-break/>

As I witnessed this spectacle, I wondered most vehemently at this new custom, as it is unheard of in other parts of Germany. I would have gladly received a report on the grounds and causes of this inquiry and investigation, but I could learn nothing certain. Rather, I understood the common saying to be that this custom has crept in through the experience and observation of certain peoples—especially this summer—namely, that all those who are witches and sorceresses, or who stand under suspicion due to certain indications of knowing the same art and being in that gang, are examined in this manner. Those who float on top are considered guilty, but those who sink are free, innocent, and without fault. Yet there is a lack of any sufficient reason that can be given for it. Therefore, in great wonder at the matter, I have seriously reflected whether some natural cause might be found and brought forward which might confirm this practice—which was devised and introduced by human counsel and deliberation—and mostly for the reason that you, Very Wise and Highly Learned Messrs. Mayors, in the presence of other gentlemen of the old Council, requested of me that I should put on paper as much as I know of this and present it to you in writing. I confess, therefore, for I cannot deny it, that the matter is altogether wonderful and strange; nevertheless, I do not believe it is so constituted that we cannot grasp it with our reason.

# On the Investigation of Witches

Therefore, I have not been burdened by presenting my simple opinion according to my limited understanding; I wish hereby to give others, who are more learned than I, cause to further consider and more extensively handle this question, upon which a person’s body and life depend.

Weyer <note>original: "Wierus"; referring to Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who was an early critic of the witch trials</note>, a Doctor of Medicine, mentions this custom in the 6th Book of *On the Deceptions of Demons* <note>original: "De praestigiis daemonum"</note> in the 7th Chapter. He says it is to be found nowhere <insert>legally</insert> and is not unjustly despised as an indication that frequently fails. I see, however, no certain proof with which he intends to defend and shield his opinion. He also cites no particularly certain example from which he might conclude that the experience and trial are deceptive and uncertain. Therefore, no one will sufficiently prove, using Weyer’s testimony alone, that this present matter is frivolous and uncertain.

Beyond this, several old jurists have considered this matter under the title and name of a "purgation" <term>purgation: a legal method of clearing oneself of a crime through an ordeal</term> and a demonstration of innocence through cold water, just as I have found in their books from your report and indication, Honorable and Highly Learned Burgomaster Cotman. Cujas <note>original: "Cuiacius"; Jacques Cujas, a famous French legal humanist</note>, in the second book of his commentary on the first book of Gerhardus Niger regarding feudal law, calls it a "judgment of cold water" <note>original: "judicium aquae frigidae"</note>; he mentions alongside this that it was in use among the Lombards but was abandoned shortly thereafter. Furthermore, Joos de Damhouder of Bruges from Flanders states in his *Practice of Criminal Matters*: At almost the same time, other purgations and common declarations were also customary, with which those who were suspected and accused declared themselves innocent; namely, when they carried a glowing iron in their hand, or walked over hot iron with bare feet, and the like. For such types of trial-pieces, the Counts of Flanders gave many privileges to their people. Additionally, the people of Ghent were also granted the favor by the Count of Flanders that they might prove their innocence with cold water.

<column-break/>

Diego de Covarrubias y Leyva, Archbishop of Toledo and a Spaniard, also mentions these customs in the fourth book, twenty-third chapter.

Furthermore, Plutarch reports that in the Island of Pontus <note>likely referring to a legendary location or a misunderstanding of "Pontus" as an island</note> there dwell certain people who possess total knowledge of the forbidden and supernatural art of magic, but they are recognized by the fact that they have the shape of a horse in one eye and two pupils in the other; these people can in no way be sunk under the water, even if they are weighed down and burdened with armor. From this, it can be recognized that even on that island, this custom was in vogue: that witches were tested through water. Many others describe this likewise, but to tell the truth, they grasp such things more with simple words than by explaining thoroughly why this usage was introduced, for no general, constant, and certain cause is cited. Truly, however, when I take to heart what I have seen, I conclude thus: Even if neither I nor Weyer can find and fathom the cause of this purgation, others will not lack them. Whatever is subject to human reason—if not the exact origins, then at least the plausible ones—can be searched out and found, so that a person's heart may rest upon them in the absence of infallible truth. This investigation of witches was introduced through human counsel and deliberation; it is therefore undoubtedly true that it was devised for a significant and important reason, whatever may be lacking in the fact that the ancients did not include it in their records.

All philosophers, both the Academics and the Peripatetics <note>followers of Plato and Aristotle, respectively</note>, say unanimously and with one mind: that which is light steers itself upwards and hastens toward every high place; but that which is heavy goes downwards and, according to its nature, desires to be at the lowest place. Hence it happens that often a large piece of wood, because it is not dense and therefore also light, floats upon the water...

From this foundation and cornerstone, the resolution of the question at hand must be sought and concluded: namely, for what reasons witches, above other women, float on top and do not sink. Here, however, someone might object and say: that the very same matter and form is found in the bodies of witches as is in other women, and as for lightness and heaviness, they possess the same qualities arising from the first and primary elements. If they were to be judged as light, other women would have to be of the same nature; therefore, it will be necessary for us to seek other aids and grounds to prove our argument.

I conclude, therefore, that from the moment witches make acquaintance and fellowship with the Devil, they lose their former properties, status, and essence; regarding also their internal form, they are entirely different people than they were before, receiving a new shape. Thus, the masters <note>likely referring to legal or theological authorities</note> can describe them as people who have their portion from the Devil, who has possessed them. For the evil angel, who is a spirit and ruler of the air, and is also a cause of all our sin and misdeeds, has so taken over the hearts and other limbs of these women that he is essentially spread through their entire substance and all its parts; indeed, because they live in impenitence and do not convert, he leaves no limb of their body. It follows then, that wherever they move, he is with them; because of this, they can no longer think or perform anything good, but instead accomplish all kinds of hideous, filthy sin and shame, commit disorderly misdeeds, and think of nothing but the harm and ruin of other creatures. For although they sometimes let themselves appear pious, God-fearing, and very holy—so that they do not even shrink from going to the Lord’s Table <note>Holy Communion</note> with other people, which has been found in some who were seized as soon as they had done so—yet such a thing happens by the command and permission of the Devil. He does this so that, while other people do not notice their wickedness, he may keep the witches all the longer in his snares and seduce them more and more; and also that they, the witches, may not perceive the deceit and knavery of the Devil, whom they consider their secret and close friend.

Since this is the case, no one should doubt that the strength and power of their entire bodies are completely changed and have lost their former properties. The nature of the evil angel, however, is like a spirit—airy and light—which quickly wanders through all places under heaven. Therefore, I would say that he, dwelling in the bodies of the witches, also makes those same bodies much lighter with his spiritual, flying, and light essence, although other people cannot perceive it. Or else, that he lifts them up with his air, which is essentially poured into them and sticks within them, so that they are held up by this lightness and, whether they want to or not, must float on top. This is, in my opinion, to be credibly proven by the fact that he often pulls them high into the air, where it is impossible for them to go because of their corporeal nature. But should someone remain in the delusion that this is only a false and imaginary thing—that they only imagine it happens, though they believe it quite certainly—I appeal instead to experience. Experience has often shown that people who never had fellowship with the Devil have nonetheless been carried by him from one street to another far away, or from a city or village into the wide field, as if by the hair, first led into the air and afterwards thrown quite hard upon the earth. I have learned that such things have happened both in other places and also at Marburg; but to cite specific examples is a hateful task. Nevertheless, someone might make this counter-argument:

# On the Investigation of Witches

->**Of the Investigation of Witches.**<-

If it is to be attributed to spiritual lightness <note>The author refers to a supernatural lack of weight caused by demons.</note> that witches do not sink like other women, then this test is nevertheless uncertain and false, since perhaps other people could also hold their breath in such a way that they float upon the water. As we see, those who hold their breath the longest can swim further and longer. However, it is known and obvious to everyone that the cause of floating is not only the holding of the breath, but much more, whoever can move and stir their limbs powerfully and properly does the best.

Now, because witches and other innocent women are entangled and bound in the same manner, they can both—one no more or less than the other—move themselves; and the external air, which those who swim in water draw to themselves, is withdrawn and prevented for them no less than for the witches, and no more withdrawn from the witches than from the innocent. Nevertheless, those who are guilty, no matter what air they try to grasp, none of them go under. For experience witnesses that all those who did not go to the bottom afterwards voluntarily confessed and declared their guilt. From this it is to be seen that Weyer's <note>original: "Wieri"; referring to Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued against the witch trials.</note> error is evident, who argues that some hold their breath and thus do not go to the bottom: because they could all hold their breath quite strongly and unhindered.

Therefore, I do not see what absurd thing would follow if I say: the witches are drawn upwards by spiritual lightness (I mean demonic, however) or by the air, or are maintained on top of the water so that they do not perish. But someone might say: does the Devil then want these women, his servants, to come away unhurt and undamaged? Dear friend, what purpose does it serve that the witches are thus pulled up and float on top? In truth, at the core, he does not seek that they be saved; rather, through his inherited natural power and the permission of our LORD GOD, he maintains, preserves, and

<column-break/>

pulls them in the water, not to the end that they should go free and live, but much more so that their demonic society and the union they have established with the evil spirits may become known to the onlookers, and they may be further plunged into unavoidable danger of body and soul. For the Devil himself, as a servant and beadle <note>A minor official or church officer; here used to describe the Devil acting as God's executioner.</note> who is ordained to carry out GOD'S command, wants to report them in this way to the authorities and the whole people; he wants to show that their misdeeds must be punished (and they must be, whether he wills it or not) so that they receive their reward, which they have honestly earned. All those whom he has driven to commit a transgression, he very gladly leads into extreme ruin, especially at the time which is appointed by God.

Now, if someone were to ask me for natural proof of this trial by cold water, how would I answer—yet not without basis? The working cause would be an airy lifting in their body, which is caused by a similar lightness that is within them. But why such a thing happens would be so that the nature of such people might be brought to light and made manifest. Since no mortal human can see the devils, who are spirits, or see their substance—for they are invisible and incomprehensible—the Devil has hit upon this use of the purgation <note><term>Purgation</term>: A legal or ritual clearing of guilt, in this case through the water ordeal.</note> as a convenient and fitting means which people can see, so that even though his essence and body are hidden, his will and recruitment may be recognized. After diligent consideration of all these things together, I conclude, most wise and highly learned Lords Burgomaster, that it is improper that one should despise and consider as naught this serious practice in Lemgo <note>A German town famous for its intense witch trials in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note> regarding the inquiry of witches through cold water. For although we have no express command regarding this in Holy Scripture, it does not follow in the least that it has no grounds for its origin in Nature. This conclusion—

Much more foolishly is it argued that this trial of sorceresses is against nature, and therefore not to be tolerated, because every human being, when bound and ensnared, easily sinks. Thus conclude those fellows who do not know the foundations and simple principles of the natural philosopher <note>original: "Naturkündiger"</note>, who teach that many things occur beyond nature which are nevertheless not directly contrary to nature; and in that this trial is beyond nature, it appears therefrom that something special is indicated thereby—namely, that the bodies of sorceresses are created much differently than those of other people.

Furthermore, because this is not mentioned in the Holy Gospel, it follows that it is godless and not to be upheld. And this, most wise and highly learned Lords, is what I have brought together at your request.

Herewith, however, it shall be free to all and every theologian, jurist, and philosopher to judge this according to their pleasure, since this question alone is common to all at once. # Counter-report of Hermann Neuwald, Doctor.

<column-break/>

The raging arch-enemy of all Christian believers, the Devil, has turned the entire human race away from God the Almighty and subjected it to himself through no other means and ways than through vain and foolish superstition. For when he enchanted them through the presumed hope of higher wisdom, excellent power, and authority, and gradually joined himself to them, he thus plunged them into eternal destruction. Even in this our time, the murderous spirit does not rest, but prowls around us like a roaring lion, so that he may satisfy and appease his insatiable hunger. He certainly does not lack power and authority, since although he has lost God's favor and grace, his power is not entirely barred or shut in, so that he might not deal with us as he pleases. And although the power is great and overwhelming, finding no equal on the face of the earth—as Job 4 <note>likely referring to Job 41:33</note> testifies—yet a simple human can do more in external matters than that very spirit of terror; for otherwise he would be held back by physical resistance. A human can, how or whom he will, steal another's treasures in a violent and thievish manner, which is impossible for the Devil, who cannot take or accept them even by God's secret hidden counsel, even if it were commanded of him. On the other hand, if God does not hinder him and he sneaks in; he is not master of money and goods. A thief, indeed, by natural opportunity, if he remains otherwise unhindered, lays hands on

himself to the property of others; in the same manner, the Devil besets us, yet only as one who is hemmed in and surrounded. Our Lord God also permits him a great deal of power, but only at such times when He wishes to use him as a tool for the spreading of His Divine Name and for the effecting of the salvation and blessedness of Christian believers, as the history of Saint Job clearly demonstrates. For in this way, all things are made subject, so that the Devil is not, and may not be called, a Creator; he cannot even stir up rain, dew, bad or good weather, which are the works of God alone, as Jeremiah speaks. However, the matter that causes wind and rain can be driven hither and thither by the Devil to terrify people, so that they think everything will be smashed to pieces, go to the ground, and fall into a heap. Sorceresses and witches often confess how they poured water into a hole they had made, and thereby caused a terrible and harmful storm; but this is false, mockery, and a delusion. For the Devil, being a swift observer of nature <note>original: "Naturkündiger" — one who understands the secrets of the natural world</note>, broods upon and measures the preceding signs of a coming tempest, and then persuades and cheats the foolish, unwise women into believing it was brought about through their doing and murmuring, albeit with his, the Devil’s, assistance. By this means, he gains great standing with them, so that they must stand in fear of him. Now, what he does and can do, God permits him; however, because we honestly deserve and earn it through our sins, we cannot be angry with God. Augustine explains himself on this matter with these words: <note>original Latin: "Voluntas Dei est prima & summa causa omniū corporalium specierum & motionum..."</note> *The will of God is the primary and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions, and nothing happens visibly in the whole of this most ample and immense Republic of creation that is not either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments.* God's will is the first and highest cause of everything that lives and moves on Earth; nothing happens in this great, extensive community of all created things in a visible way which has not been previously decided in the hidden, invisible, secret council chambers of the Divine Majesty, and is further commanded or permitted according to the unchangeable eternal justice of God, which both punishes and rewards.

<column-break/>

Now, so that the arch-murderer, the Devil, may gain more approval and expand his kingdom further, he weaves deceptive and swift nets. He wishes to mimic God’s power and miracles like an ape <note>A common medieval/early modern trope: "Simia Dei," the Devil as the Ape of God</note> and imitate them; thus he deceives and convicts the ignorant. How he has undertaken such things among the people of God, but mostly among the heathens, can be seen from the idol-temples that existed here and there, as histories report. These churches were initially built to honor God, but later, as human wickedness took the upper hand and the Devil continually drove and incited them toward the worst, they became gruesome, devilish, idolatrous churches. In these, to the detraction of Divine honor and Majesty, the Devil was worshipped, received sacrifices, and prophesied long in advance concerning secret and future things. We do not wish to cite or bring up the examples of how he has pursued God’s honor and Majesty through imposition and listfulness, for the sake of the horror and impropriety of the matter.

And although we now have God’s word bright and clear, the Devil nevertheless outwits the hearts of many people with his malicious pranks and makes them his own property, all under a false, colored appearance. It is a wonder, in such great clarity of God’s word, that there are still people present who allow themselves to be ensnared in such a piteous and miserable way, as we find with the necromancers <term>Schwarzkünstler: practitioners of the "black arts" or ritual magic</term> and sorceresses. The necromancers and soothsayers <term>Wicker: diviners or practitioners of folk magic</term>, even if they are bound to the Devil in a different manner and cause less harm to their neighbor, must nevertheless suffer the same punishment, since they have taught and practiced forbidden arts against God’s command, as the Scripture judges concerning them. More justly... <note>The text cuts off at the catchword "licher" (more justly/fairly)</note>

# Through the Cold Water

...likely receive the same punishment, for whom a similar sentence is pronounced and an equal penalty is recognized. It appears, however, and is plain to see, as if the **witches** <note>original: *Zauberinnen*</note> learn their art and bind themselves to the **Devil** <note>original: *Teuffel*</note> for the purpose of avenging themselves against their enemies; some to satisfy their disordered, lecherous lusts; some for the sake of gluttony, dancing, and merriment, just as some have a desire to know future things and to reveal secret matters, and more of the like. This one joins for this reason, that one for that, although they are inclined toward all such things. All such dealings are exceedingly foul, as is known to everyone; nor do they always deceive, as experience shows, but we will not treat further of that now.

Through the help of their established **covenant** <note>original: *Bündnuß*</note> they are capable of much, yet everything does not always succeed, according to how their power and authority is bridled and hedged in. If God does not permit it and allow them something, their powders, signs, and incantations are in vain; although they are always found to be powerless, yet through the strength of their alliance, they sometimes achieve their desired ends. Of this, it is said, **Isaiah** speaks in the 28th Chapter: *You have said, we have made a covenant with Death, and with Hell we have made an agreement.* <note>Isaiah 28:15</note> Such covenants established with the Devil are directly contrary to God's word, for He forbids all false idolatry; they are against all honor and equity, and result in the harm and misfortune of one's neighbor. Therefore, the authorities should not forget their office in these cases, and by no means turn a blind eye to those who are convicted, but rather apply diligent industry and labor so that such godless, cursed devil-folk may be cast out from the Christian community before the misfortune spreads too far and poisons and ruins careless, simple people. However, one must look closely and take diligent care that no one proceeds too hastily in these matters, nor allows suspected or doubted people to be executed suddenly before all circumstances are weighed. In this regard

<column-break/>

there has often been a deficiency, as we are able to remember. But let no one think my opinion is that such devil-folk do not exist anywhere, or that they should not be punished in their bodies; rather, I advise and pray that one would look diligently and industriously to ensure we do not believe common rumors too much, nor give any room or place to frivolous and ungodly **probation** <term>probation: a trial or test used as evidence in court</term> and inquiry, which many people agree with, thus turning from certain and steadfast determination to powerless, shameful things, wherein the Devil does not rest.

Now, because a writing by **Wilhelm Adolf Scribonius** of Marburg in Hesse—written to an honorable Council at **Lemgo** and also brought to light there through printing—has come to my hands at this time, in which he argues that the authorities do no wrong when they investigate witches in this manner: namely, that their thumbs are tied crosswise to their big toes and they are thrown naked into the water; if it be the case that they float on top, they are guilty; if they sink to the bottom, then no guilt is found in them. Therefore, I have seen fit that it is well worth the labor that I investigate the matter. I also confess and willingly admit my own simplicity as much as possible—so that I do not disparage other people or prefer my own work—that the matter is at once sublime and important, having sprouted from gross, blind misunderstanding and grown strong through long usage. The initial origin of this custom cannot be known, yet it deceives and outwits us; it first wins our favor and will secretly, afterwards entirely and openly; at last it gains and achieves so much prestige that it is held equal to, or even higher than, a laudable statute. It did not just begin this past summer, as he writes, but was in use eighteen years ago in **Saxony** and **Westphalia**. Whether right or wrong was done therein, and whether this proof and inquiry by **cold water** <note>The "swimming test" for witches</note> is valid among legal scholars...

# On the Investigation of Witches

...must be properly investigated and fathomed. The natural causes and reasons cited in this regard are not to be given the slightest credit.

Accordingly, we wish now to mention something of the ancient and long-standing customs, and to discuss to some extent the cited customs and manners of other peoples, to see whether they can support and confirm the matter at hand; likewise, whether they be godless or Christian, forbidden or unforbidden. Subsequently, the natural causes shall be lawfully weighed and inspected, so that nothing is overlooked. By this, however, no prejudice is intended against any learned or more experienced person. I must confess that it is difficult even for ingenious and highly wise people to guess in all matters what is false or true, right or wrong. For it often happens that both favor and hatred—by which consulted people are driven—and sometimes also self-interest, blind their eyes to such an extent that they cannot see the truth. Thus the matter becomes strayed and confused through their favor into friendship, and disfavor into resentment, or greed into advantage, and sometimes also through immature, careless judgment. God-fearing people should proceed differently in this, for it is not a matter of a "hollow nut" <note>German idiom: "taube Nuss," meaning something worthless or trivial</note>, but concerns the temporal and eternal welfare of many people.

The authorities, who sit in God's stead and are zealous for His justice, should administer their office in such a way that they begin nothing rashly or without a sufficiently conscientious basis, lest they be lamented and cried out against as guilty of innocent blood. It may well happen that in such disorderly "Devil's baths" <note>A metaphorical reference to the chaos of witch trials or perhaps specifically the water ordeal</note>, which bring about only the misfortune and ruin of men, many innocent persons are condemned to the fire. Therefore, all pious authorities should be diligently exhorted that nothing should be undertaken in this matter insolently or dangerously, so that no one suffers pain or harm.

We compel no one here to agree with our opinion (for we should be sworn to no single master), but everyone shall retain the power to judge for themselves, and may bring forward something better and wiser. Even if we do not reach the truth entirely, we will nevertheless strive not to stray far from it. As far as concerns Jacobus Cuiacius <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a famous French legal humanist</note> and Gerhardus Nigrus <note>Gerardus Niger, a 12th-century jurist known for his work on feudal law</note>, it is to be known that Cuiacius wrote an explanation of the first book of Gerhardus Nigrus regarding feudal laws <term>Lehenrechten: the legal system governing the relationship between lords and vassals</term>, and sets forth therein three kinds of means by which one may declare oneself innocent: by oath, by combat, and thirdly by a glowing iron, cold or hot water, and the like. The first is proven and accepted; the others are common and customary. In feudal law, only the oath is valid. Emperor Frederick permitted in some cases the proving of one's innocence through combat, but Cuiacius rejects this as ungodly and un-Christian. Among the Lombards, it could not be abolished, being an old custom, as their King Luitprand <note>Original: "Limbrecht"</note> himself confesses. And in Papal law it is also forbidden. The reason: though David fought Goliath lawfully in this manner, one should not make a law out of it. What was permitted in the Old Testament as a "figure" <note>A symbolic precursor or type</note> should not be followed in the New Testament, as Tiraquellus <note>André Tiraqueau (1488–1558), a French jurist</note> posits. Besides, it is against God's word: *Thou shalt not kill*, *Thou shalt not tempt God*. And often he who has a good cause remains on the field <note>i.e., dies in battle</note>, dying in a just defense. Whoever wishes to accomplish that which cannot happen without God's miraculous intervention is tempting God; for in combat one hopes and seeks that God will help not only the strongest—which commonly happens—but the one who has a good cause, even if he is lesser in power and strength, which proceeds in a miraculous way against the common course of nature. Martialis <note>The Roman poet Martial</note> looks to this when he says:

Procopius also reports that near Rome, on Emperor Nero’s Way, there was a track or racecourse of great size where tournaments and combat were held. We, however, wish to pass over such things and hold for certain that all of this is a godless undertaking, which is detrimental to the common good; for due to certain singular errors of princes and lords, entire governments and communities often receive harm or perish altogether.

The second trial <term>probation: a legal test or trial of guilt</term> occurred by means of a glowing hot iron, which was also known to Sophocles; if one grasped it and held it without injury, he was judged innocent; those who took damage from the burn were declared guilty. Empress Cunigunde, the consort of Emperor Henry II, when she was under suspicion of adultery, had glowing plowshares placed under her feet according to the custom of the time and walked over them eleven times. Maria Augusta, Queen of Aragon and consort of Emperor Otto III, was convicted of adultery through the experience of the glowing iron and was punished in her body for it. # Through Cold Water
### X
<meta>catchword: throne</meta>

...danced; afterwards they are kissed on the hindquarters with a burning torch. As soon as this is done, the goat <note>The devil in the form of a goat</note> is consumed by fire. From the ashes, however, everyone takes a portion, with which they kill their neighbor's oxen, sheep, or horses; as for people, they weary this one with a long-lasting sickness or help that one straight out of life <note>i.e., kill them</note>. At the last, the Devil cries out with a gruesome voice: "Avenge yourselves, or you shall be dead!" and soon everyone returns to the place from whence they came. Thus the Devil not only wants to imitate God in all things, but falsifies all things, for the reason that under a colored appearance of all holiness he may lead ignorant people astray and gain their sworn favor and will; yet he seeks out the utmost danger for them in all things.

<margin>III. Through cold or hot water.</margin>
The third purgation <term>Purgation: a legal method of clearing oneself of a crime, often through an ordeal</term> so commonly used, occurred through cold or hot water. Whether the same fits appropriately here, we must—since the necessity of the matter requires it—examine and inquire with diligence.

Cuiacius <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a famous French legal humanist</note> writes that such a practice was also in vogue among Christians. They have the custom—I know not, he says, whether adopted with good proof—taken from the drink which Moses commanded to be given to women who were notorious for adultery. When a woman took the drink, if she were guilty, immediately the "water of the curse" passed through her, her belly swelled, and her thigh wasted away; she was a spectacle to all the people. If she were innocent of the deed, the drink brought her no danger and was without any harm to her. These are three kinds of trials and inquiries that have been in use, full of all superstitious curiosity, which have been pushed into the world by the loathsome Devil. Because people now argue whether, in the conviction of witches, one can use the trial with cold water, and also cite the Law to prove it, we must look into this more deeply. 

Cuiacius, who is short and round <note>original: "kurtz vnnd rund," meaning concise and direct</note> in his writing, seems from these words—*argumento nescio an bono* <note>original Latin: "by an argument, I know not if it be good"</note>—to allow his displeasure with this practice to show. He accuses the Westphalians of ignorance, though with veiled words; from what preceded, one can well discern his meaning. He also understood very well that the Jewish ceremonies and specific commands are now abolished, and we are not subject to them. Furthermore, I say also that this trial by the "water of the curse" was a Sacrament, which the theologians call a "Sacrament of Jealousy," and it has been discarded along with the others. 

Beyond that, there is a great inequality between these [modern] ceremonies and those which Moses recorded. In this [modern] case, no holy office is performed; God is not called upon over the innocent. They thus have a custom that is supported by no human proof, much less can it be demonstrated from God's command or human laws. They have thus fallen into a thoughtless habit, the origin of which no one knows, which was perhaps devised by magical reports (this shall not be said of all) and presented with great wonder to the people, who have a lust for new spectacles and deceptive sins. For who is more in doubt that those same men are sorcerers, whom the point of the sword obeys, whose bullet does not leave the barrel of the gun, and who, in torture and painful questioning, use magical plots to endure that which cannot be overcome by heavy martyrdom? Thus one art cheats the other.

Finally, it is to be wondered which land-swindler devised this practice and invented the method of binding the feet crosswise, since Moses commanded the taking of the water with solemn ceremonies.

This foolish sinking upon the water notwithstanding, Damhouder <note>Joos de Damhouder (1507–1581), a Belgian jurist</note>—as also Cuiacius elsewhere—mentions the trial by cold water with the usual ropes, which, as I admit, are used because of the talk and the danger of drowning. But now the question is: is such a thing consistent with the Law?

That Damhouder is a patron of this solemnity...

This manner, when the oath goes before it, looks as if it might be acceptable; but whether it is entirely right is too high for me, and I must refer it to learned theologians and jurists to judge. These were thus three current and common purgations, the beginnings of which are full of superstition, and for that reason are rightly rejected and abolished. For how the Devil brought this poison to men, who are inclined to all kinds of superstition, and smuggled it in through unholy and false pieces of testing, is clear as day. The cunning and crafty deceiver seeks only one thing: that he may lead people into superstition and turn them away from God, showing them shadows of Divine Majesty and Omnipotence, making them obligated and bound to him through daily acquaintance. I also do not think that one should fail to give place to those mentioned in Papal Law regarding this testing: namely, that therein lies the desecration of God's name and a daring and proud temptation, which a person should avoid like a mad dog or a poisonous snake. For although some articles are godless and unchristian, and also full of superstition, we do not refuse at all to agree with those which accord with God's word and prefer the truth to lies. Nor can we very well believe that some Popes were so unlearned, or negligent, cold, and lazy in the investigation of Divine matters, that they should understand nothing and inquire nowhere in such things, but were instead drowned in idleness—which, however, the majority of them honestly did.

# On the Investigation of Witches

We must by no means remain silent regarding godless matters. In other lands, there are almost identical signs by which such servants of the Devil are recognized, such as the roaming of the **Werewolves** <note>original: "Beerwölffe"</note> in the furthest borders of Livonia <note>A historical region on the eastern shores of the Baltic Sea</note>, during the "Twelve Nights" as they are called—that is, the twelve days that immediately follow Christmas. These werewolves gather in packs of several thousand; they are led through woods, waters, and other uninhabited places. Their leader is a limping boy who walks in front; if they do not follow quickly, a great, tall, monstrous fellow follows behind them, who whips them with an iron scourge so unmercifully that the lash marks are seen long afterward. After the passing of the twelve days, they come to themselves and regain their former shape, for they believe nothing else than that they have been wolves; thereupon the whole crowd disperses. That such things happen in Livonia is true, beyond all contradiction. But whether the people truly become wolves is a difficult and lofty question. Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and writer on demonology</note> is of the opinion that they do, and wishes to provide proof from Nebuchadnezzar, who was changed into an ox; likewise from Lot's wife, who became a pillar of salt. Also from the rods of the Egyptian wise men, which were turned into snakes; and finally from the companions of Ulysses, who were transformed into swine. For my part, there is no doubt that it happened thus with the wise men in Egypt and the sorceress Circe, of whom Homer writes in the *Odyssey*, yet it was through deception and true sorcery. For the Devil wishes to have the appearance of being able to accomplish that which belongs to God alone, and thus he lets us see something that in truth is not so, but is a mere phantom <note>original: "gespenst"</note>, just as King Saul's sorceress did when she raised Samuel, and Simon the Sorcerer, when he falsely wished to imitate the miracles of the Apostles. Physical matter is by no means so subject to the Devil that he can change its form and properties. Although Thomas Aquinas holds otherwise on this matter, Augustine holds the opposite with these words: *It is not to be thought that this matter of visible things serves these transgressing angels at their beck and call.* <note>original Latin: "Non est putandum istis trangressoribus angelis ad nutum seruire hanc visibilium rerum materiam."</note>

<margin>

No one should be stuck in the delusion that the matter of these visible things is subserviently subject to the transgressing devils at their pleasure. Here, however, we do not wish to deny that the Devil, with incredible haste and agility, could have snatched away the rods and placed snakes in their stead, thus blinding and enchanting those standing around. Regarding what is cited about Lot's wife, who was transformed into an immovable stone, I consider it ungodly to detract in the slightest from Holy Scripture and GOD'S omnipotence. Concerning King Nebuchadnezzar's transformation, in my opinion, it is somewhat doubtful, and can hardly be drawn upon as help and proof for the transformation of werewolves. Firstly, if it truly happened in that way, it is to be ascribed to the mighty hand of our LORD GOD, which is impossible for the Devil to imitate. Thus, it does not protect the foolishness of the werewolves at all. Furthermore, the Scripture does not say that he was transformed into an ox, but rather that he ate the same food as the irrational beasts, and his wit, understanding, and senses were gone—which, according to Bodin's statement, remain unmoved in those who are transformed. For after the passing of seven years, he came back to his senses and used normal food. It also does not prove that the natures are the same. # On the Investigation of Witches

...to the end that one might also detect the witches.

I believe also that from this arose the proverb which <margin>Book 8, chapter 2.</margin> Caelius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), an Italian philologist</note> mentions: *The water is stuck* <note>original: "Hæret aqua."</note>. He sticks or hangs in the water. Ulpianus <note>A Roman jurist</note> also opines that it is spoken of those who are made dishonest. Therefore Julius Pollux uses the term *to wash* <note>original: "$\pi\lambda\acute{\upsilon}\nu\epsilon\iota\nu$, id est, lauare"</note> for *to revile* <note>original: "<unclear>λοιδορεῖν</unclear>, couitiari"</note>, to scold someone and speak ill of them.

This following practice, customary among the Papists <note>A derogatory term for Catholics used by Protestant writers of this era</note>, fits this habit not poorly: On certain days they throw a wooden image of St. Peter into the water with these words: "If St. Peter's image will not procure us a beautiful, pleasant rain in this upcoming need, then let it go to the bottom." For this is not unlike our current custom when witches are tested by cold water: those who sink are innocent, but those who float on top against nature are guilty. Thus this wooden idol, if no rain was to be hoped for, they wished that it should go to the bottom against the nature and property of wood. And in the same manner God is tempted in this piece as in that, and it is devised out of superstition.

Truly, whoever wishes to learn of future weather in this way does nothing other than tempt God and doubt His omnipotence; he wishes to prescribe measure and goal to our LORD God in His government. This water test is likewise a meddlesome temptation without God's express command; it has no grounds or causes. But because it is godless, it can succeed and happen for the sake of human sin and wickedness, which have caused many false miracles to occur through the Devil's deceit. These have immediately gained a reputation among blinded, superstitious peoples as if they were divine revelations, which is clear from the oracles and prophecies of idols, and can be seen in the wise men of Pharaoh and Simon the Sorcerer. Dear people, why is it now that we turn to false and uncertain things, which bring with them the desecration of God's name and our own destruction?

<column-break/>

No less ungodly and loathsome are similar experiments, which are quite common among the common rabble and especially among women, when they wish to see whether someone shall live or not. To find this out, they bake unleavened cakes on New Year's Eve and subsequently throw them upon the water; if a cake goes under, then he in whose name it was made dies. For bread that is well-baked must float on top against nature, just as was thought of the wood. But if the bread remains on top of the water, which is according to nature, then they say he will live. Others practice this on St. Matthias's Eve, but are just as blind as the previous ones. From the bread they are eating, they bite off one or more pieces in this or 그 name, then likewise throw them into the water, wishing to judge from this how long one shall live. If the morsel of bread goes under, they do not doubt, but believe and say for certain that the person's life is in danger; if it stays on top, they become secure and comforted, fearing no danger of death. If the bread hangs in the middle of the water, that signifies a dangerous illness, but one not harmful to life. The rabble drags themselves along with this, and such things rarely deceive; they come true almost every time. But they think this is an unforbidden thing that can be tolerated, not understanding what an abomination and loathsome cruelty is hidden therein. They commit just as great a sin as those who bind witches and set them upon the water to find out who is guilty or innocent, just as those others wish to give tidings of one's life and death. It is certain, however, that these experiments are very many, which have been pushed and brought to the human race by the Devil in a cunning way—to those whose ears itch for new things—not so that we could use them without harm and danger, but much more so that he, the Devil, might turn our hearts from God and bring us to himself through superstition, and stick us in idolatrous error.

And according to the testimony of Augustine, the more these things <note>superstitious charms or trials</note> seem to succeed and happen, the more we should flee from them and hold them in suspicion. For just as a true Christian faith has great effect in godly, pious people, so also a false and evil unbelief—stirred up or earned by God’s permission—brings about a wicked and terrible end. Daily we also find among the unbelievers, whom God draws to punishment because of their mistrust, or those whom He sees are drowned too deeply in loose delusions, that by God’s providence many such things occur to them, and they are thus confirmed in their opinion, so that their blindness becomes greater and they may fall into the snare they prepared for themselves. Sometimes our Lord God looks through His fingers <note>an idiom meaning to "overlook" or "permit for a time"</note> and allows such things, as seen with Pharaoh’s sorcerers; but this is for the testing and warning of the pious, and for the punishment of the godless. But as for what Scribonius says—that Weyer <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who opposed witch trials</note> provides not a single specific example where the opposite result is proven—I grant him that. And even if it were not to fail <note>i.e., if the water test always "worked"</note>, we must nevertheless abolish it because of the superstition which is contrary to true religion, and which has the appearance of human wisdom but is rooted not in truth, but in lies. # Through the Cold Water.

By habit, when one is struck by this artillery <note>The author uses "artillery" as a metaphor for the arguments used by proponents of the water ordeal.</note>, it easily falls to the ground and opens up, especially when this experiment is stripped of our reason and is scolded as erroneous and fallible. This we have, according to our judgment, clearly proven from the previous sections, and now also confirmed with the laws, insofar as the truth may receive approval and protection among the godly. How can it be revealed to our nature, and be perceptible and known to the same, that which is foisted upon us as a deceptive thing? How can a brand-new and erroneous habit stand in the place of a proven statute? Let us therefore, in the absence of thorough reasons and powerful laws, present no deception or misleading spectacles to the common people, since other safe and certain means are available which do not exceed the well-ordered constitution and statute of God and the authorities, so that we do not offend the Divine Majesty, nor bring any human into danger and distress.

Now we wish to turn to the argument spun from nature, which is entirely physical, taken from the lightness of the body; and we wish, as much as is possible for us, to make diligent inquiry. But because the author himself <note>Referring to Wilhelm Adolf Scribonius, a prominent defender of the water ordeal.</note> suspects it is at once ineffective, he meets us and anticipates us with a protestation, saying: in other women there is the very same matter and form as in the female witches. He must therefore show us other ways and causes for this outcome, because he notices that the lightness and *raritas* <note>original: "raritas" — thinness or lack of density</note> of the body cannot provide it. Indeed, one writes of women that they have softer and thinner skin than men, but that same fact, because it is understood only of softness and tenderness, does not take away the weight and softness of the body so that it could not sink, as experience shows. Thereupon he seizes another principle and foundation, and says: the witches, soon after the alliance is established and the contract concluded, are deprived of their

<column-break/>

previous form by their confederate, the Devil, and gain a strange and new one. The Devil also takes possession of them and their being, together with all their limbs, in the flesh. Therefore, because he, the Devil, is a spirit, he concludes that they cannot go to the bottom because of the lightness they have received. This is thus brought up and reported by Scribonius, but with what justification, we must further discuss.

First, however, it is false and unjust that their essential form should be changed by this alliance and another brought in. For no union changes the essence of a human being, whether the same happens with God, or with the Devil, or otherwise with men. Thus God has established a covenant with us without any perceptible transformation of nature, and it behaves in the same case with other contracts as well. Nor does it hurt, as some pretend, that the persons are unequal: for a *pactum* <note>original: "pactum" — a legal pact or agreement</note> or agreement is a consent and harmony of minds over a matter being dealt with, which happens without any change of the bodies, whether in the qualities or the substance itself. Furthermore, whoever pretends that the Devil changes the form of a thing is witless and not in his right mind, and is also poorly versed in the *principiis Philosophicis* <note>original: "principiis Philosophicis" — philosophical principles</note>.

God's mighty command, which gave to every thing the power that it can leave its image behind it, is the sole origin of form. And because the Devil can bring no creature into being, what should it be then, that we wish to ascribe to him an effect of the form in the matter? Which GOD has reserved for Himself, especially regarding what concerns human beings. From this the ancient theologians have rightly said: The Devils, when God permits it, can bring about through the internal power of substance that which may be brought about through *motum localem* <note>original: "motum localem" — local motion or physical movement</note> and the joining together of both *agentium* and *patientium* <note>original: "agentium vnd patientium" — active agents and passive subjects</note>; but the nature of a thing they can in no way change, contrary to

the nature of matter, as it was implanted by God. Because it follows that in every physical matter there must be a suitable opportunity and readiness to receive a form, and since the devils cannot provide this, it follows that no form can be introduced through their assistance. And even if a new form and shape were to appear through the workings of the <term>Covenant</term><note>The pact between a witch and the Devil</note>, it would necessarily have to abolish the previous soul and introduce a new one to give the body its shape and form. For as long as a witch is and remains a human being, she must attribute such things to the soul alone. But that it is impossible for him <note>the Devil</note> to substitute a new one is proved clearly and brightly by the seduction and ruin of Man. For the initial perversion of our first parents, which occurred through the Devil's cunning and instigation, did not destroy the essential form, but rather the qualities—which nevertheless suitably belong to the essence—were touched in the soul to some extent. Should the slightest disruption of the substance occur, it would have to perish immediately. If we were to say that, we would be viewed as if we wanted to defend the error concerning <term>Original Sin</term><note>likely referring to the Flacian controversy regarding whether sin is a substance or an accident</note> which has been brought back onto the path by some in our time. Therefore, because no new form arises from the agreement, nor is it poured in by the Devil, it is null and void that they force us to confirm this lightness and suitability for floating on top.

Doubtless it is not unknown to Scribonius <note>Wilhelm Adolf Scribonius, a defender of the water ordeal</note> that the lightness of our bodies is to be drawn from the matter, not the form; for the form is the perfection and completion of a thing, which is not subject to the body's afflictions and other accidents, but the matter,

<column-break/>

its opportunity and preparation are subject to manifold change and movement according to the distinction of the cause. Accordingly, we seek the causes of lightness in a matter that is thin, porous, airy, and extended, which then causes some things to float on top, such as wood, mushrooms, sponges, feathers, and the like. Other matters, which are thicker, fuller, and more compressed, sink to the bottom because of their weight, like all kinds of ore grown in the earth. Since it was previously said from the knowledge of theologians that the devils can change the nature of no thing against the kind and opportunity of matter given by God: I believe that in this dispute and discord, no one will agree with him who is even slightly acquainted with the <term>principles of physics</term><note>original: "principia physica"</note>. What we have from matter, which is provided with its qualities, is wrongly attributed to the form, which is not capable of the effect of a thing; for regarding the form, it does not act itself, nor does it allow itself to be acted upon, but of the whole substance it is said that it is subject to accidental change, regarding the matter which is tempered in unequal ways, as Aristotle and other physicists alongside him teach with foundation. But so that he may appear to have good arguments, he adds here: the whole body with all its parts is essential and proven. We say the opposite: that the witches are not physically possessed, but rather regarding the mind, which is harmful to them and brings death, because they knowingly and wakingly make fellowship with the Devil; which no one has been able to say of possessed people, who also, when they are possessed, are miserably plagued, martyred, thrown, and tormented, and are also not masters of their senses at the time when he <note>the demon</note> becomes active in them, and they feel a weak body, which is nevertheless not perceived in the witches. The witches also do not use foreign languages, as Fernelius <note>Jean Fernel, a famous French physician</note> writes of a nobleman who was possessed, nor do they carry any sorrow when they inflict harm on their neighbors, much less do they have repentance for their sins. <margin>Differences between Devils.</margin>

...run about and claim that they can perform miracles, inflict harm on others through poison and sorcery <note>original: "Zauberey"</note>, and take pleasure in gluttony, dancing, and gossiping, consorting with the Devil for their own pleasure. One does not see such behavior in those who are truly possessed; rather, the possessed desire and wish—heartily and painfully—that they might be released and set free from the Devil's bonds. It therefore causes me great wonder that Scribonius puts forward such an absurd thing; even if it were as he says (which cannot be proven), it still could not protect his argument. For without any doubt, the possessed would also sink and drown if they were bound and placed upon the water in such a manner. This is clearly demonstrated by the Gospel of Matthew in the eighth chapter, where Christ delivers two persons possessed by the Devil. The devils, however, beg that they might enter into a herd of swine; this is granted to them, but the swine then plunge into the sea and drown. This history is directly contrary to Scribonius's opinion, in that it reports that the swine were possessed by the Devil and yet perished in the water.

And although Satan is called a "spirit" or "prince of the air" by St. Paul, it does not follow from this that his essence is made of a light and airy material. Rather, it means he is an exceedingly swift spirit who can travel through the air to distant, remote places in an instant; for this reason, among some people, such speed has been mistaken for a divine quality. I believe the ancients also saw it this way when they called all spirits *alites* <note>Latin: "winged ones" or "birds"</note>, which fly through the air like birds. Thus, angels are also painted with wings. That the devils rule in the air is reasonable to believe, since by God's permission they can drive winds, thunder, and storms to this or that place, in order to destroy the crops, the mast <note>forest nuts used for animal feed</note>, and the cattle in the field, and to stir up the waters. They do not rule in the air alone, but also make their way into the water and the earth, as the ancient Platonists <note>followers of the philosopher Plato</note> held, who categorized different demons: *aereos* <note>Latin: "aerial"</note>, who rule in the air;

<column-break/>

*aqueos* <note>Latin: "aqueous"</note>, who live in the water; and *subterraneos* <note>Latin: "subterranean"</note>, who have their dominion in the earth. Here we must also reject the opinion of those who say that some devils, according to their merit, have their abode in the East, some in the West, some in the North, and some in the South, and must remain and behave there as if in their ordained seats. For by nature they are restless and roam back and forth like robbers to satisfy their fury. Thus, this argument regarding the Devil's indwelling and occupation of a body carries no weight, since witches are by no means "possessed" in that sense. Even if they were, such lightness would help very little, as we have proven and shown through examples and the properties of nature.

What he [Scribonius] cites for further confirmation of his sentence—regarding the transport from one place to another through the high air—also proves nothing. It does not demonstrate any subtlety or lightness in their bodies, for such transport is not caused by the help of a light, spiritual, and flying substance. Rather, it happens through the power and might of the Devil to whom they have surrendered themselves and sworn loyalty and faith; against the nature of bodies, they are taken up and thus hover here and there. Just as Christ was led by the Devil to the pinnacle of the Temple and the peak of the mountain, his body was not changed a hair's breadth in its properties, nor was it "prepared" for such transport. Likewise, the Devil with his power can cast down and move not only humans but great mountains and buildings, as the history of Job testifies. Therefore, what he claims about a change in the nature of witches is void; likewise, what he brings up regarding their "skill" for flying is empty, since the Devil's strength and power can accomplish such things without any tangible change to the body. We do not deny here that they travel so quickly through the air, and we believe one should not agree with those who consider such things to be merely imaginary or a delusion. However, as to how it actually happens, I see that people are not yet in agreement.
