# On the Investigation of Witches

Furthermore, an objection is raised here—which Wierus <note>Johann Wier (1515–1588), a physician who argued that many "witches" were actually suffering from mental illness.</note> agrees with—that this experiment is false, based on the nature and mechanics of **swimming** when we hold our breath. But regarding the claim that holding one's breath is not the sole cause of floating, but rather a contributing factor, he speaks rightly: for he writes that the innocent, whether they hold their breath or not, always sink. That the innocent can also remain atop the water is not disputed, since the restless, roaring **murderous spirit** <note>A reference to the Devil.</note> seeks the ruin of them and all mankind at every hour. Likewise, there is no doubt that some guilty women sink, because it does not yet please God to subject them to punishment, which He, out of His secret counsel, spares for a certain time, as is known to happen daily with other sins. This is certain: the Devil seeks in this experiment—through a dangerous, doubtful, deceitful, and ungodly piece of evidence—to lead guilty persons into physical danger and the innocent into distress and anguish of the soul.

Who would not forever consider as a sin and misdeed everything that harms the soul, troubles the conscience, tempts God, and tears apart the course and order of Nature? Wierus, however, as mentioned above, posits the true cause: namely, God's permission and the power and might of the Devil, so that the authorities who use such forbidden and un-Christian means remain stuck in their conceived error. This also happens in other investigations <note>original: "explorationibus"</note> which sometimes fail to occur and at other times appear similar to the truth; yet these are not to be followed, because they proceed through evil means, which are to be entirely avoided, as Paul teaches in 1 Thessalonians 5.

The second objection—taken from the fact that they remain in the water without harm or physical danger—could well have been dismissed, because it causes the Devil the greatest pain and opposition that he cannot hunt all people into his net and snare according to his pleasure. But we have to thank God from our hearts that, against such gruesome raging and storming of Satan, He nevertheless preserves and protects some under the shadow of His wings and keeps them from such deceitful abomination. However, in that the author exerts himself greatly and introduces natural causes, he perhaps unknowingly returns to supernatural causes against his own judgment: namely, the power of the Devil, who keeps them in the water without harm by God's allowance. We accept this and believe him, as is right; but because the murderous spirit is a rogue and deceiver, and God's administration is secret and His judgments hidden, no faith is to be given to this experiment. I would say he acted thoughtlessly and without forethought in seeking out and picking at natural causes while nevertheless bringing in the supernatural at the last—since the latter are uncertain and to be rejected as against reason, while the former have their grounds and fit well within reason.

Finally, he concludes forgetfully and returns to the natural cause; he attributes this, according to his own opinion, to a spiritual "lifting up" <note>original: "auffrückung"</note> which springs from a corresponding lightness in the witches, and he calls this the **efficient cause** <note>original: "efficientem causam" - the primary agent that produces an effect.</note>. But what he intends to mean by "lifting up"—whether it is floating atop the water—is unknown to me; otherwise, I cannot well grasp what he means by **attraction** or lifting, since lightness in a body does not cause any lifting. Rather, that something is lifted and maintained in the air happens because the substance is not entirely solid, but rare and thin. What is light is also not suited for "lifting," as can be seen in the **thistle-down** <note>original: "Thanschwan" - likely referring to the downy seeds of a thistle or similar plant.</note>; it does not draw the bile out of the body, but because its substance is contrary to the nature of our body, it causes the **expulsive power** <note>original: "vim expultricem" - a medical term for the body's ability to eject waste or harmful substances.</note> and internal strength to drive out—

# Concerning the Investigation of Witches

There are three kinds [of phenomena]: either *contrary to nature* <note>original: "ἀντιφυσικὰ" (antiphysika)</note>, *beyond nature* <note>original: "παραφυσικὰ" (paraphysika)</note>, or *supernatural* <note>original: "μεταφυσικὰ" (metaphysika)</note>. Those *contrary to nature* are those which, against Nature, violate and destroy the properties and power of a being, such as Death and its active causes. Those *beyond nature* are those which, to some extent, hinder and delay natural powers, such as all kinds of diseases and their causes. Those *supernatural* are those which occur in a substance above Nature—not according to the proper course of Nature, nor out of the internal capacity of the substance, but through the special power and will of God—such as when iron <note>A reference to the miracle of Elisha making the axe head float in 2 Kings 6:6.</note> or witches float on the surface.

The last category has no fellowship at all with the former ones and is not subject to Nature or its laws. Now we must investigate into which group this trial <term>tentamen: a test or trial, specifically the water ordeal</term> of ours may be reckoned.

He [Scribonius] says it is not *contrary to nature*, because, as everyone knows, Nature is not harmed by this as it is when someone dies. He certainly admits that it happens against the course of Nature, but he nevertheless opines that it is not entirely contrary to it. If it is not unnatural, it will be necessary for him to produce natural causes, which he has attempted to do in vain. Furthermore, those things which are *beyond nature* <note>original: "præternaturam"</note> cannot be placed among natural things; therein he makes his claim, ignorantly entangling himself and disrupting the course of Nature. And if this happens thus *beyond nature* or above Nature, we desire to know the supernatural cause, such as can be noted in diseases; and it would then lack only a little for us to agree with his opinion and accept it. I see an artificial cause well enough in the entanglement that happens crosswise <note>Likely referring to the practice of binding a suspect's right thumb to their left toe and vice versa before the water test.</note>, but I see none so natural, or above Nature, which is not contrary to Nature in the form he has established. When we say that much happens above Nature which is not contrary to Nature, we understand that something often happens in many things above Nature, even if it happens through artifice

<column-break/>

in diseases, so that almost no hope remains. In such cases, we say it happens above Nature and almost as a miracle, yet not entirely so, for the causes are not to be sought outside of Nature. But if this experiment is not unnatural, it will be easy for him to find the fundamental cause of this outcome—which, however, will be entirely impossible for him from the start.

Since these are *beyond nature* <note>original: "præternaturalia"</note>, it follows according to the opinion of all natural philosophers that they be placed among the number of things unnatural or *contrary to nature* <note>original: "contra naturam"</note>, as the manifest and clear truth testifies. However, since no disruption or destruction follows, it cannot well be reckoned among the *non-natural* things. Thus, it finally remains for us to draw it under those things which are *beyond nature* <note>original: "trans naturam"</note> and are called miracles. These are either miracles *properly* so called, or *improperly*: miracles *properly* so called belong to God alone, and no creature is able to perform them, regarding either the thing itself or its creation. Without any contradiction, however, this experiment belongs among the miracles *improperly* so called <note>original: "miracula impropriè dicta"</note>, however it may happen. If it is permitted to him, the Devil can certainly keep her [the witch] up in the water, just as he can otherwise blind the eyes of the bystanders and mock and deceive them with a worthless, false experiment: as we previously cited regarding the Egyptian sorcerers and their fabricated miracles.

Therefore, let Scribonius exert himself as vehemently as he can, he will be able to persuade no one of anything regarding natural and preternatural causes, nor make his undertaking appear truthful or gain approval among sensible people. This whole business, no matter how it is viewed in all places, is full of superstition and comes from the master-craftsman, the Devil, by God's permission; therefore, it does not belong to the aforementioned causes, but we see in it a deceptive school of jugglery by the Devil. And here we shall let it rest, regarding Scribonius's grounds by which he thinks the matter is—

...have proven by examples. God the LORD has in no way permitted the Devil to be able to change forms <note>original: "formas endern"</note>, as we have previously announced. Others may say what they wish regarding the transformation of people into wolves, oxen, and other animals. One should also not believe Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1529–1596), a prominent jurist and demonologist who argued for the reality of witchcraft</note> when he claims that Nebuchadnezzar was transformed into an ox for seven whole years because he ate unhuman food; just as he writes elsewhere that the staffs of the Egyptian magicians became actual, natural snakes, and other such things which are contrary to the truth.

Weyer <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued that many accused witches were actually suffering from mental illness</note>, who has compassion for the witches and does not recognize a proper punishment for them, is rightly refuted by others. However, regarding this purgation by cold water <note>The "swimming test" where an accused person was bound and thrown into water; floating was seen as proof of guilt</note>, I believe one should not deviate a hair's breadth from his opinion, because it has always been suspicious to him on account of superstition and fraud. And the more these experiments succeed <note>i.e., the more often people float</note>, the more they are to be avoided and fled from. For God permits this out of His secret counsel, so that abuse and superstition may be heaped upon the unbelieving.

Afterward, we attacked his arguments, which were taken from the subject of the intellect <note>original: "ex subiecto intellectus"</note> and from custom itself, and we broke their power with all diligence. For our reason is hidden, nor can everything the Devil brings about—with which he deceives us and mocks us—be grasped by our understanding. The same is to be held regarding customs that are introduced and confirmed through error, as was touched upon before. As for the further arguments he draws from physics—namely, concerning the lightness of their bodies and the change of substantial form <note>original: "formæ substantialis"</note>, of hovering through the air, and lastly of bodily possession—we have treated these with equal diligence and shown the truth. For the change of form (which nonetheless has not happened nor can happen through the pact) brings no lightness to the body; rather, such is caused by a certain disposition of the matter. And this

<column-break/>

flying in the air is also not promoted by the lightness of the bodies, but it happens by force and does not belong among natural things. Where he posits that they must be possessed, that is false, as has been proven with many reasons. And even if it were so, they would nonetheless sink and drown. But the author soon forgets himself and returns to preternatural causes <note>original: "causas præternaturales"</note>, or rather supernatural ones, namely to the Devil's power, which preserves the witches by God's permission; we gladly accept such a premise, but he does not remain consistent with it. Finally, Scribonius <note>Wilhelm Adolf Scribonius, a defender of the water ordeal</note> takes up the refutations of those arguments which might hold the opposite view to this undertaking. What he has accomplished thereby will be manifest from the preceding, but especially from where we described and distinguished between natural and unnatural things. For after diligent investigation of the same, we have concluded that this experiment involving binding is partly artificial and partly supernatural, under which all miracles belong—both those properly so called <note>original: "propriè sic dicta"</note>, which God performs, and those improperly so called, which come from the Devil and do not belong under natural causes.

Now, when these arguments are examined and looked at collectively and individually, it will then be known and manifest to everyone that the author has sought out meager and wretched reasons—which are powerless to prove anything—regarding both the testimony of jurists and natural causes. As for us, if someone can bring forth something more certain and better, we will not refuse at all, but will gladly and willingly agree with them.

At this point, we wish to add by way of admonition that those who sit in government can well abolish this entrenched custom with good reason and right. For it is unhindered and unforbidden to cancel and do away with everything that a Christian may not think of, much less use with great offense. Therefore, let all authorities who [use] this purgation in the investigation of witches...

### The 11th Little Treatise.

# A Christian Reflection and
### Remembrance of Sorcery: whence it comes, what it is, and how manifold it may be; whom it can harm or not; how this vice is to be resisted, and how those afflicted by it are to be converted or also punished. Written by

### Augustin Lercheimer of Steinfelden.
<note>Augustin Lercheimer was the pseudonym of Hermann Witekind (1522–1603), a humanist scholar who argued against the excessive cruelty of the witch trials.</note>

# Augustin Lercheimer’s
# Reflections on Sorcery / whence /
### what / and how manifold it may be / etc. The ground / cause / and power of Sorcery.

Whoever wishes to speak, judge, and pass sentence rightly concerning sorcery <note>The original German "Zauberey" encompasses witchcraft, magic, and sorcery</note> must be so minded and prepared that he does not only understand and concern himself with physical, visible beings: but also knows and considers from God’s word, and from experience, that everywhere the earth, water, and air are full of Devils and evil invisible Spirits: who envy the human race and are hateful and hostile toward it: because it was created and ordained by God for the blessed life, joy, and glory, from which they are cast out for eternity on account of their pride. Therefore, they hover around us day and night, wherever we go or stand, at home or abroad, whether we sleep or wake: plotting and striving without ceasing, watching every moment for opportunity and occasion, how they may damage us in property and goods, in body and soul, turn us away from God, and finally pull and plunge us with themselves into eternal destruction.

Which presence of the Devil in all places is shown by the words of our Lord Christ in Matthew 12, where he says: *When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he wanders about, takes seven others with him, and enters back into him,* etc. <note>original Latin/Greek context translated here from the German paraphrase of Matthew 12:43-45</note> Likewise Paul, in Ephesians 2 and 6, calls the Devils *princes and powers in the air*, with whom we have to struggle. Likewise 1 Peter 5: *Be sober and watch: for your adversary the Devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.*

We read in Roman history, when they had fought with their exiled King and did not know on which side the most had perished, the Devil cried out from

<column-break/>

a nearby forest, that they had lost one fewer than the enemy. So diligently had he counted them. There was a student at L. <note>Likely Leipzig or Louvain</note> who longed to know how his beloved was doing at home: he walked with his companion out of the city into the field. There he invited and questioned Satan: who immediately presented himself invisibly and told him where his beloved was at that hour, and what she was doing. It is a common proverb, *where one calls the Devil, there he is present.* Likewise, *one does not need to paint the Devil on the wall, he comes well enough without that.* As happened in Silesia at St. to the three drinking companions, who painted him with coal on the wall, spoke and drank to him: they were strangled by him there that night, and found dead in the morning and buried under the gallows.

In the time and presence of Emperor Henry the Fourth at Goslar in the church on Pentecost, a quarrel arose between the Abbot of Fulda and the Bishop of Hildesheim, as to which of them should sit nearest to the Archbishop of Mainz. They came from words to blows, so that on both sides many were slain in the church; after the strife was stilled, and the Sequence <note>A liturgical hymn</note> in the Mass was being sung, in which the last verse is, *This glorious day You have made,* <note>original: "Hunc diem gloriosum fecisti"</note> the Devil sang from up there under the vault, with a coarse, loud voice, *This warlike day I have made.* <note>original: "Hunc diem bellicosum ego feci"</note> When the Counts of Scheyern in Bavaria (from whom the Counts Palatine of the Rhine descend) four hundred years ago made their castle Scheyern into a Benedictine Monastery, and those who had a share in it consented to this: there was one among them, named Arnold, whom it did not please. He threw a glove into the air and said, "There Devil, I give you my share." Quickly he was there, snatched the glove

# Considerations on Sorcerers

From these and other countless indications, it is manifest that evil spirits are present everywhere: and all of this is done to harm and ruin us humans. They attempt this with us in manifold ways—with one person in this manner, with another differently—according to how each individual is naturally inclined and minded, or toward what they are predisposed: toward honor, wealth, revenge, unchastity, gluttony, anger, strife, and brawling. Or according to each person's status, opportunity, and concerns, such as: young, old, man, woman, poor, despised, troubled, faint-hearted, etc. The devils pay diligent attention to all of this, noticing it quickly, as they are sharp-witted, clever, cunning, old, practiced, experienced, and malicious spirits. They direct the temptation and the attack according to how they find each person's nature and character.

However, the fact that their schemes and temptations do not succeed or progress with all people is due to the Almighty, gracious God. He calls, chooses, and preserves some here and there in the knowledge and invocation of Him, in His service, and in trust in Him, in the hope of eternal life through His Word and Holy Spirit. He protects and guards them against the devil through the good, dear angels, in such a manner as is pleasing to Him and good and wholesome for us, His children. He does this for the sake of our Redeemer and Savior Jesus Christ, who crushed the serpent's head and destroyed the works of the devil <note>original: "Gen. 3. vnnd 1. Johan. 3." referring to Genesis 3:15 and 1 John 3:8</note>.

Thus Satan attacked the pious Job, robbed him of his children and possessions, and also plagued his body: but yet no further and no longer than God permitted and allowed him. Job well understood and took this to heart, and therefore said: *The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away.* <note>Job 1:21</note> He does not say the devil has taken it from me. The devil would have had to let him keep it if the LORD had willed it. For that he cannot do the slightest evil without permission from GOD (good he never does

<column-break/>

at all) is to be inferred from the fact that he dared not enter into a sow without the permission of the LORD Christ <note>original: "Matth. 8." referring to the Gadarene swine in Matthew 8:31-32</note>, and that he dared not touch Job's life because it was forbidden to him by God. All the hairs of our head are numbered, none of which falls without God's will.

Although these evil spirits are "thousand-artists" <note>A term for a master of many tricks or a great deceiver</note>, knowing and being able to do much that surpasses all human science, arts, and powers; nevertheless, no one should think that they know, can, or have the power to do everything they want, even if God were to slacken the reins and allow them to use all their art and power as they pleased. For such would be an omnipotence that belongs to God alone and to no creature, neither angel, evil nor good. The devil is no "heart-knower" <term>Heart-knower: A translation of the German 'Herzkündiger', meaning one who can read the secret thoughts of the heart, a power reserved for God alone</term>; he does not know the thoughts of men without external signs. He can raise no dead; make no barren woman conceive; keep no human alive without food, as Moses, Elijah, and the LORD Christ were sustained by Divine power. He is unable to transform any human into a wolf, dog, or cat; no water into wine; no copper into gold; no stone into bread, as the LORD could have done when he was tempted by him in the wilderness. Therefore, in an ancient Council at Ancyra in Galatia <note>The Council of Ancyra, 314 AD, often cited in medieval law to debunk the physical reality of shapeshifting</note>, such a decree was made by the Holy Fathers:

Whoever believes that any being can be changed into something better or worse, or that another form or shape can be given to it, by anyone other than the Creator of all things alone, is worse than a pagan and an infidel. And this shall be publicly proclaimed by preachers: that whoever believes such things has lost the true faith; he belongs not to God, but to the devil in whom he believes. So far the decree.

Otherwise, the evil spirits perform many wonders, partly through natural means...

# Augustin Lercheimer

Means / partly through their own power / either truly or with trickery and phantoms / like the sorcerers in Egypt / who imitated Aaron before King Pharaoh / they did not make snakes, blood, or frogs in truth / but in appearance / as the scholars of the Holy Scripture understand and interpret it. And the spirits do all such things to mislead, deceive, and harm people / yet not beyond the goal and measure / as said / set for them by God: whose righteous and fatherly will it is / to thus punish our sins / or to prove and exercise our patience in suffering and steadfastness in faith and confidence in Him.

Whoever does not know and consider such things / should not presume or take it upon himself to judge sorcery. It is a spiritual, supernatural matter / which should not and cannot be judged according to external common ways / like other misdeeds: it requires a higher and broader reflection: it belongs not only to those experienced in the Law / but also to scholars of the Holy Scripture, physicians, and naturalists / to all of whom it gives work to do.

The evil spirits / who are the companions, associates, and helpers of the sorcerers and witches / are the ones who effect all that the sorcerers think / according to their false delusion and appearance / is effected and carried out by them. Humans they are / humans they remain / they can and are able to do no more now, neither to harm nor to benefit / with words or with deeds / than before / before they entered into a covenant and society with the spirits. Indeed, the Devil commonly and frequently makes them weaker and more contemptible in soul and body / than they were before. He withdraws their reason / displaces and corrupts their senses / sickens them in health / lames them / gives them watery or inverted eyes / a hideous, loathsome face / a crooked mouth / stinking breath / a death-colored countenance / etc. He cannot improve them / and even if he could / he would not do it.

<column-break/>

### What Sorcery is / and that the Devil does not serve for nothing.

Sorcery is a presumed indication of hidden things / (which in Old Frankish is called *vorsagen* <note>foretelling</note>: in Saxony / *wicken* <note>divining</note>: among us / *warsage* <note>soothsaying</note>) and is a presumed doing and acting more and more often to harm than to benefit / or even only to satisfy lust and curiosity thereby / through the fellowship, inspiration, assistance, and help of the evil spirits / to whom the sorcerers and witches have given themselves as property / or have otherwise involved and bound themselves / intentionally or incautiously / for the sake of such service: and it is a misuse of holy and unholy words, gestures, or things to create and bring about something supernatural: For even such things cannot happen without the Devil's operation / whether the people who deal with it know it / or do not know it / thinking the power is in the words, gestures, or things / whose nature, kind, and property nevertheless do not allow for such a thing / nor were they created for it.

The evil spirits allow themselves to be used for such business / and perform such services / not to please the sorcerers and witches or for nothing: but so that they may thereby / when the opportunity arises / plunge them here into temporal and there into eternal destruction. They break the necks of those who have surrendered to them / when the appointed time of the obligation is out / or otherwise kill them / as it is convenient and opportune for them. As happened to a very wanton and from youth on wicked rogue / whom I will not name for his father's sake. He also played this Devil's game / traveled on a cloak with his good companion / etc. When his time had expired / he traveled from home to another place to visit his friends and relatives. As he sat at the table with them / his head was unexpectedly twisted backward / and he remained thus dead. People thought he had merely looked behind him / but it was the invisible Devil who did it to him.

# Thoughts on Sorcery

<sig>Z 3</sig>

...the spirits drive them until they are stabbed, drowned, fall to their deaths, or otherwise perish because of their curiosity, magic, and sorcery, or until they are thrown into prison and the fire. For the Devil is so rebellious and hateful toward the human race that, even when he cannot harm the soul, he still cools his temper and takes pleasure in the plague, torment, pain, and death of the body: as he did to Job and others, and still does daily. In the Papacy <note>original: "Babsthumb"; referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> he had introduced the custom that those possessed by him were placed in cold water, struck with rods, and tormented and martyred in other ways to such an extent that it was a misery to behold: as if he, the Devil, felt such things and they caused him pain, yet he actually took his pleasure and joy in the fact that the human being was thus tormented.

Years ago at the Imperial Diet <note>original: "Reichstage"; the deliberative assembly of the Holy Roman Empire</note> at R. <note>likely Regensburg</note>, there was a sorcerer or practitioner of the black arts <note>original: "Schwartzkünstler"</note> who, before his end—knowing that the Devil would come for him according to their contract—turned back to God and gave a good Christian confession and sign of the same. Nevertheless, on the appointed night, he was strangled by the Spirit, so that in the morning he lay before his bed on his back, with his face turned downward toward the floor. However, the highly learned and famous theologians and Doctors of Holy Scripture, who were gathered there at that time for a colloquy <note>a formal theological discussion</note> and from whom he had previously sought and received counsel, instruction, and comfort, and to whom he had made his confession, did not despair of his soul's salvation. For just as God wills that evildoers be punished by the authorities and shamefully executed as an example to others, but does not therefore reject or condemn the soul; likewise, He perhaps wills that even if these people repent and He receives the soul into grace, they are nonetheless physically defiled by the Devil as a mirror and deterrent to others. Thus, when he has brought it to the point that the poor witches burn, then the heart of that malicious one <note>the Devil</note> laughs, even though he may not have the soul.

<column-break/>

<margin>Which people, and for what reasons, devote themselves to sorcery.</margin>

Not all kinds of people are fit or suited for sorcery and this Devil’s covenant and guild: even if they are otherwise so devoted to, surrendered to, and drowned in physical, worldly things and affairs—striving so diligently and incessantly for property, honor, and pleasure—that no spiritual or heavenly thought ever enters their minds. They regard and consider the honor and service of God (for which they were created) and the state of their souls after this life as little as a beast does; thus they are already the Devil's companions and property. Rather, he approaches and attacks with this temptation specifically those—and allows those to be most taken by it—whom one calls *Melancholics* <note>original: "Melancholicos"; in the 16th century, this referred to a temperament prone to deep, often dark or obsessive, thinking</note>. These are people who deal with deep, heavy thoughts, who are not satisfied with their status, possessions, ability, or circumstances, and who vehemently strive in every way for something higher and better: or how they might otherwise fulfill their desires or turn away their adverse troubles. One thinks of how he might support himself without labor and have a good life in idleness; another, how he might come to honor and great prestige; another, how he might rescue himself from poverty, persecution, or danger; another, how he might take revenge on his enemy, etc. Now, when through such diligent brooding and anxiety they can see and find no reasonable or proper means and ways to attain such things and reach their set goal, then the Devil is there, offering them his service and help, provided they will alienate themselves from God and cling to him. They then consent and follow him all the more easily and sooner because they were already previously turned away and estranged from God and abandoned by Him through the aforementioned fleshly, sinful thoughts and desires. Or he puts thoughts into their minds as to how they should begin it. Or he leads them to such companions from whom they may learn it. Herewith he lures and accustoms them so gently and gradually to himself, until he has them in his net and captured, and works his will with them.

# Augustin Lercheimer

That he <note>The Devil</note> however tempts, seduces, and brings to himself more women in this case than men, the cause is that women are more easy-going in belief, more easily persuaded, and more inquisitive than men. Just as Eve, out of frivolity and because she wished to know good and evil, obeyed and followed the Devil sooner than Adam, to transgress God's Commandment. In addition, women are beyond measure vengeful: therefore, when they cannot avenge themselves with their own power, they hang themselves upon the Devil: he teaches them and helps them, so that they do it with sorcery, as they believe, or also with poison.

->**On Soothsaying Sorcery.**<-

These sorcerers are not rightly called by us "Soothsayers" <note>German: *Warsager*, literally "truth-sayers"</note>, because they tell many more lies than truth. They have arisen and been shat into the world by the Devil for the reason that men are inquisitive; they wish to know that which they should not know, and cannot know in a proper way and manner: just as in the beginning Adam and Eve let themselves be moved and driven by such desire to eat of the forbidden fruit of the knowledge of good and evil: whereby they placed themselves and their descendants out of God's Kingdom and into the Devil's power. That same nature, along with other evil inclinations, has been inherited by us from them and clings to us.

We are thus created by God, and it is thus ordained by God, that what we can know must be present and at hand, in such a way that we perceive it with our senses, namely: by touching, by seeing, by hearing: or it must be announced to us by others who have experienced it in like manner, through words or through writing. For example, when my friend is over twenty miles away from me, I cannot know how he fares through proper, natural means ordained by God, except that someone indicates it to me with words or writing, or brings me my friend's words recorded. Because we, however, have no

<column-break/>

satisfaction in such means and in such knowledge, and seek a special kind against God's order, above and against nature, the Devil is there, and gladly lets himself be used for it in many ways. He seats himself inside the bodies of certain people whom he finds prepared and convenient for it, speaks and answers through them concerning hidden things about which he is asked, so far as he knows it and God permits him to answer. For he does not know everything, nor must or may he reveal everything he knows. The soothsayers in Egypt could not tell their King Pharaoh, nor those in Chaldea tell their King Nebuchadnezzar, what both their dreams meant: the Spirit of God in Joseph and in Daniel could do it. When Dr. Luther in the year 1521 traveled back home from the Diet of Worms, and by the command of his Prince, Duke Frederick of Saxony, was intercepted in the forest near Eisenach and led to Wartburg Castle, so that he would be safe there from the Emperor's ban and persecution—which only eight persons knew and faithfully kept secret—no soothsayer, of whom many were sought for that reason in Germany and Italy <note>original: *Teutsch vnd Welschland*</note>, was able to indicate where the monk had gone.

Such a soothsaying devil sat in the maiden at Philippi, Acts 16, and revealed many secrets through her: by whom Paul did not wish to be praised, but commanded him to be silent and come out. Likewise, in the city of Münster, while it was besieged, there were two maidens possessed by the devil, who indicated to the King <note>The Anabaptist leader Jan van Leiden</note>, the tailor, what this or that person kept for themselves in money and jewels, and did not hand over to him as he had commanded.

A highly learned, credible man, an Italian <note>original: *ein Wahle*</note>, writes that he saw in his home in R. <note>likely Rome</note> a woman named Jacoba, who had a devil in her belly that wished to be called "Curly-Hair" <note>original: *Kraushärlein*</note>. When one asked him about something, he answered with a clear, distinct voice from within himself, without the tongue and mouth of the woman. But yet only of things that had either happened, or were currently in existence and at hand. Concerning future things he was silent or lied. For the Devil can [know nothing] of the future—

cannot speak with certainty of future things; he strikes at them like a blind man at a sow: he hits the mark occasionally, but fails most often. Besides these soothsayers possessed by the Devil, there are other idle, useless, and harmful knaves and rascals who join themselves to him and have bound themselves to him by contract, so that he might be at their will and ready to reveal hidden things to them. They do this so that they may gain a following among the common man, a reputation, and money, thus supporting themselves in idleness against the Commandment of God, who said: *In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.* <note>Reference to Genesis 3:19</note> They deceive the people: they bring many an innocent person to their death, or rob them of their honor and good reputation. <margin>1 Samuel 28</margin> For such service, the Spirit presents himself to some, either visibly or invisibly—as he did to the sorceress in the form of Samuel <note>The Witch of Endor</note>, and to the student at L. <note>Likely referring to Leipzig</note>. This is how the spirit of Johannes Carion <note>A famous 16th-century astrologer and historian</note> answered him when he held the hand on which he wore the ring (in which the spirit sat) to his ear.

Sometimes they use a basin of water, a mirror, or a crystal, in which the spirit forms and depicts the persons and things one desires to know. They also take a sieve, set it up, speak special words over it, and then name the suspected persons. When the one who is supposed to have done the deed is named, the sieve moves. There are countless such ways and manners which I do not know, nor do I desire to know, which the Devil has taught his followers for the purpose of divination and soothsaying—indeed, to deceive people out of their money. As has been said, they thereby rob the innocent of honor, reputation, and life. They often put themselves in trouble and danger when the accused and indicated persons cannot be convicted. Not to mention how highly they—both the sorcerers and those who seek them out—sin against God by seeking the truth from the Devil and taking refuge in him, who is a liar and the father of lies, a murderer, and the declared, irreconcilable enemy of God and all mankind. We should regard him as such, from whom nothing but evil is to be expected and awaited. If he speaks the truth at times and does good, it happens so that he may be believed another time in a greater and more harmful matter, and thus people may be all the more deceived and injured.

If someone has lost a hen, or a sack has been stolen, he runs immediately to the soothsayer, who points someone out to him. Whether that person did it or not, he denies it. # Augustin Lercheimer

The fortune-teller pointed to her maid; she was whipped with rods by the executioner, and the lost item was found shortly thereafter in a place where no one had looked before. In the land of Jülich at <unclear>H.</unclear>, a peasant could not find his horse in the pasture: he asked a priest, a fortune-teller, about it. He answered him that someone had ridden it away across the Rhine. The peasant followed after him and encountered a man; he said the horse the man was sitting on was his, for it was exactly like his own. The other denied it. The Devil had murder in mind with this, but through God's providence and grace, it failed.

I know of it, and could name the persons and the place, where a poor fellow was identified by a fortune-teller as having stolen a precious jewel in a house where he was accustomed to come and go. He was subsequently imprisoned and, after confessing under unendurable torture, was hanged. After a few days, the lost jewel was found again behind the chest. Then they took him down from the gallows and buried him, and thus the matter was "well settled" <note>The author uses "wol außgerichtet" sarcastically to highlight the tragic injustice</note>. Therefore, one should stay away from such devilish questioning. If you have lost something, seek it and recover it in a right, proper, and harmless way: such as, "lay a little salt on it" <note>A common folk idiom or superstitious joke of the time, implying patience or simple domestic effort</note>, and you shall have it soon; or comfort yourself: think that God wished to punish you with the loss.

Also, let everyone refrain from inquisitive searching into future things: do and endure in the present what God imposes, and entrust to Him that which is known to Him alone and to no Devil. Indeed, even if Satan knows something of the future in part, according to his nature and swiftness, as mentioned above, he nevertheless directs the answer toward deceit, seduction, and the ruin of you and others. When the rich, powerful King Croesus in Lydia <note>A historical King of Lydia (reigned c. 560–546 BC) famous for his wealth</note> wanted to go to war with Cyrus, the King in Persia, he had the fortune-telling spirit visited and asked how the war would turn out. The spirit gave him this answer through a woman: "You will destroy a great

<column-break/>

empire." Croesus understood this to mean the empire of Cyrus, his enemy, which he would destroy. But when the opposite occurred—his empire was taken by Cyrus and he was captured—he sent back to that same Devil and reproached him for having deceived him. The Devil said no to that. He, Croesus, had indeed destroyed an empire, namely his own. Therefore, he had spoken correctly. The cunning villain either did not know which of them would win, or if he did know, he wanted to incite and lure him into war with the ambiguous answer, which Croesus interpreted to his own side.

The Emperor Nero desired to know how long he would live: the evil spirit gave him the answer that he should beware of seventy-three years. Now, he was still young, about thirty years old, and was therefore happy that he had so many years left to live. But he did not understand what the Devil meant. For soon thereafter came an old warlord and commander of 73 years, named Galba, who deprived him of the Empire and made him so anxious that he stabbed himself. Those were the "73" that would do it to him.

Here one might say: "Yet I see that the Devil knows the truth even of future things." As previously indicated, he hits the mark once in a while, just like a poor archer who shoots often and hits the target occasionally. Sometimes affairs are so fashioned, are so driven, and have come so far, that he perceives and foresees the outcome—especially when he has authority from God to help bring it about, so that he has the game in his hands; then he can speak the truth of it. This is how Johannes Carion <note>A German astrologer and historian (1499–1537) famous for his chronicles</note> hit the mark when he wrote several years before the Schmalkaldic War <note>A conflict (1546–1547) between the forces of Emperor Charles V and the Lutheran Schmalkaldic League</note>: "The House of Saxony shall be crushed by its own beams," meaning the discord between the two lords, Johann Friedrich and Maurice. He who lies all the time is never trusted; he who wishes to deceive must occasionally speak the truth and keep faith. Since, therefore, through fortune-tellers and those who run to them, the Devil is honored, God is blasphemed, and innocent people are slandered, shamed, and injured, and discord—

Preachers should also depict this vice in its true colors from the pulpit at appropriate times, so that the common man may learn what an abominable and dangerous thing it is, and so the Authorities may be reminded of their Office and what they are bound to do in this regard.

->**Of those who take the Devil to help**<-
->**in their professional business**<-
->**and otherwise.**<-

Humans are so greatly inclined to seek and use other higher, more powerful means—beyond and above the modest, permitted, and customary ways of their professional business and dealings—than what Nature (according to human character and situation) is capable of by God’s ordinance. Thus, some take evil spirits as assistants to advance their art, to accomplish something special and great, and to show off wonders, merely for the sake of vain glory or even for some small profit. Such people are deprived of God’s protection, grace, and benefits; they live and hover every moment in Satan’s power and dominion, in danger of body and soul, expecting no good end and having no hope of salvation.

<column-break/>

For no one can serve two opposing masters: Belial has no fellowship with Christ, nor darkness with light. He who lets himself be served by the Devil should know that he must give himself to him as a reward, unless he converts—which is uncertain whether it will ever happen. For to sin intentionally in reliance on future repentance is counted among the sins against the Holy Spirit, which God is accustomed to punish with final impenitence and hardening of the heart.

People of this kind are sometimes found even among the learned, who wish to surpass all others. But because their understanding, diligence, and ability are too small and weak for it, or because they are weary of the labor, they accustom a Spirit to themselves, who reads to them what they desire, shows them in which book and in which place this or that is to be found: tells them what is written in books that perhaps lie hidden, unknown to any man—indeed, those that perhaps once existed but are now decayed, torn, or burned, which the Devil well remembers and knows what was written therein. When such people then present such high, hidden art and wisdom in their speeches and writings, people marvel at them, and they are held in great esteem. But such fame and praise are bought far too dearly. There was recently such a fellow in Germany <note>original: "Teutschland"</note> who, otherwise unlearned, composed books in this manner; in one of them, he confesses and boasts that he took something from books that are not written. That sounds unbelievable, yet it can be so, if one understands it as books that were once at hand but have now perished and vanished, which the Devil has in his memory and knows by heart. This rogue was in special regard with a great Lord, whom he deceived, as has often happened and still happens to others when they believe such glib talk and support them. In the beginning, it seems as if it were something, though it is nothing: it does not last long and soon takes a foul end.

Thus one finds physicians who wish to know the cause and cure of all illnesses, the power and effect of all herbs and other medicines, so that no patient of theirs should die; they are not satisfied with a moderate art: they involve themselves with the Devil, who indeed surpasses all physicians and naturalists on Earth in mastery. He helps them how and as far as he wishes, and as it is permitted to him by God: but not for nothing, as the outcome is accustomed to prove.

A master gunner, whom I knew, boasted that he could hit anything that was within range so that he could reach it, even if he did not see it. He allowed himself to be used in the city of W. <note>likely Worms or Wittenberg</note> during the siege. But this I know, that such a thing is not artistic or natural, but devilish, dwelling within such fellows: and that they will afterwards dwell with him: unless they turn from him to God in time.

Of this sort are the fencers, the brawlers, the warriors, whom the Devil stands by for a while under obligation, protecting them so that they are not hewn, stabbed, or shot. Like that commander who came fleeing from the battle into the city of B., where he shook the musket balls out of his sleeves as thick as peas. None had been able to wound him. Dr. Luther says he saw a young fellow who pressed his bare belly against a sword point and pushed against it so hard and so long until the

Some gamblers can throw whatever they wish, and know what cards their opponent has in hand. I saw one of them who told another to shuffle the cards however he liked. Afterward he took them, held them in one hand behind his back, and with the other hand drew one card after another, saying every time beforehand which card he would draw, and then drew it. This and the like is not natural or human: therefore one should hold nothing else of such fellows than that they are departed and estranged from God, devoted to, secret with, and embodied by the Devil. Every God-fearing person, concerned for his salvation and blessedness, should guard himself against them as against the Devil’s residents and tools, as those who have not only to expect the eternal damnation of their souls, unless they do penance: but also must always be anxious and stand in fear that the evil spirit will one day prove his faithlessness toward them, abandoning them so that they perish, or even be killed by him.

He told them to hold fast to God and our Lord Christ: he taught and commanded them to pray, saying he would help them pray so that the charm would be taken from them. This happened, so that they saw and recognized their daughter again as before. Thus, faith and prayer are powerful things to resist and drive away the Devil and his temptations and afflictions; he who otherwise befuddles, deceives, and overpowers us out of God's righteous will and permission.

### Concerning Common Jugglers.

The base folk who travel about the lands with their juggling-bags, plying their trade at church fairs and on other holidays in cities, market towns, and villages, making pastime and laughter for the common man for money: they perform some antics and wonders in a natural way, merely with agility that the onlookers do not notice. As when they let wine flow out of someone's nose; they have it in a sponge in their hand against the nose and squeeze it out into a small tube, so one thinks it runs out of the nose. They lock someone's mouth shut so that one thinks the lock goes through both lips, though it only presses them tightly together. Such antics might be tolerated and pass by if it stayed at that, and they did not display supernatural, inhuman spectacles with the Devil's assistance, whereby pleasure and honor are given to him, and displeasure and dishonor to God; and it is scandalous and dangerous to the onlookers that they allow the Devil to delight them and provide joy and laughter. If something evil or harmful should happen to them from him, to whom would they complain or give the blame other than themselves or the authorities who permit such devilish pastimes and games? ### Concerning Great and Magnificent Sorcerers and Jugglers.

But how can one rightfully and fairly forbid the common, lowly people from this devilish trade when those who should warn them, keep them from it, and punish them for it, are themselves involved in it? Such as certain highly intelligent scholars, and certain Princes and Lords, who take their pleasure and pastime in it, and even use sorcerers for fortune-telling in their business. Where the Abbot carries the dice, the brothers may play freely. But such Abbots will experience in their time that the word of our Lord Christ—*He who knows the will of his Lord and does not act accordingly shall suffer many stripes* <note>original: Luke 12:47</note>—is not powerless. And that in the Book of Wisdom it is not written in vain: *The powerful shall suffer torments powerfully* <note>original: "Potentes potenter tormenta patientur" from Wisdom of Solomon 6:6</note>. Those who should improve the people with their good examples should not offend them with evil ones. The common man follows such examples, both good and evil, all the

<column-break/>

sooner and more frequently the higher and more respectable the persons are from whom they come. For he thinks everything they do becomes them well because of their high status; and if he does it, it will suit him just as well. Thus, the Lords are a great—indeed the primary—cause for their subjects doing good or evil.

I will make no mention here of any ancient, famous pagan sorcerers, but will instead cite some of our own within Christendom (which is a shame) to demonstrate how poorly it becomes such persons, and how it is less fitting for them than others to deal with such godless, dangerous, and scandalous things.

His Papal Holiness himself, Sylvester the second of that name, a Frenchman by birth, had learned the <term>Black Art</term> <note>Necromancy or demonic magic</note> in Spain from a learned Saracen. He became Pope through this, with the condition that he would belong to the Devil, whom he had enclosed in a brazen <insert>brass</insert> head, from which it answered him whenever he asked a question. Once, he inquired of it how long he would live in Papal dignity. It gave him the answer: his Papacy would come to an end when he came to Jerusalem. Now it happened in the fourth year of his Papacy that he performed Mass in a church called "The Holy Cross in Jerusalem" <note>A church in Rome, not the city in Palestine</note>. He immediately became ill and died, though he had thought he would never come to Jerusalem. In this manner, as mentioned above, Satan uses ambiguous speech to deceive men. After this Pope, the Popes one after another were sorcerers, as the histories or chronicles show, down to the incarnate devil Hildebrand <note>Pope Gregory VII</note>: eighteen in number.

And in our own times, Pope Paul the third, alongside other unspeakable vices, was afflicted with and notorious for sorcery; he kept many prominent sorcerers with him. The servants of these "holy fathers," the brood of priests and monks, have followed their example vigorously, considering sorcery not only to be no sin, but even a praiseworthy art and virtue. Indeed, it has finally come to the point that **Magic** <note>original: *Magiam*</note>—that is, the **black art**—is professed and taught in several high schools. I have seen several writings of those who pursued and were devoted to such study, written so diligently and cleanly with wonderful foreign words and signs, and adorned with red ink <note>rubrication</note>, that even the Bible is not usually copied so beautifully.

The highly learned and world-famous **Albertus of Lauingen** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and bishop famous for his scientific and philosophical works, though later legends accused him of magic.</note>, who was called "the Great" because of his intellect and skill, was not satisfied with the excellent gifts with which God had adorned him; he also defiled himself with this "devil’s dung," practicing sorcery for his own fame and for the pleasure and delight of great lords. After he had resigned the Bishopric of Regensburg and was a preaching monk <note>Dominican</note> in Cologne, Emperor William, a Count of Holland, came there from Aachen from his coronation, along with many princes and lords, for whom Albertus prepared a magnificent banquet in winter around Christmas time. Albertus, the "entertaining monk," had to be present as well. To honor the lords and for their pleasure, he caused the hall to become green and bloom with trees, herbs, foliage, and grass; the cuckoo, lark, and nightingale sang as if it were in May. The Emperor took such delight in this that he gifted Albertus’s fellow brothers in Utrecht a stately estate, rewarding such a highly punishable sin as if it were a good deed and a virtue. No doubt he was of the opinion that it was no sin because it was done by a monk, by such a holy father, in the presence and with the approval and rejoicing of so many ecclesiastical prelates.

In our fathers' time, seventy

<column-break/>

years ago, there lived **Johannes of Trittenheim** <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), Abbot of Sponheim, a famous polymath and cryptographer often accused of necromancy.</note>, a very learned and wise man; but in this he was not wise: that he was far too devoted to and intimate with the Devil. Although he wanted to protect his reputation and claimed that everything happened by natural means, no sensible Christian who reads or hears of his doings believes him. He was Abbot at Sponheim in the Hunsrück (where the Devil was Abbot, according to the proverb) where he had established an exceedingly precious library <note>Trithemius built one of the largest libraries of his time at Sponheim.</note>. From there he was driven out by the Duke—I know not for what reasons—and by his brothers, the monks, who envied him because of his skill and great name in all lands, and the favor he held with many Emperors and Princes; they also hated him because he maintained discipline and compulsion in the monastery more harshly than they wished. He said his spirit had revealed to him several years before that he would not die as Abbot of Sponheim. This Abbot performed many wonders, namely many ghostly apparitions, through which he became known, pleasing, and intimate to the lords.

This story, which I will now tell of him, I have heard several times from respectable and credible people. Emperor Maximilian I, the highly praised, had as his spouse Mary, daughter of Charles of Burgundy, whom he loved heartily and whose death he mourned vehemently. The Abbot knew this well and offered to bring her before his eyes again, so that he might delight in her countenance, if it pleased him. The Emperor allowed himself to be persuaded and consented to this dangerous curiosity. They went together into a private chamber and took one other person with them, so that there were three of them; and the sorcerer forbade them, on their lives, to speak a single word as long as the ghost remained. Mary came walking in—just as the deceased Samuel came to Saul <note>A reference to the biblical Witch of Endor (1 Samuel 28).</note>—strolling quite elegantly past them, so similar to the living Mary that there was no difference at all and not the slightest thing was lacking. Indeed, in observing and wondering at the likeness, the Emperor remembered that she had a small black mole on the back of her neck; he looked for it and found it to be so when she passed by a second time. Just so precisely does the Devil know how every person is created...

Then a horror came over the Emperor; he signaled to the Abbot that he should take the phantom away, and afterward spoke to him with trembling and anger: "Monk, perform no more such pranks for me." The spirit of this same Abbot waited upon his service in such a manner, and was so willing and ready for him at all times and places, that when he traveled across the country and perhaps came to a cold inn, the spirit would carry food and drink to him from elsewhere. He once traveled through Franconia <note>A region in south-central Germany</note>, and among his companions was a prominent man, a Councilor to the Emperor and the City of N. <note>likely Nuremberg</note>, who recounted this: That they had come to an inn where there was nothing good to eat or drink. Then the Abbot merely knocked on the window and said, *adfer*, that is, "bring." Not long after, a dish with a cooked pike was handed through the window, and beside it a bottle of wine. The Abbot ate and drank from it; the others felt a loathing for it and did not partake—as I also would have done. I would rather, and should rather, die of hunger than let myself be fed and watered by the Devil. Of this, our Lord Christ gave us an example and teaching when Satan advised him to make bread out of stones; He answered him: "Man lives not by bread alone, but," etc.

Where did the Devil get the pike and wine? Did he create them? No. He cannot do that, as proven above. He stole them perhaps from some rich, magnificent kitchen and cellar. When the cook had prepared the fish to be served, it was snatched away from him so that he did not know where it had gone; and he

<column-break/>

doubtless fell into suspicion and trouble with his master, as if he had embezzled it. The wine he obtained easily, since he has a key to every cellar.

Such stealing and taking by the evil spirit I will prove with this true history. In O. on the Rhine <note>likely Oppenheim or Oberwesel</note>, several noblemen have their estates where they stay whenever they come to the city. In one of these, called the Fr. Court, a citizen held a wedding. When the guests had returned for the evening meal and sat at the table, and fish were being boiled—when they were ready and were about to be taken from the fire and prepared—a violent wind blew down the chimney and through the windows and door, blowing out all the lights and overturning the kettle over the fire so that it was extinguished. At this, they were all terrified, as can be imagined. When they had regained their senses and come to themselves, relit the lights, and searched for where the fish were, not an eye or a tiny bone of a fish was found. In the meantime, they served the guests nuts until they had fetched and prepared other fish, and afterward apologized and recounted how it had happened. Where did the fish go, if not to the Abbot, or a sorcerer like him, who had invited guests and cooked nothing for them?

Here I am reminded of such a fellow who was at the court of H. <note>possibly Hesse or Heidelberg</note>, and once performed a strange, shameful piece of jugglery <note>term: "Gauckelwerck" - deceptive magic or illusions performed by a conjurer</note> for his guests (I know not if he had also cooked for them), in which a particular demonic power was noted. After they had eaten, they desired that for which they had primarily come: that he should perform a juggling trick for their pleasure. Then he made a vine grow out of the table with ripe grapes, one of which hung before each person. He told each to grab and hold his grape with one hand, and with the other to set the knife upon the stem as if he intended to cut it off. But he was by no means to cut. Afterward, he left the room and came back: there they all sat, each holding himself by his own nose with the knife held against it. Had they cut—

# Augustin Lercheimer

For these guests neither saw nor felt that they were holding their own noses; they believed they were holding grapes. <note>This refers to a popular folk tale where a sorcerer makes guests believe their noses are clusters of grapes to prevent them from cutting them off.</note>

The aforementioned Abbot’s disciple was a famous practitioner of the black arts <term>Schwarzkünstler: a necromancer or black magician</term> named Cornelius Agrippa, who carried the Devil with him in the form of a black dog. This dog indicated and performed for him whatever he wished and whatever he, the Devil, was capable of. I heard this from one who had been his servant: he wanted to leave him secretly, and at a time when his master was not at home, he gathered his belongings and made himself ready for the journey. When Agrippa came home and stroked the dog—which lay upon the pallet bed—with his hand across its back, he turned to the servant and asked why he wished to leave him? This Agrippa boasted that he and the Abbot possessed such an art that no thing was so far away or could happen that they could not know of it within 24 hours, and that this happened in a natural way. Claiming that this happened in a natural way is a palpable, shameless lie, intended to persuade people that black is white and that the evil spirit is a holy angel. When his time, which the Devil had promised him, was up, and he felt that he must die, he unfastened the collar from the dog—upon which stood strange writing and characters—and spoke to it: "Go hence, you cursed beast, you have ruined me for eternity." With that, the dog ran and leaped into the Rhone, which flows past Lyon, where this occurred; and Agrippa died, and the dog remained in the water and was never seen again. This sorcerer had been knighted by the Emperor and styled himself "Imperial Councilor": whereby little honor was done to his Christian Imperial Majesty, that a public apostate from God, and one who belonged body and soul to the Devil, gave himself out as his councilor.

<column-break/>

I could still speak of several potentates and regents of more recent times who have questioned sorcerers and sorceresses, taken them for counsel, and kept them in their presence. But enough of this unpleasant, hateful truth, which I write not to vex or defame anyone, but with good intentions: to show what a hideous, scandalous thing it is for a human being, especially for a Christian believer, and what a gruesome sin it is before GOD, that the authorities use, protect, nourish, and honor such public, intentional, wanton tools of the Devil. They should instead banish them from the land or punish them with death if they will not desist; considering how earnestly GOD commanded His people to remove such from their midst (Deuteronomy 18), as Saul did (1 Samuel 28), and what the old Imperial laws command regarding their punishment. Also, that God punished King Manasseh and King Ahaziah for the reason that they consulted sorcerers, soothsayers, and the Devil.

Yet, praise God, one sees and experiences that now among us there is less of the black arts and devilish jugglery, and it is now held to be more of a sin than was customary before the Holy Gospel came to light again. <note>A reference to the Protestant Reformation and the "rediscovery" of the Bible.</note> And it is to be hoped and wished that this vice decreases more and more from day to day until it vanishes entirely. This would happen all the sooner if the authorities were more diligent in their oversight and ensured that the people were rightly taught and governed with earnest discipline and good examples; and that we were not only Christians and Evangelical in mouth, name, and appearance, but in deed and from the heart. Regarding the sorceresses and witches, things are not yet improving; they will not yet disappear or cease, and are still rumored in several places—few here, many there. Of this, in my opinion, the least cause is not that they are so easily and suddenly executed and killed. More on this follows.

# Considerations on Sorcery

<margin>Concerning sorceresses, witches, or hags; what their supposed actions are.</margin>
The reason why Satan teaches more women than men to practice sorcery has been indicated above: namely, because they are more gullible, inquisitive, and vengeful than men. Therefore, they are more convenient and ready for the Devil to deceive, mislead, and destroy through his cunning malice, out of the enmity he bears toward the poor human race. What then does he teach the witches to do, and what are they capable of? They make weather—untimely, immoderate rain, wind, thunder, hail, snow, hoar-frost, and frost—so that corn, wine, and other fruits in the field and in the woods are ruined. They bewitch their neighbors' cows so that they give no milk, or so that the milk will not turn to butter; they cause cattle, calves, horses, sheep, sows, and other livestock to fall ill and die. They afflict children through speech <note>likely referring to "bespeaking" or verbal charms</note>, through looking at them <note>the "evil eye"</note>, or by touching them; they make men and women blind, deaf, lame, or consumptive; they bring into their bodies toads, hair, sow-bristles, straw, threads, shoe-patches, etc. They take away from men the strength for the marital act <note>impotence caused by "ligature" or knot-tying charms</note>. They can disguise and change themselves into cats, dogs, goats, donkeys, wolves, geese, etc. Many of them gather at night in special, designated places, where they hold banquets, dance, and commit lewdness with evil spirits. They ride or travel there on horses, goats, sticks, forks, brooms, distaffs, etc. These and other such harmful, gruesome "miracles" are said and believed of these women. However, whether this is true and not a false delusion in those who believe it of them—and whether it is not merely a vain, devilish imagination and dream in the witches themselves—and whether what supernatural things they do or think they do happen not through them, but entirely through the Devil: this we wish to consider briefly.

<margin>Whether witches can make weather.</margin>
Making weather is the work of God and of no human being, let him be as clever and powerful as he will; I say nothing of the fact that an old, mad, powerless woman should be capable of such a thing. God speaks to His people in Leviticus 26: He will give them rain in its season if they walk in His commandments. And David sings in the 147th Psalm: That the Lord covers the heaven with clouds and lets it rain upon the earth, and that He gives snow like wool and scatters hoar-frost like ashes; He casts forth His ice like morsels; no one can stand before His frost. In the 4th chapter of Amos, God says: "I caused it to rain upon one city and caused it not to rain upon another." Zechariah 10: Ask God for timely rain; it does not say, "ask an old woman for rain." If women could bring rain to us in dry times, or do away with rain when it is untimely and superfluous (for whoever can do the one can also do the other), why then would we need to pray so often in the church, in the congregation, and in the Litany for good, fruitful weather?

<column-break/>

It is without doubt a great sin and an insult to God that we value His power and His work so carelessly, slightly, and contemptuously that we attribute it to humans, and do not recognize that from Him comes good, timely weather to help and benefit us, and bad, untimely weather to punish us. He occasionally permits Satan to stir up a harmful wind, thunder, or earthquake in some place—which is not impossible for him as a spirit powerful in the air and in the fickle, unstable <term>meteoris</term> <note>meteors; in this period, the term referred to all atmospheric phenomena including rain and wind</note>—yet no more often, no further, and no differently than God allows him, setting the goal and prescribing the measure. Of this we have a clear testimony in Job, whose children he killed by collapsing the house they were in with a storm-wind, and destroying his flock along with the shepherds with fire from the sky. In addition, we read in authenticated pagan histories that the Devil protected his temple at Delphi in Greece, along with the city, against enemies with hail, thunderclaps, and earthquakes. Which God permitted him out of His hidden yet righteous will: He who uses the Devil...

# Augustin Lercheimer
<note>Augustin Lercheimer was the pseudonym of Hermann Witekind (1522–1603), a scholar who argued against the cruel persecution of witches.</note>

[God] uses [the Devil] like an executioner against people because of their sins, in this way as in others: to plague and punish them with fire, with pestilence, and other diseases.

That witches have no power in these matters, no more than other people, is obvious and undeniable. For how should they raise water into the air and make it rain, they who cannot obtain a pitcher of water—no, not even a tiny drop from the brook or well where they live—for their own necessity, except by going there, drawing it, and carrying it home like anyone else? When there is a time of drought, they are unable to make any rain fall upon their little garden or field; or when it is a wet year, they cannot keep the rain away and bring sunshine upon it. How should they be able to create lightning and thunder in the air, they who cannot make a spark of fire when it has gone out at home, but must fetch it from the neighbors or strike it from a stone like other people? If ever a Prince of the land held a battle with his enemy and called them to his aid, they would not be able to make or stir up one little hailstone, one grain of sand, or one little breeze to blow in the enemy's face and hinder him for their Lord's benefit. Indeed, the Devil himself cannot do it, even if he wanted to serve the witches, without God's permission and leave. This is seen in the sacrifice of the Prophet Elijah on Mount Carmel, where so many priests called to their Baal—that is, to the Devil—to light the wood and the sacrifice, but he could not. But when Elijah called upon his and our God, then fire fell from Heaven, consumed the wood, the sacrifice, and the water that had been poured upon it and stood around it. God is the LORD of the world and of nature, not the Devil, much less a poor, old, powerless woman.

Here someone might say: "If they do not do it, why then do they confess to it?" Answer: It is a superstition, a vain and false delusion, which their master the Devil gives and suggests to them, so that they think he does such things at their will, according to their contract and agreement; yet nothing happens in the weather except what Nature gives by God's ordinance. Now, when a storm is at hand, which the Devil—as a sharp-witted and swift <term>naturalist</term><note>original: "naturkündiger" - one who understands the laws of nature</note>—soon notices, he announces it to the witches, asking if they want to make a storm and saying he will help them. Then, as he has taught them, they perhaps boil hog-bristles in a pot, or take sand from the brook and throw it over themselves, or carry out similar foolishness; then it rains, hails, or thunders, as the season of the year dictates. Who is so senseless and doltish as not to see and understand that this is only a vain delusion and the Devil's trickery? That a boiling pot or sand thrown into the air should have the power to awaken a storm? Even if the foolish, stubborn, miserable women did not perform such gestures, the storm would nonetheless come. We read in the books of the ancient Greeks that their witches also charmed the Moon away from heaven so that it disappeared. Then the people rang bells and small chimes and struck upon brass basins until it came back up. This is how it happened: The Devil, as a skilled <term>astronomer</term><note>original: "Astronomus" - here meaning one who can predict celestial events</note> and stargazer, showed them when an eclipse of the Moon was at hand; then they gave out that they would pull the Moon from heaven at that hour. Thereby they were held to be great, miraculous women. The clanging did nothing to make the Moon return; it would have regained its former shine without that, as happens now and always.

The Devil does not give such indications to the witches every time, but only occasionally, so that he may keep them in his company and subjection. If it were up to him and every witch—of whom there are so many in the world—to make weather at their pleasure, what kind of existence would that be?

# Reflections on Sorcery

Even if someone wishes that my horse should go lame, it does not happen for that reason, even if it should occur at that very hour, since there is no such power in words. But if he strikes it in the feet with an axe, he injures it for me. If someone desires to ruin and blind my eye, paints an eye on the wall, stabs into it with an awl, and speaks as many evil words over it as he wishes, he achieves nothing by it, even if my eye should suffer harm immediately afterward. If the milk disappears otherwise, know that the Devil weakens the cows so that they dry up, or he steals the milk and carries it to the poor witches, or wherever else he wants. They then milk it out of their distaff <note>A tool used in spinning wool, often associated with witchcraft in folklore.</note> or out of a post, as it appears.

"Yes," you say, "but the Devil still robs me of my milk for the sake of the witches; they are the cause of my damage." I say no to that. The Devil can do not the slightest bit more to please the witches than God allows, in order to punish your unbelief and sin. Therefore Job spoke—whom you should follow in this—"The Lord has taken it away" <note>Job 1:21</note>; he does not say the Devil or the witches have taken it from me. Indeed, you demonstrate your unbelief and sin sufficiently—and perform an acceptable service to him (which he sought with the stolen pail of milk)—by suspecting innocent women and bringing them into evil rumors. <column-break/>

out: in front of whichever house she stops, from that house comes the sorcery. That woman must be a witch to you; you believe the lying-teller and your cow with the breeches. If you kept your house in the fear of God and in trust in Him, you would not live more recklessly or idolatrously than a heathen, and such things would happen to you much less often. And when they did happen, you would know how to conduct yourself rightly as a Christian: suspecting no one but the Devil, blaming no one but yourself, and seeking counsel and help from no one but God.

I must relate here a ridiculous yet Christian diversion of such bewitchment of cows. I knew a world-renowned Doctor of Holy Scripture whose wife complained to him that the cows would give no milk. He then asked for a pot with a little milk, added his own dung to it, stirred it together, placed it in the cowshed, and said: "Eat that, Devil, and leave me my milk." The next day, the cows gave milk again as before. Not that the evil spirit allows himself to be driven away with filth and sticks, but rather the defiance and the contempt—accompanied, no doubt, by prayer—vexed and drove away the proud spirit. The Doctor did not accuse or scold any witches, nor did he ever beat the milk-pot with a stick, as others are accustomed to do, thinking that Satan thereby strikes the witches who steal the milk, when he himself is the thief and not they.

Diseases and death happen to cattle in many ways and for many reasons, just as they do to humans, even if there were not a single witch in the whole world. How often does a plague come into an entire herd from foul air, which is poison to the cattle; or from bad water, or from the fodder and pasture. Sometimes a poisonous vapor arises in a stable, from which the cattle become sick. Often a beast catches a poisonous herb in the pasture, or swallows a harmful worm there or in the manger. When it becomes sick from this, people insist a human must have done it to them: an "evil eye," an "evil mouth," or an "evil hand" must have intervened. How easily something happens to little, tender children that makes them weak, even if no witch ever looks upon
