That certain strange things—needles, nails, yarn, brushes, hair, etc.—pass out of the body from above or below, or are even cut out of the skin, is not true; it is a devilish phantom <note>original: "gespenst," meaning an illusion or apparition</note> which he brings about in an imperceptible way. Sometimes it happens that tooth-pullers and similar rascals who attend such sick people have these things in their sleeves and secretly let them fall into the basin: or they nimbly thrust them into the wound so that they make the sickness and their own skill and effort seem greater and thus receive a better reward.

### Whether Witches and Sorcerers are Transformed into Cats, Dogs, Wolves, Donkeys, etc.

That such a change is impossible for the evil spirit to effect was proven at the beginning of this writing, where the sentence and decree of the Council of Ancyra <note>A 4th-century church council that declared the belief in the physical transformation of humans into animals to be heretical and an illusion</note> was cited: that God alone can transform essences. It was also noted that when Satan wanted to find out if the Lord Christ was God, he offered him stones to turn into bread, so that He might show His divine power. Thereby the

<column-break/>

Devil gave it to be understood that he lacked the power to do such a thing: if the Lord Christ could do it, then he would hold Him to be almighty and God. Therefore, those who write about and accuse witches and sorcerers of truly being such animals in the form they appear are mistaken and err, ascribing to Satan divine power and attributes. It is only a phantom, a deception of the eyes, in which the evil spirit forms another false shape instead of the right and true one, as was proven above with the maid who had become a cow. And in the thoughts and minds of those who believe they are cats, dogs, or wolves, it is a vain delusion arising from a sickness which physicians call *melancholia* <note>In the 16th century, melancholy was seen as a physical imbalance of "black bile" that could cause vivid hallucinations</note>: in which people imagine strange, wonderful things that are nothing. Satan finds his way into this, strengthening and increasing such imagination for his advantage and to the harm of men; this sickness is to him like filth is to a sow, and so he wallows in it.

In Athens, there was one afflicted with this who thought all the ships sailing to and fro were his: when they arrived, he was happy and welcomed them; when they sailed away, he escorted them; until his brother came home and entrusted him to the physician, so that he became healthy again. Ajax, the great warrior, came upon a flock of sheep and hewed and stabbed at them, thinking they were his enemies. Sometimes physicians have encountered patients of this kind who thought they had a nose several yards long and guarded themselves from afar so they would not bump into anything. Likewise others, who thought they were made of glass and feared they might fall or be run into and broken. Likewise, others thought they were dead and would not eat; they would have died of hunger had they not been provided with counsel. Galen <note>A famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose writings dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> writes of one who, in his own opinion, was a rooster: when he heard a rooster crow, he swung his arms like wings and crowed as well. Thus, it is an easy art for the Devil to make such people believe the delusion that they have been changed from humans into animals. To further confirm that it is a delusion in them, and a phantom to those who see them as cats, dogs, or wolves, I will relate several true histories beyond the proof shown above.

# Considerations on Sorcery.

from which one may undoubtedly conclude and decide that those who oppose this deny both experience and the truth: which testifies and proves that God alone is capable of such transformation of one animal into another, and it is possible for no Devil nor creature.

When I was studying in my youth in the year 1547 at Frankfurt an der Oder, during the lifetime of the highly learned and highly intelligent Mr. Dr. Jodocus Willichius <note>Jodocus Willich (1501–1552) was a famous physician and humanist scholar.</note>, it happened in the month of August that in the land of Mecklenburg, near the noble Maltzans <note>The von Maltzan family, a prominent noble house in Mecklenburg.</note>, in their neighborhood, a large hound with a white collar came running into the courtyard of their subjects. The hunting dogs attacked it, biting at it. Since they could not overcome it, the stable boys also came running with forks and spears, striking and stabbing at it. Thereupon it suddenly became a human, an old woman: who begged for mercy and grace, that they should spare her. She was seized and taken into custody. From this affair Dr. Willichius, a physician by profession, took the occasion and cause to dispute publicly in the High School <note>The University.</note> regarding such changes of humans into animals: he proved and maintained it with the consensus of all the learned men who were there, that it was only a delusion of the eyes <note>original: "verblendung der Augen"</note>, which in this story happened not only to the humans but also to the dogs. In this dog-specter, the Devil had advised and helped the woman until she thereby came into imprisonment; there he had brought her far enough and then abandoned her.

I once went with a minister, a good friend of mine, into the house of a Governor who held a werewolf (as such people are commonly called in German) captive. He had him brought before us so that we might hold a conversation with him and inquire what kind of business it was with such people. The man behaved like a madman, laughed, and jumped about as if he had come not from the dungeon but from a life of luxury. He confessed, alongside much other Devilish deception and specter-work, that on Easter night he had been at home with his servants in the form of a wolf, which place was more than twenty miles from there, and a river lay between them twice as wide as the Rhine at Cologne. We asked:

<column-break/>

how did you get across the water? I flew over it. How did you get out of the prison? I pulled my feet out of the stocks and flew out the window. What did you do among your people? I walked around and saw how they lay and slept. Why did you return to the prison? I had to; my Master wanted it so. He boasted greatly of his Master. When we told him that was an evil Master, he said: if you can give me a better one, I will accept him. He knew as much of God as a wolf does. It was a pitiful thing to look upon and hear the man. We prayed and obtained his release, otherwise he would have had to burn. May God improve such judgments.

Shortly before, it had happened in the same place that a peasant came into the Governor’s house and ate supper there. After he had eaten and drunk well, he suddenly fell backward from the bench as if a stroke had hit him. The Governor, who understood the matter (as he thought), let him lie there untouched and told the servants to go to sleep. In the morning, a dead horse was found outside the city in the pasture; it had been hewn in two with a scythe, which lay nearby. The Governor had the peasant, his guest, arrested. He confessed he had done it. He said a "Host" <note>Likely a reference to the "Wild Hunt" or a spirit procession.</note> had been flying around there like a flickering flame, to which the werewolves are enemies and must pursue; he had struck at it with the scythe: but as it hid under the horse that was walking and grazing there, the blow went through the horse. Thus the man confessed what he had not done, but rather what he had dreamed, just like the previous man. The former lay with body and soul locked in the tower, therefore he could not be twenty miles away at home: this one lay with body and soul the whole night in the room, therefore he could not be out in the field committing the deed. The Devil did it and imagined it so strongly to him in deep sleep and dream that he believed and confessed it was his work. He was burned because of it.

That the Governor forbade touching the guest as he lay there happened for this reason: he believed, like many others, that the soul had departed from such people and performed the things which they afterwards confess. But if one touches them in the meantime,

# Augustinus Lercheimer
<note>Augustinus Lercheimer was the pseudonym of Hermann Witekind (1522–1603), a professor at Heidelberg who argued against the extreme persecution of witches, attributing much of their "magic" to demonic deception.</note>

otherwise the soul would not return, and they would remain dead. Some writers in these times describe this false opinion—that the soul is separated from them—in their books regarding this matter, and they wish to persuade us of it against all reason and truth. For a body without a soul is dead: since death is nothing other than a separation of the soul from the body. But whoever is dead, no Devil can make living again: which is the work of God alone, who has nothing to do with this sorcerous business.

Thus these examples clearly show that when the body of a sorcerer or sorceress takes a form other than human, it is then a phantom <note>original: "gespenst"</note>; and where such a phantom-beast is injured in a foot or another limb, the human body is likewise injured. As a credible learned man shows this proof in his book: namely, that in Padua, in Italy <note>original: "Welschland," a historical German term for Italy or Romance-speaking lands</note>, a wolf ran about, and someone came upon it and hacked off all four of its feet. Immediately thereafter, the wolf became a human who had lost hands and feet. The Devil makes them run on hands and feet and puts a wolf’s face on them, just as that great sorcerer (mentioned before) turned the lesser one into a lily: when the top was chopped off, his head fell away. One also understands from the cited examples that these are often dreams—that they run about in such a form. Whatever harm they do in wolf-form with their bodies present (where the Devil gives them a wolf’s strength, or even greater) or through a dream by killing cattle or humans, it is Satan who does it; which they afterwards confess as their own act and must suffer for it.

That the Devil can and does occasionally carry the human body from one place to another is testified—besides the recently mentioned story of the woman whom he led in the form and gait of a dog—by many other examples, of both evil and good spirits: such as the Angel who carried the Prophet Habakkuk out of the land of Judah to Babylon and back again <note>A reference to the story of Bel and the Dragon in the Apocrypha</note>; likewise

<column-break/>

the spirit that snatched Philip away after he had baptized the chamberlain from Ethiopia and was found at Caesarea <note>Acts 8:39-40</note>. We read that the Devil carried Simon the Sorcerer (of whom mention is made in the Acts of the Apostles) around in the air at Rome and let him fall so that he broke his neck. As he did to Faust at Venice, who, however, escaped with his life. At Halberstadt, in Saxony, there was a learned Cathedral Dean named Johannes Saxonicus, a great practitioner of the black arts who lived 300 years ago; on Christmas night, when every priest may perform three Masses, he held the first at Halberstadt, the second at Mainz, and the third at Cologne. It is a very well-known story, occurring fifty years ago in the March of Brandenburg, that an innkeeper denied before a court that he had a mercenary's money which had been entrusted to him for safekeeping. He denied it with these words: "If I have it, may the Devil fetch me." Immediately the evil spirit grabbed him, standing there like a man, and carried him away. I myself heard from a sorcerer that he, along with 17 others from Saxony, traveled uninvited to a wedding in Paris—more than a hundred miles away—on a cloak; but they quickly made off when they noticed people in the hall whispering about what kind of guests these were and where they came from. Truly, that same sorcerer had red eyes, which he perhaps got from such traveling. Thus Faust once traveled during Shrovetide with his company, after they had eaten supper at home, for a nightcap from Meissen in Bavaria to Salzburg into the Bishop’s cellar—over sixty miles—where they drank the best wine. And when the cellar-master happened to come in and addressed them as thieves, they made off again, taking him with them as far as a forest; there Faust set him atop a high fir tree and left him sitting, flying away with his companions. In short, it is beyond doubt and undeniable that spirits, although they themselves have no body, nevertheless carry bodies and physical things from one place to another: as can also be gathered from the aforementioned, when the Devil brought the Abbot the dish with the pike and the bottle of wine.

# Considerations on Sorcery
->Aa iiij<-

But yet he <note>The Devil</note> rarely carries the witches away to other places, even though they are seen there and believe themselves to be there. For it is a phantom and a dream. They smear themselves with ointment, which their master has taught them to prepare, and smear the broom or fork as well, upon which they wish to ride. Soon a deep, hard sleep overcomes them (like the werewolf, who needs no ointment, therefore it does not contribute to it) which gives or creates for them such explicit, apparent dreams through the working of the Devil, that they believe no differently than that they are traveling here and there to a feast, being there with others, some of whom they know and some who are strangers to them: they speak, jest, dance, and commit lewdness with their lovers, the devils. Thus they are so strongly deceived in their delusion that they do not doubt it to be so: they say and boast of it among their own: they confess it when they are captured and questioned under torture: just as the werewolves confessed they had been in places where they had not come. That this is so has been recognized from experience, and may be recognized daily by whoever pays attention to it: applying oneself more to the fundamental, certain truth than to judging and erring according to the opinion and talk of the simple, ignorant common man.

The highly esteemed and eloquent Doctor Johannes Geiler von Kaisersberg <note>A famous priest and preacher in Strasbourg (1445–1510) known for his vivid sermons.</note>, sometime preacher in the Cathedral at Strasbourg, relates such a story. A pastor, as the occasion arose, had preached on sorcery and said that the riding of witches did not happen truly and in deed; they only dream that they ride to foreign places, seeing, hearing, and doing something special there, of which they afterwards tell and boast to others. As he now leaves the church, an old woman, a witch, speaks to him, who was vexed that he thus annihilated her art: she said she wanted to prove to him in deed that it was not dreams, if he would go home with her to her house. He goes with her. There she places a kneading trough or tub upon the bench and smears herself with an ointment. Soon thereafter she falls asleep, and in her sleep she moves, waving her hands back and forth, throwing them up high as if she were flying, jumping, and hopping as if she were dancing. She carried this on

<column-break/>

so long until she overturned the trough and fell out of it onto the earth. After she had lain there a while and struggled, she awoke, jumped up, and said to him: "There you have seen how I traveled away and came back: I have been here and there, I have seen and done this and that, etc." "Yes indeed," he said, "you have traveled. You sat in the trough for a while and slept, thereafter you fell out onto the floor and lay there also for a while until you awoke. Feel above your eye; there you have fallen and made yourself sore and bloody." Thus the woman was convinced of her false delusion, and the pastor was strengthened and assured in his mind and opinion regarding the riding of witches—that it is not real: that just as this woman traveled out in the trough, in the same way, and not otherwise, others ride on brooms, forks, and sticks.

Doctor Luther <note>Martin Luther, the Protestant Reformer.</note> was also of this opinion; he held nothing at all of the riding: he considered those who believe it to be foolish, frivolous people. And as for the saying that witches sometimes come together at night in a house in the form of cats, making a cry and a biting there, and if someone stabs, strikes, or throws at them so that they are wounded, one then finds wounded women in the neighborhood who must have been the ones. To this he answers: The Devil had wounded them at home in their beds, where they lay and dreamed they were there in the form of cats.

Indeed, such thoughts and opinions of Dr. Luther are not absurd or unbelievable. In the court of Emperor Maximilian I, there were two noblemen, one of whom had sworn death to the other out of enmity. One was stabbed to death in his bed at night: the other's sword was found hanging bloody in the scabbard before his bed the next morning. These were two strong, important indications that he had done it; namely, he was his mortal enemy and his sword was bloody. But he could prove that he had not left his lodging that night. He confessed, however, that he had dreamed that night that he stabbed him. It is manifest that the Devil did it, who can do the same to the witches.

# Augustin Lercheimer's

I could here cite many other brave, wise men who likewise consider this "witch-flying" to be nothing; I will leave them out for the sake of brevity. It is truly against all reason and all understanding that a grown, elderly person—even in a trough or a tub, as the aforementioned woman thought she did—should fly through a smoke-hole <note>A chimney or vent for smoke in a traditional cottage.</note> that is often so narrow that a fist could hardly pass through, or a cat crawl through it. I will not even mention that the white veils, with which they have adorned themselves for the dance, would be soiled with soot in the smoke-hole. Indeed, they sometimes confess that they slipped through a tiny hole through which one could hardly stick a finger. Whoever believes such things can also believe that fire is cold and ice is warm. It is a foolish thing indeed to think that an old, weak, sick woman, who can hardly walk with a stick, has the desire and strength to go to a dance as young girls run from one village to another for that purpose. There is more to a dance than red shoes: "strong legs are also required," as the proverb goes.

But one sees, you say, the witches in such dances and recognizes them. **Answer:** If someone sees one, he sees no human or physical being, but rather a <term>specter</term> <note>original: "gespenst" — an illusion or phantasm created by the Devil to deceive the senses.</note>, through which many an innocent woman falls into bad reputation and loses her life. And I consider those who claim to show the witches' dances, who recognize and denounce the persons there, to be such fellows who are also related to the Devil, serving him in his lies and murder, and receiving commission and pay from him for it. To prove and explain this, I will relate one or two wonderful stories.

In L. in Westphalia, witches were being burned; it did no good, for there became all the more of them. Now there was an adventurer there who knew the witches' dancing place and used to go there to mark them and denounce them. Among other women, the rascal also denounced the Judge's wife to him; and since the Judge desired to see her present at the dance, the fellow offered to lead him there at a certain time. He said yes. And the day and evening when the witches would come together was named to him by the informant. Now, so that the Judge could convict his wife, he invited several of his

<column-break/>

brothers-in-law as guests on the appointed evening. While they sat at the table, the informant came and whispered in the Judge's ear that it was time. He commanded his wife to entertain the guests and make them merry, saying he had urgent business to attend to in another place and would soon be back with them. When he came to the witches' dance, he saw there, among others, his wife dancing about, whom he had nevertheless left at home. He came back home and asked the guests if his wife had remained with them the whole time. They said yes: she had not stood up from them once. Then he confessed and related where he had been and what he had seen; there he learned for the first time, after he had judged and killed so many witches, that such gatherings are the Devil's specter and deception. Had he not had certain experience that his wife had remained at home with the guests the entire time, she would have had to burn, because she was seen there at the dance.

A Zurich Theologian <note>Likely a reference to Ludwig Lavater, who wrote a famous treatise on ghosts and spirits.</note> writes in his book on specters that the Bailiff over the Zurich territory, a modest and earnest man, told him: He was riding out early one morning in summer with his servant, when he saw on the pasture, to his great horror, a well-known, pious, and honest man committing an act of bestiality with a horse. He therefore rode back to the man's house, who was still lying in bed and sleeping. The man came out and spoke with the Bailiff: he had not gone anywhere that morning, nor the whole night. Had the Bailiff not investigated the matter so cautiously, the innocent man would have been arrested and tortured until he confessed, and would have been executed thereupon. Therefore, you Judges, watch yourselves well in this spiritual, Devilish, and deceitful business; do not over-hurry yourselves; do not believe your sight here as in other matters, much less the public outcry: so that you do not lay hands on and sin against innocent people, whom Satan hates and whose lives he seeks; so that you do not incautiously serve the Devil, you who are appointed as God's servants.

Furthermore, he deceives the senses of touch and feeling, so that a person grasps something and yet does not feel it (as was said before regarding the noses <note>A reference to a common folk tale where the devil makes people believe they are holding a nose when they are not</note>), or thinks he feels something when it is a delusion and nothing at all. Sometimes he takes a dead body upon himself (for he cannot create one) from the gallows or from a battlefield or elsewhere; he carries, moves, and uses it as if it were alive for as long as it pleases him.

To prove this, I will recount what I heard from the pious and highly learned Master Philip Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a famous German reformer and collaborator with Martin Luther</note>, alongside many hundreds of other students. In Italy, at Bologna <note>original: "Bononien"</note>, there was a lute player who, for two years after her death, walked, spoke, ate, drank, and played the lute just as she had before while she lived. This continued until, at a banquet, a sorcerer took notice of her and said to the guests, "This person is dead." Not far from R. on the Tauber <note>Likely Rothenburg ob der Tauber</note>, there came into the house of an honest, pious man one who looked like a nobleman, with two servants, one of whom could play the pipe and the other the violin. He claimed he was there because he desired his chaste, well-bred daughter in marriage. He arranged feasts, banqueted, danced, and was merry, as suitors or recruiters are wont to be. The host noticed that things were not going right, that it was knavish

<column-break/>

work and a deception. He said to the guest that it was an unequal marriage—noble and commoner do not fit together—and that he should seek elsewhere and leave him be. The guest would not desist and came back another time. Then the host invited a minister of the church, with whom he spoke across the table from the Holy Scriptures. This annoyed the guest, who said that when one wishes to be merry, one should speak of other things. Then the host burst out and said, "You are knaves and our enemies; you have come to harm me and mine, but you shall fail, God willing. Never can children be conceived from such spiritual or physical intercourse, although some think that "changelings" <term>Wechselbelg: a folklore belief in a fairy or demon child substituted for a human one</term> come from it. Primarily, one should observe in these supposed witches' dances and intimacies that the evil spirit intends to show and make understood that he holds dancing, unchastity, harlotry, and adultery (which are caused by and follow from dancing) in high regard. From this has come, in my opinion, the practice of the preachers under the Papacy <note>The Catholic Church</note> to frighten the people away from dancing with these words: "As often as two dance together, man and woman, the Devil dances as the third between them." Which was certainly not said without cause, as those understand who have come to their years and think deeply on the matter—what a powerful spark and unchastity it is, both for the onlookers and the dancers. Of which I could well say something...

<note>Augustinus Lercheimer was the pseudonym of Hermann Witekind (1522–1603), a scholar who argued against the persecution of witches, suggesting instead that social vices and lack of faith were the true problems.</note>

...promises he had made; this once occurred on a dance floor—if it were not too coarse and foul, and therefore not to be mentioned to chaste ears. For this reason, the theologians of our time, whom they call Calvinists <note>Followers of John Calvin, known for their strict moral codes.</note>, who insist that the authorities should forbid and abolish dancing as a cause of great sin and shame, are not to be scolded and reviled in the way many ignorant and indiscreet people do: those who have not learned, or do not consider, that he who wishes to avoid sin must guard himself against the occasion and opportunity to sin.

Indeed, to spite and defy the Calvinists—the "heretics," as they call them—those preachers who wish to be considered good Lutherans teach and incite the youth, not only with words, telling them not to heed the melancholy, sad Calvinist spirit or to cease their pleasure and joy; but they also lead them by example, "putting lice in the fur" <note>A German idiom meaning to cause trouble or create a nuisance.</note>. When they are at a wedding or otherwise a guest, the Superintendent, the Pastor, or the Deacon leads the line, dancing at the front, swinging the girls around in their long academic gowns and wide cloaks. They imagine that such behavior suits their Reverences quite well, and they even "make the dance good" with their presence, according to the common proverb. They never learned in school—or they have forgotten it or disregard it—what the wise, honorable Heathen Cicero says: that no one who is in his right mind dances at an honest, chaste banquet. <note>original: "nemo enim fere saltat sobrius, nisi forte insanit" — Cicero, Pro Murena.</note>

They do not know that in the Council of Laodicea in the year 370, it was decreed and resolved that Christians should not dance; and when the church servants are at a wedding and the pipers and fiddlers enter, they should then depart, so that by their presence they do not approve or validate such extravagance and lewdness. They do not know or consider what Augustine wrote on Psalm 32: It is better to plow the field on Sunday than to dance. They do not take to heart that our Lord Christ earnestly forbids everyone in general, and therefore especially the teachers and leaders, to give offense to anyone; and that they nowhere read in the Bible, nor in the histories of honorable Heathens, that men and women, boys and girls, ever

<column-break/>

danced together in the manner that happens among us. They have never read, or did not notice, that at all times since the beginning of Christianity among us, honorable, earnest, and brave men have punished this extravagance of dancing and desired to abolish it.

A hundred years ago, a small German book was printed in Heidelberg, in which, among other coarse common vices, there was a complaint about dancing in these words: **"The dance in itself, by its nature, as it is currently performed, is evil. To dance or to watch the dance, and especially on Sunday, is a mortal sin. And according to what the Divine teachers generally hold, as the world is now shaped, a dance rarely occurs, even on a workday, without mortal sin—be it at weddings or otherwise—for many reasons. Therefore, it is faithfully advised that for your wedding, you invite very few people, without dancing and gluttony."** So far the booklet.

Emperor Frederick III said he would rather lie sick with a fever than dance. The aforementioned Doctor Johann Geiler von Kaysersberg <note>A famous and fiery cathedral preacher in Strasbourg (1445–1510).</note> used to say from the pulpit and elsewhere that no dance, however moderate and chaste it might wish to be, happens without great sin; and he used to admonish and warn honorable matrons and mothers of households not to let their daughters go to such dances. Thus, their Reverences may see from this—if they did not know it before—that our dances were considered punishable and vice-ridden by chaste, honorable, and righteous Christians long before Calvin was born. But I have strayed too far into the subject of dancing, though not without occasion and cause; I will now return to the matter of witchcraft.

# Reflections on Witchcraft

is added; this is done by our sworn enemy, the Devil, through God's providence and permission, as a punishment for our sins, or to test and try the steadfastness of our faith and our confidence and trust in Him. Therefore, when your child falls ill, the calf dies, or the cow will give no milk, do not accuse or blame, nor bring into ill repute your neighbor, who could not have done this to you with words and foolish gestures, even if he had wanted to and attempted it. Never prick a waxen image; do not throw the milk pail with the intention that the witch might thereby be pricked and struck, as some do—which is to drive out witchcraft with witchcraft. Instead, endure it patiently like all other adversities of which this miserable life is full, not for the sake of the witch, but because of our sins.

Remember that it is God's will that you be so plagued, as Jeremiah says in Lamentations 3 <note>Lamentations 3:37-39</note>: Who can say that such a thing happens without the Lord's will? And that neither evil nor good comes [except] through His will? Why do people murmur so in life? Let each one murmur against his own sins. Pray to God in faith in our Lord Christ, that He may better your evil and turn away your misfortune, as He commanded and promised us in Psalm 50: Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you. You and your household should not live like cattle or like heathens. Recite your Creed daily, which is called the *Symbolum* <note>original: "Symbolum" – a Greek-derived term for a creed or "watchword"</note> for this reason: it is, as it were, a password and field sign of the warriors of Christ. When the Devil hears the password, "I believe in God, etc.," he flees from you, because he perceives that you belong to and serve the great, mighty Lord, and that you defy him.

Pray in the morning when you rise, and in the evening when you go to sleep. Do not go to the table without prayer, as the sows run to the trough. Pray with devotion, especially this: "lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." In such cases, use certain holy verses, such as Romans 8: "If God be for us, who can be against us?" Psalm 27 <note>The text cites Psalm 26 following the Vulgate numbering</note>: "The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?"

<column-break/>

etc. Psalm 91 <note>The text cites Psalm 90 following the Vulgate numbering</note>: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. He says to the Lord: my refuge and my fortress, etc." What does it matter? The devils, with all their sorcerers and witches, will surely leave you in peace. Nothing is accomplished with herbs and smoke, or with crosses; faith and prayer must do it.

Furthermore, you can do no greater harm to the Devil and make him more despondent against you than by despising him and defying him in faith, as the Doctor <note>Likely referring to Martin Luther</note> did when his cows were bewitched. One reads of Emperor Frederick I <note>Frederick Barbarossa</note>: when he besieged Milan, a sorcerer was sent out of the city into the camp to kill him with poison. When the prisoner threatened the Emperor that if he did not let him go, he would bewitch him to death, the Emperor paid no heed, had him executed, and he could not harm him.

That unchaste devilish knave Faust <note>The historical Johann Georg Faust, the inspiration for the legend</note> stayed for a while at Wittenberg and sometimes came to Master Philip <note>Philip Melanchthon, the famous reformer and colleague of Luther</note>, who then read him a good text, scolded him, and admonished him to desist from such things in time, otherwise it would come to a bad end—as indeed it did. But he paid no heed. Now, it happened once at ten o'clock, as Master Philip went from his study to the table, that Faust was with him, whom he had severely scolded. Faust said back to him: "Master Philip, you always attack me with harsh words; one day, when you go to table, I will make all the pots in the kitchen fly out through the chimney, so that you and your guests shall have nothing to eat." To this, Master Philip answered him: "You shall leave that well alone; I shit on your art." And he [Faust] let it be. Another old God-fearing man also admonished him to repent. In "thanks," Faust sent a devil into his bedroom as he was going to bed to frighten him. It went about the room, grunting like a sow. The man, well-armed in faith, mocked it: "Oh, what a fine voice and song that is for an angel who could not stay in heaven, and now goes into people's houses transformed into a sow, etc." With that, the spirit retreated home to Faust and complained to him how he had been received and dismissed; he did not want to be there where one reproached him for his fall and ruin and mocked him for it.

# Augustin Lercheimer

## On the punishment of witches or
## sorceresses.

Almost no vice is punished so diligently, earnestly, and harshly as witchcraft: even though the poor, miserable women do little or no harm to anyone—unlike other evildoers whose lives are truly criminal, as proven above—and their guilt is entirely obscure and unprovable. God creates the weather according to the order of nature: humans and animals cannot be harmed or killed by mere thoughts, words, or gestures used by witches, but only by poison or physical deeds. That, however, is not sorcery; it is something else and does not belong here. And even if they smear sticks, brooms, or forks and ride them to the dance—which in fact does not happen—they certainly do no harm to anyone by it: let them dance until they are tired of it, since we tolerate all other people dancing whenever they feel the urge.

Although this is the case, they are nonetheless thrown into prison based on common rumor according to old custom: there the wretched women lie in the dark, where the evil spirit is more welcome and powerful than elsewhere, making them more subservient and his own through terror than they were before. Indeed, in such lonely darkness, he often persuades and threatens even those who are not sorceresses and have never had fellowship with him, until they become his companions. After the Devil comes the executioner with his gruesome instruments of torture. What woman, seeing that before her eyes, would not be so terrified that she would confess not only what she knew or thought she had committed, but also things that had never even entered her mind to do?

Upon such forced, delusional, false, and void reports, they are then condemned and executed: and they would rather die than be so tormented in such a prison by the Devil and the executioner. And such proceedings are praised not only by some jurists, but also by theologians in the books they have written on this matter; they strengthen the judges in this, incite them to it, and are so hateful and harsh toward the miserable women that they say

<column-break/>

one should believe all kinds of witnesses against them, even the dishonest and the slandering, so that they may be blotted out and exterminated. They are so zealous here for God’s honor, though they otherwise act quite slowly regarding it in other matters. They cite many examples of high and respectable judges who have condemned witches to death. To this one should answer them as <term>Demosthenes</term><note>A famous Greek orator known for his logical rigor.</note> answered his adversary: do not say "it happened thus," but say "it happened *rightly* thus." <note>original: "sage nicht es ist also geschehen/ sondern sage es ist also recht geschehen."</note>

This example pleases them particularly well, as if it were very convenient for proving their opinion. A butcher was walking through a small forest at night when he heard a noise and dancing: he approached, and the dancers vanished. He saw silver cups standing there, took them, and brought them to the authorities. They threw those into custody whose marks were on the cups as sorceresses, along with others who were named by them, and executed them all together. That they were indeed sorceresses is to be inferred from the fact that they confessed against others, whom the Devil had conjured in their minds in a dream, as if they had been there together. They had been lying at home, sleeping and dreaming; meanwhile, the Devil was awake, took the cups from their cupboards or containers, and carried them to where he knew his servant, the inquisitive and daring butcher, would pass by, so that the women would lose their lives because of it. Had they brought them there themselves, they would not have left them behind when leaving, lest they be betrayed by them and robbed of the cups. It was the work of Devils, not humans. Who would desire to hold a feast and dance at night in a smoky forest, in wind, cold, and rain? Their cups were found, therefore they were there. With the same logic, the authorities in a prominent city in Germany were once deceived into hanging an innocent locksmith because his lockpicks were found in a place where money had been stolen from chests. Another had secretly snatched the lockpicks from him and used them for the theft, which the thief later confessed after he was caught.

<summary>Lercheimer argues that witch trials are based on forced confessions and demonic deception rather than physical evidence, criticizing theologians and jurists who encourage the execution of the innocent. He uses the story of the butcher's cups to illustrate how the Devil frames women for crimes they only dreamed of committing.</summary>

# Considerations Regarding Sorcerers

Indeed, some who ought to exhort the judges toward equity and leniency are so hostile and unmerciful toward the poor witches that even when a husband testifies for his wife—stating that she never left his side in bed during the night she was allegedly seen at the [witches'] dance—they then argue and contend that a phantom lay in the bed while the true body was outside. Dear friend, why do you not turn this around and interpret it for the best: that the true body lay in the bed, and the false one was outside? This is exactly what the judge mentioned previously discovered regarding his own wife. Does that laudable rule not apply to you: <term>Semper in dubiis benigniora præferenda</term> <note>Latin: "In doubtful matters, the more liberal/kind interpretation is always to be preferred."</note>? Namely, that in doubtful cases, one should always prefer the milder path over the harsher one.

It is the duty of theologians—as those who understand this spiritual business better than those who deal with worldly matters—to instruct the authorities. The greater part of the authorities look more to custom and follow it rather than understanding or considering what the root of witchcraft actually is. Theologians should exhort and move them toward kindness and mercy, following the example of <term>Saint Ambrose</term> <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan known for his influence on church-state relations.</note>, who rebuked the Emperor <term>Theodosius</term> with harsh words because he had allowed many people in the city of <term>Thessalonica</term> to be killed in anger without sufficient or just cause.

As for the harm and evil that people believe and say witches inflict upon humans: this is merely a vain, bare will without action, as proven before. God punishes this will to do evil—with Him, the intent counts as much as the deed—but the worldly authorities should not. Even when a witch passes her hand over livestock (unless she has actual poison in it) and speaks evil words, this is only an indication of her will; it does no harm to the animal, for the hand and words do not possess such power to kill or make livestock sick. However, if the Devil physically leads them somewhere in the form of cats, dogs, bears, or wolves (which rarely happens to women, but more often to men) where they steal, rob, tear apart humans or cattle, or otherwise cause damage: that is a physical act like any other and is therefore to be punished. In such cases, the evil spirit helps them so that they are stronger than they would otherwise be.

<column-break/>

Are witches then, outside of this specific case, innocent and blameless? God forbid that I should say such a thing. Indeed, I say that sorcerers and witches are so sinful and vice-ridden that they could not be sufficiently punished by all the penalties and pain that all the authorities on the entire earth inflict upon miscreants. This is because they have turned away from and renounced God—their Creator, Redeemer, and Savior, whom alone they should serve and whose property they should be—and have promised and surrendered themselves to the Devil. What sin can be greater than this? How can a person be in a worse state? It would be better for such people if they had never been born.

But now, alas, it is not only sorcerers and witches who are thus separated from God and belong to the Devil's household; the whole world is full of them, including the majority among us who wish to be called Christians and Evangelicals. Therefore, the Lord Christ calls the Devil a "Prince of this world." He says to the unbelieving Jews in <term>John 8</term>: "Your father is the Devil." Likewise, in <term>1 Timothy 6</term>: "Those who strive for riches, the covetous, fall into the Devil's snare." And in <term>1 John 3</term>: "He who sins is of the Devil." Dear friend, how many people do you expect to find on earth who do not strive for riches, or who do not at times sin against their conscience and thereby, according to these verses, fall into the Devil's power? The authorities punish none of these, nor should they; yet the witches must burn simply because they have surrendered themselves to the Devil.

Here, people appeal to the Law of <term>Moses</term>; it must apply here: "You shall not let a sorcerer live." Likewise: "Whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord shall die the death." "Yes," they say, "those other sins happen in secret, so we commit them to God and let Him punish them; but the witches make it too coarse and too public." Well, let it be so. But what will you say to this, and how will you answer: That the godless rabble, the mercenary soldiers, openly and publicly treat God with scorn and contempt—

<summary>The author argues that witchcraft is often a matter of sinful intent rather than physical reality, criticizing judges who ignore alibis and urging authorities to prioritize mercy over tradition. He contends that while spiritual apostasy is a grave sin, it is a common human failing that does not always warrant the unique physical cruelty of the stake.</summary>

# Augustinus Lercheimer

fess openly—even boast—that if the Devil would give them something, they would serve him. Is it not common among hucksters and merchants that for the sake of a single batzen or kreuzer <note>Small denominations of silver coinage used in the Holy Roman Empire</note> they often deny God within an hour and dedicate themselves to the Devil? "As true as God exists," they say, "it costs me this much." Now, it does not cost them that much; therefore, there is no God for them or with them. Likewise: "If it costs me less, may I belong to the Devil." But since it does cost them less, they are indeed surrendering themselves to the Devil. They do this so commonly and without shame that there is a proverb: "No one should care about a huckster's oath."

What is more: when someone has committed perjury before the authorities—be it for money, out of favor, or out of hatred—whereby God is made a liar by him and consequently denied, he is punished only by being declared dishonorable from then on, or being banished from the land, or perhaps losing two fingers. Where does the Law of Moses remain here, that "the blasphemer shall die the death"? <note>Leviticus 24:16</note> I will not repeat here what was said before regarding the soothsayers, jugglers, and the grand, famous sorcerers and practitioners of the black arts, who are not only left unpunished but are even supported, gifted, and honored—even though they should be punished more severely than the women, because they are men.

Here someone might interrupt me and say: "We admit it is wrong that the [male] sorcerers are not punished, or punished too little; but is it therefore wrong that the female witches are executed according to the Law of Moses?" Answer: Our authorities are not bound to the civil laws of Moses, neither in this case nor in others, to punish this vice or others according to them. These laws were specifically given by God to the **Jews** according to their nature and circumstances, so that they might have a distinct policy and government from other nations, which was to remain until the Messiah came. After He came, that policy was abolished and set aside. When the Apostles Paul and others preached the Gospel here and there in the pagan world, in Rome and other places, they nowhere advised or commanded that the existing laws of the land and city be abolished or changed, and that the Law of Moses be accepted and kept instead.

<column-break/>

Paul did not command or incite the Governor Sergius in Cyprus, whom he had converted, to kill the sorcerer Elymas <note>Acts 13:6-12</note> who opposed him, according to the Law of Moses. Every nation has its own particular nature and circumstances; the laws must be established and arranged accordingly.

What need is there for many words? The statutes of Moses do not hold sway with our authorities. Yet to defend the sharpness and severity against the poor, insane women, Moses must do his best <note>i.e., the authorities cherry-pick Moses only when they want to justify killing witches</note>. Moses commands a thief to return what was stolen and as much again; our authorities hang him on the gallows and take the stolen goods for themselves. Thus the thief steals for them, and the victim must go without his property, in which the authorities should have protected him. Moses commands that whoever strikes father or mother, or whoever curses them, shall die the death; a disobedient son shall be stoned by the people. Where is this kept among us? Even if the authorities know of it, they do nothing about it. Moses wants male and female adulterers to be punished with their lives. How many Princes and other rulers are there among the Evangelicals <note>Protestants</note> who do this? Of Bishops and Abbots I will not speak; since they have forsworn marriage, their regime cannot tolerate such a law, nor can it exist alongside it. Likewise, no Jew shall take usury <term>usury: the practice of lending money at interest</term> from another; I believe we Christians keep this commandment by lending to one another for nothing! The freedoms <note>original: "freiheiten," referring to legal exemptions or sanctuaries</note>, of which there were several in the Jewish land by God's command, and which the Popes among us had established in excessive numbers, our authorities allow to lapse for fair reasons. Likewise, God had ordained for His people through Moses the keeping of the beautiful and useful Jubilee Year, namely that landed and immovable property had to be sold in such a way and with the condition that in the Jubilee Year—which was every fiftieth—it would revert to the seller. That is a strange and unknown thing among us. In Numbers 15 <note>original: "Nu. 21." - likely a citation error for Numbers 15:32-36</note>, someone gathered wood on the Sabbath day; Moses, by God's command, ordered him to be stoned. What happens among us on our Sabbath or Sunday, unpunished, during the sermon and divine service?

But because the Law of Moses regarding the punishment of witchcraft makes our authorities so moved and zealous to [execute] the witches...

# Considerations on Witchcraft

burning <note>referring to the execution of witches</note> should also remember that it is their duty to ensure in their territories and among their subjects what Moses ordained and what was maintained in the Jewish polity <note>The "Jewish polity" refers to the civil and religious laws of the Old Testament Israelites</note> to prevent and guard against witchcraft. If the authorities see and do the one thing <note>punishment</note>, let them also see and do the other which happened alongside it and ought to happen still. The Jewish land was everywhere and at all times full of divine service, teaching, and sacrifice, discipline and compulsion. All people had to appear in Jerusalem three times a year to hear and learn the law of God there, and to receive other ordinances conducive to an honorable life and good morals from the high priests and elders. Throughout the entire land, in every corner, there were synagogues or parishes, where everyone was required to present themselves every Sabbath to hear God's word, to pray, and to give alms; they had to observe the new moons and many other ceremonies. And these parishes were all well-staffed with people, of whom there were many thousands in such a small land. Furthermore, women after childbirth, when the days of their purification were over, had to travel to Jerusalem and offer sacrifice there—some, truly, over a long and rough road. They had to bring the firstborn of men there and redeem them with money, and sacrifice or redeem the firstborn of cattle. Since the people were so urged and compelled toward divine service and had so much practice in it, it was not unjust that those who turned from God to the Devil were severely punished.

What happens in this regard among us? One finds many villages where there is no pastor at all; perhaps three or four villages share a single pastor between them. How he can provide for them all can be imagined, even if he is capable and diligent, of whom there are few. No one, neither man nor woman, is exhorted—much less compelled—to go to church on Sunday or other feast days. The men are busy hauling grain or wine to the city, or have other business; the women wash, scrub, and clean the house because they have worked in the fields all week. If they happen to come once a year, such as at Christmas or Easter,

<column-break/>

into the church, those under the Papacy <note>referring to Roman Catholics</note> only look at the jugglery of the Mass; they hear nothing in the sermon but fables and human trifles. Among us Evangelicals <note>Protestants</note>, it has come to the point that the pastors think they have performed their office well if they have spent an hour speaking, regardless of how it suits their listeners or what fruit and improvement they gather from it. From this it comes that the majority of the parishioners know nothing at all of God, of His will, fear, obedience, or prayer. As recently in a small country town, a citizen's wife about sixty years old, when she was about to die and was exhorted by a virtuous, God-fearing neighbor woman to cast all worldly thoughts from her mind and to concern herself with God and pray, she said: "She could not pray." Thus she passed away like a heathen, and entered heaven "like a cow through a mouse-hole" <note>A proverbial expression meaning something is impossible or highly unlikely</note>.

Therefore, it is no wonder that the Devil takes root among such people and teaches them superstition and witchcraft. Then the authorities step in, throw them into the towers <note>prisons</note>, and thereafter into the fire, as if they had thereby fulfilled their office. It is exactly as if a schoolmaster were to whip his pupils when they have done wrong, without having previously taught them what wrongdoing is. Just as one should not only punish adultery and harlotry—which, alas, seldom happens—but also forbid dancing and other occasions and causes for it. Just as one should not only hang thieves, but also take foresight and prevent, as much as possible, anyone from becoming a thief: by letting young people learn a trade or something else so they can support themselves healthily in the future, and appointing overseers for them so they do not squander what they inherited from their parents, and then, having wasted it and not knowing where to turn, take to stealing. Other idle rascals should not be tolerated in the community.

Here I expect the rulers and judges will say: "What you propose regarding church teaching, discipline, and compulsion as was held in Judaism to prevent witchcraft, that is difficult for us in our territories and govern—"

**Answer:** It is more difficult than simply ordering the executioner to lead out and burn several women. Because that which should happen and precede this—to prevent this vice—cannot be done, you should consider that equity requires one not to proceed with such hardness and severity in punishment. *Too sharp makes a notch* <note>A German proverb meaning excessive severity is counterproductive</note>: *Too much justice is injustice.* I do not doubt that many a judge and pronouncer of sentences in these witch-matters has a zeal for God's honor against them; but one must ensure that this zeal flows from right understanding and knowledge of the matter, with consideration of how these persons are made, and how they fell into this pitiable misfortune and sin. They are commonly poor old women with troubled hearts and deranged senses, to whom the Devil has presented and forced himself as convenient instruments. These then perhaps lead other young women astray. For they think they are doing well, and therefore wish to make others partakers of their "prosperity."

That some respectable, wealthy women also fall into this number of witches happens, in my opinion, through false accusations which the Devil brings about in this way: When the poor witches dream that they are perhaps at a dance or living in luxury, he makes them imagine that they see such women there; they afterwards report that these women were also in their company. Thus they fall into ill repute and are subsequently thrown into prison. There the Angel of Darkness <note>The Devil</note> finds them, moving them with flattery or with terror to surrender to him and confess themselves as his companions. Then comes the executioner with the torture; he makes them so anxious and causes them such pain that they confess more than they know. Thus no discretion is used, and there is no mercy toward the poor, miserable, foolish, seduced race of witches; it is nothing but sharpness and severity. Yet, very often, those who administer and attend this court—while they punish the unbelief in other

people—cannot themselves recite the Articles of the Christian Faith, or do so only rarely. Their faith stands upon their granary full of corn, upon their cellar full of wine, upon their stalls full of cattle, upon their treasure and riches. And those who wish to be seen as guardians and upholders of both tables of the Ten Commandments know as little what is in the first as in the other. Indeed, they themselves practice sorcery during such trials.

To investigate whether they be witches, some have this custom: They tie the right hand to the left foot, and the left hand to the right foot, and thus throw them into the water. If they float, then they are witches; if they go to the bottom or sink, then they are not. What spirit has suggested this to you, dear Lords? A human body—especially when hands and feet are bound so that it cannot move—goes to the bottom; though the clothes may hold it up for a while, it sinks once the water penetrates them. If such a body floats without help, the Devil holds it up so that he may strengthen you in your delusion and kill the human being—the innocent just as easily as the guilty. They order their clothes changed and their hair shorn, as if their strength were therein, like in Samson’s hair. The executioner sprinkles them with holy water or with baptismal water so that they might confess. Also, it is an indication to them that they are witches if they do not weep—as if this happened only to them and not also to other young and old men and women, either by nature (as I have seen) or from immoderate sadness and other accidents. Before the court and during the procession, they are placed in tubs and carts so that they do not touch the ground. For if that happened, they would escape and do great damage, causing great misfortune.

This is purely superstitious business; and therefore, while you punish others, you commit the same yourselves. You want to drive out sin with sin; that is washing off filth with filth. You also deceive yourselves by thinking—and holding it as a sign—that you do the Lord right by killing them because they lose all their strength

I side with those who believe it is much fairer, more lenient, and also more Christian to root out sorcery in this way: that the pastors instruct the people about this deception of the Devil, warn them against it, and frighten them away from it by showing how great a sin it is and what will happen to them because of it in and after this life. In the time of Dr. Luther and Philipp <note>Philipp Melanchthon, a key Protestant Reformer</note>, the black-magician Faust, as mentioned above, stayed for a while in Wittenberg. This was allowed to happen in the hope that he would convert and improve himself through the teaching that was then in vogue. M., who loved to drink and gamble. He offered to provide him with enough money, provided he surrendered and signed himself over to him, not with ink, but with his own blood. He said, yes. The Doctor noticed that he had money and wondered where it came from, as he knew his parents had sent him none. He took him aside and investigated where he had gotten it. He confessed how it had happened. The Doctor was terrified by this: he complained to Dr. Luther and others, who summoned the student to them, scolded him, and taught him what he should do to be released from such an obligation. They prayed to God for him: they defied the Devil for so long that he brought the contract back. Thus the youth was snatched from the jaws of the Devil and preserved, and brought back to God; he was not immediately put in the tower and afterward into the fire. Following this example, one should apply diligence and work harder to convert and improve such people than to kill and destroy them.

Since few judges, lay assessors, and jurors understand this, but follow their ignorant zeal and custom, it would be desirable for the high authorities to take notice and entrust such courts to sensible, experienced, and modest men. Or where these cannot be had, that the verdict should be sent from the Chancellery, which should have a certain formula established—not only by lawyers but also with the advice of theologians, since it is a spiritual matter, and also physicians, since the Devil brings people into these snares of his according to the nature of their <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of bodily humors, thought to influence temperament and susceptibility to the Devil</note> and the accidents of the mind. And that the cities and communities which have the power of high justice <note>The legal authority to carry out capital punishment</note> but no skilled persons, should...

> Since it has come to our attention that some in our land, and also those settled nearby, presume to practice sorcery: to conjure devils and to tell fortunes: whereby our subjects are led not only into useless expense, but also into superstition, and sometimes honorable people are placed under evil suspicion and false slander and accusation. Now, since such devilish undertakings with sorcery, blessings, fortune-telling, and other such things are an abomination before God the Lord in Holy Scripture and earnestly forbidden by all laws: Therefore, we intend not to tolerate any sorcerers, fortune-tellers, devil-conjurers, blessers, and other such idolaters in our Electorate: but rather to strictly banish the same from our lands, so far as they will not desist from such ungodly ways, or in certain cases to punish them in body and life. We also will that such devilish fortune-telling, whereby perhaps innocent people are wickedly slandered and brought into harmful suspicion, shall not be believed, and based upon it in law

<column-break/>

nothing shall be adjudicated: but rather it shall be held as shameless lies. And our subjects, who until now out of curiosity or superstition have run to such fortune-tellers, sorcerers, and blessers within or outside our territory, shall henceforth entirely abstain from the same. In the event, however, that one or more are found disobedient in this, that person or persons, male or female, shall be earnestly punished with the tower <note>imprisonment</note> or otherwise, according to the occasion of their transgression and their person.

So far the Palatine decree.

That is framed leniently and modestly: if they desist from the practice, they are to be forgiven and spared. Against this equity, a jurist has recently written quite to the contrary, saying that witches should not be spared, even if they do penance. He proves it thus: At <term>Ut.</term> <note>likely Utrecht</note> someone ate meat on a Friday: he, like a heretic, had forfeited his life. He did penance, yet had to die nonetheless: though the mercy was shown to him that he was executed with the sword and not with fire. Is that not a clever argument and a strong proof? "Fit like a peasant's shoe" <note>a sarcastic proverb meaning the logic is clumsy or forced</note>. Woe to us heretics (for which he holds us), woe to you witches, if he were able to use sword and fire against us and you, whom he considers equal. Likewise, the aforementioned decree says: those who run to fortune-tellers shall be punished with the tower, not killed, regardless of the fact that Moses commands it. For because this is such a high, difficult, and doubtful matter, one does right, and without danger, by following mercy more than hardness and severity.

A fine, humane saying and rule is this: that it is better to acquit ten guilty people than to condemn one innocent person.

Therefore, you Lords, moderate what is excessive in this judgment and punishment, and amend what is done unjustly therein: just as some of you now never so hastily and easily let the thieves...

Ensure that they are dealt with fairly and leniently, seeking their improvement and restoration rather than their destruction. Then, certainly, fewer witches will appear in your lands and territories; conversely, the more you kill, the more there will be.

Experience shows this to be true, and the reason is easy to understand when one considers the nature of the Devil. The highly esteemed and world-famous jurist Mr. Andreas Alciatus of Milan <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550), a famous Italian legal scholar who argued that "witches" were often just mentally ill.</note>, who lived forty years ago, writes that an inquisitor and witch-burner in a diocese in the Italian mountains burned over a hundred witches, and the more he burned, the more there were. Finally, the peasants took up arms and forced the witch-burner to stop, leaving the Bishop to be the master and judge in the matter. The Bishop sought advice from Alciatus, who advised him to go slowly, for these were people with deranged minds who should more rightly be taken to a doctor than to the fire. Because of such lenient advice, the aforementioned aggressive jurist <note>Likely referring to a critic of Alciatus, such as Jean Bodin or similar proponents of the witch trials.</note> scolds him as a friend and defender of witches, as if he alone had understanding and everyone else had goose-heads.

I heard from a fine, sensible fellow, a man from Luxembourg whose father had been a mayor or official there: that another mayor, his neighbor, complained to him that he did not know what to do, as he could not stop the witches in his care; the more he burned, the more there were. This man gave him the advice that he should stop the burning to see if that might help. He obeyed him, and it so happened that the sorcery decreased and vanished over time. For when the Devil saw that he could no longer bring about murder with his cunning and deceit, he let it be, leaving the poor women in peace and quiet.

It also serves to prevent this evil if husbands love their wives and are not too harsh with them, lest they fall into resentment and melancholy, thinking: "The Devil led me to this block of wood <note>A derogatory term for a harsh or unresponsive husband.</note>, may he lead me away from him again." In such thoughts and minds, the Devil soon builds his nest and takes his seat, like a louse in a scab. Likewise, parents should not be too bitter or rough toward their children, nor stretch the bow too tight, but allow them timely, honest pleasure and joy: marry off their daughters in good time, and keep a good eye on them so they do not go idle, since idleness is a pillow upon which the Devil rests softly and gladly; and keep them from evil company. He who touches pitch defiles himself with it. If such foresight, diligence, and earnestness were applied by the authorities and subjects, both in general and in particular, to drive out, resist, and prevent this monster, it is to be hoped and certainly expected that it would decrease and fall into decline. May God help with this.

**Blessing** and **conjuring** <note>The German "Segnen und beschweren" refers to the use of folk magic, charms, and superstitious incantations to heal or protect.</note> is the undertaking to increase, decrease, or even take away the power of creatures through words, gestures, or strange figures, and to give them another power against their nature and properties, contrary to God's will and order. In the Creation, God assigned to every thing its own power and effect, in which it should remain and by which He sustains it. Or, if he does accomplish something and brings it about, the evil spirit does it through deceit and only in appearance, for the seduction and ruin of man. # Augustin Lercheimer

other figures possess such power in themselves to change, improve, or diminish creatures. One group understands this out of ignorance, not realizing that it is not a righteous process, but that Satan is present and working through it. The priesthood under the Papacy was full of this abuse, superstition, and devilish work, and consequently, it was in vogue among the common man; much of it still remains among us Evangelicals <note>Protestants/Lutherans</note>. What was the most prominent part of the Mass other than a magical blessing? There the priest spoke the five words or eight syllables, *Hoc est enim corpus meum* <note>original: "This is my body"</note>, over the bread, breathed upon it, made three crosses over it with his chin, and believed that the bread thereby became the body of Christ. In the same way, he transforms the wine in the chalice into the blood of Christ, even though such power is not given to words and syllables. They conjured the Holy Spirit into baptismal water, holy water, salt, oil, wax, herbs, stones, wood, and the very ground when they consecrated churches, altars, and graveyards. They blessed cakes, meat, eggs, *etc.* On Easter Eve, they even consecrated the fire so that it would do no harm; yet I have, alas, experienced our village burning to the ground just five days later. The nature of fire is and remains such that if it is neglected, it causes a conflagration. They baptized and sanctified bells, giving them the power to drive away evil spirits with their sound, to still storms, and to prevent them from doing harm as far as the sound could be heard. Oh yes, indeed—I saw it myself in our little church: the thunder struck the bell-ringer while he was ringing; he lay dead, still holding the rope in his hand. Who can recount all the jugglery and deceit they practiced? If a peasant woman had a sick cow, the pastor came with his surplice or choir robe and breviary, went into the stable, read over the cow, sprinkled her with holy water, made crosses over her, and gave her consecrated salt. Whether she recovered because of it, I do not know.

<column-break/>

Among the common people, there was no end to such superstition and abuse. If someone’s nose bled too much, or if one was wounded, they stilled the blood with "holy words" about the piercing and blood-flow of our Lord on the cross. If someone had some other injury on their body, an old woman would take a "cross-penny" <note>a coin marked with a cross</note> or a gulden, rub the injury with it, and mumble certain words; this was then thought to help. A noblewoman, not unknown to me, had a ring made for her husband in which these words from the Evangelist were engraved on the inside: *Os non comminuetis ex eo* <note>original: "You shall not break a bone of him" (Exodus 12:46/John 19:36)</note>. The ring protected her husband so that he never broke a bone, even though he often fell dangerously from his horse. If someone wore the beginning of St. John’s Gospel written around their neck, no evil spirit could harm them; they were free from the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, storms, thunderclaps, and other evils. Poor people hung a little piece of bread in a cloth around their children's necks, as they still do among us.

Other "blessers" and conjurers can enchant swords and weapons so that they do not cut, stab, or otherwise wound, as is their nature and property. They can dance on sword-edges with bare feet without injury; they hex the bows and rifles of others so that they miss, and bless their own so that they hit—of which I have spoken before. Jo. St. <note>likely Johannes Stabius or a similar contemporary figure</note>, a priest and famous astronomer, had a blessed herb; if he held it against a lock, it would open, even though God did not make it grow for that purpose, nor did it have such power from a blessing. The Devil was involved, who pulled the locks open. Some can, through conjuration, lure mice and rats out of houses so that they follow them in heaps, like piglets following a sow. they lead them out into the water and drown them. But whether these are real mice or a phantom, those who hire such fellows may experience and know for themselves whether they notice fewer mice in their houses afterward. ->Report or confession of several witches who were recently burned at N.<-

The first, a poor widow, had gone into the forest nine years ago to gather wood. There the evil spirit came to her in the form of a forester. He asked why she was so sad, and if her husband had died. She answered, "Yes." He said: "If you will take me and obey me, I will give you enough money." He persuaded her with many words until she consented; she renounced God and committed herself to him, the Devil. After this, he lay with her. Four weeks later, the lover returned to her and handed her a broom, upon which she rode with him to a nearby heath to dance. There were ten other women there, only two of whom she knew; one of them paid the musician his fee. There they agreed to destroy the acorns, but it did not succeed. She bewitched a neighbor's horse to death with the help of her lover because his wife would not lend or sell her a measure of lentils. And another time, she stroked another neighbor's horse over the back with her hand in the name of all the devils, after which it died not long after, because he would not sell her a measure of barley. She had relations with her lover only twice.

The second had lost a cow twelve years ago. As she was searching for it, sad and distressed, she met a man in black clothing; she took him for a citizen of N. He addressed her: "Koni, <note>A diminutive or nickname for Kunigunde</note> be my lover; I will show you your cow and teach you an art so that the cow always comes home by itself." She answered: "God forbid me

from that." Thereupon he vanished immediately. As she was returning home, he met her again and persisted as before. She refused. The following day, the cow was lost again. While she was searching for it, the guest found her again and gave her such good words and promised her so much that she finally complied with him, denied God, and pledged herself to him. She let him lie with her, from which she perceived that he was a devil. He gave her money in her lap; when she poured it out at home, it was moss. She regretted that she had involved herself so with the Devil. Once, in her husband's absence, her lover led her on a small brown horse into the forest to the heath to dance, where twelve other women were present, who collectively decided they wanted to destroy the hazelnuts and acorns. To a dog that had done her harm, she gave bread to eat with a black salve prepared by her lover, from which it died. Once, she went with another woman, a witch, to another village to the baths; there they saw several lords <note>or "masters"</note> dancing in the field by the road. As they stood and watched, both of their lovers came and led them there so that they also danced. When the dance was over, they made a hailstorm to destroy the grain and grapes, but it passed without damage and fell into a forest. In the year [15]76 at the dance, she, along with others of whom she knew only three, contributed to the destruction of the grain and the damaging of the grapes through frost and mildew. The beadle <note>a minor church or law official</note> had mocked her several times, for which she bewitched one of his cows to death; for another, a yearling calf, because he had struck her son; for another, two sheep, because he was the cause of her husband having to pay two guilders as a fine. <margin>Consideration of these confessions of the five witches.</margin>

I wish to briefly examine, consider, and weigh these witch reports or confessions, not to oppose or insult anyone: but as an example and a mirror, in which one may see to some extent what kind of thing this witchcraft is, what people and for what reasons they commit themselves to it: and for the proof and strengthening of my above-written report on this matter. I know well that it is futile and unjust to master and criticize things that have already happened and cannot be changed, but rather that one should speak the best of them. For it is too late, and advice after the deed is done. These women are dead, just as many thousands have been killed and are still killed daily. However, one should judge and arrange future things by the repetition and consideration of past things, so that what was failed in those may be improved in these. With this intention, and no other, have I undertaken to weigh these reports.

All together, these five women fell into the Devil's snare out of sadness, melancholy, and despair: not out of lust, wantonness, or curiosity. They were poor, troubled women; two miserable widows who were stuck in want and sorrow with their children. The first, while she gathered wood in the forest in worry and gloom to carry home on her head, was tempted by the evil spirit: who could easily win and take over such a troubled woman's heart with his swift rhetoric: whose thoughts, wishes, and sighs were directed and went solely toward how and from where she might be helped. Should such a cunning, crafty villain not persuade and move such a person with flattery and threats to join him, especially one who knows little or nothing of God and His promises, of faith, and trust in Him? The same holds true with the other widow, who in the evening, when she had laid her poor orphans to sleep, thought and worried about what they would eat tomorrow: she knew no way out: then the Devil approached, finding there a mind and heart that was convenient and ready for him. The second woman goes about seeking her cow with fear and gloom, of which she perhaps had no more than the one: and so that he, the Devil, might keep her in gloom until he had taken her over, he caused her to lose the cow again the next day and have to search for it with pain. The third woman is ill-tempered and sad that her husband had gambled away their supply of money. There Satan also had a desired game: he promises to give her back what she had lost and more besides. Thus he brings her to himself. The fourth, Catharina, had a violent, angry, vengeful mind; she should have been a soldier. It rightly caused her pain that she was so lied to and slandered by the other woman, but the anger and fury were too great and beyond measure. Therefore the villain also joined himself to her, offered her his service, and holds her as he wishes.

Since these unhappy women were driven to such misfortune through poverty, misery, loss, and other adversity, over which their senses were troubled and displaced—as the physicians and other naturalists <note>original: "naturkündiger" - early scientists or natural philosophers</note> judge of them—and since they had little report or knowledge of God's word, of faith and prayer, or of the Devil's cunning and malice, through their own and their protectors' neglect and negligence, as can be judged from their speech—they only name their Creator, and know as much of our Lord and Savior Christ as a Jew or a Turk <note>A common 16th-century idiom meaning "very little" or "nothing at all" regarding Christian doctrine</note>: so it should be considered and taken to heart whether one might not proceed somewhat more graciously, fairly, and mildly with such people. For indeed, in all matters, the circumstances are the most important thing, which must be looked upon, according to which one must judge and the verdict...
