# The Second Part.
### Which treats of the marks and testimonies by which witches are recognized and convicted.

<margin>Natural signs.</margin> Signs or testimonies are of two kinds according to the Doctors of Medicine <note>original: "Artzney Doctorn"</note>: namely, those that designate and those that distinguish the things of which they are signs. Through the former, the nature, power, and deeds of the sorcerers are recognized; through the latter, however, they are distinguished from certain other almost similar evildoers. Although in our time few witches are found who do not have manifold misdeeds about them and are found guilty, as is evident from the first part.

Thus (I say) the true characteristics of witches are taken from their nature, peculiar deeds, and works: such as that they allow themselves to be so far seduced by the Devil that they deny and blaspheme God, surrender themselves to the Devil, and commit many great, unspeakable sins. Therefore, whatever form these take, it is certain that they are guilty of witchcraft.

<margin>Civil signs.</margin> But when they are not known through the aforementioned signs and yet are nonetheless suspected, one must also use other signs by which they can be recognized and convicted, which are then required and taken in a political <note>meaning "civil" or "legal"</note> manner, both by the accusers and the judges. And such signs are not of one kind, but are taken either from their own confession, or from the testimony of other people, or from common outcry <note>public rumor</note>, or from their own and public deeds, or from painful tortures <note>term: "peinlichen tormenten" refers to judicial torture used to extract confessions</note>, or finally from certain experiments and special experiences. But because there are various opinions regarding this, I will briefly say something about each one—not that I wish to prescribe anything to the secular courts (to whom such things properly belong) as if I were a legislator, but that I might, as is customary in difficult matters, also indicate my good opinion in general. For the opinion of the warlord introduced by Homer has always pleased me, who said that in pressing necessity no man's counsel is to be rejected. Likewise the saying of the venerable old Hippocrates, who says: That it is not at all improper, when a particular necessity is at hand, to also request the help and counsel of other people; for in such times even the understanding often do not think of many things that another might perhaps soon find.

<margin>On medical precepts.</margin> <note>Latin: "De præc. medicis."</note>

<margin>Own confession.</margin> As for what first concerns the own and voluntary confession, these are indeed very powerful in all courts, without which a penal sentence is not easily passed. But one must nevertheless diligently consider how the same was created, and whether it was enticed through cunning or extorted through threats. Likewise, what kind of people made the confession: whether they perhaps failed the truth out of error or out of madness. For it is hardly to be believed, and is very rarely heard, that those who are accused unto death, and yet have hope that their deed may remain hidden, would—so long as they are not senseless or otherwise misunderstood—willingly want to report their misdeed themselves. How then: could the witches perhaps be mistaken in their deeds? Perhaps it may be that they sometimes err, namely when they are so harshly possessed and detained by Satan (for they themselves are often most of all bewitched by Satan) that they do not know or consider what they prattle. Likewise, should they perhaps at times be as if mad and misunderstood? Truly, such is also easily to be believed of some of them, that it happens to them as if they were so deranged and weakened in their senses, or lurked upon by Satan in deep sleep, that they babble quite loathsome and false things themselves, which one should not easily believe or trust. Just as one perceives in those blinded by jugglery <note>or "illusion"</note>, who cannot judge rightly from what they see, what they otherwise boast that they have seen. But I have said (at times) that they are not all nor at all times misunderstood. For some of them also keep house and servants, raise children, farm...

<margin>From the Digest, on the rules of law: "That which happens rarely."</margin> <note>Latin: "ff. de reg. Iur. L. vt quæ raro." A legal citation referring to the rarity of certain events.</note>

<margin>Cardanus, on the variety of things, book 15, chapter 80.</margin> <note>Latin: "Cardan. de variet. re. 15. cap. 80." Reference to Girolamo Cardano, a famous polymath.</note>

<margin>Testimony of other people and common rumor.</margin>
Related to the signs just mentioned are the testimony of other people and common rumor. These provide very uncertain information, and therefore little trust should be placed in them. The former [testimony], however, cannot be boldly rejected, provided it is provided by sufficiently qualified persons; but how this should be done, one must consult those learned in the law. A wise man says that one should learn to mistrust—that is, not to believe everyone—just as the Poet says:

<margin>Exodus 20, Matthew 18.</margin>
> You should not quickly place
> Your trust and confidence in everyone.

And Ignatius says that he who believes quickly is light-minded of heart.

How can it then be just, and not against God, as the aforementioned writer relates and seems to praise, that solely upon the testimony of three witches (who were also punished with death for it), three others were immediately accused, arrested, and tested with the uncertain water ordeal <note>The "water test" or swimming test involved binding a suspect and throwing them into water; floating was seen as proof of witchcraft, as the "pure" element of water supposedly rejected the guilty.</note> in the presence of many thousands of people in a prominent city, and publicly defamed? Should the testimony of such women, burdened with great vices, carry so much weight in capital cases that such great shame and misery (which honor-loving women would rather suffer death than endure) might rightfully be imposed on previously unsuspected persons? Yes, I say, [to rely] on the testimony of such witches, who are regarded by the mentioned writer himself as half-demonic because of an assumed demonic substance and an altered internal human form and shape (for if he meant the external, it would be a certain indication that he himself were robbed of his internal [reason]—

<column-break/>

But who would give the slightest credit to those mad and insane or raging hags, or to these lies and spirits of the morning <note>original: "Morgeistern," likely a reference to deceptive spirits or "lying spirits" from the beginning/morning of time.</note>? Legal scholars do not boldly allow all kinds of people to give testimony, especially in criminal matters, and expressly exclude those who are infamous or are enemies. But who is more shamefully infamous than witches? Who is a greater enemy to the human race than Satan, whose substance the witches essentially partake in, according to that writer's opinion? Therefore, it is not fitting to accept the testimony of these evil creatures who seek nothing but the ruin of mankind. And as to how dangerous it is to believe such things, although I could demonstrate this with many arguments and examples, I will nevertheless, for the sake of brevity, relate only a single one here, which occurred a few years ago in Verden, where at that time the brave Claus von Eppen was the commander. He held two women in custody on account of witchcraft, of which they were accused by another piece-of-a-woman <note>A derogatory term for the accuser.</note>. But after the accused were punished with fire <note>Burned at the stake.</note> according to the form of the customary laws, the accuser also fell under the suspicion of the magistrate and was immediately arrested and painfully interrogated. She then confessed that she herself was guilty and the two who were burned had been innocent; for which reason she was also rightfully punished by death.

### Doctor Johann Ewich.

necessities and according to the described laws, they must nevertheless be applied and used with great caution, so that through overly sharp and immoderate pain, life itself—along with the confession—is not pressed and forced out of the accused (as I know of some to whom this happened, to the no small shame of both the judge and the executioner). For there are some of such delicate complexion <note>original: "zarter complexion"; referring to a person's physical and mental temperament</note> that they cannot endure even the least torture and would much rather confess everything they are asked than suffer the inhuman and cruel torture for long. On the other hand, there are others who endure all kinds of pain before they will confess anything, even though they well know that their deed is public knowledge and their own conscience convicts them. What then can one achieve with these instruments <note>referring to torture devices</note> among such people to certainly learn the truth of the guilt? Therefore, it seems much more advisable to follow the law of Labeo, the ancient legal scholar, and not use such torments until one is already certainly informed of the principal deed. This should not be demanded through painful questioning, but should be known beforehand through other means, and the torments used afterward only to learn the circumstances, not the main facts. For those experienced in the law know that in criminal matters, the evidence ought to be clearer than the sun at midday, which kind of evidence truly cannot be obtained from the accused through torment and torture. Those who sit in judgment should rightly consider this, so that they do not become guilty themselves before God, who is a punisher of all injustice and all tyrannical processes, and who says that judgment is His, and threatens that He will demand the blood of the innocent from the hands of the judges.

# Of Witches

<margin>Soothsayers and exorcists.</margin>
In some places, people use soothsayers and exorcists, or "devil-banners" <note>original: "Teuffels banner" — those who claim to drive out spirits</note> (perhaps because they wish to drive out the devil through Beelzebub) to recognize witches. These men are not very different from the witches themselves and are commonly church servants or "spiritual people," as they are called, who are believed to be able to point out both the sorceresses and the bewitched as if with their fingers. You ask, in what manner? With some, it is through a special little prayer or held ceremonies; if someone, they say, comes into the house carrying a sack or something similar and desires something, "Look, that is the one! Seize her, hold her fast, and strike her bravely." These soothsayers also sometimes show the witches or other evildoers in a mirror. But no wise man can praise such things. For this image and likeness flows neither from natural nor human ways, nor through the working of the Holy Spirit, but from the agility of the much-experienced Satan, who has always been such a clever Doctor and forever suggests, boasts of, imagines, and forces this vain and deceitful art upon mankind.

Likewise elsewhere, when they wish to interrogate witches under torture <note>original: "peinlich wollen verhören" — specifically referring to judicial torture</note>, they shave the hair from all parts of their bodies, as if their art resided in it—just as Samson’s strength resided in his hair—and as if this smoothness, provided the torments are added to it, were an excellent sign for recognizing witches. But they have also learned this experience and "testing-art" from the executioners <note>original: "nachrichtern"</note>, who are commonly disregarded people and in whom little trust is to be placed in this matter, since they seek their advantage from the shedding of human blood (oh, what wretched gain!).

<margin>Marks, or brown spots imprinted upon the witches.</margin>
These same men (as I am informed by credible people) also say that they can notice certain marks or brands which Satan has imprinted on the witches, and thereby recognize the guilty. But they report that no one but they—namely the executioners <note>original: "scharpffrichter"</note>—can distinguish these signs. Oh, what thick, fat, shameless lies! For while it is possible that they speak of marks, it is nonetheless untrue that the hangmen alone should see them. Our ancestors held that the Chrism <note>term: Chrism — the consecrated oil used in baptism</note>, which is usually smeared on children's foreheads at baptism, was scratched out by Satan, thus leaving a wound-mark behind. But since in our time the Chrism has mostly fallen out of use in the churches, the rogue Satan and his frivolous disciples, Master Hans <note>note: "Meister Hans" was a common euphemism for the executioner</note>, etc., would gladly persuade us that the mentioned signs should be hidden behind the ears. But tell me, if they are true spots, how does it happen that other people cannot see them too? It would have to be that our eyes alone were blinded, and not the executioners'. If they are not true signs, then certainly the hangmen themselves must be more deluded and blinded by Satan than others. From this, it is to be concluded that these things must also be vain deceit and false signs, to which no room should be given in well-ordered courts: however much some protest that they have perceived them to be true. For it is to be feared that these are more false imaginations than certain experiences, which they have adopted out of ignorance and therefore useless wonder at the things they think they have seen.

<column-break/>

Finally, another sign was invented some years ago and has now come into use by almost everyone for recognizing witches: namely, that one binds their hands and feet crosswise together and thereafter throws them three times (note the mystery!) into the water. This they call the "water-test" <note>term: Wasserprob — the ordeal of water</note> or "purification through water," perhaps because they wish to purify and justify or absolve the innocent with it. For when those who are suspected sink, they are held to be innocent; but if they do not sink, but remain on top of the water, then they are [guilty]... <note>The sentence breaks off here; the catchword "schül-" indicates the next page begins with "schuldig" (guilty).</note>

# Doctor Johann Ewich.

...held guilty. This is truly a superstitious invention, and I know not whether it comes from those same masters previously mentioned—namely, Satan and his gullible pupils, the executioners—and has been offered and promised to the authorities in several cities and lands as something consistent with nature and reason, and has thus been accepted and paid homage to by them. I would, however, dearly like to know whether those who sink are immediately held to be innocent or not: for if they are not deemed innocent, it follows that those who use this trial do not hold it to be true. Likewise, I would like to know whether they consider those who do not sink to be certainly and firmly guilty. For if they do not believe that, they prove once again by their actions that they themselves hold their experiment and trial to be uncertain. That they do not immediately and certainly hold those who do not sink to be guilty is sufficiently testified by the fact that they also require many more signs for this, and as they themselves admit, they dare not condemn or punish anyone based on this sign alone. What then is this unusual work and tomfoolery <note>original: "Alfangerey," meaning nonsense or trickery</note> other than a tempting of God, or a devilish mockery, and the beginning of a sorrowful and wicked tragedy? Regarding this, an executioner <note>original: "Schärger"</note> said laughingly and mocking these "masters of the trial" that they follow the way of the cooks. For just as cooks first clean with water the capons they prepare for a meal and afterwards roast them, so do these men also prepare for Moloch <note>A biblical figure associated with child sacrifice by fire; here used to symbolize the burning of victims.</note> his dishes and burnt offerings. Hey, hey, dear Christians, what are you doing?

<margin>

</margin>

It can happen (says the oft-cited writer) that a spiritual lightness is poured into the witches by Satan, who has taken over and possessed them, making them much lighter than they were before (though we do not perceive such a thing), so that they cannot sink to the bottom. Or perhaps Satan—who is essentially poured out through their entire substance and through every part and limb of their entire substance—draws the witches upward or to himself because of the similarity of spirit (for Satan’s nature is spiritual, light, airy, and easily travels through all places of the lower heavens), and thus holds them up in the water, etc. Truly, this is a pretty fable, if it were not at the same time dangerous and godless. It seems, however, that those who judge the matter in such a way are perhaps deceived by thoughts of the magnet, or of amber <note>original: "Agstein"</note>, or perhaps of the kidneys and bladder. For just as steel and down are attracted by the former, and bile and urine by the latter, so they perhaps think it happens between Satan and the witches. But let us leave the joking aside and answer the matter in earnest.

# On Witches

<margin>
Augustine, *On the City of God*, Book 2, Chapter 44. <note>Original: "August. de cret. sciendum. 2. 44." The author cites St. Augustine to lend authority to the argument against superstitious fables.</note>
</margin>
...that such things are an old-wives' and ungodly fiction. Regarding Satan, however—that he is a spirit, indeed a nimble, swift, and powerful spirit—no one can deny. That he is also capable of much and performs much within witches, as the greatest and foremost of unbelievers, can also be denied by no one. Yet, nevertheless, he does not have the power to create geese or other water-fowl out of human beings, nor can he make that which is naturally heavy to be light, except through arts also known to men, namely through boiling, grinding, distilling, etc. In what manner he knows how to prepare those old, aged crones—though they remain living creatures—I do not regard. Or, if he can do that, why do they not also cast themselves down from the heights so that they might soar in the air like the birds of heaven? For the one would be as easy for witches as the other, if they truly received spiritual lightness through the art of Satan. If they thought, however, that such a thing might perhaps be dangerous for the innocent, they could surely bind them in such a way that they do not touch the earth, and thus do not injure themselves. Just as is the custom among the Italians <note>Original: "Welschen," a historical term for Romance-language speakers, particularly Italians.</note> that they give those whom they wish to punish for some minor misdeed a *strappado* <term>strappado: a form of torture where the victim's hands are tied behind their back and they are hoisted up by a rope</term> (as they call it). But this is no less shameful than if another were to say that witches do not sink in water because the baptismal water, previously used for the salvation of their souls, had been desecrated in them; and therefore, common water could no longer serve them for the necessity and rescue of the body. See what superstition does not imagine for itself! Therefore, this is altogether a vain fantasy and a devilish mockery, which should rightly not be suffered in Christian courthouses, regardless of whatever other outcomes—upon which only the unwise gaze—might follow from it.

How does it happen then, someone asks, that witches nevertheless do not sink in water? Doubtless it is thus: that Satan places his hands beneath them and holds them up by force so that they cannot sink. For since

<column-break/>

he is a spirit, he can do many things quickly and easily for which bodily creatures are unfit. For if in living animals the power of the spirits <note>Original: "facultas spiritus animalis" — the "animal spirits" thought in medieval medicine to move the limbs.</note>, although still greatly burdened and hindered by the body, is nonetheless most powerful, then truly the spirit—namely Satan—is much greater and stronger, since he is devoid of such bodily heaviness. For what else is it but their spirit or soul that can move the powerful, great sea-monsters called whales so readily? What power drives the heavy-bodied elephants forward so quickly that they surpass many other much lighter animals, more suited for running, in speed, if not that which is most subtle and agile within them, namely their spirit? Indeed, even the wind, which is a vapor of the earth or the water and akin to spirit, travels so powerfully over water and land that it can move entire houses, castles, towers, cities, cliffs, mountains, and the whole sea, tearing through valleys and overturning things from their foundations.

<margin>
Power of the spirits.
</margin>

Since this is then so (as has been said), the airy—or to put it better—the hellish spirit Satan, formerly called Lucifer, and thereafter a Father of Darkness because of his pride and the abuse of the powers given to him by God, can accomplish much more (I say) when God permits him. But God often and frequently permits him to use his freedom and power, just as He also allows certain tyrants and wild beasts and lets go of the bridle so that they may plague us—namely, according to His hidden yet always righteous counsel, because we have deserved it, or so that He may incite us to repentance and increase the faith within us, or so that He may make His glory greater through victory over His enemies and demonstrate to the churches His providence, His faithfulness, and His special grace and goodness. But when He does not do such things according to His hidden wisdom (for He is, as the Prophet says, wonderful in His counsel and mighty in His deed), but rather...

# Doctor Johann Ewich.

but rather looks through his fingers at Satan’s plots <note>original: "sicht... durch die Finger," an idiom meaning to turn a blind eye or connive</note> (so that everyone may well understand how I return to our subject), how easy it is for Satan to lead his cunning ones, the witches, through the air, water, stone, and fire, and to prevent them from falling, or sinking in the water, or being harmed in other ways, as long as he thinks it advisable. Therefore, it is unnecessary to invent new and unheard-of wondrous talk and miracles (for which some have all too great a desire) and to present them to gullible people or uninformed authorities as if these things were in accordance with natural truth (they should rightly say supernatural, since they speak of the spiritual kinship of Satan with the witches), and to put them up for sale, as it were, so that they may seem to know all things and appear quite clever and subtle. For since the same has happened to many others who are not witches—indeed, even to the God-fearing, and even to Christ himself—that they were thus led here and there by Satan, and brought quickly from one place to another, and that without any change or disruption of their internal form and essence, what wonder is it that such things also happen to witches?

<margin>Matthew 4.</margin>
<margin>Daniel 14.</margin>

Since this is now the case, in the manner we have described, it is much more reasonable to believe that nothing essential is changed in the body of the witch, but rather it happens through the power of Satan, who is a swift and mighty spirit, that the witches float on top of the water or travel through the air, etc. And since (as was said) such things can happen to others, both the guilty and the innocent, it is wrong to place faith in that uncertain, dishonest, and supernatural experiment or experience which those people call "unnatural" (which indeed) can have no natural cause, because it goes beyond the limits of

<column-break/>

nature—unless two contrary things could be true at the same time. One should not wish to believe it and surrender oneself more and more to Satan’s mockery, for truly it is a work of mockery by Satan (the water test, I say). For those who thus dispute and conclude: "these stay on top of the water, therefore their internal form and essence have departed from them, and they are witches"—these same people are mistaken and fall into the deceptive trap which the <term>Dialecticians</term> <note>Scholars of logic and formal argument</note> call *non causam ut causam* <note>Latin: treating a non-cause as a cause</note>, which brings great shame and contempt upon the learned and those who are ambitious for the sake of their teaching.

This <term>consequence</term> <note>logical deduction</note> and conclusion is also worthless when one says: "this custom was invented through human good judgment, therefore it did not begin without a certain cause." For in that way, one could easily defend all kinds of error, all superstition, and all heresy that float within the Church.

<margin>Digest on the Rules of Law: L. quod initio & L. quod contrat.</margin>

Also, it is not enough to say, as Plato once said, that one should believe the words of the ancestors even if they provide no reason for them. For such a thing is also dangerous, and Plato himself was not always of that same opinion, but taught much differently at other times: namely, that one should hear the reason together with the authority or prestige of the person, so that the teaching is not deemed deficient and powerless. For that one should believe bare words—that cannot be accepted from any other human speech, except only from those whom we know spoke from the Spirit of God; thus we Christians recognize and hold only Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles.

<margin>Galen in his commentary on the nature of man, in the preface.</margin>

Likewise, it is not at all to be praised when someone says: "if the cause is not certain, it may nonetheless be provable, and human reason may certainly trust it." For in our matters, wherein life and death are dealt with, one can rightly never be too cautious, and especially the authorities, who must pronounce the sentence

# On Witches

...and to impose the appropriate punishment for the misdeed, one should not be satisfied with all sorts of arguments, nor indeed with all sorts of customs, so that they hurry to the execution. For in criminal matters, the laws demand entirely certain and clear evidence. For <margin>Custom. 38. ff. on laws. <note>A reference to the Digest of Justinian (Corpus Juris Civilis), specifically the section on legal customs.</note></margin> custom, when it is evil, is called an ancient error and tyranny. A good custom, however, and one that is laudable, has its beginning in truth, equity, and justice; its foundation and ground are taken from Holy Scripture, philosophy, and from the law. Everything that cannot be clearly proven by one of these three should rightly be considered void or godless. I do not say, however, that it must be contained and expressed in those very words (for we do not conclude so foolishly as to say: "the water ordeal of witches is not explicitly taught and commanded in Holy Scripture, therefore it is to be rejected"), but rather that it should and must be derived and proven from the basis of the aforementioned teachings; that is what we mean and nothing else. The doctrine of the Church (says Theodoretus <note>Theodoret of Cyrus, a 5th-century influential theologian and bishop.</note>) should not only be provable, but also firm and true. Since, then, the wondrous and abominable "Water-Baptism" of witches does not have such a certain and firm ground and demonstration—indeed, it is contrary to the same and amounts to a tempting of Divine Omnipotence (as Pope Lucius III <margin>Decree. chapter ext. on canonical purgation. <note>Referring to a papal decree by Lucius III (r. 1181–1185) condemning trial by ordeal.</note></margin> himself confesses)—one need not doubt that it was devised and introduced by the Teacher Satan or by his followers, such as executioners, torturers, godless idolaters, false Christians, sophisticated and unholy philosophers, witless soothsayers, and the like. All of these together, as far as this point is concerned, are servants and "baptizers" of Satan; for through this water ordeal—just as through a new baptism—they take those who were previously held to be Christians and incorporated into Christ through the Sacrament of the Church, and now, in the presence of many people, they assign and incorporate them into Satan (as much as lies in their power), just as the Molochites <note>Followers of the biblical deity Moloch, associated with child sacrifice by fire.</note> did in ancient times with their children through fire. This certainly cannot happen without great godlessness. Therefore, we should not deal with or trust in such experiments and superstitious practices or customs, but should seek much more certain and stable grounds if we wish to convict and punish witches: namely, those which consist in the actual, specific, and consistent self-confession of the witch; likewise from their <margin>Note: Rightful testimony against witches.</margin> conduct and works, which are known and possible to Nature; and finally, from their religion and confession of faith, properly brought forth and introduced.

And so let this be the end of the second part: in which, if perhaps someone wished to interpret it poorly—that I, as in the previous parts, have cited the abuses and lies with more words than I have used to confirm the truth—he should know that the truth is also taught and confirmed when errors are pointed out and abolished. For the truth is simple and requires no long speech; indeed (as Aeschylus says), three words are enough for the truth. But on the other hand, as Tertullian says, untruth and lies are manifold and must be either confirmed or refuted with many words; for evil, to which errors and lies belong, is infinite according to Aristotle's opinion. <margin>Galatians 5. <note>Likely a reference to the "works of the flesh" vs. the "fruit of the Spirit."</note></margin>

<column-break/>

### Maxims and Rules of the Second Part.

The sin of witches is not simple, but is mixed from many misdeeds.

In difficult and obscure matters, it is not improper to request the help of other people and to hear their advice.

Voluntary and self-originated confessions, provided that error or deception does not interfere, are very powerful.

# Doctor Johann Ewich.

Some witches are at times merely insane and melancholic <note>melancholy was then considered a physical ailment of the "black bile" that caused delusions</note>. Indeed, they themselves are severely enchanted by Satan.

Common rumor or gossip does not provide certain knowledge.

Neither torture nor the accusations of the ungodly provide sufficient testimony.

Satan is generally a liar and always an enemy of mankind; therefore, he is an unfit witness, as are his servants and followers, the witches.

The use of torture and painful interrogation <term>peinliche Fragen: judicial torture used to extract confessions</term> should only be undertaken once the primary guilt is already known.

The dungeon or prison should be a place of custody, not a punishment in itself.

The experiments and experiences <note>referring to folk-magic tests</note> that are now commonly used are dangerous and deceptive in the matter of witches.

The examination or water ordeal <note>the "swimming test" where an accused person was thrown into water to see if they floated</note> is a mockery of Satan and has no foundation in truth.

Satan is a powerful and clever spirit.

The spirit is the strongest and most powerful part in all creatures.

God occasionally lets loose the reins of his and our enemies for certain reasons: namely, to test and exercise our faith, or to demonstrate his strength to the enemies and to make his glory magnificent. Likewise, to show his goodness to the believers and to ratify and strengthen his promise to them.

Bad custom is a tyranny and an ancient error; conversely, good custom is similar to and in harmony with justice and integrity.

### The Third Part,
### Concerning the Punishment of Witches.

Now there remains the third part, in which to deal with the chastisement and punishment of witches, and to consider how one should proceed therein according to law and equity. And here I must once again ask all sensible people, but especially the legal scholars and the authorities, that they will not think ill of me that I, a physician <term>Medicus: a medical doctor</term>, should pass judgment on those things which

<column-break/>

properly belong and pertain not to me, but to them as the priests of justice and sword-bearers against the unjust. Which I (indeed) gladly acknowledge and concede. But since physicians are nevertheless commanded to promote and preserve the health and wellness of the body, when innocence is defended and unjust punishment and torture are advised against, then the welfare of the body is also promoted in that act. I ask, therefore, that I be heard, for I desire not that sin or guilt be shielded, but that justice be protected and the truth be upheld.

Firstly, as to whether witches should be punished as guilty parties and evildoers: on this, I believe, no one will doubt much, provided he believes that it is an exceedingly great sin to turn from God to Satan and to incite others to similar godlessness. But as was said before from Hippocrates <note>original: "ex Hippocrate"</note> that "experiment is perilous," so it may with more equity be said here also that "judgment is difficult." <note>A reference to the first Aphorism of Hippocrates: "Life is short, art is long, opportunity fleeting, experiment perilous, judgment difficult."</note> But whether they should be punished according to the Law of Moses <note>The Old Testament legal code</note>—in whose time, as some believe, our modern witches hardly existed—I hold it unnecessary to investigate too closely. For what he did or did not do in this case does not concern us, who are not subject to his civil policy and worldly government.

For it is in the interest of the common good that wickedness be punished and piety be shielded.

# On Witches

Although there are certainly various opinions on this matter—as there were in the previous two chapters—nevertheless, the greatest and best part of the sensible world holds that, whatever may be said of the origin and timing of witches, and whether they were known to the ancients or only arose in later times, they are nonetheless (I say) not unworthy of punishment; though they are not all to be punished in the same manner. For one must never act with rashness, nor forget modesty and mercy.

<margin>Matthew 7</margin> <note>Likely a reference to "Judge not, that ye be not judged."</note>
A great portion of the common people (would to God it were not also the case among the most prominent) are for this reason more hostile toward witches than toward certain other evildoers—who are nonetheless equally in God's disfavor—because they fear more misfortune from them and hear of greater deeds from them than from others. For they hold the opinion that the more they hate the witches, and the more harshly they address and handle them, the less they can be harmed by them. They believe, therefore, that few authorities, judges, and other servants of justice are injured by them. It is as if one were protected through boldness, just as physicians are preserved against the poisonous disease of the pestilence <note>The Plague</note> by preventative medicine; see where a wicked delusion and barbaric error often lead seductive men. Therefore, such people tremble before witches no less than before the gaze of a Basilisk, or before the sight of a night-specter, or the Devil himself. Yet this fear comes from nowhere else than from error and false delusion regarding the witches' high-mighty arts and wonder-deeds. But nothing should rightly terrify us except sin, and a bad conscience on account of sin. These two (I greatly fear) will make these people more anxious than anything else: for the works of witches are not worth so much terror.

<margin>Francisco Vallés, *Controversiarium medicarum*, Book 4, last chapter.</margin> <note>Vallés (1524–1592) was a famous Spanish physician.</note>
It is true that judges and their servants are seldom harmed by witches when they are in custody,

<column-break/>

which a highly learned man considers to be for the reason that, in prison, they can neither help themselves nor harm others, because they do not have their medicine <note>Magical ointments or potions</note> with them there, nor can they prepare it there, nor hold conversation with their familiar paramour, Satan, lest they betray themselves. (For they are a fearful kind of people). But these reasons seem to be too lightly esteemed and uncertain. For their medicine, prepared with their ceremonial mirror-fighting <note>A reference to scrying or catoptromancy</note>, has little power, as was said before. But to speak with Satan, since he is an invisible spirit, is indeed possible and easy for them at any time. Therefore, it seems much more credible that they cannot do harm for the reason that God especially protects the authorities as His servants at that time: and that He wills that through them wickedness be punished. Or also, that Satan at that same time withdraws his help from them and provides no assistance, as he now waits and hopes for his reward—that is, the ruin and destruction of the witches—for which he alone has lurked, and for which they were taught and served him. But let this be said in passing.

<margin>Why witches cannot do harm in prison.</margin>

Now I return again to the punishment of witches, and I certainly deem it right that they are to be punished: yet the same punishment should only be imposed upon the truly guilty, publicly and lawfully convicted. One should punish them, but according to the nature of the misdeed, the age, the length of time, and according to other circumstances. However, as far as the punishment should be extended against them, a God-fearing, cautious judge will know how to be modest, or at least how to conduct himself somewhat according to the following manner. Children who are still without understanding, likewise the very old who have become like children again (in both of whom Satan sometimes also practices his deceits), just as in other sins, cannot be rightly punished, but one should, as much as possible, inform and teach them better.

# Doctor Johann Ewich.
## Gg iiij

as far as the human will is concerned, many are unfit and powerless in this regard, so one must act cautiously here. Just as in the previous case where the personal physicians were consulted, here too one should consult the "physicians of the soul" and theologians who best understand the nature, tricks, and sophistry of Satan. It is true that without a means (as was said before in the first part), no creature can accomplish anything; but when the means is unsuitable for the matter and furthermore unknown to us, it is entirely dangerous and difficult to judge these things, even though they happen daily among men. Therefore, a rational and modest authority must, following the example of the Church (as has been said), entrust many things to the omniscience of God, and not measure and judge everything according to the "sharpness of the law" <note>original: "Spitze der rechten"; a reference to the legal maxim *Summum ius summa iniuria*—the highest law can be the greatest injustice</note>, which is then called the greatest injustice.

<margin>Whether the will should be counted as the deed.</margin>
But if someone wished to defend without distinction the idea that here the will should be counted as the deed—especially if the will was made manifest through the action, which is also consistent with written law—he should know that, conversely, it must be considered whether the deed (as just mentioned) can be viewed as useful and necessary for that purpose. For if not, it is to be counted more as a folly; and whoever would rely upon it would commit a blunder in **Logic** <note>original: "Dialectica"</note> which the learned call a **fallacy of accidents** <term>Fallacia accidentis: a logical error where one mistakes a coincidental or accidental trait for an essential, causal one</term>, when one takes an accidental, improper cause for a proper one. For not every kind of work or effect follows every deed or work, just as every eclipse of the sun or moon, or the positions of other stars, is not followed by every kind of storm or other effect. Likewise, not everything that follows the mentioned eclipses is a specific effect of the same, even though the star-prophets <note>astrologers</note> often wish to persuade us of such.

<margin>C. ad Le. Cor. de sica. Item ff. de rer. & Ver. sig. L. fugitiu' <note>Citations to the Codex Justinianus and the Digest regarding the Cornelian law on assassins and the definitions of fugitive slaves.</note></margin>
It is (alas) all too well known that many a man sits in judgment who is armed only with such fallacies and deceitful talk, yet is nonetheless bold and

<column-break/>

daring enough to pronounce judgment. Many also refuse to be guided, and thus make many foreign matters their own—if not before men, then at least before God. For they should know that they occupy and serve not a human judgment seat, but God’s, and are like God’s stewards who will have to give an account of their commanded office when God summons them and removes them from office. Then, no one will be excused by their ignorance if they have passed themselves off as a master. For God wants dogs and wolves as judges in His town hall just as little as He wants statues, or children, or other persons unfit by reason of age or intellect. And it is rightly and wisely ordained that there should be certain higher courts or supreme courts to which appeals may be made from the lower ones, so that the latter may learn something from the former, or the former may correct and improve what the latter perhaps did not consider or overlooked. Therefore, I must once again object to the excellent man **Lambertus Danaeus** <note>A prominent French Calvinist theologian (1530–1595) who wrote on witchcraft and law.</note>, who dared to criticize the custom of the King of France because the lords are permitted to appeal to the Parliaments—that is, the highest courts—which is otherwise not always granted to other great miscreants. By this procedure and evasion, he believes that many guilty parties slip away and go unpunished, which he regards as a great neglect. But this godly man and, by his profession, a **theologian** <note>original: "Schrifftgelehrter"</note> (to whom patience rather than severity is more becoming), should rightly not take this delay poorly, since he could have learned this verse even from the pagan poet:

> One can never deliberate too long,
> When one must pronounce a sentence of death.

Likewise, since he well knows that among the ancient people of God <note>the Israelites</note> it was the custom that there were several grades in the courts, and every matter was recognized by these or those judges according to its nature and importance...

But who would say that our matter of witches is not very difficult and obscure, since it is not so apparent to the eyes of men, being for the most part prepared through the cunning and deceit of Satan? Nor is it as minor as other common sins committed daily by men. These two reasons (I hold for certain) were wisely considered by the aforementioned Kingdom <note>likely referring to the legal precedents of France or another major jurisdiction mentioned previously</note>. Therefore, it is more certain (to repeat what I said before) that in the aforementioned obscurity, one should not proceed boldly, nor rush headlong to the extreme punishment, until the matter is sufficiently understood. Following the example of cautious physicians: when they are perhaps not fully informed of the nature of the illness, they are accustomed to use light and tolerable medicines, not those that put the patient in danger or might otherwise bring particular harm to the body. But when it is handled differently in our witch-dealings, the great calamity, confusion of the authorities, grumbling, and rebellion it causes among the common people is plain as day and known to everyone; for the examples are at the door and cry out almost everywhere with a loud voice.

<margin>What happened in Venice.</margin>
Some years ago, in the Lordship of Venice, the punishment of witches was carried so far that almost all women would have been exterminated from the land with fire, had the high authorities not looked into it and mitigated the matter.

<margin>Brunswick.</margin>
Not long before this time, in the land of Brunswick, the matter began with lowly persons and was brought to noble, indeed almost to the highest persons, not without great shame.

In the Bishopric and Diocese of Offenburg, this same tragedy was played out two years ago with a few people, but it proceeded and was handled over time in such a way that it made a bloody <term>catastrophe</term> <note>the final disastrous conclusion of a drama</note> and end for many. And if one does not yet provide more wisely, or wishes to watch the play for too long, it could happen (which may God graciously avert) that this same action might reach the most honorable people. For <term>Moloch</term> <note>a biblical figure associated with child sacrifice by fire; here used as a metaphor for the insatiable fire of the stake</note> has a particular pleasure in such burnt offerings, which he partly prepares himself, and partly they are prepared for him by others through the inexperience and frivolity of the people, unlawful processes, and the multitude of the godless, of whom the world is full, and in which Satan works powerfully through the righteous judgment of God. For it is certain, as far as the guilt of men and judges who pronounce the sentence is concerned, that too often the punishment falls upon not a few who are without guilt. Oh, what an unspeakable injustice! This is not only highly burdensome and shameful to the miserable executed persons, but it also brings eternal slander upon the entire lineage and all their kindred. Would it then not be more laudable that, according to that famous opinion, one should let several go who are not sufficiently convicted, rather than put the innocent to death? But I leave this to be considered by the fair and cautious authorities.

# Doctor Johann Ewich.

Whether it be right, is known to God. If one were to say that the apple was poisoned <note>original: "vergifftec"</note>, it is a wonder that the mother received no harm from it: And it is even more a wonder that afterwards, when she was pregnant again, the same thing happened to her every time. For although reasons could be thought of whereby the womb was weakened and could no longer carry a heavy fruit—which indeed happens to others—nevertheless, as long as other more demonstrable and more credible causes can be found, it is not fitting that one should immediately loosen this knot in the manner of King Alexander <note>A reference to the Gordian Knot; meaning to solve a complex problem by force or execution rather than reason.</note>; that is, to hand it over to the executioner and chop it through with the sword.

Another story was told to me by an honorable and credible person, concerning a witch who confessed she had killed his father with poison. But in what manner? She had (he said) smeared the handle or the ring on the door with a special poison, and when he touched it, he was harmed. That might perhaps have been possible, but since without doubt others likewise grasped the same ring and were not harmed, it remains an incomprehensible thing, or rather a lying imagination and deception of Satan, whereby he led the sick into mistrust, fooled and bewitched the witch herself, and kept the judges and others in superstition. For what is poisonous must remain poisonous, to one as well as to another (I speak of humans, not of other creatures); otherwise, it is altogether a fantasy and mere imagination (of whose power and effect I spoke previously in the first part) and can accomplish nothing in foreign subjects or bodies.

In the Land of the Mark, a cloistered person <note>A nun or monk.</note> was suspected of witchcraft and therefore arrested and interrogated under torture <note>original: "peinlich verhöret"</note>. She then confessed that she had made the others sick only with wishing and cursing (for they were all burdened with bodily

<column-break/>

weakness). And when she was asked how the sick might be helped again, she answered and said freely that when she was put to death and executed, then it would become better for the others. But after her death, it was found that they were all possessed by the devil. Thus the spirit of lies and murder brought this about through God’s permission (for His judgments are in every way wonderful and unsearchable).

In the year 1551, when I was studying at Toulouse <note>original: "Tholosa"</note> in France, two witnesses were produced and heard in the Parliament against a prisoner. These testified that they had once been in the city (for they were strangers, living several miles away from Toulouse) and had this countryman of theirs with them. When they wanted to travel home together and it became quite late, so that they had no hope of arriving home that evening, he told us (they said) to be at peace, for he would surely bring us across. We went out (they said), and immediately we encountered several well-equipped horses; he commanded that we should mount them without terror or fear. So we did, and arrived home without delay, nor did we perceive any discomfort, except only that it seemed to us as if the air, because of the fast traveling through it, cut our faces, etc. The accused also confessed himself that he had once been captured and sentenced to death, but when the court believed he was hanged, it was not he, but the judge’s mule that hung on the gallows. This was a ridiculous thing, and he was nonetheless punished with fire as a sorcerer <note>original: "Zauberer"</note> by the sentence of the Parliament (though he was actually guilty not of our present sin <note>Likely referring to the specific theological definition of witchcraft being debated</note>, but of the black art <note>original: "schwartzekunst"; ritual magic</note>). # On Witches

One can tell the most absurd stories, yet there are always some who believe them; and to confirm evil habits and false opinions, they recite them as true histories in town halls as well as in other places. Thus, it is found here in truth what Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, a famous Greek physician and philosopher whose works influenced Western medicine for centuries.</note> said: Preconceived opinions make the hearts of men not only deaf, but also blind. "Thus and so," they say, "it happened: this occurred and that occurred, and this and that followed upon it." God forbid that the Devil should become a creator! You speak of gruesome things, indeed of many miracles. But listen in turn to what I wish to say. Have you never heard or seen that someone vomited up something they had never previously taken in? I am not speaking of that which perhaps, through a failure of nature, never grew in a human body, but of that which *can* never grow in a human: as we have cited several examples of that kind in the first part. Many things are falsely told and many things are boldly believed. But it would be far too long if one wanted to recount many of these stories, or rather these "Nuremberg tales" <note>original: "Nürenbergischen tantmar" — likely a reference to tall tales or nursery rhymes, implying the stories are childish fictions.</note>. It is enough that one knows that Satan is a master of a thousand arts, indeed the greatest of all jugglers <note>term: "Gauckler" (juggler/illusionist) — used here to mean a deceiver who creates optical illusions to trick the senses.</note>, as has now been often said; for whom it is very easy to represent many such things to our physical eyes, and through the physical eyes, also to seduce the eyes of the spirit and understanding, so that through error he may lead the unwary not only to unbelief but also to misdeeds. Therefore, we should distance ourselves from the old serpent—namely, from false speech and its disciples, bold gullibility. Here we are not dealing with "the shadow of an ass" <note>A Greek idiom referring to a dispute over something completely worthless or trivial.</note>, but with how one may maintain a good conscience: likewise with the life and death of people for whom Christ died. It is just as great an abomination before God, as the Prophet says, to condemn the innocent as it is to justify the guilty.

However, so that a Christian judge may know what a heavy sin that authority takes upon itself which condemns an innocent person, he should know that whoever does this, first violates his conscience <note>original: "conscientz"</note>, sickens his faith, and thus becomes damnable before God himself and a murderer. Secondly, he impresses such a mark of shame upon himself that even after his death it remains and clings to his entire lineage and all his friends; he tears apart human society, which he ought rightly to preserve, in that he exterminates a piece of it and cuts it off just like a limb from the body. Lastly, he both grieves the holy angels, whom God has appointed as guards over mankind, and rejoices Moloch <note>A Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice, used here to represent demonic bloodlust.</note> and the evil spirits, who take pleasure in murder and unjust death. And enough of this; we do not wish to push this further. That we have said something of this, however, was caused by the occasion and the injustice of the matter, so that some might be reminded of prudence. We will therefore now return to our intended subject matter.

# Doctor Johann Ewich.

treat with great care: Likewise, that they at times punish those who have not dealt with poison more severely than with the pillory and the rod: which I (indeed) would not wish to advise against, if they would leave aside the blasphemous, vain art of jugglery <note>original: "Gauckelkunst" - referring to deceptive magic or sleight of hand</note> (as has been said).

The third reason why witches are to be punished was that, although they are not the actual and immediate cause of some of their misdeeds, nevertheless, because they commit them with the help of Satan (with whom they are also allied, whom they call upon and petition for this purpose), it appears as if they perform them themselves, and are therefore guilty and punishable. Just as it is held when one incites another to theft or murder, which he himself does not wish to do or perhaps cannot do, this cannot then be reckoned as a mere wish or simple ill-will (which are not punished in court). For it is a very different thing to command or ask others to do something, than merely to wish or desire in the heart that something should happen. But I say that this is only so far as those who are asked can do it by God's permission; otherwise, it would be a useless wishing, which God alone punishes: or the folly of a senseless person, who is not usually punished. Therefore, this reason can, in my opinion, be better referred to the first or the following. For as far as the rule of law is concerned—what one does through another, is as much as if he did it himself—it is to be believed that he who framed it did not think of Satan's contract with the witches. For since the contract is against good morals, and occurs between unequal creatures, one of whom is not capable of nor subject to civil law, such a contract is in itself void and does not belong to human dealings. For spiritual natures cannot, properly speaking, make contracts with men and be bound to them: since words such as contracts, alliances, obligations, etc., are words of the law, to which,

<column-break/>

as has been said, the spirits, who are no member of human society, do not belong. And since it also remains always uncertain what Satan's part in it is—whether that which happened followed according to the supposed obligation of Satan with the witches—whether that, I say, happened through the finger of God or through the work of Satan or not, it would be improper and unjust to impose the punishment of an uncertain deed upon certain persons. For we are speaking here of the acting causes, not of the guilt. Witches are otherwise guilty before God in many other ways, even if some committed deeds cannot rightfully be attributed to them.

That some also say: "The doer and the one who consented are equally guilty," is indeed true before God, but not always before men, and this rule of law can have just as little place in this devilish business as the other just mentioned. Unless the judge thought that he could punish Satan with fire or the like, or also knew for certain how to prove that Satan himself carried out the very misdeed in question. But regarding this, enough has been said for our purpose.

There remains the last and greatest reason of all why witches are to be punished, namely the denial of God, or the terrible blasphemy associated with it, the falling away from God to Satan. For this reason, not only the learned but also the politicians <note>secular authorities or statesmen</note> and sensible magistrates deem the witches worthy of death—and specifically death by fire—as <margin>Many codes concerning evildoers and magicians. <note>Latin: "K. multi cod. de mal. & then." refers to various legal codes regarding 'maleficos' (evildoers/sorcerers) and 'veneficos' (poisoners).</note></margin> Ulricus Molitor <note>A 15th-century legal scholar known for his influential dialogue on witches.</note> testifies in his Dialogue on Witches and Devil-possessed Women, and proves from the written laws; whose opinion we also gladly support.

These then are now the principal reasons why witches are to be punished, which, if they are put forward (so that we may finally make an end of this treatise), excluded from all prejudice, solely in the fear of God, with Christian caution and modesty— <margin>Deuteronomy 28.</margin>

# On Witches

With discretion, and having carefully weighed all the circumstances previously mentioned, one may and should treat the aforementioned witches or sorceresses (just like blasphemous heretics, to strike fear into the secure and crude people, which is the primary final cause of Divine punishment) according to the form of lawful punishments, and demonstrate an example of severity against great sins. No sensible, God-fearing person can despise or contradict this.

<margin>Conclusion or Closing.</margin> And so we have until now, as briefly as possible, dealt with the three parts of the witchcraft matter. The first (to briefly repeat the summary) concerns nature, powers, and deeds—how much one should attribute to witches or not. The second concerns testimonies or signs by which they are to be recognized, and that one must not accept all kinds of testimony, nor believe all kinds of signs, nor immediately punish the suspected and judge the accused and punished as guilty (for here many <term>fallaciae</term> <note>Latin: fallacies or deceptions</note> and dangerous errors are often committed). Rather, as is proper in criminal cases and required by the laws, one should only accept such signs and testimony that are certain, indubitable, and indeed clearer than the midday sun. The third part has shown that witches are indeed to be punished, but not all with equal severity, nor with indiscretion or ferocity.

In all of this, if I have written differently than others, this should not be attributed to my stubbornness or self-conceit, but rather to my conscience and the weight and difficulty of the matter. For just as this subject has always been dark in itself, it has been made even darker by the differing opinions of those who have dealt with it. If I have failed or erred anywhere, the pious and learned will kindly improve it upon discovery; but that which is in accordance with the truth, they will accept with grateful hearts. I wish to have the matter itself, and this my opinion or <term>prophecy</term> <note>Here used in the sense of a formal declaration or testimony</note>, entirely subjected to the spirit of the prophets and the judgment of the wise, so that peace and truth alone may shine forth in all things and maintain their place everywhere.

JESUS CHRIST the Son of God, who came to destroy the works of darkness, may He punish and hinder Satan, so that he does not bring it to the point where the most noble creature, namely man, is seduced and ruined to the shame and disgrace of God, but rather is made daily more and more ready and fit for the honor and praise of the same (for which he was created), Amen.

### Maxims and Rules of the Third and Final Part.

**W**itches are worthy of punishment, but not all with equally heavy punishment. The Law of Moses does not bind Christians according to its external form, but only according to its inner truth.

It is in the interest of the common good not only that misdeeds be punished, but also that innocence be upheld and protected.

<margin>Code on Judgments, Law: "It pleased..." <note>Reference to the Codex Justinianus, a fundamental work of Roman law.</note></margin> One should deal with witches discreetly, not insolently, even in punishment.

Age, childhood, error, teachability, and repentance merit a milder punishment when they are to be punished.

The judge should not rush the <term>sentence</term> <note>The formal legal judgment</note>, especially in <term>penal cases</term> <note>Cases involving physical or capital punishment</note>, for the judgment is heavy.

<margin>Code on Laws, Law: "The laws..."</margin> Ignorance of the law excuses no one, much less the judge.

It is a grievous thing to condemn the innocent; God does not leave innocent shed blood unavenged.

It is dangerous to judge concerning the death of a human being when one does not know for certain that they are guilty.

<margin>Law: "An absent person," Digest on Punishments. <note>Reference to the Pandects/Digest of Roman law.</note></margin> It is better to let many guilty people go free than to punish one innocent person.

Bad examples from those in authority give cause for many grievous sins.

# The Opinion of Johannes Trithemius

Sin prevents and robs one of the grace of God. However, we become like the good angels through the uprightness of our will, provided we demonstrate and testify to the godliness of faith in Christ through holy and necessary works. And just as the fulfillment of a good will makes pious men like the angels, so does a perverted will make godless men like the devils. Therefore, the more perverted evil and godless men become through the malice of their own will, the more similar they also become to the devils in affection and disposition. From this comparison arises a friendship and fellowship, and further, from day to day, a trust and confidence. From this trust follows a power and dominion of the lesser over the greater—be it a genuine power or a presumed and deceptive one. Therefore, when it appears as if evil people have power over the devils, this happens only because of their great malice; namely, when they pervert themselves so far that they resemble the devils and either surpass them or at least become equal to them in their malicious will.

For the devils are not all equal to one another in malice and understanding; rather, one is much more cunning, swift, intelligent, and malicious than the other. For after they fell from the high throne <note>Referring to the fall of the rebel angels from Heaven</note>, certainly those who are closest to the surface of the earth and dwell in caves and dens are much coarser and more foolish than the others, so that they even allow themselves to be frightened by men with swords, rods, and threatening words, as one sees in possessed people. But the devils who have their dwelling somewhat further from the earth are of a more subtle nature and unite or compare themselves less with men. However, the more perverted the will of malicious men is, the more they compare themselves with the devils with whom they come into acquaintance; they thereafter become bolder and obtain a dominion over the devils in whose fellowship they are—not indeed with earnestness and true power, but

<column-break/>

under a presumed appearance and deceit. For in order that the devils may willingly keep such people (who have once surrendered themselves to them) in their malice, they comply with them under the appearance of a presumed mastery and compulsion, and they pretend as if they are forced by power to do that which they actually like to do of their own accord. Certainly, no man obtains any true power over the devils except he whom faith in Jesus Christ makes acceptable and pleasing to God through the merit of His holiness. For thus says the Holy Scripture concerning those who truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ: *He gave them power over the unclean spirits.*

<margin>
Matthew 10.
Mark 16.
</margin>

Therefore, only those evil men have the right to command devils whom malice has made equal to them, equality has made friends, and friendship has made their own and subject. Just as it is said and often happens that a servant of lowly origin, through long-term residence, becomes powerful over a great prince, obtaining everything he desires from him without contradiction, making it appear as if the master is ruled and governed by the servant rather than the servant by the master. So it also often happens that evil and perverted people, accepted into the fellowship of the devils, become very presumptuous and bold over time and obtain a presumed power—I will not say a friendly, voluntary dominion over them—which they have earned with their evil will by becoming equal to them. Hence, they obtain everything they desire from the devils whom they resemble, by virtue of an express or hidden agreement and pact, unless they are hindered by God's permission and cannot grant their request. Yet they do not comply at all times with all godless and evil men, but only with those who have entered into a pact with them. Such as evil women and witches who have betrothed themselves to the devil, and the summoners of the dead, whom one commonly calls <term>Necromantics</term> <note>original: "Necremáticos"; those who practice necromancy or spirit summoning</note>, who worship the devils.

Exodus 22.
</margin>

# Of Witches and Monsters.

There are, however, two kinds of people who can command devils without sin. The first are those who, through the merit of their holiness, are beloved by God and have received power from Him to trample the head of the ancient serpent <note>A biblical reference to defeating the Devil, from Genesis 3:15</note>. Such were the Apostles in the early Church, their successors, and disciples, of whom the Lord says in the Holy Gospel: In my name they shall cast out <margin>Mark 16</margin> devils, and if they take up serpents, it shall not harm them. The others are those who, by virtue of their ordination and the office entrusted to them in the Church, have received authority to drive out devils from men. This office and work is commanded to the **Exorcists** <note>original: "Exorcistis"</note>, that is, the conjurers of devils in the Church, specifically when they are ordained and consecrated by the Bishop.

On the other hand, there are also two kinds of people who desire to command devils, yet how unjustly they presume to do so is proven by their own unchristian and wrongful pacts and alliances. The first and most harmful are the witches and monsters <note>original: "Hexen vnd Vnholden"; 'Unholden' refers to malevolent spirits or those in league with them</note>, who make alliances with devils and surrender themselves with special solemnity and confession to a devil as his own property and into eternal servitude. But what great misfortune these harmful people cause in your realm, O most wise Emperor, no man can sufficiently express. For they first of all deny God, the Christian faith, and Holy Baptism; they sacrifice themselves, body and soul, to the devils; they lame, damage, and kill men and cattle with their sorcery; and they cause all manner of diseases through God's providence <note>The text suggests God allows this as a trial or punishment</note>. Because they allow themselves to be used in the service of devils by virtue of the established alliance, they presume to achieve everything they lust after through the appearance and help of the same. Therefore, they are to be tolerated nowhere, but are to be utterly rooted out in all places and ends, just as God <margin>Exodus 22</margin> the creator of all things commanded when He says: "Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live." Some witches and monsters summon the devils with incantations. Some lure them with blessings and sacrifices; others bring them forth with shameful things and ceremonies, so that they might appear to help them in their godless undertakings. It is therefore no wonder that these same evil women supposedly command the devils, whom they resemble in the godlessness of their perverted wills, and with whom they are one through frequent association to the detriment of the human race.

The other evil people who wish to command devils are commonly called **Necromancers** <note>original: "Necromāt," meaning those who conjure the dead or spirits</note>. They deal with bans and incantations and boast that they can thereby bring devils together into a circle, or enclose them in a crystal or another vessel, and show them there visibly. These harmful people deal only in deceit and superstition, and commit many more and worse acts than any pious man might imagine. So that they may have the devils more willingly at their service, they commonly offer them the most shameful sacrifices, make an express pact with them, and drag about many and various books filled with lewdness, godlessness, and deceit. Nevertheless, they use names as if these books were written by the ancient philosophers and wise men, and by displaying them, they deceive many cautious and inquisitive people, plunging them along with themselves into the devil's pit. They falsely claim great and unbelievable things, so that people who hear of them must marvel at it; they say they can force the evil spirits with their little rings, figures, images, bans, and incantations to show themselves in a circle, crystal, or other vessel, and that they must give distinct answers to each and every question. They claim all this, to be sure, but in our times very few are found, even among the wicked, whom the devils obey in such a manner. For God, for weighty reasons, does not permit it, so that inquisitive people—who otherwise have a desire for new things—do not learn to seek counsel and help from devils in times of need, setting aside the Christian religion. But without doubt, all those to whom the devils obediently appear upon their incantation and demand have bound themselves through an express or hidden Pact and

Between contrary and unequal things, no friendship or fellowship can endure; rather, it must show much more of nothing but enmity and resistance. Nor can any unity or friendship exist between those who are contrary to one another and of unequal will. Yet they pretend as if they were compelled and forced to such service. Therefore, Your Imperial Majesty should not wonder that it often appears as if the devils show obedience to evil and godless people, who—as has been said—are aligned not only in evil will, but also in the harming of the poor human race...

But why can pious and God-fearing people not command the holy angels of God, with whom they nevertheless share the same good will? For although there are people to be found in the Church of God who, through their righteousness, are helpful and serviceable to many people for their salvation, few in our times reach so far that the devils fear them for the sake of their holiness and merit, or that the holy angels receive them into their fellowship and company. ### Concerning the Might and Power of Witches and Monsters.

But from where does such great power come to the monsters <note>original: "Vnholden" - a term for demons, sorcerers, or monstrous beings</note> that they can often perform many strange and wonderful things in a single hour, which a pious person would not be able to do in the whole time of his life? To answer this question briefly, it will be necessary to report that all power stems from God, without whom no creature can do anything. For Christ says in the Gospel: *Without me you can do nothing* <margin>John 15</margin> <note>original: "Ioan. 15."</note>; therefore it is evident that people have and obtain all power to accomplish anything, be it evil or good, from nowhere else but from God. Therefore, the Holy Bishop Augustine says: The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily creatures and movements, and nothing at all happens visibly in the whole wide world that is not commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and incomprehensible hall or court of the Most High Emperor, according to the incomprehensible justice of rewards and punishments. Therefore, Most Gracious Emperor, there is no doubt that all power of the witches and monsters, by which they perform wonderful and terrifying things with the help of evil spirits, comes from God the Lord, whom no one can resist, nor can anyone move or stir a single finger without His help. And the holy teachers conclude that neither the devils nor the witches and monsters can harm humans or cattle, unless it be that Almighty God wills it, permits it, and gives them power to accomplish that which they have resolved in their evil will. Without God's will and consent, no creature is able to do anything. For if something could happen without God's will and permission, it would necessarily follow that God is so weak that He could not prevent it, and must allow a thing to happen against His will. But since every human being, insofar as he is God's creature, is in God's power, he can do nothing without the will of Him from whom he has both the willing and the doing; therefore, what the witches and monsters do, they do by God's permission, and can do nothing without His will. For just as Almighty God has instituted certain Sacraments in His Church, which, for the sake of His presence, show and accomplish their healing effect among those who handle them worthily—for He who ordained them works salvation through them—so also has the Devil (who seeks nothing higher than to be like God) established certain signs as "sacraments." This is all done by their mind, which is displaced and snatched away into the company of the Devil. Experience teaches us that witches and sorcerers have scooped butter out of fast-flowing waters at such a time when it could in no way have happened otherwise than through the Devil's help. Likewise, when they have become enemies to a person or livestock and wish to kill them, they become quite mad and insane, and strive without ceasing for how they may avenge themselves.
