# Of Witches and Sorcerers.

The Devil wishes to imitate the Church of Christ in all things; but just as one who is not ordained cannot consecrate <note>original: "conficieren"</note> or present the Body of Christ, even if he speaks the words belonging to the consecration and hallowing, so too the Devil never—or at least very rarely—serves anyone who is not bound to him by oaths, no matter how diligently he is summoned or what customary signs and marks are used. For if he complied with everyone who called upon him without a prior covenant, so many witches and sorcerers <note>original: "Hexen vnd Vnholden"</note> would not need to surrender themselves to him as his own property. From this it also follows that many who apply themselves to this ungodly art, and wish to bind the Devil in a circle, mirror, or other vessel with their gruesome conjurations, nevertheless achieve nothing; either because God thwarts them with His power, or because the Devil despises such a curious person who is not beholden to him.

For three parts belong to sorcery <note>term: "Zauberey" (magic or witchcraft)</note>, without which no sorcery has ever been accomplished: namely, a mad and malicious witch or sorcerer, the voluntary cooperation of the Devil, and above all things, God’s permission. If any one of these is lacking, the sorcery cannot proceed. For if God does not permit it, neither the Devil nor the witch can achieve anything; and if the Devil did not assist the will of the wicked woman, her sorcery would have no impact. Conversely, if the witch were not there, the Devil could not complete the sorcery either; for the Devil uses the will of the mad witch just as a master craftsman uses a tool for work, and without her, he could do no harm.

<margin>Distinction of evil spirits.</margin>
And just as one devil surpasses another in power and shrewdness, so too not all witches and sorcerers have equal power. Rather, their power is fashioned according to whether each receives a coarser or more subtle devil as a helper. For there are many kinds of devils, distinguished into certain grades and orders because of the places to which they were cast when they first fell from Heaven. The first race of

<column-break/>

devils is called **Fiery**, because they hover high in the air and never come to the lower places before the Last Judgment; instead, they remain always below the circle of the moon and have no fellowship with men on Earth. That they remain below the moon is testified by St. Augustine in the book *On the Christian Combat* <note>original: "de agone Christiano"</note>, where he says: the devils do not dwell in Heaven where the sun and stars are, but all make do below the circle of the moon. In my opinion, this is also what moved Apuleius to say that the devils are fiery spirits. Aristotle also testifies to this, saying that people have often seen small winged creatures flying about in glowing furnaces, who spend their whole lives in the fire; for they come forth with the fire and also perish within it, and when they vanish, they return to the place from whence they came. These have no fellowship with sorcery, for because they keep to the fire, they cannot, due to their subtlety, take on a coarse body in the air.

<margin>II.</margin>
The second race of devils is called **Aerial** <note>original: "Aerium"</note>, from the air, because they dwell in the air near us and travel about. These can indeed come down to the lowest places, take on bodies from the thick air, and sometimes appear visibly to men. Through God’s permission, they often disturb the air, stirring up thunder and storms, and they are all inclined to harm and destroy the human race. Like men, they all have their affections and impulses; they are especially full of pride and envy, are driven by constant temptations, have no permanent body, and do not always remain in one place. They are not all of the same form, but take on many different shapes and change them often according to their varying dispositions when they are summoned by the magical words of witches and sorcerers, or moved by anger to do harm. For they are accustomed to show themselves with great violence and madness, and when one...

Thus, witches and sorcerers <note>original: "Hexen vnd Vnholden"</note> are so much more powerful with the help and assistance of the devils, depending on whether each one receives a higher and more powerful devil as a helper. St. Athanasius says in the *Life of St. Anthony* that the air is full of devils, just as the great Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> previously said: That in all places and ends of the entire world there are devils. <margin>III.</margin>The third kind we call the Earthly Devils, and we do not doubt that they were cast out of heaven and fell to the earth because of their sins. Of these, the holy bishop and martyr Ignatius Theophorus <note>Ignatius of Antioch</note> writes in a letter to the Ephesians thus: "There is nothing better than to have peace, whereby all arrows of the heavenly and earthly spirits become powerless." Some of these devils dwell in the woods and forests and do much to harm hunters. Some stay in the wide fields and lead travelers astray at night. Some take their pleasure in frightening people with ghosts; some prophesy future things so that those who hear it will hold them in high regard; some apply great diligence to how they may darken, harm, and kill senseless and melancholy people. As we have often experienced, St. John Chrysostom writes in the 3rd book *On Providence* to Stagyrius, a monk, thus: "Great sadness does greater damage than all devilish works. For whoever becomes master of the devil, he overcomes them all through sadness; when one rids oneself of the same, one has nothing to fear from the devil." This kind of devil very rarely associates with witches and sorcerers because of their inconstant and frivolous mind. Since they would rather frighten many than wait upon a single woman. Yet they occasionally let themselves be found in glass, crystal, or mirrors, as they have promised to foolish people, and give answers to women's questions when they are summoned by their magical words. They indicate to them if the one who comes to them has cursed them or spoken ill of them on the way. There is a great difference between these sorceresses and others: for what others have destroyed through their sorcery, these promise to set right again. But because the sorceress commonly drives out one sorcery with another, all Christians are commanded by the Church to avoid them entirely.

These are fierce, impetuous, restless, and spiteful; they stir up storms on the sea, sink ships to the bottom, and kill many in the water. These devils, as often as they take on a visible body, commonly appear in the form of a woman, rarely in the form of a man. The fifth species is called *Subterraneum* <note>Latin: "Underground"</note>, because it likes to dwell in caverns, caves, and wide, deep valleys. Some of such Devils guard the treasures which greedy people have buried in the earth; they snatch, steal, guard, and carry them sometimes from one place to another, so that they do not fall to the lot of people again. This species of Devils does not usually have any fellowship with witches and monster-beings.

<margin>VI.</margin>
The sixth species of Devils is called *Lucifugum* <note>Latin: "Light-shunning"</note>, because they shun and flee the light and never let themselves be seen by day; they also cannot take on any physical form except at night. Their work is to run about in the darkness. These Devils are of an unfathomable, dark, cold nature, malicious, restless, and violent; they attack people who encounter them by night, and often bring some to their deaths, either by breathing upon them or by touching them. This kind of Devil cannot get along with witches and monster-beings, cannot be subdued with magical words, and has a loathing for light, the human voice, and all noise. The spirits called *Aerios* <note>Latin/Greek: "Aerial" or "of the air"</note>, who dwell in the air, serve the witches and monster-beings the most in their <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "Zauberey"</note>, for they are much more subtle, bold, and daring than the others. The earthly spirits, as has been said, do indeed help the witches and monster-beings as well, yet because they are of a lesser rank and power, they cannot inflict great harm. Thus it is now certain that witches and monster-beings have a measured power, and they can do no greater harm than God the Lord permits to the Devils; and when He does not allow it, they are capable of nothing.

# The Opinion of Johannes Trithemius
<note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a German Benedictine abbot, polymath, and influential writer on cryptography and the occult.</note>

Why the righteous God and zealous avenger of all evil permits and allows such sorcery, through which the human race is so heavily damaged—and indeed, not only the wicked, but also many innocent people are badly plagued and executed.

I remember well that I recently gave Your Imperial Majesty this oral answer: Whatever the faithful, pious, righteous, gracious, and merciful God does, He does justly. For He is a righteous God, and there is no sin or unrighteousness in Him; rather, He does and permits everything by right. Now, if one asks <margin>God also permits evil.</margin> why God allows such evil things, we answer: because He is righteous. Your Imperial Majesty should not consider this answer of ours to be an absurd one. For it does not at all presume against the goodness of God, as He has just causes for why He permits much evil. If He allowed nothing evil in this world, it would then be to His disparagement. For if God did not let evil happen, then man could not sin, and would be entirely without sin—which cannot be said with truth regarding human nature, as the Creator of all things gave it a free will from the beginning. For since man is a creature and not the Creator Himself, he must be able to turn himself toward both good and evil, since his essence comes from the highest Creator of all creatures, just as all things stem and exist from their first origin; but to create something belongs to God alone, who alone is immutable and eternal. Whatever is mutable, however, must by necessity eventually cease, but is preserved through the goodness of the Creator as long as it is not abandoned by its origin or beginning. Therefore, it was not fitting that man should be created without sin in his first formation, which by nature belongs only to the immutable and eternal Creator of all things. However, whenever it is granted to man—such that one believes he cannot sin—even then, neither the free will nor the capability is removed or withdrawn; rather, the will toward the good is confirmed and strengthened. And whenever this grace is granted to a person, it is a gift of grace and not a natural work. As the Holy Scripture says: God created man from the beginning and gave him free choice. To speak of it properly, it cannot be that a mortal man, conceived in original sin, has both a free will and yet cannot sin. Therefore, the holy Bishop Augustine says: "The first freedom of the will was to be able to sin. The last, however, in holiness, will be greater: to not be able to sin." <note>original: "Prima libertas voluntatis erat, posse non peccare; novissima erit multo maior, non posse peccare." Trithemius is paraphrasing St. Augustine's City of God.</note> Therefore, if man could not sin, he would also not have his free will. Although Almighty God takes no pleasure in sin, He justly lets man sin and do evil so that free will may endure, and that both virtue may receive the reward of good works, and wanton malice may receive the punishment of sins. For no one does good or evil against his will. Therefore, Almighty God justly lets men—to whom He gave free will from the beginning—sin and do wrong.

<column-break/>

<margin>Proverbs 15.</margin>
<margin>Reasons why God permits evil.</margin>
The holy teachers of years past have indicated many reasons why Almighty God allows so much evil to happen through the cooperation of the devils, which we wish to recount briefly and in order, one after another.

<margin>1st Reason.</margin>
The first is that the exceeding power of God—who alone is immutable and surpasses all—may be revealed. But the creature is mutable and not to be compared with the immutable Creator. Therefore, one reads in the Fourth Book of Moses <note>The Book of Numbers.</note>: God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent of anything. In the Fifth Book of Moses <note>The Book of Deuteronomy.</note> it stands: God is faithful and there is no evil in Him; righteous and pious is He. In the Book of Tobit it is written: Lord, You are righteous, and all Your deeds are right, and pure goodness and faithfulness. And in the Book of Job we read: Far be it that God should be godless, and—

and the Almighty God is not unjust; rather, He repays man according to what he has earned, and strikes each according to his deeds. Therefore, every person who rightly recognizes their own ignorance and weakness easily perceives how they are as nothing compared to God. That God justly allows man to sin is so that his free will is preserved, and the majesty of the great God may be made known to mankind.

<margin>II. Reason.</margin>
The second reason is so that the unfathomable wisdom of God may be revealed to mortal men—which knows how to make something good even out of our evil—when He allows the sin of one person to serve for the improvement and meritorious work of another. For if He did not allow evil to happen, who among us would understand what was good? Since God creates and ordains the good, but does not create evil; He does, however, ordain it, so that the evil committed by men does not fall into total disorder. Human malice cannot hinder God's will, nor can man achieve anything unless God permits and allows it to him.

<margin>III. Reason.</margin>
The third reason that God permits sorcery <note>original: "Zauberey"</note> is to demonstrate His great grace and goodness toward those who have sinned and turned back to Him. For if God did not allow His creatures to sin, He could not show them His grace again; and if there were no sin, God could not be merciful. But because we all sin in manifold ways, God has much to forgive, and the faithful and gracious Creator finds poor sinners everywhere upon whom He may prove His mercy. Therefore, the holy Bishop Augustine says: "If the sickness were slight and minor, one would not respect the physician, nor seek him out." But if one does not use the physician, the sickness would not be averted. Where sin is powerful, grace also becomes powerful, and alone makes a distinction between the redeemed and the damned, whom the common guilt—which crept in and corrupted everyone soon after

<column-break/>

creation—holds all together. Thus God has mercy upon all His works.
<margin>Psalm 144.</margin> <note>Likely referring to Psalm 145:9 in modern numbering: "The Lord is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works."</note>

<margin>IV. Reason.</margin>
The fourth reason for Divine permission <note>original: "Göttlichen verhengtnuß"</note> is that the Creator demonstrates His justice upon those who have indeed sinned but have not performed penance. For if all men were pious and no one sinned, the justice of God would have nothing to punish. So that the justice of God may also have its place, the creature sins through God's permission. For the Lord is just, and repays each according to his willful deeds.

<margin>V. Reason.</margin>
The fifth reason is the majesty and dignity of created man. For if God did not allow man to sin, he would be esteemed less than the irrational animals, which have their free natural movement without any compulsion; and although they lack reason and understanding, they still have their natural free impulse and path which they follow. If one were to compare man against them, he might be esteemed much lower if he did not have his free will. But God has left man with a free will, over which neither kings nor princes can command.

<margin>VI. Reason.</margin>
The sixth reason is the praise of virtue and constancy in goodness. For we praise a pious man because he did not sin, even though he could have done so, but instead remained steadfast in his good purpose through the help of Divine grace.

<margin>VII. Reason. 2 Thessalonians 2.</margin>
The seventh reason why God permits the Devil to cause so much misfortune through witches and sorcerers <note>original: "Hexen vnnd Vnholden"</note> is so that those who do not believe the truth, but take pleasure in lies, may be seduced and deceived by the Devil as the inventor of lies. For it is fair and right that all sorcerers and witches, who cast the healing doctrine of Christ to the wind and reject it, should be deceived by the devils and [cast] into the abyss of Hell for eternal punishment.

# Concerning Witches and Sorcerers.
## [Signature: Ji]

I shall recount, one after another, the reasons that I have found among the ancient and Christian teachers.

<margin>1st Reason.</margin>
The first, indeed, is the testing of faith and the proof of temptation among Christians, so that those who are disciplined through sorcery <note>original: "Zauberey"</note> may perceive from their physical afflictions what kind of trust and love they truly hold for God in their hearts. It is not a difficult thing to have patience when one is fortunate and well. But to ask for and expect help from the Savior of the faithful with humility and patience during misfortune—that can be done only by steadfast and true-believing Christians. The holy Job, who had previously shown himself to be very God-fearing during times of peace and outside of danger, had to first experience in his tribulation what kind of constant trust he had in God. Here it is also to be noted that those who are taught and corrupted through the sorcery of the Devil or witches sin against both the commandments of God and the Church when they seek out or consult the nearest sorcerers and devil-conjurors, either themselves or through others, to restore their health. For they have neither upright faith nor love for God. They value the health of the mortal flesh higher than God Himself, and seek their salvation and health not in Christ, but in the Devil and his servants; they would rather be healthy in the Devil's name and live a blessed life of labor than suffer a little here for the honor of Christ and hereafter enjoy eternal joy with Him. But he who does not visit the sorcerers and would rather live in poverty and sickness in obedience to Divine commandments than end his life in wealth and physical health against God, he truly loves God and keeps himself steadfast in the right Christian faith. Most Christian Emperor, one should not tolerate among Christians such blinded and unbelieving people who help the bewitched through sorcery, reveal theft and adultery with the help of the devils, or prophesy future

<column-break/>

things from crystals and mirrors. I beg Your Imperial Majesty not to give a hearing to those who, out of ignorance of the Divine Law, believe such messengers of the Devil are useful people to the Empire because they know how to drive out sorcery with sorcery. For this harmful healing of the body is the death of the soul; it causes men to fall away from the Creator of all creatures and to cling to the apostate and damned devils, with whom they shall also be eternally damned after death.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin>
The second reason why Almighty God allows even innocent people to be bewitched and harmed is for greater merit; namely, so that after the trial and proof of their faith, they may deserve and obtain a crown of honor that is all the more glorious. For as St. Augustine says, man himself does not know what he can suffer or what he might not be able to endure. Sometimes he fears he cannot withstand and bear that which he actually can; when the temptation comes and, as it were, questions him, he finds himself to be a man who previously did not know what he was. Before the temptation began, neither the Chief Apostle Peter nor others knew of him that he was so reckless and weak. But when it came to the encounter, his hidden weakness became manifest. Therefore, temptation is the best test of man, as the Holy Scripture testifies: Just as the furnace proves the new pots, so tribulation proves the senses of man. It is good to be patient when things go well and no tribulation troubles the heart. The righteous must suffer much, but our Lord Jesus Christ helps them out of it all.

-># The Opinion of Johannes Trithemius<-

Since it is only fair that he who wantonly falls away from the truth and becomes an adherent of lies should be plunged into destruction by the devil.

<margin>VIII. Reason.</margin>
The eighth reason is the revelation of Divine power and authority over all created beings. For when Almighty God occasionally permits and allows the devil to do great things, but on the other hand turns away other minor things, he thereby gives it to be understood how weak the enemy of the human race is, and that he must be obedient to the Divine Majesty in all things. For the devil is capable of nothing by himself, but everything he does, he accomplishes through God's providence and permission.

Thus the main reason for which Almighty God permits sorcery <note>original: "Zauberey"</note> is the justice of God, through which he maintains and preserves in correct order the free will which he initially gave to man. But since all power that creatures have received from their Creator is measured and circumscribed, it appears from this that neither the devil nor man—however evil his intentions might otherwise be—is capable of everything he would like to do. The will is indeed free, but the power has its determined goal and measure. If the devils were capable of everything they wished to do, nothing on the entire earth would be safe from them; instead, they would throw everything into a heap. But that the devils have only a measured power is sufficiently proven by the example of Holy Job, whom Satan dared not touch further than was allowed and permitted to him by God. No man in the whole world, however pious and strong he might be, would be able to withstand the devil's wrath and raging if they had free power to harm whomever they wanted at any time. Before the suffering of Christ, they exercised greater power. After

<column-break/>

Christ died for us on the tree of the Cross, however, their power was thereafter greatly diminished and lessened, as our Savior says in the Gospel: <margin>John 12</margin> <note>original: "Ioan. 12."</note> *Now shall the prince of this world be cast out.* For Christ's humility and the constancy of the saints have greatly weakened the power of the devils, so that they may well be called the instigators, but not the establishers of evil. Also, the devil would have no power over us if he did not obtain strength from our sins. Therefore the Scripture admonishes us and says: <margin>James 4</margin> <note>original: "Iacob. 4."</note> *Resist the devil, and he will flee from you;* and again: <margin>Ephesians 4</margin> <note>original: "Ephes. 4."</note> *Give no place to the devil.*

To conclude my speech: I believe one can sufficiently understand from the reasons recounted how the question of why God permits so much evil is to be answered. For although the devils always have evil in mind, their power is never unjust; since they have the evil will from themselves, but the power to accomplish the evil they have from God alone—and let that be said of those who do evil.

<margin>Reason why God also lets pious people be bewitched and harmed.</margin>
But why does Almighty God permit the devils, through witches <note>original: "Hexen"</note> and monsters <note>original: "Unholden" - often used for demons or malevolent spirits</note>, to harm such people who are baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity and believe in the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ? For if they only did harm to the bodies and goods of evil, godless, and unbelieving people, but had to spare the pious, God-fearing, and believing, then one could hold that the permission of God was fair and right. Now, however, pious and innocent people are also frequently harmed by devils through sorcery, and sometimes even deprived of their lives—to say nothing of the damage and loss that the bewitched must suffer in temporal goods. This causes heavy thoughts for many: why Almighty God, who allows nothing evil, permits and ordains such things.

# Opinions of Several Highly Learned Men

<margin>Psalm 73.</margin>
The wicked <note>original: "losen"</note> are not in trouble as other folk are, and are not plagued like other men. Therefore, their defiance must be a precious thing, and their gluttony must be called well-done. Their person struts like a fat belly. It is a special grace of God that he visits pious and God-fearing people—whom he knows are created such that they cannot be humbled through good days—with the Cross <note>A common metaphor for suffering or divine trials</note>. For many are humbled through tribulation who would have been made proud by great fortune. Lastly, the worry and fear of sorcery <term>Zauberey: witchcraft or magic</term> drives a pious person to fear his God and to call upon Him for help and assistance, so that he remains secured and preserved against the Devil’s assault. But no proud or presumptuous person should think that he is free and safe from the Devil’s sorcery. For when God withdraws his hand from a puffed-up, gluttonous person, he has nothing more certain to expect than the Devil’s deceit.

<margin>IV. Reason.</margin>
The fourth reason is so that a distinction remains between the good and the evil. For the Holy Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles concerning pious people who are pleasing to God:
<margin>Acts 14.</margin>
> We must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

<margin>2 Timothy 3.</margin>
And **St. Paul**, the lover of Christ, says in an Epistle:
> All that will live godly in Christ Jesus must suffer persecution.

<margin>Proverbs 3.</margin>
The wise King Solomon also says in the Proverbs:
> Whom the Lord loveth he correcteth, and hath delight in him, even as a father in his son.

It is glorious and well-suited for a Christian to suffer adversity for God’s sake, whether it comes from evil men or from the Devil. Power is given to the Devil and his servants to offend the pious and the righteous, not to their destruction—as the common, coarse rabble <note>original: "Pöfel"</note> thinks—but much more to the great and certain comfort of the soul. For when a pious person leads a godly life, never

<column-break/>

offending or harming anyone, doing no one injustice, loving, fearing, and honoring God his Lord with his whole heart, and diligently keeping His commandments before his eyes, and yet is nonetheless plagued by sorcerers in body and property, or even in both together, then he is certainly a blessed man who, after enduring the trial, shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to all who love Him. When one lives piously in the unity of the Christian faith in the Catholic Church, and suffers adversity in this world for God’s sake and endures it patiently, it is a sign that God loves him and will make him blessed. Therefore, we read in the Scripture concerning evil and godless people thus:
<margin>Job 21.</margin>
> Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, and increase in goods? Their seed is established in their sight, and their offspring are with them; their house has peace from fear, and the rod of God is not upon them. They grow old in good days, and in a moment they go down to hell <note>original: "Helle"</note> with a fright.

For it is a certain sign of damnation if you live sumptuously here on Earth and resist God with sins and vices, even if you have great wealth, a healthy body, and good fortune.

<margin>V. Reason.</margin>
The fifth reason why Almighty God allows pious and godly people to be plagued by the evil and godless is the perfect purification of the mind <note>original: "gemühtes"</note>; for as the Scripture says:
<margin>1 Kings 8. 2 Chronicles 6.</margin>
> There is no man so righteous on earth that always doeth good and sinneth not.

But because God lets no sin go unpunished, He ordains for pious people, according to His mercy, bodily punishment for their sins; but for the evil and godless, according to His justice, He ordains eternal pain and punishment. And thus, according to His great mercy, He transforms for the repentant the eternal pain into a temporal punishment, which they either here...

For the plagues of the godless serve as a healing medicine for the pious and godly people, but for the originators and perpetrators, they lead to eternal damnation.

<margin>6th Cause.</margin>
The sixth cause is that the person who is attacked and enchanted by the Devil may thereby be moved to repentance and conversion, and as is necessary, resolve in his heart to improve his life. For Almighty God does not hasten so quickly to vengeance and punishment when we have sinned, but waits for our improvement until the appointed time; but when we do not convert, He comes with punishment when we least expect it. And because we do not wish to recognize ourselves as sinners and convert while in good peace, we must finally recognize it late enough. Therefore the Prophet says in the person of God:
<margin>Psalm 89.</margin>

<margin>7th Cause.</margin>
The seventh cause why God permits the devils to practice sorcery <note>original: "Zauberey"</note> over pious and innocent people is that He wishes to suppress their wantonness and opportunity to sin; for there are many poor, sick people who please God well—pious, devout, and humble—whom poverty and physical weakness keep in the love of God. If these people were to float along in wealth and honors, they might soon abandon their holy purpose and fall into all manner of sin and vice. It is not beneficial for all men

<column-break/>

in their salvation to float along in honors and wealth with a healthy body; nor does a long life always make a person more pious. Therefore, when Almighty God wishes to show His mercy to the elect, He allows pious, righteous, and innocent people to be burdened with much adversity. He withdraws wealth and honor from them, sometimes through the devils, sometimes through evil men, or through some other means and ways, because He knows they would misuse such things. Thus, through poverty and misery, He keeps them in the humility which they could easily have forgotten amidst great goods and high standing. He also frequently sends great and heavy illnesses to their house, because the desired physical health could have given birth to great illnesses of the soul. Finally, He even allows some to be executed through sorcery, thereby cutting off and strangling the desire for sin into which they might have fallen had they lived longer. Therefore the Scripture says of a pious man:
<margin>Wisdom 4.</margin>
> He was taken away, lest that wickedness should alter his understanding, or deceit beguile his soul. <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom, often cited in funeral contexts to explain early death.</note>

<margin>8th Cause.</margin>
The eighth cause of Divine permission <note>original: "Göttlichen verhengnuß"</note> is so that men might learn to honor the Sacraments of the Church, which have a great power against all the sorcery and damage of evil spirits. For whoever uses the Sacraments and ordinances of the Catholic Church with proper reverence is seldom harmed by devilish sorcery. We have often heard that the witches and monsters <note>original: "Hexen vnd Unholden"</note> themselves have confessed that the Devil's power is violently broken by hearing Mass and other consecrated things of the Church. For one does not consecrate such things in the Church in vain, but so that they may be terrifying signs which we can show to the devils as seals of Divine protection and shield, with which we are guarded from the young—

# Concerning Witches and Sorcerers.
<note>original: "Von Hexen vnd Unholden." The term 'Unholden' refers to malevolent supernatural beings or sorcerers.</note>

## Page 367

even if they had confessed something and evidence <term>Indicia: legal signs or clues of guilt</term> was present that they might be guilty. Even then, they were not immediately seized. Instead, first and foremost, in the places where they resided and where the suspicion and rumors regarding them were greatest, the officials conducted a diligent inquiry into all suspicions and circumstances—such as harm to livestock or people—to determine whether the matters arising in the <term>Inquisition: the formal judicial inquiry</term> had actually occurred in reality. 

If it was then found that such inquiry and experience agreed with the previous suspicion, rumors, and reports, and there were strong presumptions that the suspected person might be guilty, only then was that person taken into custody and imprisoned. They were then earnestly questioned regarding the suspicions and accusations, though initially without the use of <term>Tortur: judicial torture</term>. 

If they were unwilling to confess anything voluntarily, the church ministers and preachers were brought in to attempt, through the Word of God, to see if they could bring forth a voluntary and unforced confession (to which more credit is given than to those extracted by force) through Christian remembrance and admonition, for the sake of the salvation of their souls and true repentance for their sins. 

If this also proved ineffective, they were legally charged for the <term>peinlich frage: the "painful question," a legal euphemism for interrogation under torture</term>. Once this was permitted by a judicial ruling—and never undertaken without such a legal ruling—they were then put to the question. Whether they confessed something during the torture or not, the church ministers nonetheless continued to admonish them toward a later true confession for the sake of greater certainty. 

And if they admitted guilt and persisted in it, the criminal proceedings were continued against them as is proper, and whatever sentence was judged was executed upon them. Thus, everything was handled with all good foresight and discretion (which is highly necessary in such slippery matters where the Devil can easily introduce and use all kinds of blindness and deceit, thereby attempting to harm even innocent people). Your Graces did not wish to withhold all of this from the other already written correspondence as a dutiful reply. Dated the twenty-second of June, in the year [fifteen] sixty-three.

->To our highly esteemed good Friend and<-

And namely, for the first, the N. N. <note>N. N. stands for *Nomen Nominandum*, used here to protect or omit the specific names of the accused women</note> confessed to the seventh interrogatory that she had several times had fellowship with the Evil Foe.

To the eleventh, that she danced with him and was often present at the dance.

To the fifteenth and sixteenth, that she was present twice when they deliberated and made fire and weather <note>Weather-making was a specific category of witchcraft believed to destroy crops</note> to the damage of people, cattle, vineyards, fruits, and other crops, etc.

To the twenty-seventh, that she bewitched cattle and milked several cows, one of which died, etc.

N., N. N., and N. N., and boiled the herbs in N. N.’s house.

To the twenty-third and twenty-fourth: she bewitched people and cattle.

Confessed to the seventh, ninth, tenth, and eleventh: she had (as one gathers from the answer) often had fellowship and danced with the Evil Spirit.

### The Fourth N. N.

Confessed in general: she had (as one notes) often had fellowship and danced with the Evil Foe, and helped make the weather and frost around Walpurgis; they boiled the herbs which the Evil Spirit gave them in the field; she, the N. N., bewitched a gunsmith at N. so that he can neither stand nor walk.

And it is the confession of them all in common: they took money from the Evil Spirit, which then undoubtedly enticed and caused them to follow him in such a manner.

But because they are Christians and have accepted Baptism and the Gospel of Christ, they should have rejected such fellowship and dealings with the Evil Spirit, and refrained from the Devil’s art such as sorcery, etc., which is so strictly forbidden; as Augustine mentions and describes in Book 1 of *On Christian Doctrine*, [defining] what kind of fellowship and doing such is. <note>original: "Inquiens, omnes artes huiusmodi vel nugatoriæ vel noxiæ superstitionis ex quadam pestifera societate hominum & dæmonum quasi pacta infidelis & dolosæ amicitiæ constituta, penitus sunt repudiandæ & fugiendæ Christiano, vt translatiue habetur, in ca. illud quidam. in fin. 26. q. 2."</note> Saying: **All arts of this kind, whether of trifling or noxious superstition, arising from a certain pestiferous association of men and demons, as if constituted by a pact of faithless and deceitful friendship, are to be utterly repudiated and avoided by a Christian.** As is held in translation in the chapter *illud quidam* at the end of [Canon Law] 26, question 2.

# On Witches and Monsters.
## Ii iij

Therefore, such acts are considered <term>Maleficia</term> <note>original: "Maleficia"; refers to harmful magic or "evil-doing"</note> and great misdeeds, and the perpetrators are held to be enemies of Christ, and both are condemned, as per the chapter *Sortes* and the chapter *peruenit* 26. question 5.

Furthermore, these practitioners of this diabolical religion are called evildoers, enemies of the human race and of human society, and foes of the common welfare, in whatever part of the world or in whatever rank they may be established; and they are to be punished with a penalty worthy of their own crime, as per Julius Caesar and the Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius in the law *Et si excepta*, and the final law in the Code concerning Evildoers and Mathematicians <note>In Roman law, "mathematicians" often referred to astrologers or diviners.</note>.

Their art or damned diabolical profession is called <term>Malefica</term> for this reason: because it always tends toward evil, as Paolo Grillandi relates in his treatise *On Heretics and Fortune-tellers*, question 2, collection 3. Also question 3, number 20.

And if the deeds committed and confessed by these four accused women are rightly weighed, one finds that they are not minor, but the greatest misdeeds imaginable. For they do not only damage, weaken, and ruin people, cattle, crops, and other earthly things, etc., but also—to say nothing of the perpetrators' own souls—they insult the <term>Divine Majesty</term> <note>original: "Göttliche Maiestet"; a legal term for God, mirroring "Lese-majesty" or treason against a monarch</note> itself in the highest and most public way. This occurs not in one, but in many ways, which in this case can be attributed to them both literally and by interpretation: such as <term>Apostasy</term> <note>abandoning the faith</note>, <term>Prevarication</term> <note>betrayal of duty</note>, <term>Blasphemy</term>, <term>Sorcery</term> <note>original: "Sortilegium"</note>, <term>Incantation</term>, and the like.

Now, among all sins, vices, and misdeeds, the vice of insulted <term>Divine Majesty</term> is the highest, heaviest, and greatest; for it is far more serious and unjustifiable to grieve or insult the eternal and heavenly Majesty than the temporal and earthly Majesty. As is read and noted in the chapter *Vergentes in senium* and there in the notable gloss on the word "more seriously," and in the authentic *Gazaros* in the Code on Heretics and Manichaeans.

Furthermore, a sin committed against God is greater than one committed against man, because that which is committed against the Deity or against divine Religion results in injury to all and is a public

<column-break/>

crime committed, per the chapter *Sicut qui Ecclesiam* 17. quest. 4. and the chapter *cum secundum leges* on Heretics, book 6, express text, in the law *Manicheos* after the beginning of the Code on Heretics and Manichaeans.

And the vice, sin, or misdeed is so much greater and heavier as the Person against whom the sin and offense is committed is more worthy. As from the gloss (bringing forth examples) in chapter 1, on the word "Especially" regarding calumny, and the clear text in the chapter *A Christian Man*, Distinction 40. Bartolus in section *Si vero* number 2, in the authentic on not alienating or exchanging, collection 2.

Since, then, the transgression, misdeed, or sin against the <term>Divine Majesty</term> itself is much higher and greater than if it were done against any human—as the above-cited chapter *Vergentes* demonstrates—it follows necessarily from common law that it must be punished in the highest and sharpest manner. For the mentioned laws and their scholars ordain and will that the pain or punishment be equal to the misdeed and offense. As is the text in the chapter *fœlicis*, section *Illud autem* (there): "The judge shall measure the punishment from the guilt, so that the vengeance proceeds according to what the excess demands," etc., and in the section *præmissis* (there: "The punishment should be proportioned to the crime," etc.) on punishments, book 6. Panormitanus in the chapter *Nisi specialis*, number 5, on the office of the legate.

As Pietro Filippo Corneo, Counsel 57, number 6, volume 1, explicitly indicates with these round words serving our case, saying: "Punishments should be commensurate with the gravity of the crime, for he who sins more seriously should be punished more seriously," alleging the chapter *Sicut dignum* on Homicide, with similar cases.

Thereupon, for the explanation of such aforementioned points and the highest misdeeds committed by the four accused women, it is to be noted and observed how such things are punished or ought to be punished by common laws.

And there is a great difference in such a case between the pain and punishment of Spiritual Law <note>Canon Law</note> and those which would be imposed by Secular Law.

But because in this case, regarding the <term>Criminal Accusation</term> <note>original: "Peinliche anklage"; a formal charge involving physical or capital punishment</note> that has occurred, nothing can be done with the punishments of Spiritual Law—

For although we concede that all such operations are not primarily performed by them, the witches, but by the Devil through God’s permission and for the sake of our sins, it is nonetheless also true—as daily experience shows and can be witnessed with many true examples—that witches, by means of their consorting with the Devil, may indeed do harm to people, cattle, and the fruits of the field. Therefore, they are his slaves <note>original: "Mancipia"</note>, hang upon him, and do all his will, even if they do not know otherwise. And even if they do not surrender themselves to him with express words, nor deny God, they are nonetheless attached and devoted to the Devil through their works. They certainly can have no right invocation, repentance, faith, trust, or love for God (who suffers no fellowship with Belial <note>A biblical name for the Devil or personification of worthlessness</note>), even if they go to the sermon or the Holy Supper deceptively to maintain appearances and break the people's evil suspicion.

Since such women also cause public and notorious damage, whatever it may be, we are of the opinion (let Dr. Wier write what he will) that they should be punished from life to death according to the Law of the Lord in Exodus 22 <note>A reference to Exodus 22:18: "Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live."</note>, etc., and according to the Imperial Laws and common custom. This is to punish such a highly forbidden vice and also to provide security and peace to the neighbors and other pious people who must otherwise live in constant fear of such evil women.

<column-break/>

As the late Dr. Martin Luther was also of such an opinion, as indicated in the previously mentioned advice, and is further confirmed by Johannes Aurifaber in the mentioned Dr. Luther’s *Table Talk* in the 26th Title. There he writes, among other things, that Dr. Luther spoke in the year [15]38, saying that one should have no mercy on the thieves of eggs, milk, and butter, and that he, Dr. Luther, would burn them himself, as one reads in the Old Law that the priests began to stone the evildoers, etc. Now, if one should have no mercy on such milk-thieves, etc., how much less should one have mercy on those who steal one's bodily health, lame them, torment them with gruesome pains, and often even kill them? As Dr. L[uther] himself relates at the beginning of that same 26th Title, several examples occurred to his mother, a pious pastor’s wife (who was bewitched to death), and to himself.

Thus, we have our opinion and good consideration, round and clear, regarding the *Thesis* <note>The general principle or theoretical case</note>: whether, when, and how to proceed with punishment against witches or sorceresses.

However, as far as the *Hypothesis* <note>The specific application to the current case</note> is concerned—namely, whether such actions should be taken against the aforementioned imprisoned and accused witches—

We cannot decisively determine anything on that point, nor resolve it ourselves, because of the deficiencies indicated and mentioned above.

But since these deficiencies will be no deficiencies to Your Honors and Graces, as you well know the women and all their circumstances, or may hereafter specifically inquire, we wish to leave the final decision of this matter—and how much weight is to be given to the evil confessions of these imprisoned women <note>original: "confessionibus istarum carceratarum"</note>—to you.

### The final opinion of the advocates at N. N. concerning the three cited sorceresses.

That sorcerers and sorceresses, on account of such their <term>malefice</term> <note>harmful magic or criminal wrongdoing</note>, may be sentenced to death and punished, there is no doubt; for such is expressly ordained in both Divine and Imperial Secular Law, and has also become the established custom everywhere.

However, it must also be clearly proven that such persons, who are to be so sentenced and punished, are indeed sorcerers and sorceresses.

Therefore, in the present case, concerning the three arrested female persons suspected of sorcery, the entire deliberation rests solely upon whether it is proven that they are persons worthy of such punishment.

Now, we find in their <term>confessions</term> <note>original: "vergichten," a legal term for a confession made under or after torture</note>, as well as in the inquiries made regarding them with other persons, not many acts showing that they have done specific damage to cattle and people through weather-making or other sorcery.

For N. N., the first, confesses no more (as far as the damage is concerned) than that she bewitched N. N.’s wife so that she got a bad leg; likewise, she gave N. N.’s little child <term>Welsh-seed</term> <note>likely a reference to a poisonous plant or foreign seed used as a toxin</note> for its "great fog" <note>possibly a reference to a respiratory ailment or "clouding" of the senses</note> (to which her <term>paramour</term> <note>the devil or a familiar spirit</note> also contributed his part), so that it subsequently died; which confessions are then also strengthened by the inquiry.

So N. N., the second, has only confessed of two

<column-break/>

storms which she helped to make, from which the vineyards froze; likewise, that she gave N. N.’s child a "grip" <note>a touch or a sudden seizure</note>, which subsequently died; of which also much is found in the inquiry, so that it is believable that it was done by her, N.

Likewise, the third, N. N. (who has not been involved in such dealings for much more than two years), confesses no more than that she poured a drink—which her paramour had taught and commanded her—into the wine that N. N. drank in her house, from which he became ill, wasted away, and died; which confession is also strengthened by the inquiry. The rest, concerning the two dead cows of her father, is contradicted by her brother, though he himself is suspicious in this matter and not entirely credible.

Now, whether these three should be punished for so few misdeeds, just like other well-practiced and harmful sorceresses, is a matter for consideration.

But alongside this, it is also true that the aforementioned N. confessed that she surrendered herself to the Evil One three years ago, and N. N. that she did so eleven years ago, and in the meantime stayed with him, and did his will as often as he wanted, and had <term>intercourse</term> <note>original: "gemeinsamet," implying both social and sexual association with the devil</note> with him consistently.

And although we might consider such intercourse to be a fantasy, it is nevertheless certain that the women believed no differently than that it truly happened so, and that on their part, there was no lack of good will, even if it had actually happened that way.

So N. N. has likewise confessed that two years ago, she also surrendered herself to the Evil One and promised to follow him with a hand-clasp of loyalty.

From this, <term>apostasy</term> <note>original: "Apostasia," the total desertion of the Christian faith</note> and the denial of God are publicly evident, which <term>malefice</term> alone (as committed against the first commandment of the first table <note>The first of the Two Tables of the Ten Commandments, concerning duties to God</note>) is to be punished <term>capitally</term> <note>original: "Capitaliter," by death</note>.

Now, when the above-mentioned pieces, which each of the arrested persons further committed—though they be few, yet they include several <term>homicides</term> <note>original: "Homicidia"</note>—are added to the fact that they presumably committed much more in so many years than they have confessed, and...

Because it is also to be feared—even if mercy were shown to these three female persons to spare their lives—that they would nevertheless have no peace from the devil, to whom they once surrendered themselves and whose will they have done so much; rather, just as before, they would be compelled to remain attached to him. # Of Witches and Monsters.
->Aaa ij<-

...denied God, renounced Him, and cursed Him, while the others did not do so at all.

They also caused varying degrees of damage with their sorcery (although I do not hold such matters in high regard); specifically, the last woman, <term>N. N.</term> <note>N. N. is a standard legal placeholder for a name, similar to "Jane Doe."</note>, performed no sorcery at all, nor did she do anything else except that she was led to the dance twice, had relations with him <note>the Devil</note> only that many times, and is said to have been involved in such dealings for only two years. All of this is according to the aforementioned confessions, which were not taken with the greatest diligence; the questioning could certainly have been done better and more completely.

In addition to this, it must be considered that these five persons all (as I understand from the court records) recognize their seductions, express regret for them, and wish to turn back to God. <note>Latin: Et ita pœnitentia suâ profitetur &c.</note> *And so he/she professes by his/her repentance, etc.*

Now, however, there is a great distinction between those witches who have denied God and those who have not; those who have caused harm and those who have caused no harm; likewise, those who persist in their errors and hold fast to their idol or paramour, and those who renounce the same and hold again to God. From this, it is to be concluded that regarding their punishment, the aforementioned persons should by no means be treated with equal severity.

It is true that it is commanded in Exodus chapter 22: <note>Latin: Maleficas nō patieris viuere</note> *You shall not suffer a sorceress to live,* and as the late Doctor Luther translated it into German: "The witches you shall not let live." Doctor Luther also wrote to this effect in his book *On the Councils and the Church* and elsewhere, stating that such people should be burned, using these words:

"The Devil, God’s ape, also works nothing but what is temporal; or where it is meant to be spiritual, it is pure deception. For he cannot thereby eternally forgive sins and bring salvation, as he lies through holy water, masses, and monkery—even if he can make a cow give her milk again, which he himself previously stole through his prophets and priests. Among Christians, these are called the Devil’s whores, and where they are caught, they should be burned with fire as is right—not because of the theft of milk, but because of the blasphemy by which the Devil strengthens his sacraments and churches against Christ."

But I understand all of this with the aforementioned distinction regarding those truly 

<column-break/>

apostate, stubborn, and harmful true witches; but not regarding those who are merely seduced through phantasms <note>Latin: per phantasmata</note> (as shall be further explained hereafter) <note>Latin: Et quæ vlterius ad actus nouos non progressæ sunt.</note> *And those who have not progressed further to new acts.*

Paulus Grillandus writes thus in his treatise on sorcery, question 7, number 36: <note>Latin: & nota vnum valde singulare, quod istarum apostasiarum duæ sunt species...</note> *And note one very singular thing: that there are two species of these apostasies. One is that which simply falls back from the faith and follows the worship and obedience of the demon. The other is that which, after denying the faith of Christ, casting it behind and throwing it out of the heart, baptizes itself again expressly in the name of the Devil and takes another name upon itself. Although both species are condemned, the former, if she recants her sin, is admitted to penance and avoids physical punishment just like heretics (as in the Law regarding Manichaeans in the Code on Heretics). The second species, however, is never admitted to penance in a judicial court so that she might avoid physical punishment, even if she were to abjure that profession a thousand times and wish to return to Christ, etc.* From which it could be concluded in our case that not even the first witch, Anna Gerhardes, should be afflicted with physical punishment, since she simply denied the faith—much less the others, who did not deny the faith at all.

But be that as it may, in the present matter I am briefly of the opinion that the first four might be executed with fire together. This is not precisely because they were led to the dance at night and had fellowship with the evil spirit (since such things are uncertain, doubtful matters upon which nothing should be grounded, as will follow hereafter), but because, in addition to attaching themselves to the Evil One, they surrendered themselves entirely to his will—whether he actually and truly dealt with them or not—and carried it out. Furthermore, they caused apparent harm by making weather <note>The belief that witches could conjure storms or hail to destroy crops.</note> and damaging and ruining people and cattle. They also persisted in such heretical vice for many years: the fourth for thirty years, the second for fifteen years, and the other two (the first and third) for four or five years (according to their own words). It is entirely to be presumed that over such a long time they committed much more harm and evil than they admit in their confessions, etc.

Also, such blasphemous and highly damaging vice must be punished for the sake of the common good, as an example and a horror to the wicked and frivolous, and for the 
->pious<-

# Opinions of Several Highly Learned Men

But in order to ensure safety, and so that people may be free from further worry regarding such women, should they not be earnestly punished according to the aforementioned commandment of the Lord: <term>maleficas non patieris vivere</term> <note>Latin: "You shall not permit sorceresses to live" (Exodus 22:18).</note>?

Yet, alongside this, every diligence should be applied so that they are best maintained in the repentance of their misdeeds and conversion to God. Thus, even if earthly life cannot be granted to them without great offense and worry to the pious, they may still be made partakers of God's grace after their punishment has been endured. However, as for the suggestion that they should be dragged to the place of execution by irrational beasts <note>i.e., horses or oxen</note>, as mentioned in the previously cited counsel, I consider this to be consistent neither with the law nor with common custom.

As far as the fifth person is concerned, N.N. <note>A placeholder for a name, similar to "John/Jane Doe"</note>, since she was present at these dealings for only a short time through the seduction of her own biological mother, and otherwise practiced no sorcery, did no harm, nor acted in any other way than being taken once or twice to the dance and (in her own opinion) having fellowship with the Evil One—but now she regrets this and has turned back to God—I would not only refuse to condemn her to the fire like the others, but would also not burden her with any particular physical punishment, according to the teaching of <term>Doctor Paulus Grillandus</term> <note>A 16th-century Italian jurist known for his writings on witchcraft and crime.</note>. Indeed, it seems to me that for the reasons mentioned above, and in view of her youth (especially since the others themselves partly say she came to it innocently), she might be shown mercy in such a way: that she be banished from the city of N. (so that she is out of the sight of the people who held and might still hold her in suspicion), but be allowed to swear an oath to remain within the territory of N., so that one might keep a better eye on her to ensure she conducts herself in a truly Christian and pious manner. She would then live under such great and constant concern that, should she make herself suspicious or suspected in the slightest way again, she would immediately have the judge and sentence upon her neck.

That I do not give so much weight to the "night-traveling," the dancing, or the fellowship, is moved by the fact that I find many excellent learned men of old

<column-break/>

and also in our own times, who state and demonstrate most impressively (even with the authority of the Canons of the Holy Fathers) that this night-traveling and such nocturnal dances and banquets, as well as the physical mingling that the evil spirits are said to perform with women, is a pure dream, phantom, deception, and an unbelievable and impossible thing. This is despite the fact that the <term>Inquisitores haereticae pravitatis</term> <note>Latin: "Inquisitors of heretical depravity."</note> (for their own profit) and others have heavily reinforced such unbelief through many fabricated, untrustworthy examples—as found in the <term>Malleus Maleficarum</term> <note>The "Hammer of Witches," a famous 15th-century treatise on hunting witches.</note>, the *Formicarius*, and the aforementioned <term>D. Grillandus</term> and others who cling to the Papacy—and have made them seem believable, even against all reason and natural understanding.

> For it was decided long ago in a council <note>Referring to the Canon Episcopi, a medieval legal text.</note> that such witches and sorceresses are not transported locally to those places where they say they have been, but only phantasmally, through the illusion of demons. As is reported in Chapter *Episcopi* 26, question 5, where among other things it is said: "Therefore, priests throughout the churches committed to them must preach to the people of God with all urgency, so they may know these things to be entirely false, and that such phantasms are brought into the minds of the faithful not by a divine spirit, but by a malignant one. For Satan himself, who transforms himself into an angel of light, when he has captured the mind of any woman and subjugated her through unbelief, immediately transforms himself into the shapes and likenesses of various persons. Deluding the mind he holds captive in dreams, showing now joyful things, now sad, now known persons, now unknown, he leads them through pathless places. And while the spirit alone suffers this, the unfaithful person thinks this happens not in the soul, but in the body. For who is not led out of himself in sleep and nocturnal visions, seeing many things while sleeping that he never saw while awake? Who indeed would be so foolish and dull-witted as to think all these things, which happen only in the spirit, also occur in the body? For the Prophet Ezekiel saw and heard the visions of the Lord in the spirit, not in the body, as he himself says: 'I was in the spirit.' And Paul does not dare to say he was snatched up in the body."

Therefore, such transportations happen only phantasmally, which is further demonstrated with many arguments by Giovanni Francesco Ponzinibio in his treatise *On Witches*, number 45 and following; and in our century by the most learned men, Martín de Arles, Theologian, in his treatise *On Superstitions*, chapter 6; and Girolamo Cardano, book 18, regarding the "ointment of witches" in *On Subtlety*, and again in book 15, chapter 80, *On the Variety of Things*, where he elegantly provides the reasons...

-># On Witches and Sorcerers.<-

->Kk iij<-

<note>The text begins with a series of citations from Renaissance scholars who argued that witchcraft was often a result of mental illness or demonic deception rather than physical reality.</note> ...yields an increase of such absurd delusions.) And Giambattista della Porta of Naples <note>original: "Ioan. Bapt. à porta Neapoli"</note> in book 11 of *Natural Magic*, chapter 26. And finally, Johann Weyer <note>original: "Ioan. Vvierus Grauianus"</note>, in the book *On the Deceptions of Demons*, book 2, chapter 31.

The same must be felt and said regarding the illusions of demonic intercourse <note>original: "dæmoniaci concubitus"</note>, of which we spoke above; these things often happen even to honorable and upright matrons, as Martin de Arles testifies in the said *Tract on Superstitions*, chapter 7. Cardanus also says this in chapter 80, and Weyer demonstrates it most diligently and copiously in the said book, from chapter 33 through chapter 43 inclusive, with many reasons and authorities alleged therein. Among others is Cassian, who says: "In no way is it to be believed that spiritual figures can naturally copulate with women." Since things stand this way, I do not see by what law—unless it be the "highest law," which is also called the "highest injustice" <note>A reference to the Latin maxim *Summum ius, summa iniuria*, meaning that the law applied too strictly becomes an injustice.</note>—that fifth woman, N. N., could be condemned to the punishment of death and even of fire (which is considered the most severe), solely on account of such illusions, when in other matters she was harmless. Certainly, in a doubtful matter, it is no less just than it is safe to follow the more merciful interpretation. As the jurist Marcellus says in the law *Ea quae*, section 1, in the Digest *On the Rules of Law*, and the laws *Quoties* and *In ambiguis* in the same title.

Regarding the second point, namely those women who were accused by the one now in custody of having been seen at her **Devil’s Dance** <note>The "Sabbath" or gathering of witches.</note>, etc. To that I answer again briefly: if one or more of them had been under such evil suspicion and rumor before this accusation, and if there were sufficient <term>indicia</term> <note>Legal "indications" or pieces of evidence required to justify torture or formal charges.</note> and signs that they might belong to such a category and company, then they might well have been taken into custody even without such an accusation, and dealt with as highly suspicious persons.

But what such <term>indicia</term> and signs are, which are sufficient for such suspicion of female sorcerers, are explained in the 44th Article of the **Imperial Constitutio Criminalis Carolina** <note>original: "peinlichen Halßgerichtes Ordnung," the unified criminal code of the Holy Roman Empire established in 1532.</note> with these words:

"Likewise, if someone offers to teach people <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "Zauberey"</note>, or threatens to bewitch someone else, and such a thing happens to the person threatened; also if one has special fellowship with sorcerers and witches, or deals with such

<column-break/>

suspicious things, gestures, words, and behaviors that suggest sorcery, and the person is otherwise notorious for the same. That gives a legitimate sign of sorcery and sufficient cause for <term>judicial torture</term> <note>original: "peinliche frage"</note>, etc." Where these important and clear signs and <term>indicia</term> are lacking, the authorities should by no means be moved to arrest others whom the imprisoned witch names, for the following reasons:

**First**, that such poor women are themselves deceived and never actually came to a dance (as is proven above), but what they see is nothing other than a dream through the deception of the Evil Spirit; and what he represents to them, they see. Therefore, one should not rely at all on their deceptive accusations.

**Second**, because it is known that the Evil One is particularly hateful and hostile toward pious people, and for that reason he attacks them however he can. It would be easy for him to practice this against any honest woman (whom he can easily represent to such [imprisoned] women in their sleep, according to the text in the canon *Episcopi* <note>A medieval legal decree stating that the "Witches' Sabbath" was a mental delusion caused by the Devil, not a physical reality.</note>), if such deceptive and uncertain accusations were to be followed.

**Third**, because we know from experience that often such evil women have falsely accused innocent, pious, and noble women, partly out of hatred and envy—because they are suffering and would like to see the whole world burn if they must burn—and partly because they hope that if the authorities refuse to seize such [noble] accused women, they might then also have to let the prisoners go free and unpunished.

# On Witches and Sorceresses
## Section Ak iij

Even with a probable public rumor, a judge ought not to proceed even to an arrest, according to Angelo Aretino in his *Treatise on Crimes* <note>original: "tract. malefic."</note> under the heading "Public Rumor"; indeed, according to Mario Socini in his *Treatise on Citations*, Article 11, Question 24. Furthermore, the crime must be fully established before an arrest is made, as reported and followed by Egidio Bossi in his *Criminal Treatise* in the title on arrests. For this reason, Jodocus Damhouder in his *Handbook of Criminal Matters* <note>original: "Enchiridion rerum criminalium"</note> in the title on citing the accused or arrest, number 7 and following, vehemently attacks those officers of justice who, by their own whim, rashly arrest anyone reported to them at any time without an urgent cause and based on "wind," as he calls it. For he writes that a no small injury is done to one so arrested—indeed, an irreversible disgrace—as witnessed by Baldus in the first law on the restoration of integrity. Many points are also alleged in Law 4, paragraph "If anyone has been condemned," number 22 and following, regarding the judgment of matters; for that reason, such officers should be subject to no small punishment. Paris de Puteo also notes this in his *Treatise on Syndics* under the word "Torture." Furthermore, a confession extracted through torture without preceding legitimate evidence <note>term: indicia; legal signs or clues that suggest guilt</note> is null, even if ratified immediately afterward or after an interval while the accused remains in custody of the same judge, nor does it prejudice the one confessing, according to Mathefillanus, Hippolytus de Marsiliis, and Thomas Grammaticus.

And although it might be said here that "one does not break a hunting-right for a single fox" <note>A proverb suggesting that the law shouldn't be too concerned with the rights of "lowly" people</note> and that it does not matter much if one deals harshly with such lowly women, etc.; yet it is not fitting for us to respond or advise in any way other than what is consistent with the Law.

Whether, in the present case, the reputation or the common outcry that has pursued these two women—as well as the evidence and indications brought forward alongside it—are sufficient to take them into custody and, consequently, to torture them, is what must be further discussed.

As far as the common outcry is concerned: although we note that the Council and the community at N. N. <note>A placeholder for a specific town name</note> hold these two women in high suspicion, it is nevertheless of no small concern to us that they did not dare nor wish to indicate or mention them by name in either their first or second petition <note>original: "Supplication"</note> which was recorded.

<column-break/>

Even though they mention in their first petition that there has been a "mumbling" for a good thirty years about evil women who are said to be in N., and that even the young children on the streets know to speak of it, etc. Which is nonetheless somewhat strange to hear: that in such a long time, no more acts of sorcery <note>original: "Zauberey"</note> have been perceived in these women (if they are indeed the ones meant) than have come forward now, and that they should have been allowed to go unprosecuted for so long.

When one wishes to speak of a reputation or common outcry to be used as proof in criminal matters <note>original: "maleficiz sachen"</note>, much more is required for such an outcry to be proven as "public rumor" <note>term: fama publica; a legal standard of widespread, credible reputation</note> and made credible.

<margin>Many things are required for the proof of public rumor.</margin>
For the proving of rumor—so that it is worthy of faith, proves a matter at least semi-fully, or has the force of sufficient evidence—many things are required. Especially that it must have arisen from persons worthy of faith and fit to give testimony, and not from malicious, envious detractors or suspected enemies (as per the chapter "It Behoves" on accusations). And that this rumor emanated from entirely probable causes, as noted by Angelo and Lancillotto Corrado. Where, concluding near the end, he says that the opinion of the common rabble is not called "rumor," but only that which draws its origin from several causes that induce the people to speak or believe so; otherwise, it is not rumor, but the "vain voice of the crowd." Furthermore, rumor by itself constitutes no evidence. Bartolus, Baldus, and Thomas Grammaticus agree. Gabriel Saraina says that if the rumor for which someone is tortured is so "naked" that it has no arguments in its favor except the confession of the tortured person, even if they persevere in it, it is nonetheless invalid. Hippolytus de Marsiliis teaches the same.

Thus, it might well be precarious if the Lords Envoys, all the persons of the Council...

The question is whether one is authorized to question the three detained female persons—as alleged witches—under <term>torture</term> <note>original: "peinlich zu fragen" - literally "to ask painfully," the standard term for judicial torture.</note> once more, beyond the two previous sessions of torture already endured; or whether they should be released from such painful questioning and be acquitted and discharged from the established <term>criminal process</term> <note>original: "Malefiz proceß" - a trial for capital crimes.</note>?

In examining this question, it appears at first—since in such criminal matters the alleged evildoers cannot be irrefutably convicted or proven guilty through living testimony or otherwise—that the Imperial Laws <note>Refers to the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the legal code of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> require, and it is otherwise just in itself, that no punishment may be undertaken against the detained unless he does it himself and is [convicted] through his [own confession]...

Regarding this accusation, none of them offered a defense; therefore, the common man took this to heart, and the outcry and suspicion grew ever more violent against the suspect women, so much so that the entire community is up in arms, etc. Now, however, the legal scholars commonly conclude that *public fame induces semi-full proof, and that it takes the place of one whole witness.* <note>original Latin: "quod fama inducat semiplenam probationem, quodque vicem vnius testis integri obtineat."</note> [Citations of Bartolus, Jason, and other legal authorities follow]. The Canonists conclude the same... and that is the common conclusion. But a whole witness who testifies regarding a crime creates sufficient evidence for torture... Therefore, the same shall apply to public fame.

**Secondly**, that these three imprisoned persons were accused by the women who were burned for witchcraft a year ago at N. N., saying they had been their playfellows and had practiced sorcery and witchcraft with them. *Those who speak while exhausted by lashes, torments, and fire, the truth itself seems to speak,* says Tully <note>Cicero</note> in his *Topics*.

Such a statement gives sufficient evidence for torture; for in common law it is not held that one who sees death before their eyes and is about to die would jeopardize the salvation and welfare of their soul by confessing less or more than the truth itself is. *For the aforementioned burned women, being already established at the point of death, are not presumed to have been unmindful of eternal salvation, nor to have confessed more or less than was the truth of the matter.*
