# On Witches and Sorcerers.

as there are adultery, poisoning and the administering of toxins, witchcraft, counterfeiting, and the like, the judge should be much more inclined toward the painful questioning <note>The "painful questioning" or *peinliche Frage* is a formal legal term for judicial torture used to extract a confession.</note> than in other crimes that are committed openly. *For where there is smoke in secret crimes, then the Judge can proceed more boldly to torture than in others; and in these cases, if the evidence were lacking in some part, the judge should not be blamed for it.* So says Bossius in his criminal treatise, title on evidence and consideration of torture, number 200. Where he cites Baldus on Law 3 of the Code regarding Episcopal Audience, saying that *in crimes which are committed in secret, such as adultery, poisoning, and counterfeiting of money, the Judge ought to be easier and more inclined toward torture.* This is supported by Giulio Claro in the final question 64, at the verse "and therefore it is usually said." Since this is the case in the Law, it cannot be denied that in the present case, the judge may proceed to the painful questioning for the third time without hindrance and boldly.

Fifthly, the Doctors <note>Legal scholars and authorities on Roman and Canon law.</note> also conclude on the question of how often torture is to be repeated, that this should happen three times; and if the accused withstands it for the third time, he should be released upon an oath of truce <note>An *Urphed* was a formal oath where a released prisoner swore not to take revenge on the judge or accusers.</note> and upon bail to present himself for future cases and summons. For thus Hippolytus de Marsiliis, in his repetition of the Law "Repeti" in the Digest on Questioning, number 16, cites the authority of Paride del Pozzo in the treatise on Syndics, teaching that *the accused ought not to be tortured beyond a third time*, as noted by Angelo in the final Law, chapter on questioning. Where he says that *if a witness examined and found inconsistent and tortured said one thing, then repeated said another, he ought to be examined through torture because the first statement will not stand, nor the second, but he must be repeated a third time, and that statement shall stand in which he perseveres as the truth*, according to the gloss on the final Law of the Code on questioning, at the verse "others." And he also brings in Paolo di Castro in counsel 197, beginning "Having seen the inquisition," near the end, where he said that *one torturing beyond three times at different times would be proceeding immoderately*, by the argument of the law on testamentary trusts, section "If anyone ten" from Law 3.

It therefore appears that a judge does not do too much when he proceeds to the painful questioning for the third time, by the argument from the contrary sense, which is frequent in law.

<column-break/>

Sixthly, these women may also not be considered innocent; rather, the suspicion against them is strengthened all the more because they have already been able to endure the quite harsh torture applied to them so steadfastly without any interruption. This would otherwise not have been easily possible for a male person, who is by nature stronger and able to suffer more. Therefore, one of the consultants on witchcraft <note>Legal experts who provided formal opinions on how to conduct witch trials.</note> wished to conclude that no injustice is done to them at all, but rather that these three imprisoned persons have achieved so much by means of their sorcery that, no matter how harshly they are tortured, they could confess nothing. For this reason, they might be considered subjects to be questioned painfully with more earnestness and at the sharpest level, as the aforementioned consultant—for the reasons just cited and because these people perhaps possess other arts and circumstances than other humans—advised that one should apply for a secondary judge <note>Likely referring to a specialist or a professional executioner/interrogator experienced in "breaking" the magical silence of witches.</note> who has himself dealt with such matters.

From the previously related grounds and arguments, it appears that in the present case against the above-named three imprisoned persons, one may rightly proceed with the severity of painful questioning for the third time.

But despite all this, the opposite seems to me to be more similar to the Law and equity and more fitting, for the reasons set down hereafter.

Firstly, because public Law—also expressly established by the late Charles V <note>Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who established the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* in 1532.</note> of high and most merciful memory in the Penal Constitution of the High Courts—states that where honest indications of the misdeed for which one wishes to question painfully are not first present and proven, no one shall be painfully questioned. Where any authority or judge oversteps this, they shall be bound to give the one who was thus tortured against the Law without proven evidence proper compensation for his ignominy, pain, costs, and damages, all according to the cited Penal Constitution of the High Courts.

# Opinions of Several Highly Learned Men

...regulation Article 20 <note>Refers to the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the Holy Roman Empire's criminal code of 1532</note>, which article is all the more applicable because it is consistent with common law, equity, and laudable established customs; for these reasons, one should diligently comply with them in all criminal matters before proceeding to torture. **For no one is to be cast into prison, much less tortured, at the complaint or instance of another without preceding evidence and a specification of the crime committed,** as Julius Clarus <note>original: "Iul. clar." - a famous 16th-century Italian jurist</note> testifies this to be the common opinion in his *Criminal Practice*, final section, question 26, at the verse "Know, however," where he also says that a judge ought to pay attention to three things in particular, lest he be held liable in a judicial review <term>Syndicatu: a process where a judge's conduct was investigated after his term</term> if he causes someone to be unjustly detained. **Much less should anyone be subjected to the painful question <note>A common euphemism for torture</note> multiple times beyond the torture already endured without preceding new and sufficient evidence <term>indicia: legal signs or clues that suggest guilt</term> and marks; for such is against the manifest disposition of the laws in the Law *Unius*, paragraph 1, of the Digest on examinations, where in that place Paulus <note>A 3rd-century Roman jurist</note> says: A defendant overwhelmed by more evident proofs can be returned to examination, especially if he has hardened his mind and body against the torments; but in a case where the defendant was pressed by no proofs, torments are not easily to be applied, much less repeated, but the accuser must be urged to prove and convict that which he intends.** It is therefore a matter of high necessity that these three imprisoned women be convicted by many and new signs and suspicions, and be entirely proven guilty, before one undertakes the third torture.

Now, however, after reading and diligent consideration of the sent records, reports, voluntary and painful interrogations, and all circumstances, it is found in the slightest degree that after enduring the first and second torture, any new honest evidence, marks, or suspicion can be drawn, other than—as mentioned—the common outcry and the testimony of the two women previously burned <note>Refers to "convicted witches" who named others before their execution</note>; how flimsy and unstable these evidences and signs are in this highly important matter will be explained with grounds shortly hereafter. And even assuming that sufficient, legally valid presumptions, suspicions, and signs—which perhaps in this case against the three imprisoned persons might in some way

<column-break/>

be active and applicable—had occurred, one is nevertheless accustomed to distinguish in the following manner regarding the question of how often one may torture someone: Either the question concerns a defendant who was tortured based on existing or preceding legitimate evidence and confessed nothing, or one who was similarly tortured based on preceding legitimate evidence and confessed the crime, but afterwards does not persevere in such a confession, but when led to the judge to ratify what he said, says he did not commit the crime. Since this latter part of the distinction does not fit our terms, we deliberately omit it here. Regarding the former, if it is asked whether a defendant who was tortured based on preceding evidence (with all necessary formalities observed) and confessed nothing can be tortured again, a sub-distinction is made: Either he was competently and sufficiently tortured based on the first evidence, or lightly and insufficiently. In the first case, if he was sufficiently tortured and confessed nothing, but new evidence arrives that is stronger than the first, then the torments are repeated, according to the text in Law *Unius*, paragraph 1, of the Digest on examinations. If, however, he was not sufficiently tortured according to the quality of the evidence against him, but only lightly, then he can be repeated even without new evidence arriving.

But if the evidence appears light and not very manifest, nor very urgent, the examination should not be repeated. That a person sufficiently tortured cannot be tortured again unless new evidence stronger than the first arrives, as stated above, is held by Jacobus de Arellio and Dinus <note>Medieval legal commentators</note> in the final Law on examinations, and many others cited by Hippolytus de Marsiliis <note>An Italian jurist known for his writings on torture</note> in the Law *Repetit* on examinations, where he adds that this should be noted against cruel judges who torture daily and repeat torments and do not have other new evidence, because they are held liable in a judicial review. For they cannot return defendants to examination so many times; to which they also cite Cynus in the final Law, saying that assessors <note>Legal assistants to a judge</note> who repeat torments without new evidence or without new arguments have neither God nor men before their eyes. Finally, he concludes that this is the common opinion of all and thus to be observed in practice, because this opinion is fairer and more sustainable and more in harmony with the law.

It appears, however, from the report and letters sent by the Magistrate, Mayor, and Jurors of N.N. <note>Placeholder for the specific town name, common in legal templates</note>, that the imprisoned persons were not only tortured to a fair degree, but in the harshest and most unusual manner,

# Concerning Witches and Sorcerers.

Therefore, it should rightly remain according to the previously cited laws.

Secondly, it is also established and set down in the <term>Constitutio Criminalis Carolina</term> <note>original: "peinlichen Halßgerichts ordnung"; the Holy Roman Empire's criminal code of 1532</note> that every sufficient indication upon which one may question under torture must be proven by two good witnesses. However, if the main substance of the crime is proven by one good witness, the same constitutes a half-proof and a sufficient indication. <note>Latin: "Neque vnum indicium sufficit..."</note> *Neither is one indication sufficient unless it is extremely significant.* Bartolus, final law, number 6, on questions. Wesenbeck in paragraph number 7, on the ordinary criminal code, articles 23 and 27. *And although some Doctors hold that one indication suffices for torture, the truer opinion is that of those who distinguish: either the indication is very close to the crime and one indication suffices for torture, or it is remote from the deed, and then the accused ought not to be tortured on account of one such indication, but several are required; and they say this is the common opinion.* Bossius in the title on indications, number 71. Blancus on indications, number 15. Giulio Claro in his criminal practice, question 64, verse "But I ask." *Furthermore, even if several indications are proved by individual witnesses, they are not to be joined together, because each indication, of whatever sort it may be, must be proved by at least two witnesses.* Hippolytus in the said law "of one," section "Witnesses," number 2, and in the law "on the minor," section "of several," on questions.

Now, if in the present case one diligently observes all circumstances, suspicions, and indications by which the accused has come under suspicion, one may and can find no new, stronger, or more certain suspicion and evidence from the account of the story that would be sufficient for further torture—much less that the same should be proven by two or one good witness, as is proper. Instead, everything remains with the previous bare assertion and uncertain and insufficient suspicion, through which the first torture was presumably undertaken.

Thirdly, even assuming that sufficient indications had previously been present—

<column-break/>

it is nevertheless a matter of known law that if a person who has become notorious for a vice or misdeed is earnestly questioned under torture based on significant and highly pressing causes or <term>indications</term> <note>original: "indicia"; legal signs or clues of guilt</note>, and does not confess to the accused vice, then by enduring the torture, all indications—no matter how strong they may have been—are stilled and rendered null. For that reason, the person shall not be forced into further painful questioning.

<note>Latin: "Si enim illata reo tortura..."</note> *For if, after torture has been inflicted on the accused, he denies that he committed the crime, or confesses nothing, then he is said to have purged the indications existing against him, as if he were seen to have spoken the pure truth; and Albericus says this is observed in the rubric of the Code on questions, number 9. The same in the law "Indication," number 2, on questions, says the world commonly holds this to be so.* Therefore, the three persons currently in custody are, for the reasons now indicated, cleared and freed of all accusations attributed to them regarding witchcraft by the women previously burned; likewise of the suspicion that arose against them from common rumor, and they should rightly not be pressed into further torture.

Fourthly, the alleged statement and confession of the woman previously burned regarding the sixteen female persons—among whom were these who are said to have been her companions—cannot constitute a valid indication or sufficient suspicion to repeat the painful questioning for a third time.

For the laws and their Doctors maintain that when a person confesses something while in torture, or names and accuses another as being also guilty during the painful questioning or otherwise, that same confession and accusation is not sufficient for the other person named by the former to be questioned under torture. <note>Latin: "Confessio enim sola per se..."</note> *For a confession made by a confessed culprit against an accomplice in a crime, standing alone, produces no presumption, nor is it a legitimate and sufficient indication for torture, unless other legitimate presumptions concur.* Cynus, Baldus, Salicetus in the last law of the Code on accusations. Bossius testifies in the title on indications, number 149, that this is practiced daily.

# Opinions of Several Highly Learned Scholars

The laws of Emperor Charles V, of most noble and merciful memory, as expressly ordered in Article 31 <note>original: "31. Artickel"; referring to the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the 1532 imperial penal code</note>, must rightfully be followed within the Holy Empire. In addition to this, it does not clearly appear from the confession or testimony of the sorceress previously burned <note>original: "verbrandten Zauberin"</note> that these three detained persons ever undertook anything to harm any human being, or that they brought anyone to their death through poison or other sorcerous works. Rather, it is only stated that they were seen together at the dance <note>original: "bey sammen am tanz"; the Witches' Sabbath</note>. When viewed in the light of day, this testimony and confession does not have enough weight to generate sufficient evidence or suspicion for the first—let alone the third—bout of torture <term>Tortur: the judicial use of pain to extract a confession, regulated by specific "degrees"</term>.

For although there is a dispute between theologians, jurists, and other authors, both ancient and modern, on both sides—namely, whether the illusions of Satan occur in the spirit or in the body, and whether witches and sorceresses are locally transported—nevertheless, it was decided long ago in the Council of Ancyra <note>A church council from 314 AD often cited to argue that witchcraft was a mental delusion rather than physical reality</note> that this seeing and spirit-travel happens chiefly to witches, as is reported in the Canon *Episcopi* (26. q. 5). But there is no time now, nor is it necessary, for such a dispute to be fully argued in this place.

Since, therefore, it is not found in the previously mentioned confessions of the burned witches, nor otherwise sufficiently proven, that these three detained persons caused harm to anyone or acted in any other way than that they were allegedly seen once at the dance, such confessions are entirely uncertain and doubtful. One cannot build upon them, much less hurry to further severe martyrdom and torture, or to the fire with these poor, weak women <note>original: "Weibsbildern"</note>. Instead, every judge in these matters should and must act with greater caution and foresight, so that he is not led astray and deceived by such devilish phantoms.

Nor does it follow that "these women denounced them, therefore it is so," for a confession is far removed from the act itself, and whatever is against nature fails in its own principles, as Franciscus Ponticus says in his title on witches. It must therefore be said that since such persons are deluded by the Demon, their denunciation is not immediately to be admitted as true and certain, as noted in the law regarding age (Digest, on interrogatory actions).

According to the law, a "singular testimony" <term>Singulare testimonium: the testimony of a single witness, which was usually insufficient for conviction in capital cases</term> is powerless and without merit even in civil matters. Much more so in this present case, which touches upon life and limb, the testimony of this single person—which cannot even be compared to a proper singular testimony, considering that in the hearing of a witness many other solemnities and formalities are required—does not carry enough weight to justify the "painful question" <note>a euphemism for torture</note> without other sufficient, honest evidence. Much less is the testimony of such a single criminal person sufficient, which could have occurred for all sorts of presumed reasons. The <term>legal scholars</term> <note>original: Rechtsgelehrten</note>, as testified by Johannes Crotus in his treatise *On Witnesses*, require that such a witness be of good name and reputation. This is not at all the case with the women previously burned. Furthermore, such a confession against the women [N. N. N.] is merely a statement based on "hearsay from others," which is not admissible in civil law, let alone in <term>capital criminal cases</term> <note>original: Malefizgen sachen</note>. N.] is one [a witch] or not; also—which is well worth noting—she knows nothing else about her, except that she supposedly said such things only when she was a small girl.

All of this, if weighed and considered on the basis of truth, is not sufficient for an arrest, much less for initiating a first interrogation, not to mention repeating it. For it is manifest that no one should be held in captivity based on previous lawful <term>indications</term> <note>original: indiciis; evidence or signs of guilt</note>, reports, and specifications of the crime committed, solely on someone's accusation. Julius Clarus, the excellent and widely renowned writer, cites this in his *Criminal Practice* as a general opinion and conclusion of all legal scholars, where he says: *Even a judge who causes someone to be unjustly detained or tortured may be held liable by the Syndicate. For sufficient indications must precede, both for someone to be thrust into prison and, much more so, for interrogations [torture] to be held concerning him.*

And accordingly, in the letters to the bailiffs, mayors, and jurors at [N. N.], it is noted that [N. N.] is of a good, honest family and livelihood, and also has a pious, honest husband. It is not mentioned therein that she ever led a reckless or godless life. Although one would have preferred better reports on this, it is presumed that she otherwise applied herself to virtue. Thus, favorable presumptions are to be preferred over suspicious ones, since experience also shows that commonly poor, simple, and lowly persons employ themselves in <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: Zauberey</note>. Now, however, it is clear law: *That indications are removed by contrary presumptions in favor of the accused* (Bartolus and others).

<column-break/>

(Legal citations: Alexander, Angelus, etc.)

Finally, there is also a good conjecture and <term>presumption</term> <note>original: præsumption</note> in favor of these three imprisoned female persons: that since they were taken into custody and questioned most severely, not only kindly but also under pain [torture], they remain steadfast in their denial, insisting that violence and injustice were done to them by the burned witches. *For just as indications are taken against a defendant from his trepidation and inconsistency, so conversely, indications are taken in his favor from his constancy and perseverance, which must be diligently considered by the judge himself* (as shown by Brunus, Bartolus, Baldus, and others).

I conclude, therefore, from the aforementioned laws and all circumstances of the transcribed stories, that the frequently mentioned three imprisoned persons, collectively and individually, are not to be held further for <term>torture</term> <note>original: tortur</note>, but are to be acquitted and released from the criminal complaint. However, this is not an absolute and definitive acquittal, but rather—as things currently stand—under a guarantee of bail or, if that cannot be obtained, an oath to present or surrender themselves again to the judge if new indications should arise or if they can again be evidently convicted.

For even if the indications had been vehement, they are nonetheless purged by torture, and it is granted that this constitutes an "abolition" <note>A legal term meaning the evidence is wiped clean or the suspicion is legally cleared</note>: as taught by Salicetus in the law *Ea quidem* under the title *On Accusations*; in the law *If anyone in adultery* under the Julian law on adultery; and the law *Whoever* under the Julian law on majesty. Regarding the fourth point that was raised—that a judge, in such and similar misdeeds which commonly tend to happen in secret and hidden ways, should be much more inclined and willing to use criminal interrogation than in other misdeeds committed publicly—one lets this also pass in its own terms, namely as far as the first torture is concerned. But this does not apply when one treats and deals with the *repetition* of torture. Otherwise, through such free power of the judge, an innocent person—accused without any sufficient legitimate indication—might frequently be tortured and tormented unto death, which is directly contrary to the laws. For the end of torture is not that someone should be killed or punished by this means, but that the truth may be expressed through the application of torments. Thus, the aforementioned legal ruling has no place other than when such torture and torment is preceded by "pregnant" <note>meaning compelling or weighty</note> and just indications, and with all necessary legal formalities observed, following legitimate and sufficient indications, and then...

# Opinions of Several Highly Learned Men

...with the observation and maintenance of everything that the law requires for torture and torment to be undertaken, as the excellent and highly renowned criminalist Hippolytus <note>original: "Hippol. in l. Repetit. nu 30. ff de quæst." refers to Hippolytus de Marsiliis (1451–1529), an influential Italian jurist known for his writings on criminal law and torture.</note> teaches.

Regarding the fifth argument, concerning the question of how often torture is to be repeated: it is the opinion and conclusion of the Doctors of Law that this should occur three times. However, this is not to be understood simply or without distinction. Rather, the cited passages speak of the case where someone has once confessed and admitted the suspected crime during the painful interrogation <term>painful interrogation: a legal euphemism for interrogation under torture</term>, but afterwards retracted and denied it again. In such a case, it remains at the discretion and modesty of the judge to arrange the painful interrogation for a third time. This cannot be applied at all to our present case, namely where these three imprisoned persons confessed nothing after previous endurance of torture and harsh rackings. For further rejection of the same, I refer here—for the sake of beloved brevity—to the distinction cited above in the first argument, or the reasoning for the decision in the paragraph beginning: "Firstly, it is manifest law," etc.

The sixth and final argument is more than sufficiently refuted by the common proverb: *That which can be absent from a thing does not prove its essence* <note>original: "Non probat hoc esse quod ab hoc contingit abesse." A legal maxim suggesting that if a trait (like a confession) isn't present, you cannot assume the underlying condition (guilt) exists.</note>. Indeed, from the presuppositions laid down, the opposite is rather to be concluded: namely, because the frequently mentioned three imprisoned persons endured the harsh martyrdom imposed upon them so steadfastly without any statement regarding the supposed crime, there is a much stronger presumption in their favor that they are innocent of such accusation. As was indicated above in the last argument or reasoning for the decision in the paragraph beginning: "Finally, it is also shown," and even if some honest indication and suspicion had initially existed against them, these are hereby completely fallen, extinguished, and abolished, as was done shortly before in the refutation of the third argument or the reasoning of doubt in the paragraph: "As to the third, that..." etc., at the end of the same paragraph.

<column-break/>

It has been argued with legal grounds; however, one of the co-consultants concluded that, in view of such steadfastness and persistent endurance of great martyrdom, one should perhaps apply to soothsayers or a certain executioner who himself deals in such arts. This seems to me to be not only against the general written Imperial and Papal laws, but also against the Divine Law. For not only was this expressly forbidden by the late Emperor Charles V, of high and most merciful memory, in the Criminal Constitutions <note>original: "peinlichen halsgerichts ordnung," referring to the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina of 1532, the first body of German criminal law.</note> in Article 21, with the following words: "No one shall be taken into custody or subjected to painful interrogation upon the report of those who presume to tell fortunes through sorcery or other arts; rather, those same presumed soothsayers and accusers shall be punished for it."

Also, every judge shall be bound to reimburse the accused for all costs and damages. For that art is condemned as illicit by both civil and canon laws <note>original: "Est enim ars illa legibus & ciuilibus & canonicis vt illicita improbata." The author cites several Roman law codes (C. de malefic.) and Church decrees against sorcery.</note>. Furthermore, God Himself, in uncertain and doubtful matters, expressly and with great earnestness forbade seeking counsel from soothsayers and others who deal in such works of the Devil. Leviticus 19, where He commands that we should not join ourselves to such people to inquire of them concerning future or uncertain things. Also Leviticus 20 and Deuteronomy 18, where He threatens every soul who undertakes to inquire after something by such forbidden means and defiles themselves with such vices with eternal destruction, and that He will root them out from the midst of His people. There are also express examples in the Holy Scripture of those who were punished by God for this reason, as seen in King Saul (1 Samuel 28), Ahaziah, and others more.

Therefore, I conclude this with the proverb: *Evils are not to be rooted out by evils, nor should bad things be done so that good may come of it.* <note>original: "Maleficia maleficiis non esse eruenda nec facienda mala vt eueniant bona."</note>

Subject to the judgment of anyone perceiving what is more just and better. N. C. D.

Judges would remain unpunished.
We have cast the pretended prophecy into the fire.
</margin>

# In Conclusion, Concerning the
## Punishment and True Distinction of Sorcerers, Witches, and Poisoners.
### Drawn from Doctor Johann Weyer’s preface to the 6th Book of *On the Deceptions of Demons*. <note>original: "de præstigiis Dæmonum"</note>

<margin>
Note.
True sorcerers go unpunished.
Old, wandering, crazed women are snatched away to the fire.
</margin>

The content of the sixth book primarily concerns the punishment of sorcerers, witches, and poisoners. It is demonstrated that the true sorcerers—whom Moses, as well as secular and ecclesiastical laws, have condemned—now commonly go unpunished. Indeed, many of them have great patrons and are held in high honor by the authorities. These are the clerics and secular judges who can perform strange apparitions and provide diabolical counsel, help, and advancement through readings, conjurations, <term>characters</term> <note>magical symbols or sigils</note>, figures, rings, and the like. Now, these men are left free and unmolested, and are even regarded as respectable, extraordinary people, while the punishment is commonly and heavily laid upon poor, deluded, and old possessed women. These women are thrown into harsh, oppressive prisons—into the "murder-pits" and hostels of the Devil. Then the most wretched, cruel executioners are summoned, who should more rightly be called tyrants than servants of justice. These men invent the most gruesome torture and pain, with which they pitifully hang the bodies of the poor women and pull them apart; they also pour oil on their legs and burn them under the arms and feet. By this, it is believed they will more quickly be forced into a confession of their accused sorcery and other misdeeds, which they nevertheless did not commit, nor have any knowledge of. And when they have tortured them to death, or if they die from the practiced torment as they come out of the dark, diabolical holes into the bright air and are led to judgment or court,

<column-break/>

<margin>
Take note, you judges and executioners.
</margin>

people shout and scream without any shame, fear, or discretion, that the Devil has broken their necks; thus it must always be and remain a "true" story. However, this will be revealed in the future on the last day of our redemption, regarding those who are guilty of such inhuman torture and pain. In such intolerable stoning—especially of the female sex, who can poorly endure and suffer pain—they would rather confess to every evil that one wishes them to confess, than be tortured daily with newly invented tyrannies.

<margin>
The "test" of the witches is vain and false.
</margin>

Furthermore, the authorities—who should indeed have somewhat better discernment, especially given the renown of the Gospel—have a "test" <note>the ordeal of water</note> wherein they throw the poor bound women into the water. If they then float (which the Devil can do and can hold them up on the water to further blind the deluded authorities and promote the shedding of innocent blood), then she must always be a witch. The proof and test of this is before one's eyes, as if floating could only come from an evil will or the improper deeds of a person. Dear Lord, who taught such an art and test? Truly, no one other than the Evil Foe, who takes pleasure in this work and artistically arranges and executes it everywhere. It is indeed a pity that we allow ourselves to be led around and guided by <term>Satan’s fool’s rope</term> <note>a metaphor for being deceived or manipulated by the devil</note> in this manner, even though we think and judge no differently than that we have escaped him through the knowledge of the Holy Gospel.

The confessions of four witches: errant and false.
</margin>

# Conclusion.

as one woman known from a convent confessed: she claimed that with her words and wishes, she had weakened the other young women, and was thus led away to be a burnt offering <note>original: "Brandopffer" — a sacrificial victim of the stake</note>; yet the young women were actually possessed by the Devil, as was discovered afterward. Here, one should have considered that one cannot bring anyone into a state of weakness through mere words or wishes. Nor can one bring the Devil into a body. Another woman confessed how she had led a noble person into great misery and affliction, and it was later found that he was possessed by the Devil; yet she had to go to the fire and be burned. Another confessed how she had "bewitched" and stolen a man's livelihood using a piece of resin that she had placed under a brewing kettle. Now, one must investigate whether it were possible for resin to have such poisonous and destructive power within itself? To this I say: No. The fourth woman confessed how she had killed and aborted the fruit of the womb in another woman simply by giving her an apple. Now, it is well known that an apple does not have such power. If one wishes to claim that poison was smeared upon it, one should have first inquired into that, and whether such poison could harm only the young child and not the mother’s own body. Also, that having eaten one apple so many years ago should have caused an abortion—all of this was not sufficiently investigated. Instead, the judgment was pronounced that Master Cuntz <note>A traditional nickname for the executioner</note> should prepare the fire. Why? Because she confessed it; her confession can be produced. Now, the common written laws <note>referring to the *Ius Commune* or Roman Law</note> state that in criminal matters, the proofs must be "clearer than the sun shining at midday" <note>original Latin: "probationes luce meridiana clariores"</note>; yet one finds on the contrary that the confession is erratic, inconsistent, and false. This is also true of those who, by virtue of their confession, are sacrificed in the belly [of the fire]: that they smeared themselves with a salve and were changed into irrational animals or wolves, had run about devouring people, and after the passing of two hours,

<column-break/>

roughly became human again. This is also impossible; yet the fire must nonetheless make it "true." And all these have confessed; but just as the confession was false in one instance, so it is in the other, for the Devil has merely corrupted their fantasy and imagined things to them, so that they believe they have done that which did not actually happen. And even if they had done it, it would have happened in a deranged mind and understanding—whereas all blasphemers, drunkards, adulterers, and persistent whoremongers act with full intent and good understanding. Even then, they would have done nothing other than act against their own souls. All of this, regarding the aforementioned witches, can easily be corrected with better instruction from the Word of God, as is customary to do with all who are erring, even heretics. Thereby their souls would be won, as Saint James teaches <note>referring to James 5:19-20 regarding the reclaiming of sinners</note>; for whoever gives themselves to Satan out of poor instruction must be led back to God with better instruction. For the sword of the Authority <note>the secular government's power of capital punishment</note> is not intended for those who err in their mind, opinion, and thoughts and who show repentance and improvement with good instruction, but rather for those who break out and commit offenses against others with external deeds. Here, those worldly laws can have no standing which some put forward—those who nonetheless admit that these witches have done nothing evil to others, but only *believe* they have done it. Namely, they claim there are many who deal in evil arts which trouble and poison the elements, and who do not spare the lives of innocent people but inflict harm upon them. Since such people act against nature, they should be judged from life to death. Here one sees clearly that the Imperial Law <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the legal code of the Holy Roman Empire</note> first describes the people who should be punished and provides the reason why such a thing should apply: namely, that they are enemies of humanity who deal in evil, dangerous arts and rob and poison the elements and also injure the lives of men. Now, it has always been admitted previously that these monsters or witches <note>original: "Unholden oder Hexen"</note> do not deal in any [actual] evil arts,

# Conclusion.

<margin>
Distinction between witches and poisoners.

Also, they harm no one’s life, as has been said and acknowledged. For those who do [harm life] are no proof at all for this matter—that one should put witches to death. The Law of Moses must also be cast before one's eyes here, in his second book <note>Exodus</note> in the 22nd chapter: "You shall not let a sorceress live." This is how the Hebrew word *Mechasepha* <note>original: "Mechasepha" (מְכַשֵּׁפָה), usually referring to a practitioner of harmful magic</note> has been translated into German until now. But those same seventy old Greeks <note>The Septuagint translators</note>, who transferred the Hebrew Old Testament very well and quite faithfully and diligently, set it in Greek as <gloss>you shall not let poisoners survive</gloss> <note>original Greek: "φαρμακὸς ἐπιβιώσετε"</note> *Veneficos*, that is, poisoners, or those who kill with poison; do not let them live. For in Moses' times, it shall not be found that our [modern] witches were yet on earth, seeing as the Devil had not yet taken away the brains of old women with such phantoms. For the sorcerers of whom Moses writes in the second book in the 7th and 8th chapters, and those he also condemns in Leviticus in the 19th and 20th chapters, were only those who, through their evil and devilish art, let something appear before eyes and so blinded them that one knew no better than that what appeared before the eyes was true, which was nevertheless vain deceit. And they thus brought the common man from the contemplation of God's true works to the service of the Devil, and into idolatry through their deceitful trade and art: as one can clearly recognize from the works they did for Pharaoh against Moses and Aaron as messengers of God, so that they might cause Pharaoh and his people to persist and be blinded against the will of God in withholding the Israelites. Which they themselves had to confess when God no longer permitted the deceit and they could not bring forth the lice; they cried out, "This is the finger or power of God," as if

Therefore, one must distinguish well between the wrongdoers, which has been neglected until now; for these right, true, rebellious sorcerers and soothsayers have preferred their freedom and dignity everywhere, while the poor, straying, and possessed witches—who are also called sorceresses and have inflicted evil on no one—are burned innocently. Nor are they distinguished from the poisoners, whom Moses in the second book in the twenty-second chapter, as well as all laws, rightly condemn. But one must not mix the innocent with the guilty through a misunderstanding of the name, and thrust them into one fire together.

Furthermore, the punishment of our witches with banishment or fines, or in other fair and honest ways according to the circumstances, shall not be forgotten. However, no one must think that I wish to anticipate or set a measure for the authorities; that is not my intention at all. So one should also bear with me for presenting my simple opinion and placing it before everyone’s eyes for free judgment; he whom it does not please, let him instruct me better, and I will gladly be shown and recant. For if this my proposition is found to be steadfast, I ask that it be recognized as such, and that one does not proceed so strictly with the innocent burnt offering—as I understand is now, alas, happening most in the Reformed churches.
